entries.name: The Four-Colour Mainstream
entries.description: The genre's default register, and the one most often described rather than analysed.
entries.principle: The mainstream register is not naivety; it is a set of load-bearing conventions that make an unauthorised mandate readable as legitimate without ever arguing for it. Colour, costume, the recurring rogue and the reset to status quo do work a realist register cannot: they let a story stage lethal force weekly and remain about something other than consequence. Writers who treat this as a style to be outgrown lose the machinery along with the tone.
entries.example: The Fantastic Four under Lee and Kirby run a family argument at cosmic scale without once asking who authorised the intervention; Superman: The Animated Series demonstrates the register still works when built deliberately rather than inherited.
entries.application: If your story needs weekly intervention without cumulative legal or psychological consequence, you are in this register and should build for it rather than apologise for it. The question to answer is what the reset costs the reader's belief, and where you spend the one consequence you allow to stick.

entries.name: The Grim-and-Gritty Turn
entries.description: Violence and consequence foregrounded, and the market's most-imitated and least-understood move.
entries.principle: The turn's actual innovation was not darkness but the reintroduction of physical and legal consequence into a form built to shed it. Wounds persist, bystanders litigate, the mandate is questioned by people with standing. What imitators copied instead was affect — rain, grimace, body count — which is why the register has a reputation for adolescence it did not earn on its first outing.
entries.example: The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen are the works usually named, and both are about the mandate rather than about the violence; Marshal Law and much of the early nineties line demonstrate the imitation, where consequence is depicted and never accrues.
entries.application: Test any grim register by asking what persists into the next issue. If nothing does, you have adopted the surface of the turn and none of its structure, and you are writing the four-colour register in darker ink.

entries.name: The Deconstruction
entries.description: The genre's most contested critical term, used here with its provenance attached.
entries.principle: The word is borrowed loosely from literary theory and in comics usage means something narrower: taking the conventions apart to show what they were doing, usually by supplying the consequences the convention suppresses. It is worth keeping only if you keep the narrowness, because the loose usage has expanded to cover any dark or self-aware superhero story and now distinguishes nothing.
entries.example: Watchmen supplies the consequences of the costumed mandate and is the term's usual referent; Miracleman asks what a genuinely omnipotent being does to a world and is the harder case; the many works described as deconstructions because they are violent are the reason the term needs its provenance stated.
entries.application: Before claiming the mode, name the specific convention you are taking apart and the specific consequence you are supplying in its place. If you cannot, you are writing in the grim register and the label is doing no work.

entries.name: The Reconstruction
entries.description: Rebuilding the conventions on purpose, after the argument against them has been heard.
entries.principle: Reconstruction is not a return to the four-colour register; it is that register rebuilt in the knowledge of what the critique established, which means every convention it restores has to be earned rather than assumed. Its characteristic move is to accept the deconstruction's premise and reject its conclusion: the mandate is indeed unwarranted, and the work argues that acting anyway is the interesting choice rather than the naive one.
entries.example: Astro City builds its cases around ordinary people inside a functioning superhero world and restores the register by changing the vantage point; All-Star Superman restores the mainstream's optimism as a deliberate argument rather than a default.
entries.application: Identify which specific critique your story is answering and give it to a character who states it well. A reconstruction that never voices the objection is a four-colour story with a defensive posture.

entries.name: The Superhero Satire
entries.description: Attack rather than revision — the machinery is the target, not the tool.
entries.principle: Satire differs from both revision and parody in what it aims at: parody reproduces the form for comic effect, revision keeps the machinery and reverses its polarity, satire attacks the thing the machinery is for. In this genre the usual target is the concentration of unaccountable force and the public appetite for it, which makes the satire political before it is comic and gives it a structural problem — the reader came for the spectacle the satire is prosecuting.
entries.example: The Boys prosecutes celebrity and corporate power through the form and has to keep supplying the spectacle it condemns; Marshal Law aims at the military and the licensed hero.
entries.application: Decide early whether the reader is meant to enjoy the thing you are attacking. Both answers work; not deciding produces a story that indicts its own audience by accident and loses the argument.

entries.name: The Solo Vigilante
entries.description: One person, no institution, and a city that did not ask.
entries.principle: The solo vigilante is mode one at its purest: nobody conferred the mandate and no body can withdraw it, so every limit in the story is one the character imposes or one the world imposes physically. The form's engine is that the absence of authorisation is never resolved, only survived, which is why the durable question is not whether he is caught but what he does on the night nobody needs him.
entries.example: Batman's Gotham and Daredevil's Hell's Kitchen both run on jurisdiction the protagonist does not hold; The Punisher removes the self-imposed restraint and demonstrates what the form is without it.
entries.application: Name the body that could revoke this person's licence to act. If there is none, build the limits into the character and the city rather than into a chain of command, and make at least one of them cost something to hold.

entries.name: The Team and the Shared Universe
entries.description: Several incompatible power systems in one room, and a continuity that outlives every member.
entries.principle: A team book is not an anthology with a group shot; its subject is adjudication between systems that were each designed to solve everything. The weakest member's ceiling is the team's working ceiling, because any problem above it is solved offstage by the strongest, and the shared universe raises the same problem to publisher scale — every crisis must be one that could not have been ended by someone who is not in it.
entries.example: The Justice League and The Avengers both run on the absent-member problem and both solve it by scheduling; Doom Patrol solves it by choosing members whose powers are liabilities.
entries.application: For every set piece, name the member who could end it alone and write the reason they are not there. If the reason is repeatedly a coincidence, the roster is wrong rather than the plot.

entries.name: The Legacy Title
entries.description: A name that outlives the person wearing it, and the genre's only reliable route to a new reader.
entries.principle: The legacy title turns the codename into an office, which converts a character into a lineage and gives a serial the one thing it structurally lacks: a way to end a story without ending the property. Its recurring cost is the reversion, because the audience that arrived for the successor is not the audience the reversion serves, and a legacy handled as a temporary vacancy teaches readers that succession is a fake-out.
entries.example: Wally West succeeding Barry Allen held for two decades and made the succession the point; Miles Morales established a parallel line rather than a replacement, which is the structural answer to the reversion problem.
entries.application: Decide before the handover whether the office can be permanently occupied. If it cannot, write the succession as a stated interregnum rather than as a promise you intend to break.

entries.name: The Origin Story as a Form
entries.description: The genre's most reprinted scene, treated as a structure rather than as an obligation.
entries.principle: An origin is a mandate's warrant stated in narrative form, which is why the interesting ones are about the warrant rather than about the accident: the question is not how the capability arrived but why this person concluded it obliged them. Told in sequence at the front it leaves the second act nothing to discover, which is why the strongest versions distribute it, delay it, or tell it in a register that is not reliable.
entries.example: Watchmen tells Dr Manhattan's origin out of sequence and from inside a consciousness that no longer experiences sequence, so the telling is the characterisation; Batman Begins keeps returning to the alley and converts an origin into a recurring pressure.
entries.application: Write the sentence in which your protagonist concludes that capability obliges them. If that sentence is missing, the origin is an accident report and the mandate has no warrant.

entries.name: The Event Crossover
entries.description: A story that spans a line, sells a line, and is written by people who did not choose to be in it.
entries.principle: The event is an economic form before it is a narrative one, and its craft problem follows from that: a writer on a tie-in must serve an ending they do not control and a schedule set years ahead. What the form does well is force a shared universe to have consequences at all, because an event is the only occasion on which a publisher will permit a permanent change. What it does badly is arcs, since every book in the line stops mid-argument to attend.
entries.example: Crisis on Infinite Earths exists to solve a continuity problem and reorganises a publishing line to do it; Civil War stages the mandate question at line scale and demonstrates the form's real capability.
entries.application: If you are writing a tie-in, find the question your book can answer that the event cannot, and answer that. If you are writing the event, name the permanent change you are buying with it before you write page one.

entries.name: The Street-Level Book
entries.description: Small stakes, hard limits, and a jurisdiction of about twelve blocks.
entries.principle: Street level is a constraint on scale rather than a genre of realism, and its value is that it restores consequence cheaply: a protagonist who can be outnumbered, arrested, sued or hospitalised generates plot from ordinary obstacles that a cosmic protagonist has to have manufactured. Its failure mode is the visiting heavyweight, because one guest appearance at the wrong power tier retroactively makes every earlier limit look like an authorial choice rather than a fact.
entries.example: Daredevil's law practice supplies obstacles the costume cannot solve; Gotham Central runs the form with no powered protagonist at all and demonstrates how much of the genre survives the subtraction.
entries.application: Fix the power ceiling of your setting and hold it. If a stronger character exists in the shared world, write the reason they do not come, and make the reason structural rather than scheduling.

entries.name: The Villain-Led Book
entries.description: The mandate assumed by someone the story does not ask you to endorse.
entries.principle: Dropping the pro-social clause from the genre's definition admits this book, and it needs its own structure because the usual engine — will the intervention be justified — is unavailable. What replaces it is competence under a warrant the reader rejects, and the form works when the reader's discomfort is the mechanism rather than a side effect. It fails when it launders the protagonist by degrees until it has quietly become a hero book with worse lighting.
entries.example: Ozymandias in Watchmen is the case the genre argues about most, because the book refuses to settle whether the warrant held; The Boys' Homelander is the inverse, a villain the form presents as its own product.
entries.application: Decide whether the reader is meant to want the protagonist to succeed. If the answer drifts across the run, you are laundering, and the drift is usually invisible from inside the draft.

entries.name: The State's Superhuman and the Registration Question
entries.description: Mode two, where the mandate is conferred and the conferring is the subject.
entries.principle: Mode two puts a body between the capability and its use, and the story is about the terms: who licenses, who audits, what revocation costs, and whether the licensed hero is a public servant or a deniable asset. The registration plot is the American form of a question the Japanese and Korean traditions have asked from the beginning, and treating it as a late American invention is the back-projection this pack's organising claim exists to avoid.
entries.example: My Hero Academia builds a school system on hero licensing and makes the licence the plot's currency; the Sokovia Accords stage the same argument as a rupture rather than a premise, which is why the American version reads as a crisis and the Japanese as a setting.
entries.application: Write the revocation scene before you write the origin. If losing the licence costs the protagonist nothing, the conferral was decoration and you are in mode one with extra paperwork.

entries.name: The Pulp Prehistory
entries.description: The masked avenger before the costume settled, and the layer the genre keeps returning to.
entries.principle: The pulp hero supplies the genre's mandate structure fully formed — an unauthorised intervener with a concealed identity, a fixed method and a proprietary city — and supplies almost none of its iconography, which is why the prehistory is a lineage claim rather than an origin claim. Reading the pulps as a first draft of the superhero gets the direction of influence right and the content wrong: what was inherited was the warrant problem, not the cape.
entries.example: The Shadow and Doc Savage establish the method and the concealed identity in the 1930s; Zorro supplies the dual identity and the disguise that the earliest costumed heroes acquired directly and documentably.
entries.application: If you are reaching for the pulp register, take the mandate structure and leave the prose. The layer's durable contribution is a hero whose authority is entirely self-declared and whose method is fixed enough to be a promise to the reader.

entries.name: The Newspaper Strip Hero
entries.description: A costumed lead in three panels a day, and the format that taught the genre to recap.
entries.principle: The strip's constraints produced techniques the comic book later adopted without acknowledging the source: the daily recap, the beat that lands in the third panel, and a serial pace slow enough that a reader arriving mid-story could still follow. It also demonstrates that the genre's furniture predates the comic book, since the costumed adventurer was a mass-market daily form before the pamphlet existed.
entries.example: The Phantom establishes a costumed hero with a legacy identity in 1936, before the comic book's founding run; Buck Rogers and Flash Gordon supply the adventure grammar the early costumed line borrowed wholesale.
entries.application: Steal the recap. A serial that assumes the reader remembers is a serial with a shrinking readership, and the strip solved that problem daily for decades before anyone wrote a jumping-on point.

entries.name: The All-Ages and Younger-Readers Line
entries.description: Written to be read by children and adults at once, which is harder than either.
entries.principle: An all-ages book is not a simplified book; it is one that runs two registers simultaneously without either becoming a wink at the other's expense. The discipline it imposes is that consequence must be legible without being graphic, which forces the writer to make stakes emotional and structural rather than physical, and that is a craft constraint most adult-line books would benefit from.
entries.example: Batman: The Animated Series carries genuine moral weight under a broadcast standards regime and demonstrates the constraint improving the work; Ms. Marvel's early run holds a teenage register and an adult one at once without condescending to either.
entries.application: Test every stake by asking whether a child could state what is at risk and an adult could state why it matters. If only one of those is true, you have written for one audience and are marketing to two.

entries.name: The Licensed and Toy-Driven Line
entries.description: The story exists to sell the object, and the constraint is stated in the contract.
entries.principle: A line written to a toy or licensing schedule has its cast, its variants and often its plot beats fixed in advance by manufacturing lead times, and treating that as a defect misses what it produces: an externally imposed constraint set is a reliable generator of invention, and several of the genre's most inventive runs are licensed ones. The honest version states the constraint; the dishonest one pretends the story arrived first.
entries.example: The Transformers under Simon Furman produces a durable mythology inside a toy catalogue's requirements; Rom, Spaceknight builds a genuinely strange run around a licence that lapsed and left the character unreprintable for decades, which is the layer's characteristic risk.
entries.application: Ask what the licence requires and write toward it rather than around it. And check who owns the result, because a run whose central character cannot be reprinted is a run that leaves the shared universe when the contract does.

entries.name: The Cosmic and the Theological Superhero
entries.description: A publishing tier rather than an attitude, where the antagonist is a principle and the stakes stop being municipal.
entries.principle: The cosmic line is a layer of the shared universe rather than a mode of it, defined by a power tier at which ordinary obstacles cease to function and the story must supply moral or metaphysical ones instead. Its craft problem is that unlimited capability makes physical jeopardy inert, so the form survives only where the threat is to meaning rather than to the body, which is why it drifts toward theology whether or not the writer intends it.
entries.example: Kirby's Fourth World builds a pantheon and argues about freedom and tyranny at a scale where punching is expository; the scholarship disputes whether it belongs to this genre at all, with Charles Hatfield reading it as the culmination of Kirby's superhero work and elsewhere as a mutant cosmic fantasy, and this pack states the dispute rather than settling it.
entries.application: If nothing physical can threaten your protagonist, decide what can, and make it a claim rather than a creature. A cosmic story with municipal stakes is a long fight scene with better backgrounds.

entries.name: The Costume Without the Question
entries.description: Mode three — the furniture reproduced with no mandate at issue anywhere in the work.
entries.principle: The costume, the origin and the secret identity circulate far beyond the stories that argue anything: in advertising, in mascots, in cereal boxes, in political imagery, in cosplay and in children's television, the iconography works perfectly well with the warrant question removed entirely. This is a mode rather than a failure, and it is the genre's largest output by volume; treating it as residual is the error the critical literature makes routinely and this pack does not.
entries.example: Super Friends (1973) runs the whole visual system with no jurisdictional question anywhere in it; Spidey Super Stories, on The Electric Company from 1974, puts the costume to work teaching reading; and the Hostess advertising strips, which ran licensed DC and Marvel characters as a sales device inside the comics themselves from the mid-1970s, are the purest instance the genre has.
entries.application: Establish which mode you are in and hold it. Mode three is legitimate and lucrative; the failure is a story that gestures at the mandate question in one scene and drops it, which reads as an argument the writer lost interest in rather than as a mode.

entries.name: Tokusatsu and the Henshin Hero
entries.description: Japan's live-action costumed tradition, and a parallel invention rather than a borrowing.
entries.principle: The henshin hero is built on a transformation the audience watches every episode, which converts the costume from a disguise into a ritual and makes the change itself the form's structural signature rather than a transition to be got through. The tradition arrived independently: this pack's lineage clause does not apply to it, and it is admitted on iconographic legibility alone, which every card in this block states rather than assumes. Its mandate is usually mode two, conferred by an organisation that briefs, equips and can stand the hero down.
entries.example: Kamen Rider (1971) makes the transformation a fixed sequence and gives its hero a mandate assumed after defection rather than granted; Ultraman (1966) fuses its hero to a member of an official science patrol, so the licensing question is in the premise; Himitsu Sentai Gorenger (1975) founds the team form that the genre exports worldwide.
entries.application: If you are writing transformation, write what the untransformed body is for, because a hero who is only interesting after the change has a dead first act every episode. Note that the Manga pack is planned and not yet built, so this tradition is carded here and the debt is booked outward for pack twelve to collect.

entries.name: Shonen Battle Manga and the Power System
entries.description: A demographic category rather than a genre, and the most systematic power writing in the field.
entries.principle: Shonen is an age-and-readership bracket, not a genre, and the battle line inside it produces the most rigorous power-system writing anywhere in this genre because serialised weekly competition forces every capability to be legible, rankable and escalatable on a schedule. Its relation to the superhero runs through the mandate: where an institution assigns and can revoke, the work is mode two and belongs here squarely; where the fighting is its own end, the mandate is absent and the work enters, if at all, on iconography.
entries.example: My Hero Academia (2014) makes hero licensing the plot's currency and is mode two throughout; One-Punch Man (2009) assumes its mandate and then deconstructs it by removing all jeopardy; Naruto and Jujutsu Kaisen both run licensed-operative structures with a body that assigns missions and can withdraw them.
entries.application: Decide whether your fights are the plot or the argument, and be honest about the answer. Note that the Manga pack is planned and not yet built, so this tradition is carded here and the debt is booked outward for pack twelve.

entries.name: Mahou Shoujo and the Transformation
entries.description: The magical-girl line, which solved the double life decades before the American form took it seriously.
entries.principle: Mahou shoujo takes the two lives that the American tradition treats as a burden and makes them the subject: the transformation is aspirational rather than concealing, the powers are frequently granted by a contract with terms, and the cost is social rather than physical. Its mandate structure is unusual and worth stealing — a pact with a party who benefits, which makes the warrant question concrete in a way an origin accident never does.
entries.example: Sally the Witch (1966) founds the line; Sailor Moon (1991) fixes the transformation sequence and the team structure that the tradition exports; Puella Magi Madoka Magica (2011) makes the contract's terms the horror and is the line's own deconstruction.
entries.application: If your hero's power came from an agreement, write the other party's interest. Note that the Manga pack is planned and not yet built, so this tradition is carded here and the debt is booked outward for pack twelve.

entries.name: The British Line: 2000 AD and Marvelman
entries.description: A tradition whose distinctness is itself contested, and the export route that reshaped American comics.
entries.principle: The British line's claim to be a separate tradition is disputed on good evidence: Marvelman began in 1954 as a direct substitute for a Captain Marvel reprint licence that had lapsed, which makes the founding text a replacement rather than an invention. What is not disputed is the export: the writers 2000 AD trained arrived in American superhero comics in the 1980s and changed what the form was willing to attempt. The pack states the dispute rather than settling it.
entries.example: 2000 AD (1977) and Judge Dredd run a satirical mode two in which the licensing body is the horror; Marvelman, later renamed Miracleman after a trademark dispute, asks what an omnipotent being does to a world and is the tradition's most-cited work under two names.
entries.application: If you are reaching for the British register, take the anthology discipline — a complete argument in five pages, weekly — rather than the accent. That constraint is what the export actually carried.

entries.name: The Bande Dessinée and the French Prosecution
entries.description: France has no superhero tradition, and the reason is a statute rather than a preference.
entries.principle: The absence of a French superhero line is usually explained by cultural taste and is better explained by law. The loi du 16 juillet 1949 on publications aimed at young people gave the state a standing instrument against imported and imitative adventure comics, and the costumed line that had started after the war did not survive it. This is the clearest case in the genre of a national tradition being closed rather than declining, and it is why bande dessinée's enormous adventure tradition runs almost entirely outside this genre's furniture.
entries.example: Fantax, drawn by Pierre Mouchot under the name Chott from 1946, is the French costumed hero the statute reached; its author was prosecuted from 1955 and bankrupted by the litigation in 1961.
entries.application: Before explaining an absent tradition by taste, look for the instrument. A genre that is missing from a market usually has a documented reason, and the reason is frequently regulatory.

entries.name: The Indian Superhero: Raj Comics and Krrish
entries.description: A domestic comics line and a film tradition that reached the form by a different road.
entries.principle: India's superhero line runs on two tracks that barely touch: a domestic comics publisher building a costumed roster for a Hindi-reading readership from the mid-1980s, and a film industry that arrived at the superhero through the masked-avenger and science-fantasy traditions rather than through comics. The film track matters more to a writer, because its solutions to the double life are drawn from a star system and a song structure the American form has no equivalent for.
entries.example: Raj Comics, founded in 1986, built the line around Nagraj and later Doga; Mr. India (1987), written by Salim and Javed, runs invisibility as a social parable; Krrish (2006) follows Koi… Mil Gaya (2003) and is the tradition's most visible costumed hero.
entries.application: If you are borrowing from this tradition, take the structural device rather than the iconography — the star persona carrying moral weight the script never states is the transferable part.

entries.name: The Luchador Film and the Real Mask
entries.description: The one tradition in which the secret identity has consequences outside the fiction.
entries.principle: The luchador film satisfies every clause of this genre's claim, and it does something no other tradition does: the mask is not a narrative device but a real labour contract and a social pact, governed by rules with genuine stakes — the wager match in which a mask is put against another wrestler's hair or mask, and the taboo on unmasking outside it. A secret identity that is legally and professionally binding is the single most useful observation in the non-Anglophone material, because it shows what the convention feels like when it costs something.
entries.example: The films of El Santo, from the late 1950s, run a costumed hero whose mask was a career-long professional obligation; he was buried wearing it. Heather Levi's The World of Lucha Libre (2008) is the scholarship on the institution behind the films.
entries.application: Ask what your protagonist's mask costs while nothing is happening. If the answer is nothing, the identity is a plot device rather than a condition, and this tradition shows what the alternative looks like.

entries.name: The Black Superhero and the Milestone Line
entries.description: A standpoint tradition, and the one case where creators built the publisher rather than negotiating with one.
entries.principle: The tokenised team member and the standpoint tradition are two different things, and the distinction is ownership: a character written from a standpoint inside a line owned elsewhere is subject to the line's needs, while a publisher founded to carry those characters sets its own. The Milestone founders' move was structural rather than representational, and it is the genre's clearest demonstration that the credit and ownership questions in §6 are craft questions as well as legal ones.
entries.example: Milestone Media, founded in 1993 by Dwayne McDuffie, Denys Cowan, Michael Davis and Derek Dingle, launched Static, Icon and Hardware under a distribution arrangement that kept the characters with their creators; Black Panther, created in 1966 inside the Marvel line, is the older and structurally opposite case.
entries.application: Ask who owns the character whose standpoint you are writing from, because ownership determines who can revise it later. It is the question the genre's history answers most consistently and most uncomfortably.

entries.name: The Woman Superhero and the Costume Question
entries.description: The costume as an argument the reader can see before the first line of dialogue.
entries.principle: The costume states a claim about the body wearing it, and in this genre that claim has been made overwhelmingly by artists drawing for an assumed reader rather than by writers characterising a person. The craft consequence is that a woman hero's costume is doing characterisation the script did not write and frequently contradicts, and the posing conventions that circulate under informal names are a drawing-desk habit rather than a design decision. Carolyn Cocca's work is the standing scholarship; the coinage of the best-known term for the posing convention is not established and this pack does not attribute it.
entries.example: Wonder Woman has been redesigned repeatedly and each redesign is an argument about who the character is for; Ms. Marvel (2014), by G. Willow Wilson and Adrian Alphona, designs a costume that states a specific standpoint and is characterisation before it is iconography.
entries.application: Describe your hero's costume as if the reader will infer the character from it alone, because they will. Then check whether what it says matches what you wrote.

entries.name: The Queer Superhero
entries.description: A double life that already means something before the powers arrive.
entries.principle: The secret identity is a metaphor that arrived at this reading rather than being built for it, which is why the queer superhero is both obvious in retrospect and structurally awkward: a convention designed to protect a hero's family reads differently once concealment is the subject rather than the mechanism. The tradition's craft problem is the coming-out scene, which the genre keeps staging as a revelation and which works better as a condition the story starts inside.
entries.example: Northstar's coming out in Alpha Flight (1992) is the mainstream's first and is structured as a revelation; Batwoman's 2006 relaunch and The Authority's Midnighter and Apollo (1999) both start inside the condition instead, which is the structurally stronger choice.
entries.application: Decide whether concealment is your subject or your mechanism. If it is the subject, the powers are the metaphor rather than the plot, and the story should be able to survive their removal.

entries.name: Religion, Ethnicity and the Superhero
entries.description: The genre's oldest unstated substrate, and the difference between a heritage and a costume.
entries.principle: A hero written from a religious or ethnic standpoint has an obligation the pack's other standpoint blocks do not: the tradition being drawn on is living and has its own account of itself, so the card and the story are both accountable to it. The failure mode is the heritage rendered as an origin accessory — a language, a garment, a grandmother — with none of the tradition's own claims permitted to constrain the plot.
entries.example: Ms. Marvel (2014) writes a Muslim teenager whose faith constrains her choices rather than decorating them; the argument that Superman is a Jewish immigrant myth is contested, with Martin Lund arguing it is a retrospective invention rather than a founding intention, and the pack carries both positions.
entries.application: Give the tradition at least one claim your protagonist has to obey when it is inconvenient. Without that the heritage is set dressing and the reader can tell.

entries.name: Disability, the Prosthetic and the Body
entries.description: The genre's worst record, and its two most-cited cases pulling in opposite directions.
entries.principle: A form organised around exceptional bodies handles ordinary variation badly, and its characteristic move is the compensatory power — a disability offset by a capability, so that the body is a plot device rather than a condition. The two cases the field argues about most run opposite ways: a hero whose blindness is offset by a heightened sensorium, and a character whose paralysis was made central to her competence rather than corrected, then later reversed. The reversal is contested and this pack states the dispute rather than adjudicating it.
entries.example: Daredevil is the compensatory model and the genre's most-copied version of it; Barbara Gordon as Oracle, from 1989, made competence structural rather than compensatory and was the field's most-cited counter-example until the 2011 relaunch restored her mobility, which remains disputed.
entries.application: If a capability arrives to offset a condition, ask what the story loses by removing the offset. If the answer is nothing, the condition was never doing work.

entries.name: The Superhero as Modern Fantasy
entries.description: The power-system and chosen-one apparatus — owned by the fantasy-reference pack.
entries.principle: This book-type is handed off to the fantasy-reference pack, which owns magic-system design, the price of power, chosenness, and the magical-law and magical-education material a hero academy runs on. Fantasy asks what the world's rules are and what they cost; Superhero asks who authorised the intervention and what limits it. The distinction is jurisdictional rather than tonal: a caped protagonist inside a coherent magic system whose warrant is never questioned is Fantasy's, and a magicless protagonist whose right to act is the subject is this pack's. Fantasy already holds the comics creators this genre shares with it and carries no superhero pointer of its own.
entries.example: A hero academy whose interest is in how the magic is taught belongs in Fantasy; My Hero Academia, whose interest is in who issues the licence, belongs here.
entries.application: When the rules of the power are the point, work in the fantasy-reference pack; when the warrant for using it is the point, hold the superhero contract and hand the system across.

entries.name: The Costumed Crimefighter and the Crime Story
entries.description: The pulps and the crime apparatus — owned by the mystery-crime-thriller-reference pack.
entries.principle: This book-type is handed off to the mystery-crime-thriller-reference pack, which owns the pulp magazines, the procedural, the investigation and the whole architecture of how a crime is solved. MCT asks how a crime is solved and what solving it costs; Superhero asks by what warrant this person is at the scene at all. The seam is the mandate: a detective with a badge is MCT's, and a detective without one whose lack of authorisation is the story is this pack's. Note that MCT carries thirty subgenres and none of them is a vigilante, masked-avenger or pulp-hero card, so this hand-off points at an apparatus rather than at a card.
entries.example: A locked-room puzzle solved by a costumed protagonist is MCT's story wearing a cape; Batman's Gotham, where the police tolerate an intervener they cannot deputise, is this pack's.
entries.application: When the question is who did it, work in the mystery-crime-thriller-reference pack; when the question is who let this person investigate, hold the superhero contract and hand the crime across.

entries.name: The Superhero-Adjacent SF
entries.description: Augmentation, the multiverse and the counterpart self — owned by the sf-reference pack.
entries.principle: This book-type is handed off to the sf-reference pack, which owns parallel universes, digital resurrection, the shadow self, the body-augmentation block and the antagonist-craft material this genre's rogues gallery draws on. SF asks what changes if this were true; Superhero asks who authorised the intervention. The seam is that SF treats the capability as the premise to be extrapolated and this pack treats it as a warrant to be questioned. SF cites Watchmen in five of its cards and carries no work card for it, which is the clearest statement of where this boundary currently sits.
entries.example: A story about what a society does once anyone can be enhanced is SF's; a story about what one enhanced person decides they are now obliged to do is this pack's.
entries.application: When the extrapolation is the point, work in the sf-reference pack; when the mandate is the point, hold the superhero contract and hand the premise across.

entries.name: The Horror Comic and the Monster Hero
entries.description: The monster, the creature line and the franchise treadmill — owned by the horror-reference pack.
entries.principle: This book-type is handed off to the horror-reference pack, which owns the monster traditions, the creature line, the escalation problem and a named comics-and-manga author block. Horror asks what the thing in the dark means; Superhero asks who authorised the intervention. The seam is agency: a monster that is suffered is Horror's, and a monster that intervenes on its own warrant is this pack's. One correction travels with the hand-off — Horror's franchise-treadmill card claims the problem is worse in horror than in any adjacent genre, and this genre falsifies that, so the Superhero card cites it and corrects it rather than restating it.
entries.example: Swamp Thing read as a horror of transformation is Horror's; the same character read as an intervener deciding what he now owes a landscape is this pack's.
entries.application: When the creature is the subject, work in the horror-reference pack; when the creature's decision to act is the subject, hold the superhero contract and hand the monster across.

entries.name: The Superhero Parodied
entries.description: Parody and pastiche of the form — owned by the comedy-reference pack.
entries.principle: This book-type is handed off to the comedy-reference pack, which owns parody and pastiche and the whole comic-strip tradition. Comedy asks how the joke is built and why it lands; Superhero asks what the parodist is reproducing from. The two are complementary rather than competing: a parody needs a form fixed enough to be recognised, which is the iconography this pack cards, and Comedy's own hand-off apparatus currently has a hole exactly where a superhero card belongs. The name follows Western's precedent at its `subgenre-38`, which was renamed from The Comic Western because a hand-off must not share the name of the card it points at.
entries.example: A superhero parody whose engine is comic structure is Comedy's; the fixed conventions it is reproducing — the origin, the costume, the rogues gallery — are carded here.
entries.application: When the joke's construction is the point, work in the comedy-reference pack; when what is being parodied is the point, hold the superhero contract and hand the joke across.

entries.name: The Historical Graphic Novel
entries.description: Comics that make a claim about the past — owned by the historical-reference pack.
entries.principle: This book-type is handed off to the historical-reference pack, which owns the claim a work makes about the past and carries most of the library's serious long-form comics already. Historical asks what claim the book makes about the past and what the record supports; Superhero asks who authorised the intervention. The seam is straightforward and rarely contested: a comic set in the past whose subject is the past is Historical's, and this pack's only interest in it is where a costumed intervener is the vehicle for the historical argument.
entries.example: A comics memoir or a documented history in comics form is Historical's; a wartime costumed line whose subject is the propaganda function of the costume is this pack's.
entries.application: When the past is the subject, work in the historical-reference pack; when the costume is the subject and the period is the setting, hold the superhero contract and hand the history across.

entries.name: The Superhero Romance
entries.description: The relationship plot and the concealment that drives it — owned by the romance-reference pack.
entries.principle: This book-type is handed off to the romance-reference pack, which owns the relationship as the plot's spine, the genre's ending obligations, and the secret identity as knowledge-asymmetry between intimates. Romance asks what the relationship costs and whether it survives; Superhero asks who authorised the intervention. The seam is unusually sharp because both packs card concealment and mean different things by it: Romance's is asymmetry between people who love each other, and this pack's is asymmetry between a person and the law. Romance's own withholding-with-a-defensible-reason material is a transferable test rather than a fence.
entries.example: A story in which the disclosure is the emotional climax is Romance's; a story in which the disclosure is a jurisdictional event with legal consequences is this pack's.
entries.application: When the concealment's cost is to the relationship, work in the romance-reference pack; when its cost is to the mandate, hold the superhero contract and hand the relationship across.

entries.name: The Costumed West
entries.description: The masked hero on the frontier — owned by the western-reference pack.
entries.principle: This book-type is handed off to the western-reference pack, which owns the weird western at its `subgenre-25` and cards the frontier's costumed and supernatural line. Western asks what makes a claim to ground legitimate and what force settles it; Superhero asks who authorised the intervention. The two claims are closer here than anywhere else in the library, because a frontier with no functioning law and a city with no functioning law generate the same protagonist, and Western itself makes the observation — its town-and-marshal card says that a marshal with unlimited authority is a superhero and that the subgenre's tension is entirely in the limits.
entries.example: A masked avenger on the frontier whose subject is the contested title to land is Western's; the same figure whose subject is his own lack of a warrant to intervene is this pack's.
entries.application: When the contested ground is the point, work in the western-reference pack; when the unauthorised intervention is the point, hold the superhero contract and hand the frontier across.

entries.name: The Super-Soldier and the Uniform
entries.description: The state's enhanced combatant — owned by the war-military-reference pack.
entries.principle: This book-type is handed off to the war-military-reference pack, which owns what combat does to the people inside it, the friction of command, and the uniformed absurd. War asks what the fighting costs the people doing it; Superhero asks who authorised the intervention. The seam is the mandate's direction: a soldier's warrant is conferred, revocable and the subject of War's whole apparatus, while this pack's protagonists mostly hold warrants nobody issued. War holds one comics work in its collection, so this hand-off is written on the contract seam rather than on shared material, which is the honest form of the card.
entries.example: An enhanced soldier following orders inside a chain of command is War's; the same soldier deciding to act after the orders stop is this pack's, and the moment the decision is made is where the hand-off runs.
entries.application: When the chain of command is intact, work in the war-military-reference pack; when the protagonist acts outside it, hold the superhero contract and hand the uniform across.

entries.name: The Costumed Hero in the Weekly Magazine
entries.description: The transforming hero, the piloted robot and the tokusatsu line — owned by the manga-reference pack.
entries.principle: This tradition is handed off to the manga-reference pack, which owns the serialisation system that produced it. The distinction is not subject matter but production: this pack's genre was shaped by monthly floppies, work-for-hire ownership and an editorial continuity apparatus, and manga's was shaped by a weekly magazine, a reader survey, an uncredited editor and an author who holds the rights. **The same premise run through those two systems is two different genres.** Manga collected this pack's outward debt in full at its own build — 31 subjects, 18 carded, 10 declined with stated reasons and destinations — and each of the thirteen creators both packs card is read there from the other side, which is the point of handing off rather than duplicating.
entries.example: A powered team assembled by an institution is this pack's; the same team assembled in a boys' weekly under a survey that can cancel it in ten weeks is manga's, and the ten-week horizon is the difference.
entries.application: When the question is who authorised the intervention, work here. When the question is what a weekly schedule, a survey and an uncredited editor did to the story, hand it to the manga-reference pack — and note that the tokusatsu television line is declined by both and belongs to TV Formats.

entries.name: Name the Body That Could Revoke It
entries.description: The pack's central diagnostic, stated as a question a writer can actually answer.
entries.principle: The organising claim's operational test is a single question: name the body that could revoke this person's licence to act, and say what happens to the story if it does. Where there is no such body the work is in mode one and every limit must be built into the character or the world. Where there is one and the work engages the possibility of revocation, it is mode two. The test is worth running because it converts an abstraction about legitimacy into a scene you either have or do not have.
entries.example: Batman has no such body and the absence is the whole engine; My Hero Academia has a licensing authority and the licence is the plot's currency; James Bond has one, which is why he belongs to another genre entirely.
entries.application: Answer the question in one sentence before drafting. If the answer is a body, write the revocation scene early — it is the scene that proves the conferral was real rather than decorative.

entries.name: The Warrant Is Not the Origin
entries.description: How the power arrived and why the character thinks it obliges them are two different scenes.
entries.principle: Origin stories collapse two claims that need separating: the acquisition of capability, which is usually an accident, and the conclusion that capability creates obligation, which is a choice and is where the character actually lives. A story that supplies the first and skips the second has a protagonist whose motivation is a spider bite. The warrant is the sentence in which someone decides that being able means being obliged, and it can be revisited, doubted and withdrawn in a way an accident cannot.
entries.example: Spider-Man's warrant is not the bite but the death that follows an inaction, which is why the origin survives retelling; the Fantastic Four acquire capability in one accident and never state a warrant at all, which is why their book is a family drama rather than a mission.
entries.application: Write the warrant sentence separately from the origin scene, then check whether your protagonist could plausibly repudiate it. If they could not, it is a premise rather than a decision.

entries.name: The Intervener Has No Constituency
entries.description: Nobody selected this person, and the people they act on cannot deselect them.
entries.principle: The distinguishing feature of mode one is not secrecy but the absence of any mechanism by which the people being acted upon can decline. A police officer can be complained about, a soldier can be ordered home, a politician can be voted out; a costumed intervener can only be endured or resisted. Most of the genre's political discomfort lives in this asymmetry, and most of its craft opportunity does too, because a protagonist with no constituency has no legitimate way to learn they are wrong.
entries.example: The Boys builds its whole argument on the absence of any recall mechanism; Gotham Central runs the same city from the side of people who have one and shows what the asymmetry feels like from below.
entries.application: Give at least one character standing to object and no power to enforce the objection. That character is the story's conscience and is usually more useful than an antagonist.

entries.name: The Privilege of Violence, in Three Modes
entries.description: Who is permitted to use force, in whose name, and with what consequence — a distinction the genre rarely draws.
entries.principle: Menaka Philips distinguishes three modes in which the genre distributes the privilege of violence, and the value to a writer is that the distinction is structural rather than moral: the same act reads entirely differently depending on which mode the story has placed the actor in. The pack states the argument and names whose it is; it does not adjudicate between Philips's reading and the accounts that treat the genre's violence as incidental to its wish-fulfilment.
entries.example: Watchmen places the same act in different modes for different characters and lets the reader feel the difference without stating it; The Punisher collapses all three into one and is the case the scholarship argues about.
entries.application: For each violent act in your story, ask who is permitted to do this and in whose name. If the answer is identical for every character, you have one mode where the genre offers three.

entries.name: What the Intervention Buys, and for Whom
entries.description: The result of the rescue, named, and the person it actually benefits.
entries.principle: Intervention in this genre is almost always narrated from the intervener's side, which conceals the question of who is better off afterwards and by how much. A story that names the beneficiary specifically — this family, this block, this contract — gets stakes for free and avoids the genre's characteristic vagueness, in which a city is saved and nobody's rent changes. The strongest versions let the answer be uncomfortable: the intervention buys something real for someone who did not deserve it.
entries.example: Astro City repeatedly narrates from the beneficiary's side and derives its whole method from the shift; the standard city-saving climax names no beneficiary at all and is the pattern this card exists against.
entries.application: After every intervention, write one sentence naming who is materially better off. If you cannot write it, the stakes were atmospheric.

entries.name: The Bystander Is a Character or the Story Is Lying
entries.description: Collateral without a face is a budget line, and the reader knows it.
entries.principle: The genre stages destruction at a scale that would in reality kill and bankrupt thousands, and then declines to look at any of them, which is a choice rather than an oversight and is the single most common way a superhero story loses a reader's belief. The remedy is not more grief; it is specificity. One named person whose flat is gone does more work than a collapsing skyline, and costs a page.
entries.example: Marvels narrates the entire superhero era from a photographer's vantage and makes the bystander the protagonist; the third act of the standard city-levelling film treats the population as terrain and is the failure mode.
entries.application: Put one named bystander in every large-scale set piece and let the reader meet them before the damage. If the story cannot afford the page, the set piece is too big.

entries.name: The Hero Who Was Asked
entries.description: Mode two on the page — what changes when somebody actually requested this.
entries.principle: A conferred mandate changes the shape of every scene, not merely the politics: a requested hero has a client, a brief, a reporting line and a record, which supplies obstacles a self-appointed one has to have manufactured. It also relocates the story's central tension from is-this-legitimate to is-this-being-done-honestly, which is a different and frequently richer question. The licensed traditions have run this structure for decades and the American form treats it as a crisis.
entries.example: My Hero Academia's licensing regime makes the brief and the record ordinary features of the world; the Sokovia Accords stage the same arrangement as a rupture, which is a story about arriving at mode two rather than a story set in it.
entries.application: If somebody asked, decide who signs the paperwork and who reads the report. Those two people are your best sources of scenes and neither of them needs a power.

entries.name: When the Mandate Is Withdrawn
entries.description: The scene that proves a conferral was real, and the one most licensed-hero stories skip.
entries.principle: A licence that is never withdrawn is set dressing. The withdrawal scene is where mode two earns its structure, because it forces the story to say what the protagonist actually is once the authorisation stops — a criminal, a civilian, or a person who was never really operating under it. Mode one has an inverse version: the moment a self-appointed intervener is told to stop by someone with standing, and complies or does not.
entries.example: My Hero Academia repeatedly stages licensing loss as an ordinary professional hazard; Watchmen's Keene Act removes the authorisation from a whole population and the book is largely about who kept working anyway.
entries.application: Write the withdrawal, even if it never reaches the page. What the character does in the first hour afterwards is the most efficient characterisation available in this genre.

entries.category: Power on the Page: Staging, Scale and Legibility
entries.name: Scale Is Composition, Not Caption
entries.description: A caption that says enormous is a caption admitting the picture failed.
entries.principle: In a visual medium, power is asserted by composition — where the figure sits in the frame, what it occupies, what cannot contain it — and every word spent telling the reader that something is powerful is a word conceding the image did not. This is the most transferable thing the genre's best artists know, and it applies to prose too: a sentence that reports magnitude is weaker than one that reports what magnitude did to a specific object.
entries.example: Kirby's page architecture asserts scale through composition and rarely needs a caption to do it; the standard editorial caption announcing an unprecedented threat is the failure this card names.
entries.application: Delete every adjective of magnitude from your action beats and see what survives. What survives is what the reader actually experiences as scale.

entries.category: Power on the Page: Staging, Scale and Legibility
entries.name: The Artist Is Staging It, Not You
entries.description: In comics, the person who decides what the fight looks like is not the person who wrote it.
entries.principle: A comics script proposes staging; the artist disposes of it, and the finished page is the artist's account of the scene rather than the writer's. This is the delta against `war-military:craft-21`, which is about staging an action the reader can hold: that card assumes a single author controlling the image. Here, legibility is a negotiated outcome, and a script that over-specifies produces a stiff page while one that under-specifies produces a scene the writer did not intend. What travels between them is the beat, not the blocking.
entries.example: The Marvel Method inverts the order entirely, with the artist plotting from a premise and the writer scripting afterwards, which is a production process rather than a house style and is routinely conflated with one.
entries.application: Specify what the panel must accomplish and what must be unambiguous in it; leave the camera to the artist. Then read the pencils and rewrite the dialogue to the page you actually got.

entries.category: Power on the Page: Staging, Scale and Legibility
entries.name: The Beat Before the Impact
entries.description: The panel that makes the next panel land.
entries.principle: Impact in a static medium is produced by the preceding beat rather than by the impact itself: the reader supplies the motion in the gutter between the two, and the size of what they supply is set by how much stillness preceded it. Writers who script the hit and not the moment before it get pages where everything is loud and nothing is fast. The technique transfers directly to prose, where the same effect is produced by sentence length rather than panel size.
entries.example: The single quiet panel before a Kirby impact is the mechanism, and it is why the impact reads as force rather than as noise.
entries.application: Before every major impact, script one beat of stillness with no dialogue. If the page cannot spare it, the sequence has too many impacts.

entries.category: Power on the Page: Staging, Scale and Legibility
entries.name: Range Decides What the Fight Can Be
entries.description: How far apart they are determines which powers matter, and most fights never decide it.
entries.principle: Distance is the variable that silently selects which capabilities are relevant, and a fight whose range is undefined is a fight where the author picks the winner. This is the superhero-specific delta against two existing cards: `western:craft-19` treats distance as an antagonist in a landscape, and `war-military:combat-60` treats it as a force multiplier for the defender. Here it is a filter on an asymmetric roster — at contact range the strongest wins, at a hundred metres the fastest does, and beyond that only some of the cast is in the scene at all.
entries.example: The asymmetric roster problem is at its clearest in a team fight, where a character who is decisive at one range is a bystander at another and the writer must decide which.
entries.application: Fix the range at the start of every fight and change it deliberately rather than by drift. A change in range is a change in who the scene is about.

entries.category: Power on the Page: Staging, Scale and Legibility
entries.name: The Undrawable Power
entries.description: Some capabilities have no image, and the medium punishes them.
entries.principle: Powers that operate on minds, probability, information or time have no natural visual, which is why the genre keeps giving them arbitrary effects — glowing eyes, floating debris, a colour — that convey activity without conveying what is happening. The honest solutions are to externalise the power into a consequence the reader can see, or to stage it through a character who can be shown reacting. The dishonest solution is a caption, and it is the one most often taken.
entries.example: Telepathy is the genre's standing case and has been solved by borders, lettering and floating panels rather than by drawing the power itself, which is a lettering solution to a staging problem and belongs to the collaborative page.
entries.application: For any power without an image, decide what the reader sees instead — the consequence, the reaction, or the lettering — and commit to one convention for the whole run.

entries.category: Power on the Page: Staging, Scale and Legibility
entries.name: Collateral Is Geography
entries.description: Damage that is not located is damage the reader cannot feel.
entries.principle: A fight that moves through named, specific places accumulates weight that a fight in generic urban terrain cannot, because the reader tracks loss geographically. This is the practical half of the bystander card: the destruction becomes legible when it happens somewhere the reader has already been shown, which means the cost of a set piece is paid in earlier pages rather than in the set piece itself.
entries.example: Daredevil's Hell's Kitchen is a fixed and repeatedly established geography, which is why damage there registers; the interchangeable city of the standard climax is the counter-case.
entries.application: Establish three specific locations before the fight that will be destroyed during it. The reader will do the rest without prompting.

entries.category: Power on the Page: Staging, Scale and Legibility
entries.name: Speed on a Static Page
entries.description: The medium has no motion, so speed is a rhythm rather than a depiction.
entries.principle: Speed in comics is produced by panel count and panel width rather than by motion lines: many narrow panels read fast, one wide panel reads slow, and a character who is faster than everyone else is shown by giving them more panels in the same amount of story time than anybody else gets. It is a structural solution rather than an illustrative one, and it is why speedsters are hard to write and easy to draw badly.
entries.example: The convention of showing a fast character completing several actions inside a single moment of story time is the form's answer, and it is a page-layout decision before it is a script decision.
entries.application: Script speed as a panel budget rather than as an adverb. Decide how many panels your fast character gets inside one beat and hold that ratio.

entries.category: Power on the Page: Staging, Scale and Legibility
entries.name: The Splash Page Is a Sentence
entries.description: A full page is a unit of emphasis, and emphasis spent everywhere is emphasis nowhere.
entries.principle: The splash and the double-page spread are the medium's strongest emphasis and behave like a very short sentence in prose: their power is entirely relative to what surrounds them, and a book that opens every chapter with one has taught the reader to skim them. They are also expensive in story, since a page of grid carries several beats and a splash carries one, which makes every splash a decision to spend narrative on impact.
entries.example: The single-page reveal works because the pages before it are dense; a run that spreads every confrontation across two pages produces a book that reads in ten minutes and lands nothing.
entries.application: Budget splashes per issue before you script, and make each one pay for the beats it displaced. If you cannot say what it displaced, it is decoration.

entries.name: Why the Ceiling Is Never Reached
entries.description: The genre's central unexamined question — why a person with power does not use all of it.
entries.principle: Almost every superhero story depends on protagonists operating far below their demonstrated ceiling, and almost none of them explain why. The library has nothing on this at all, and it is the problem a working writer meets first: a character who could end the conflict on page two and does not is either restrained by something the story has established, or is being managed by the author. Only the first is craft. The available restraints are a rule, a cost, a jurisdiction, an audience, or an incapacity, and each produces a different book.
entries.example: Superman's restraint is usually presented as ethical and is therefore fragile, since an ethic can be argued with; the restraints that hold across long runs are structural — an obligation elsewhere, a consequence that accrues, a person who would be harmed.
entries.application: Name the restraint explicitly in your own notes, then check whether a reader could name it from the text. If not, you are managing the character rather than writing them.

entries.name: The Rule the Character Will Not Break
entries.description: A self-imposed limit is only interesting where breaking it is available.
entries.principle: The refused option is the genre's most reliable characterisation device, and it works on one condition: the option must be genuinely available and genuinely effective. A rule against killing is dramatic where killing would solve the problem and hollow where it would not, which is why writers who want the rule to matter must first make the case for breaking it at full strength. The rule also has to cost something on an ordinary day, not only at the climax.
entries.example: Batman's rule is the most-argued instance in the genre precisely because the story keeps making the case against it; the Punisher exists as the standing demonstration of what the form looks like with the rule removed.
entries.application: Write the strongest available argument for breaking the rule and give it to someone sympathetic. If the rule survives that, it is load-bearing.

entries.name: A Limit the Reader Can Check
entries.description: The difference between a limit and an excuse is whether the reader can audit it.
entries.principle: A stated limit that the reader can hold in mind and test against later scenes is a source of tension; an unstated one that appears when the plot needs it reads as an author's convenience, and readers detect this reliably even when they cannot articulate it. The test is simple: could a reader, at any point, predict whether the character can do a given thing? If not, jeopardy is theatre.
entries.example: The recurring reader complaint that a powerful character should have solved an earlier problem is always a symptom of an unauditable limit rather than of pedantry.
entries.application: Write your protagonist's limits as a short list a reader could reconstruct from the text. Then check each plot resolution against it, and treat every violation as a defect rather than as a note.

entries.name: Unlimited Authority Is Not a Character
entries.description: The library already uses this genre's name as a warning, twice, and both times about limits.
entries.principle: Two shipped packs use "superhero" as a pejorative craft term and both are about the same failure. The Western pack's town-and-marshal card observes that a marshal with unlimited authority is a superhero and that the subgenre's tension is entirely in the limits; the crime pack uses "the analyst as superhero" for a forensic specialist who can do everything. In both cases the word marks a character whose capability has outrun any constraint, and the diagnosis is the same in this pack's own genre: unlimited authority removes the need for choice, and choice is what characterisation is made of.
entries.example: The genre's own solution is jurisdictional rather than moral — a hero who is powerful everywhere is constrained by being wanted in three states, sued in a fourth, and unwelcome in the fifth.
entries.application: If your protagonist can do anything, take away not the power but the permission. Jurisdiction constrains without weakening, which is the trade the genre's best long runs keep making.

entries.name: The Competence That Ends the Scene
entries.description: A character who solves every problem has to be removed from most of them.
entries.principle: On an asymmetric roster, one member is always capable of ending a given scene alone, and the writer's real work is arranging their absence convincingly. Doing it by coincidence repeatedly teaches the reader that the roster is wrong; doing it structurally — an obligation elsewhere, a cost they will not pay, a jurisdiction they cannot enter — turns the problem into characterisation. The absence is a scene in itself and is usually more interesting than the fight it enables.
entries.example: The team book's standing difficulty is the member who could resolve the plot in one panel, and the durable solutions give that member a reason of their own rather than a scheduling conflict.
entries.application: For every set piece, name who could end it alone and write their reason. If the reason is a coincidence more than once, change the roster rather than the plot.

entries.name: Killing Is a One-Way Door
entries.description: In a form where death reverses, the decision to kill is the only thing that does not.
entries.principle: The genre reverses death routinely, which drains the act of killing of consequence for the victim and concentrates all of it on the killer: what persists is not the death but the decision, and the decision cannot be retconned out of the character without the reader noticing. This is the one place where the serial's reversibility works in a writer's favour, because it makes an irreversible choice available in a form that otherwise has almost none.
entries.example: A hero who kills once is changed for the remainder of a run in a way that a hero who dies is not, and the asymmetry is the most useful structural fact the reversibility of death produces.
entries.application: If your protagonist kills, treat it as the run's only permanent event and plan the run around it. If you intend to walk it back, do not write it.

entries.name: Concealment Is a Cost, Not a Convenience
entries.description: A second life the story never charges for is a costume the character takes off between scenes.
entries.principle: The secret identity is usually written as a plot generator and is more useful as a standing expense: the time it takes, the relationships it damages, the income it costs, the lies that accumulate and have to be maintained. The delta against Romance, which owns concealment as knowledge-asymmetry between intimates, is that this pack's concealment is asymmetry between a person and the law — the thing being hidden is not a feeling but a criminal liability, and the cost is measured in jurisdiction rather than in trust.
entries.example: The luchador tradition is the limit case, where the mask is a professional obligation with real-world stakes rather than a narrative device; Daredevil's law practice supplies a version of the same idea, since the day job is where the concealment is billed.
entries.application: Write what the concealment costs on an ordinary Tuesday with no crisis in it. If the answer is nothing, the identity is a device rather than a condition.

entries.name: Who Already Knows
entries.description: The map of who knows is the story's real relationship diagram.
entries.principle: A secret's structure is not the secret but the distribution of who holds it, and in this genre that distribution is where nearly all the available drama sits: the partner who knows, the parent who does not, the antagonist who has worked it out and is waiting, the institution with a file. Writers who track only the protagonist's concealment miss that every knower is a character with their own exposure, and that the interesting scenes are between two people who both know and cannot say so.
entries.example: The supporting cast of a long-running superhero book is best read as a knowledge diagram, with the tension living in the gaps between who knows, who suspects and who has decided not to ask.
entries.application: Draw the knowledge map before the plot. Every line on it is a scene, and the people with no line are the ones the reader will stop caring about.

entries.name: The Disclosure Is a Jurisdictional Event
entries.description: When the mask comes off, the law arrives — and most stories only stage the emotion.
entries.principle: Unmasking is written overwhelmingly as an emotional climax, and structurally it is a legal one: an identified vigilante is a person who can be charged, sued, subpoenaed, deposed and enjoined, and whose family becomes reachable. Staging only the feeling wastes the strongest consequence the genre has, and it is the consequence that persists after a reset, since a court record does not un-happen when continuity does.
entries.example: Civil War's registration argument treats identification as the central concession precisely because it is the one that cannot be walked back; a run that unmasks its lead and returns to ordinary patrols the following issue has told the reader that identity never mattered.
entries.application: List the legal consequences of disclosure before you write the scene, and let at least one of them survive into the next arc. Reputational and legal cost is the form of cost this genre cannot reset.

entries.name: The Mask Changes the Voice
entries.description: Two lives means two registers, and most scripts write one person in different costumes.
entries.principle: A double life is a characterisation opportunity the genre routinely wastes: the masked register and the unmasked one should differ in vocabulary, sentence length and what the character is willing to say, because the mask is permission as much as concealment. Where both voices are identical, the reader learns that the identity is cosmetic; where they differ too much, the reader loses the person underneath. The calibration is the craft.
entries.example: The convention of a lowered, clipped register under the cowl is a voice decision rather than a sound effect, and it works because it marks what the character will only say while unaccountable.
entries.application: Write one page of dialogue in each register with the tags removed and see whether a reader could sort them. If not, the mask is doing nothing to the person wearing it.

entries.name: Which Life Is the Real One
entries.description: The genre's oldest question about its own protagonists, and a structural decision rather than a theme.
entries.principle: Whether the costume or the civilian is the true self is a decision that determines which scenes carry weight: if the mask is the real person, the civilian scenes are the disguise and can be played as strain; if the civilian is real, the costume is a job and the interesting material is the return home. A story that has not decided produces a protagonist whose stakes move around, because the reader cannot tell which life the character is afraid of losing.
entries.example: Superman and Batman are the field's standing opposed answers to the same question, and the difference is legible in which set of scenes each book treats as the character's home.
entries.application: Decide which life the character would keep if forced to choose, then check that your page allocation matches. Most drafts spend their pages on the life they say is the disguise.

entries.name: The Sidekick Knows
entries.description: The genre's oddest relationship, and the succession pipeline nobody plans.
entries.principle: The sidekick is three things at once — an audience surrogate, a person who knows the secret, and the legacy title's supply line — and treating them as only the first produces the flat version. The role's real content is the apprenticeship: an adult recruits a younger person into an unauthorised and dangerous activity, which the genre stages as mentorship and which becomes far more interesting when the story lets it be examined. The succession function means every sidekick is a claim on the mantle, whether or not the writer intends it.
entries.example: The Robin lineage is the field's most-developed instance and demonstrates all three functions at once, including the reversion problem when a successor is returned to a subordinate role.
entries.application: Ask what the mentor gets from the arrangement, and let one character voice the objection to it. And decide early whether this sidekick will inherit, because the reader is already assuming so.

entries.name: The Identity That Was Never Secret
entries.description: Public heroes are a different form, and the genre keeps forgetting it has them.
entries.principle: Removing the secret identity removes an entire machinery — the double life, the disclosure threat, the knowledge map — and the stories that do it must replace it with something, usually celebrity, accountability or family. The result is a distinct structure rather than a simplified one: a public hero has publicists, litigation, an audience and no refuge, and their problem is not exposure but the impossibility of stopping being on.
entries.example: The Fantastic Four are unmasked celebrities from their first appearance and their book is a family drama with a press office; Iron Man's public identification converted a concealment structure into an accountability one and the run changed shape accordingly.
entries.application: If you remove the mask, name what replaces it in the same paragraph. A public hero without an audience problem is a private hero missing a subplot.

entries.category: The Serial: Writing Without an Ending
entries.name: Write the Arc, Inherit the Character
entries.description: You are a tenant, and the lease has terms.
entries.principle: A writer joining a continuing title inherits a character with decades of prior text, a readership with expectations, and an editorial line, and produces an arc that a successor will inherit in turn. The craft consequence is a bounded kind of authorship: what you may change is real but partial, and the durable contributions are additions rather than revisions — a new supporting character, a relocated status quo, a question the next writer has to answer.
entries.example: The runs remembered as definitive are almost all additive; the runs remembered as damaging are almost all ones that removed something a successor then had to restore, which is the reversion cost §5a's legacy section describes.
entries.application: Decide what you are adding that a successor cannot easily delete. That is your run, and it is usually smaller and more specific than the pitch.

entries.category: The Serial: Writing Without an Ending
entries.name: The Ending You Are Not Allowed
entries.description: The form's central deprivation, and the substitutes that work.
entries.principle: A serial that cannot end cannot spend an ending, which removes the device most narrative structure is built to deliver. The workable substitutes are the arc climax that changes a standing condition, the departure of a character the reader is attached to, and the irreversible decision — which is why `craft-22` matters structurally as well as morally.
