What does not work is the false ending, because a reader who has been promised finality twice stops believing the third time.
entries.example: The imaginary story and the alternate-continuity book exist precisely to supply the ending the main line cannot, which is why the tradition keeps producing them and why they are frequently the best-remembered work.
entries.application: If you need an ending, either take an irreversible decision or go outside continuity to get one. Do not simulate finality inside a line that will resume next month.

entries.category: The Serial: Writing Without an Ending
entries.name: What Your Run Accrues
entries.description: A serial's asset is the reader's memory, and it has to be deliberately built.
entries.principle: The thing a long run accumulates is not plot but reader memory, and memory is an asset that can be spent: a single panel can pay off two years of accretion, and nothing else in fiction has that exchange rate. The corollary is that accrual must be intentional. A run that introduces nothing recurring has nothing to spend later, and a run that introduces too much creates continuity debt that a successor has to service.
entries.example: The most-cited single panels in the genre are almost all withdrawals against long accrual, and they are unreadable to a new reader precisely because the value is in the deposit rather than the panel.
entries.application: Name the three things your run is accruing and the moment you intend to spend each. If you cannot name them, you are writing episodes.

entries.category: The Serial: Writing Without an Ending
entries.name: The Jumping-On Point Is a Promise
entries.description: Every issue is somebody's first, and the promise is that they can follow it.
entries.principle: A continuing title has to be simultaneously legible to a reader of twenty years and to one who has just arrived, and the techniques that manage this — the recap, the reintroduction in dialogue, the self-contained arc opening — are craft rather than housekeeping. The genre's structural readership problem is that accrual and accessibility pull in opposite directions, and a run that serves only the long reader shrinks its own audience issue by issue.
entries.example: The comic strip solved this daily for decades before the pamphlet existed, which is why `subgenre-15` treats the strip's recap discipline as a technique the comic book adopted without acknowledging the source.
entries.application: Hand any issue to someone who has read nothing and watch where they stop. That is your jumping-on failure, and it is almost never where you expected.

entries.category: The Serial: Writing Without an Ending
entries.name: The Recap Page Is Craft
entries.description: The most-skipped page in the book is the one doing the most structural work.
entries.principle: A recap is not a summary; it is a selection, and what it includes tells the reader what this issue will be about. Written well, it does three jobs — orient the new reader, remind the returning one, and prime the specific fact the issue will turn on — and the third is what separates a functional recap from a good one. Written badly it is a plot dump that spoils its own issue's emphasis.
entries.example: A recap that names four things when the issue turns on one has told the reader nothing about where to put their attention; the strip's daily reintroduction is the older and tighter version of the same technique.
entries.application: Write the recap after the issue and include only what the issue needs. If it reads as a table of contents, cut it to the single fact the ending depends on.

entries.category: The Serial: Writing Without an Ending
entries.name: Decompression Is a Budget Decision
entries.description: How many pages a beat gets, and what the collected edition did to the answer.
entries.principle: The term for extending a story across more pages and fewer beats per page has heavy industry and fan currency and no peer-reviewed treatment that this build could locate, so the pack uses it as working vocabulary rather than as established scholarship. What is not in doubt is the mechanism: writing with the collected volume in view changes the beat-per-page ratio, because a chapter that reads slowly monthly reads well in one sitting. The cost is borne by the monthly reader, and the decision is a budget rather than a style.
entries.example: The six-issue arc sized to a trade paperback is the industry's standard unit and is a production decision that became a narrative one, which is the clearest case in the genre of format determining form.
entries.application: Decide which reader you are writing for — monthly or collected — and be honest that you are trading one against the other. A book that claims to serve both usually serves the collected reader and disappoints the other monthly.

entries.category: The Serial: Writing Without an Ending
entries.name: Leave It Better Than the Status Quo
entries.description: The reset is coming; the question is what you get to keep.
entries.principle: A run ends with the book handed back, and the standing expectation is that the status quo returns. A writer who fights that entirely produces changes a successor immediately reverts; a writer who accepts it entirely produces a run that leaves no trace. The productive position is to identify the one change likely to survive — usually a character, a relationship or a location rather than a plot state — and to spend the run establishing it well enough that reverting it would look like vandalism.
entries.example: The additions that survive decades are almost always people and places rather than events, which is a reliable enough pattern to plan around.
entries.application: Pick the one thing you want to survive your run and make it useful to the next writer. Utility is the only real protection against reversion.

entries.category: The Serial: Writing Without an Ending
entries.name: The Book Outlives You
entries.description: The title is the protagonist, and it will be here after everyone currently on it has gone.
entries.principle: Western's observation that in a long-form serial the community becomes the protagonist because it is the only thing that persists applies exactly here, and this pack's `continuity` collection is built on it. For a writer, the practical consequence is that the title's identity — its register, its city, its recurring cast — is a shared asset with a longer life than any arc, and damage to it is the one kind of damage a run can do that is not repairable by the next reset.
entries.example: A title whose register is broken by a run takes years to re-establish, whereas a plot state can be reversed in an issue, which is why editorial protects tone more carefully than continuity.
entries.application: Before changing the book's register, ask whether the change is yours to make. Changing what a title feels like is a decision about the property rather than about your arc.

entries.category: The Collaborative Page: Script, Pencil, Ink, Colour, Letter
entries.name: The Script Is a Proposal
entries.description: What you write is an instruction to four other people, and each will interpret it.
entries.principle: A comics script is executed by a penciller, an inker, a colourist and a letterer, each of whom makes decisions the writer cannot fully specify and should not try to. The scripts that work identify what must be unambiguous — who is where, what changes, what the reader must not miss — and leave the rest, because over-specification produces a stiff page and under-specification produces a scene the writer did not intend. Two script traditions coexist: full script, which specifies panel by panel, and plot-first, in which the artist paces the story and the writer scripts afterwards.
entries.example: The Marvel Method is the plot-first tradition's best-known form and is a production process rather than a house style, which is a distinction the secondary literature routinely collapses.
entries.application: Mark each panel description as either a requirement or a suggestion, and keep the requirements to the ones the story fails without. Then rewrite the dialogue to the art you actually receive.

entries.category: The Collaborative Page: Script, Pencil, Ink, Colour, Letter
entries.name: The Inker Is Not a Tracer
entries.description: The line is an interpretive decision, and it changes what the page means.
entries.principle: Inking determines weight, texture, depth and the reading speed of a panel, and the same pencils inked by two people produce pages with different emotional registers. For a writer the practical consequence is that the mood you scripted is delivered — or not — at a stage you are not present for, and that credit for the finished look is genuinely shared. This is the clearest single case of §0.23's five claims: a page has a writer, a penciller, an inker, a colourist and a letterer, and naming one of them as the author is a claim about all five.
entries.example: The dispute over whether inking is authorship or execution is a live one in the industry and is the reason the credit distinction exists at all; the pack states it as contested rather than settling it.
entries.application: If a sequence depends on a specific texture — rain, dust, weight — say so once, and then accept the interpretation. And when you credit the work, name the whole team.

entries.category: The Collaborative Page: Script, Pencil, Ink, Colour, Letter
entries.name: Colour Is Continuity
entries.description: The reader tracks time, place and mood by palette before they read a word.
entries.principle: Colour does structural work that scripts rarely acknowledge: it marks flashback from present, one location from another, and one character's sequences from another's, and it does so faster than any caption. A palette shift is the cheapest scene transition the medium has. The limitation is historical rather than aesthetic — the four-colour register was a printing constraint before it was a style, and reading early work as a deliberate palette choice misattributes a technology to an artist.
entries.example: A run that assigns each of its parallel narratives a palette lets the reader navigate a complex structure with no signposting at all, which is a solution prose has no equivalent for.
entries.application: Decide your palette logic before the first issue and tell the colourist what it means, not what it looks like. A palette that carries information cannot be changed for a cover-date season.

entries.category: The Collaborative Page: Script, Pencil, Ink, Colour, Letter
entries.name: The Letterer Controls the Pace
entries.description: Balloon placement decides the order and the pauses, which is to say the timing.
entries.principle: Lettering determines the reading path through a panel and the beat between lines, which makes the letterer the person who actually controls comic timing. Balloon size sets volume, tail placement sets who speaks first, and the gap between two balloons is the pause a prose writer would render with a paragraph break. A page can be re-timed at the lettering stage without redrawing anything, and frequently is.
entries.example: The floating-panel and bordered-caption conventions used for telepathy are a lettering solution to the staging problem `craft-13` describes, which is a good illustration of how much narrative work this stage carries.
entries.application: Write dialogue in the order you want it read and keep balloons short enough to place. A long balloon does not merely look heavy; it removes the letterer's ability to time the panel.

entries.category: The Collaborative Page: Script, Pencil, Ink, Colour, Letter
entries.name: The Cover Is a Separate Authored Object
entries.description: Frequently by someone who did not read the issue, and it makes a promise the issue must keep.
entries.principle: A cover is a marketing object, an authored image and a contract with the reader all at once, and it is often produced by a different artist from a description rather than from the finished issue. The consequence is a standing mismatch risk: a cover that depicts a confrontation the issue does not contain has broken a promise, and readers count. It is also the most-reproduced single image from any issue and will outlive the story inside it.
entries.example: The cover-and-contents mismatch is old enough to be a genre joke, and the corrective — treating the cover as a promise to be honoured rather than an advertisement to be excused — is the position this pack takes.
entries.application: Describe the cover in terms of the promise it makes rather than the image it shows, then check the issue delivers it. If it does not, change one of the two.

entries.category: The Collaborative Page: Script, Pencil, Ink, Colour, Letter
entries.name: Panel Count Is Pacing
entries.description: How many panels a page holds is the medium's tempo control, and it is set in the script.
entries.principle: Panel count per page does what sentence length does in prose: a nine-panel grid reads deliberately and holds tension, a three-panel page reads fast and open, and alternating between them is how a book breathes. The writer sets this in the script and therefore owns the tempo even where the artist owns the staging, which makes it the single largest pacing lever available to a comics writer.
entries.example: The nine-panel grid used as an argument about inevitability rather than as a layout preference is the technique's most-cited application, and it demonstrates that panel count can carry meaning rather than merely rhythm.
entries.application: Write your panel counts as a rhythm across the issue before you write dialogue. If every page holds five or six panels, the book has one speed and the reader will feel it as flatness.

entries.category: The Collaborative Page: Script, Pencil, Ink, Colour, Letter
entries.name: Write to the Page Turn
entries.description: The medium's only concealment device, and it is determined by pagination.
entries.principle: The page turn hides what comes next, which makes it the medium's equivalent of a chapter break and its only true reveal mechanism, and it lands on fixed pages — so a beat placed one page early is a beat spent. Writers who script without tracking pagination surrender the device entirely. The convention is direction-dependent: a tradition read right to left turns the other way, so a script written for one and published in the other loses every reveal it built.
entries.example: The reveal on the recto after a turn is the standard placement, and its power comes entirely from the fact that the reader physically cannot see it early.
entries.application: Number your pages and mark every intended reveal against a turn. If a reveal falls mid-spread, move it or accept that it is not a reveal.

entries.category: The Collaborative Page: Script, Pencil, Ink, Colour, Letter
entries.name: Name All Five Claims
entries.description: Writer, penciller, inker, colourist, letterer — and the record usually names one.
entries.principle: Authorship of a comics page is five separate claims, and the reference record, the credit box and the popular account routinely collapse them into a single name. This is not a courtesy problem; it is an accuracy problem, and it is the substrate of the genre's longest-running disputes. For a working writer the practical form is simpler: know which claim you are making, and know that the page you are proud of was made by four other people as well.
entries.example: The genre's founding credit disputes are all disagreements about which of the five claims a given person held, and several of them ran for decades because nobody had stated the question in those terms.
entries.application: When you describe a comic, name the claim you mean. "Written by" and "created by" are different sentences, and the second is the one that starts arguments.

entries.category: The Rogues Gallery and the Recurring Antagonist
entries.name: The Gallery Is a Portfolio
entries.description: Not one villain but a set with coverage, which is a design problem SF's antagonist cards do not have.
entries.principle: SF's `character-18`, `-20`, `-21` and `-22` build one antagonist well. A rogues gallery is a portfolio, and its design question is coverage: each member should test a different capability, a different limit and a different part of the protagonist, so that the set spans the character rather than repeating one confrontation in six costumes. A gallery where every member is a physical match is a gallery with one card in it.
entries.example: Batman's gallery is the field's model because its members test intellect, resources, restraint, sanity and identity separately; a hero whose enemies are all stronger versions of themselves has no gallery, only an escalation ladder.
entries.application: Chart your gallery against the protagonist's attributes and find the uncovered ones. The gap in the chart is your next villain, and it is a better brief than a power set.

entries.category: The Rogues Gallery and the Recurring Antagonist
entries.name: The Enemy Who Cannot Be Beaten
entries.description: SF's escalating threat assumes a final confrontation. This form has none.
entries.principle: `scifi:character-22` requires a villain's danger to be earned and rising, which is correct for a bounded story and unavailable here: a recurring antagonist must be defeated repeatedly and therefore cannot escalate indefinitely without either becoming unbeatable or becoming a joke. What replaces escalation is variation — a returning villain should arrive with a different method, a different objective or a different relationship to the hero, so the tension comes from not knowing which version has come back.
entries.example: The recurring antagonists that survive decades are the ones whose subsequent appearances change register rather than volume, and the ones that exhaust themselves are the ones that only ever get stronger.
entries.application: For each return, change the question rather than the power level. If the only difference is that they are harder to beat, you have spent the character.

entries.category: The Rogues Gallery and the Recurring Antagonist
entries.name: The Revolving Door
entries.description: The prison that cannot hold anyone is a credibility problem the genre has never solved.
entries.principle: No pack in the library holds a card on the escape-and-recapture cycle, so this one differentiates against a gap rather than against a neighbour, and the gap was verified rather than assumed. A gallery requires its members to return, which requires the institutions that hold them to fail, repeatedly and visibly. Handled carelessly this destroys the reader's belief in the setting's competence and, worse, in the protagonist's project — a hero whose captures never hold is doing nothing. The workable responses are to make the failure a subject rather than a mechanism, to vary the reason each time, or to have the protagonist notice.
entries.example: The asylum that cannot contain its inmates is the field's standing case and is strongest where a story treats the institution's failure as its own scandal rather than as a plot convenience.
entries.application: Write the reason this specific escape happened and let a character be angry about it. An escape nobody in the story finds outrageous teaches the reader not to care either.

entries.category: The Rogues Gallery and the Recurring Antagonist
entries.name: The Villain Is an Asset on a Balance Sheet
entries.description: The economic layer SF's antagonist craft has no reason to consider.
entries.principle: Nothing in any of the ten shipped packs treats an antagonist as owned property — the search returns nothing at all — so this card has no neighbour to differentiate from and states the gap instead. A recurring antagonist in a shared universe is corporate property with a licensing value, a film pipeline and a claim on future writers, which constrains what any single run may do to them. You will not be permitted to end them, and if you are, it will be reversed. This is not a complaint but a design fact, and the writers who work best inside it choose changes that add rather than remove — a new relationship, a revealed history, a lasting humiliation — because those survive where a death does not.
entries.example: The recurring villain who is killed and returned within two years is the pattern, and the runs that landed permanently are the ones that changed what the character wanted rather than whether they existed.
entries.application: Assume your antagonist will be used by someone else next year. Write the change you would want to inherit.

entries.category: The Rogues Gallery and the Recurring Antagonist
entries.name: When the Rogue Is More Popular
entries.description: A commercial fact that becomes a craft constraint, and it happens more often here than anywhere.
entries.principle: This genre produces antagonists more popular than their protagonists with unusual regularity, which creates a real structural problem: a villain the audience is rooting for cannot generate jeopardy, because the reader wants what the threat wants. `scifi:character-20`'s sympathetic logic is a virtue in a bounded story and a liability across a serial, where the sympathy compounds with every appearance until the protagonist becomes the obstacle.
entries.example: The villain-led book is the industry's structural answer, and `subgenre-12` cards it — but note what it costs, since a rogue promoted to protagonist stops being available as a threat.
entries.application: Track whether the reader wants your antagonist to succeed. If they do, either commit and write the villain-led book or give the protagonist the better argument for once.

entries.category: The Rogues Gallery and the Recurring Antagonist
entries.name: The City Produces the Enemy
entries.description: The gallery is characterisation of the setting, and reading it that way generates plots.
entries.principle: The library holds nothing on a setting generating its own antagonists; the nearest entry is a crime pack card about a detective agency, which is a different claim. A rogues gallery is a portrait of the place that made it: a city whose villains are all financiers is making a different argument from one whose villains are all failed scientists or all costumed obsessives. Read this way the gallery stops being a cast list and becomes a diagnosis, and new members arrive from asking what this city would produce next rather than from asking what power is unused.
entries.example: A gallery dominated by industrialists, chemists and the institutionally mad describes a city with specific pathologies, and the best runs treat that description as the book's actual subject.
entries.application: Write one sentence describing what your city keeps producing. Every subsequent villain should be an instance of it, or a deliberate exception you can defend.

entries.name: Adaptation Selects for Iconography
entries.description: What crosses media is the costume and the origin; what does not is everything else.
entries.principle: Western's `craft-54` asks what survives adaptation and what does not, in general. This genre's answer is unusually consistent and worth stating as a rule: the iconography travels almost perfectly, the mandate question travels poorly, and the continuity does not travel at all. That selectivity is why adaptations converge on the origin — it is the only part of ninety years of material that is self-contained — and why they struggle with anything that depends on accumulated reader memory.
entries.example: The origin is retold in almost every screen adaptation regardless of how well known it is, which is a structural consequence of what the medium can carry rather than a failure of imagination.
entries.application: Identify which of your three layers — iconography, mandate, continuity — the adaptation can actually carry, and put the story's weight there rather than in the layer that will be cut.

entries.name: Ninety Years Will Not Fit in a Film
entries.description: Continuity is the one asset that cannot be adapted, only referenced or rebuilt.
entries.principle: A serial's accumulated reader memory is its most valuable asset and is worthless in adaptation, because the new audience has none of it. Adaptations therefore either rebuild the accrual from scratch across a long-form run, gesture at it with references that reward only existing readers, or discard it. All three are legitimate; what fails is treating an unearned reference as if it carried the weight the source's decades gave it, which reads to a new viewer as an assertion of significance rather than significance.
entries.example: Long-form television can rebuild accrual over seasons in a way a single film cannot, which is why the adaptation of a decades-long serial into a two-hour structure keeps reducing to an origin.
entries.application: Decide whether you are rebuilding, referencing or discarding — and if referencing, count how many of your references are load-bearing. Any that are will not land.

entries.name: The Costume Is the Hardest Problem
entries.description: A design that works in ink frequently does not survive contact with a body and a camera.
entries.principle: The costume is the genre's most portable element and its most technically difficult, because a drawn figure has no fabric, no weight and no wind, and colours that read as heroic on newsprint read as fancy dress under lighting. Every adaptation therefore negotiates between recognisability and plausibility, and the negotiation is a characterisation decision rather than a design one: what the costume is made of, who made it and why says as much as its silhouette.
entries.example: The recurring adaptation choice between the source's primary colours and a darker, textured redesign is an argument about which register the adaptation is in, and audiences read it as one immediately.
entries.application: Decide what your costume is made of and who made it before you decide what it looks like. Both questions are characterisation and only the second is design.

entries.name: The Adaptation Becomes the Canon
entries.description: For most of the audience the screen version is the character, and the source then answers to it.
entries.principle: Screen adaptations reach audiences orders of magnitude larger than the comics, with the consequence that the adaptation's version of a character becomes the default and the source line frequently revises itself toward it. Elements invented for adaptation are routinely imported back into the comics, which makes adaptation a source of canon rather than a derivative of it, and complicates any account of the genre that treats the comics as primary.
entries.example: Elements first created for radio and animation have been absorbed into comics continuity repeatedly, so the direction of authority between source and adaptation runs both ways and has since the 1940s.
entries.application: When you write for the source line, know which version of your character the audience already has. You are either working with it or against it, and both are choices worth making deliberately.

entries.name: Casting Is a Continuity Decision
entries.description: An actor's tenure is the adaptation's version of a legacy title, and it behaves the same way.
entries.principle: In screen adaptation the actor is the continuity: a recasting is a soft reboot whether or not the story says so, and an actor's departure ends a run the way a writer's does in the source line. This makes casting a structural decision rather than a production one, and it means the adaptation inherits the legacy title's whole problem set — succession, reversion, and an audience attached to the previous holder.
entries.example: The recasting of a long-held screen role produces exactly the reception pattern a legacy handover produces in the comics, including the demand for the original's return, which is `continuity`'s reversion problem arriving in a different medium.
entries.application: Treat a recasting as a succession and plan it as one. Announcing continuity while changing the face is the version audiences reject.

entries.name: The Screen Cannot Do a Splash Page
entries.description: The medium's strongest emphasis has no direct equivalent, and the substitutes are different in kind.
entries.principle: A splash page works because the reader controls the dwell time and can stop; film controls duration and cannot be stopped, so the equivalent effects — the held shot, the score, the slow push — work by different means and on a different schedule. Writers moving between the media consistently over-value the hero-shot, which on the page is an emphasis the reader chooses to accept and on screen is time the audience is required to spend.
entries.example: The held reveal is film's nearest equivalent and costs seconds of screen time that the page gets for free, which is why an adaptation that reproduces every splash reads as slow.
entries.application: For each moment of maximum emphasis, ask who controls the duration. If it is the audience, you can afford more of them; if it is you, you can afford very few.

entries.name: The Sky Beam Ending
entries.description: The genre's most-mocked structural habit, and the reason it keeps happening.
entries.principle: Third acts converge on an impersonal, city-scale threat because scale is the easiest way to signal stakes and the hardest way to generate them: a threat with no face cannot be argued with, cannot be understood, and cannot lose anything, so the climax becomes a demolition. The films that escape it do so by keeping the antagonist a person with a position through the final act, which costs spectacle and buys everything else.
entries.example: The impersonal aperture threat is the pattern's shorthand; the counter-cases are all films that resolve on a conversation or a choice between two people while the spectacle runs behind them.
entries.application: Name who the protagonist is arguing with in your final act. If the answer is a phenomenon, the ending is a demolition and the audience will read it as one.

entries.name: The Shared Universe Is a Release Schedule
entries.description: On screen the shared universe is a production calendar, and it constrains stories years ahead.
entries.principle: A screen shared universe commits stories to a slate fixed by production lead times, which means an individual film's ending may be determined by another film's start date. This is the event crossover's economics arriving in a medium with far higher costs and far less flexibility, and it produces the same craft problem: writers serving an ending they do not control, and books that stop mid-argument to attend a crossover.
entries.example: The tie-in problem is structurally identical across both media, and the workable response is also identical — find the question your instalment can answer that the slate cannot, and answer that one completely.
entries.application: Identify what your instalment can finish on its own. An episode of a schedule that finishes nothing is a trailer with a running time.

entries.name: The Secret Headquarters Is a Set
entries.description: Mode three's most literal case — a piece of iconography that exists to be looked at.
entries.principle: The cave, the tower, the satellite and the mansion are among the genre's most reproduced images and among its least narratively necessary, which makes the headquarters the clearest instance of the furniture circulating on its own account. That is not a criticism; it is a description of what it is for. A headquarters does real work as characterisation and as a fixed geography the audience learns, and almost none as plot, and confusing the two produces long scenes of people walking through a set.
entries.example: The headquarters is reliably among the first elements any adaptation builds and among the first any toy line reproduces, which is mode three operating exactly as `subgenre-19` describes it.
entries.application: Use the headquarters to establish geography and character and then get out of it. If a scene's only content is the room, it belongs in the title sequence.

entries.name: The Mandate Audit
entries.description: Run before the second draft, and again after any scene where the protagonist intervenes without being asked. This is the pack's central diagnostic and every other checklist here assumes it has been run.
items: Who could revoke this person's licence to act, and what happens to the story if they do?
If the answer is nobody, is the absence of authorisation ever felt by anyone on the page?
What is the mandate's warrant — capability, grief, guilt, contract, inheritance, or the bare fact of being able?
Can the protagonist state the warrant in their own words, and would they still hold it if challenged by someone sympathetic?
Which of the three modes is this story in, and does it stay there?
If it is mode two, where is the revocation scene?

entries.name: The Mandate Collapse Test
entries.description: Run once at outline stage, on the premise rather than the draft. Five minutes, and it tells you whether you are writing this genre or another one wearing its costume.
items: Remove the extraordinary capability and the mandate. Does the story collapse or does it stand?
If it stands, which genre does it actually belong to, and would that pack serve the writer better?
Is the work legible to a reader as standing inside the superhero system — by iconography, by documented lineage, or by its own framing?
If it enters on lineage, can you name the specific exchange rather than asserting a tradition?
If it enters on iconography alone, is that a deliberate mode-three choice or an accident?

entries.name: The Restraint Pass
entries.description: Run whenever a reader or editor asks why the protagonist did not simply solve it. That question is always a symptom and this pass finds the cause.
items: Name the restraint that keeps the protagonist below their demonstrated ceiling.
Is it a rule, a cost, a jurisdiction, an audience or an incapacity? Each produces a different book.
Could a reader name it from the text alone, without your notes?
Does it cost something on an ordinary day, or only at the climax?
For each plot resolution, check it against the restraint. Every violation is a defect, not a note.
If the restraint is ethical, has anyone argued against it at full strength?

entries.name: The Power-Legibility Pass
entries.description: Run on every action sequence before it is drawn or shot. A fight the reader cannot follow is a fight that did not happen.
items: Is the range fixed at the start of the sequence, and does it change deliberately rather than by drift?
At this range, which capabilities are relevant and which characters are effectively absent?
For any power without a natural image, what does the reader see instead — the consequence, the reaction, or the lettering?
Is the same convention used for that power everywhere in the run?
Is there a beat of stillness before each major impact?
Could a reader draw the sequence from the script alone? If not, which panel is ambiguous?

entries.name: The Bystander Ledger
entries.description: Run after every large-scale set piece, before the next one is written. The genre's most common way to lose a reader's belief is to destroy a city nobody lives in.
items: Is there at least one named bystander in this set piece, met before the damage?
Name who is materially better off after the intervention. One sentence, specific.
Name who is materially worse off, including anyone the protagonist did not intend to harm.
Are the destroyed locations ones the reader has already been shown?
Does anyone in the story have standing to object, and are they given a voice?
Does any of this cost persist into the next issue?

entries.name: The Jurisdiction Pass
entries.description: Run at outline and again before any confrontation with police, courts or another hero. This is the constraint that limits a protagonist without weakening them.
items: Where may this character legally act, and who has authority in that place?
Who could arrest, sue, deport, enjoin or deputise them, and has anyone tried?
What happens when they cross a boundary — a city line, a border, a private property line?
If another hero operates here, who yields and on what basis?
Does the story treat institutional failure as a scandal or as a convenience?
Is any of this asymmetry — that the people acted upon cannot decline — ever stated by someone inside the story?

entries.name: The Credit Pass
entries.description: Run on every card, page or reference to a comics work before it ships, and on every biography you write. Authorship here is five claims and the record routinely names one.
items: Which of the five claims is being made — writer, penciller, inker, colourist, letterer?
If a single name is given, can it be corroborated, and who else held a claim?
Is "created by" being used where "written by" is meant, or the reverse?
Was any credit added later, and if so, when and by whom? A restored credit is a different claim from one held from the start.
Is any of this contested, and if so are both positions sourced?
For a pseudonym: is it personal, publisher-owned, a rotating house name, or a character persona?

entries.name: The Continuity Debt Pass
entries.description: Run at the end of every arc, and before pitching the next one. Continuity is an asset and a liability on the same balance sheet, and this pass tells you which side you are on.
items: What has this arc accrued that a later story can spend?
What has it obligated a successor to service or explain?
Is any new element load-bearing for a future story that has not been written?
Could a reader arriving at this issue follow it? Where exactly do they stop?
Does the recap select the one fact the issue turns on, or list four?
Which period and which publisher does each rule you have stated actually apply to?

entries.name: The Reset Cost Pass
entries.description: Run whenever a story reverses something — a death, a reveal, a status change. The reset is the genre's most-used device and its least-examined one.
items: What exactly is being reversed, and who in the story remembers that it happened?
What did the original event cost, and does any of that cost survive the reversal?
Is there a consequence that cannot be reset — a legal record, a reputation, a decision — that could carry the weight instead?
Have you promised finality to this reader before? How many times?
Is the reset the story's subject or its mechanism? Only the first is defensible more than once.

entries.name: The Legacy and Sidekick Handover Pass
entries.description: Run before writing any succession, and before introducing any sidekick, because a sidekick is a succession claim whether or not you intend one.
items: Can this office be permanently occupied, or is the vacancy already scheduled to end?
If a reversion is planned, is the succession being written as an interregnum or sold as a promise?
What does the successor do that the original could not? If nothing, why is this a succession?
What does the mentor get from the arrangement, and has any character objected to it?
Who is the audience for the successor, and does the reversion serve them?
Does the successor know the secret, and what does that knowledge cost them?

entries.name: The Rogues-Gallery Audit
entries.description: Run when a gallery starts to feel repetitive, and before adding a new member. Repetition here is almost always a coverage problem rather than a quality one.
items: Chart each member against the attribute of the protagonist they test. Which attributes are uncovered?
Is any member only a stronger physical match? That is an escalation ladder, not a gallery.
For each recurring antagonist: does the next appearance change the question, or only the power level?
Why did this specific escape or return happen, and does anyone in the story find it outrageous?
Does the reader want this antagonist to succeed? If so, has the protagonist been given the better argument?
What does this gallery, taken together, say about the city that produced it?

entries.name: The Whose-Continuity-Is-This Pass
entries.description: Run before asserting any fact about a long-running character, in a card, a pitch or a script. Ninety years of contradictory publication means almost every statement needs a scope.
items: Which version of this character is the claim about — which run, which continuity, which medium?
Has this been retconned, rebooted or reset since? In which direction?
Is the fact you are citing from the source line, from an adaptation, or from a reference work that merged them?
If the adaptation and the source disagree, does your reader know which one you mean?
Are you describing a character or an office? The answer changes who the statement is about.

entries.name: The Which-Mode-Is-This Pass
entries.description: Run per scene when a story feels tonally unstable. Most instability in this genre is an unmarked mode change rather than a tonal failure.
items: Is the mandate assumed, conferred and in question, or absent altogether?
If the furniture is present but no warrant is at issue anywhere, the work is in mode three — is that deliberate?
Does the story gesture at the mandate question in one scene and drop it? That reads as an argument abandoned rather than as a mode.
If the mode changes across the work, is the change marked for the reader?
Are you judging a mode-three work by mode-one standards, or asking a mode-three work to carry an argument?

entries.name: The Adaptation Fidelity Pass
entries.description: Run before adapting into or out of this genre, and before writing a source-line story that assumes screen knowledge. Fidelity here is about which layer travels, not about how much is kept.
items: Which of the three layers is this adaptation carrying — iconography, mandate, or continuity?
Is the story's weight in the layer that survives, or in the one that will be cut?
Are you rebuilding accrual, referencing it, or discarding it? If referencing, how many references are load-bearing?
What is the costume made of, who made it, and does that answer say what you want about the character?
Which version does the audience already have, and are you working with it or against it?
If recasting: is this being planned as a succession, or announced as continuity?

entries.name: The Own-Language Sources Pass
entries.description: Run on every non-Anglophone work, creator or award before a claim about it ships. Applies to the Japanese, Korean, Franco-Belgian, Hindi, Spanish and Portuguese material this pack cards as its own.
items: Is the original title given, in its own script where one exists, alongside the release title?
Is the year the original's, not the translation's or the export release's?
Has the claim been checked in an own-language source, or only in English secondary material?
For an award: was the awarding body's own record reachable? If not, say so and state no award rather than an unsourced one.
Is the relationship to the American form borrowing, parallel invention, or documented exchange — and what is the evidence?
If it is parallel invention, does the card say the lineage clause does not apply?

entries.name: The Inherited-Claim Pass
entries.description: Run last, on the sentences you did not think you were asserting. This genre's received wisdom arrives as background rather than as a claim, which is exactly why it passes unchallenged.
items: List every factual claim in the piece that you did not verify because it seemed obvious.
For each: where did you learn it, and is that source the awarding body, the publisher, or a summary of a summary?
Does any Hall of Fame or award claim name the body it belongs to?
Is any periodisation doing analytic work that it cannot bear — a metal age used as a date?
Is any hedge in the text a claim about your own process, and did you actually run that process?
Is any statement about a creator's record a negative you have bounded, or a negative you have assumed?

entries.name: The Accident That Confers
entries.description: Capability arrives by chance, which is the genre's default and its least interesting half.

examples.text: Four people acquire capability in one accident and the book never asks whether it obliged them, which is why it works as a family drama and not as a mission.
The accident that blinds and the accident that enhances are the same event, so the cost and the gift cannot be separated even rhetorically.
Deliberately withholds any conferring logic — three boys find a hole in the ground — which exposes how much narrative weight the accident normally carries and how little it deserves.
A ring selects a bearer for unstated reasons and the film treats selection as characterisation, so the protagonist's central quality is having been chosen by a prop.

entries.name: The Dead Guardian
entries.description: The genre's most reproduced motive, and the one most often mistaken for the whole origin.

examples.text: The death is caused by the protagonist's inaction rather than by an enemy, which converts a bereavement into a debt and is why this origin survives sixty years of retelling where its imitators do not.
Refuses the murder as a scene almost entirely and builds the book out of its consequences, demonstrating that the death is a premise rather than a dramatic asset.
Retells a death the audience has already seen and adds a parental mystery it does not resolve, so the motive is diluted by a second motive that goes nowhere.

entries.name: The Inherited Mission
entries.description: The obligation arrives from a predecessor rather than from an event.

examples.text: Builds an entire generational argument out of inherited mandates that nobody living chose, and lets the inheritors resent the inheritance.
The mandate is an office with a succession ritual, which makes the mission institutional and the film's central question constitutional rather than personal.
Stacks a second inherited mission on the protagonist's own and gives neither room, so both read as backstory rather than as obligation.

entries.name: The Origin Retold
entries.description: The most-reprinted scene in the genre, and the one that changes most between tellings.

examples.text: Dr Manhattan's origin is told out of sequence from inside a consciousness that no longer experiences sequence, so the telling is the characterisation rather than a preamble to it.
Keeps returning to the same few seconds, which converts an origin from a fact established once into a pressure that recurs.
Competent, complete and sequential, which is exactly the problem: an origin delivered straight through leaves the second act nothing to discover.
Retells a story every reader knows and justifies itself by changing what the origin is about rather than what happens in it.

entries.name: The Origin Withheld
entries.description: Refusing the explanation, and what it buys.

examples.text: Decades of deliberate withholding made the absent origin the character's most valuable asset, and the eventual explanation is widely held to have spent it.
The antagonist supplies three incompatible origins and the film endorses none, which makes the absence itself menacing rather than mysterious.
Withholds without a design, so the audience reads absence as omission rather than as choice — the failure mode this trope has when nobody decides what the gap is for.

entries.name: The Chosen Instrument
entries.description: Selection rather than accident — and the delta against Fantasy, which owns chosenness outright.

examples.text: Selection is a contract with terms and a counterparty who benefits, which makes the warrant concrete in a way an accident never is.
Stages selection as an explicit audition with a stated criterion, so the story can ask whether the criterion was right.
Layers a selection mythology onto a character whose interest was always the will to use the ring, which subordinates a choice to a destiny.

entries.name: The Self-Made Hero
entries.description: No accident and no selection — training, money, or engineering.

examples.text: Capability is built on camera by a person who could stop at any point, which relocates the warrant from what happened to him to what he decided to do about it.
The founding case, and the reason the powers clause of every definition of this genre has to be loosened until it nearly breaks.
Interrogates the self-made hero by removing competence, which is a genuine argument and one the book abandons once the violence becomes enjoyable.

entries.name: The Origin That Is a Crime Scene
entries.description: Somebody did this on purpose, and the origin comes with a defendant.

examples.text: The transformation has an identifiable cause inside a specific community and civic geography, so the origin is also an account of a place.
Treats the origin as an assault with a perpetrator still at large, which converts the standard flashback into an unresolved criminal matter.
Multiple origins delivered as a dossier montage, which makes each a case file rather than a story and demonstrates how little an origin survives compression.

entries.category: The Mask and the Two Lives
entries.name: The Civilian Job That Pays for the Cape
entries.description: Somebody has to fund this, and the answer characterises the hero more than the powers do.

examples.text: The law practice is where the concealment is billed and is the source of most of the plot's obstacles, which is what a day job is structurally for.
Repeatedly narrates from ordinary working life inside a superhero world and derives its whole method from the shift in vantage.
Retains the newspaper job as furniture without letting it generate a single obstacle, so the second life is a costume change rather than a life.

entries.category: The Mask and the Two Lives
entries.name: The Person Who Nearly Knows
entries.description: Suspicion held just short of certainty, and the tension it generates for free.

examples.text: Built a decade of series tension almost entirely on characters approaching a conclusion the format could not let them reach.
The founding instance, and the one that established near-knowledge as a renewable resource rather than a plot to be resolved.

examples.work: Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice
examples.text: Resolves the near-knowledge instantly and off-handedly, discarding a structure the genre normally spends years on.

entries.category: The Mask and the Two Lives
entries.name: The Confidant
entries.description: The person who knows, and what knowing costs them.

examples.text: The confidant as an accessory in the legal sense, complicit in an unauthorised activity and rarely permitted to say so.
Gives the confidant a professional relationship to the concealment, which makes the secret an arrangement with terms rather than an intimacy.
Introduces a child confidant for one act and discards the relationship entirely, which is the trope used as a device rather than as a character.

entries.category: The Mask and the Two Lives
entries.name: The Unmasking
entries.description: The scene the genre stages as emotion and which is structurally a legal event.

examples.text: Treats public identification as the central concession in a constitutional argument, which is the only major treatment that gets the register right — the consequence is jurisdictional, not romantic.
Ends on a voluntary disclosure that converts a concealment structure into an accountability one, and the sequels inherit the change rather than reversing it.
Stages disclosure and then removes it by supernatural means, which tells the reader that identity was never a standing condition.

entries.category: The Mask and the Two Lives
entries.name: The Public Hero
entries.description: No secret at all, and the different machinery that has to replace it.

examples.text: Unmasked celebrities from the first issue, with a press office and a public, which makes the book a family drama with an audience problem.
Heroes are corporate-sponsored broadcast personalities ranked by points, which takes the public hero to its logical end and makes the sponsorship the plot.
Public heroism as pure product, argued so hard that the trope stops being a structure and becomes the thesis.

entries.category: The Mask and the Two Lives
entries.name: The Costume as Permission
entries.description: The mask does not conceal so much as license — a different voice, a different set of things sayable.

examples.text: Rorschach's account of which of his two faces is the real one is the genre's most-quoted statement of this trope and its most disturbing.
Takes the mechanism literally and outside this genre, which is why it isolates the trope so clearly.
Permission granted so completely that nothing is at stake in granting it, which is the trope with its constraint removed.

entries.category: The Mask and the Two Lives
entries.name: The Name Given by the Press
entries.description: Somebody else names the hero, and the name sticks whatever they think of it.

examples.text: An institution hostile to the hero controls the vocabulary the public uses about him, which is a structural relationship rather than a running joke.
Names arrive from a public that also sues, and the film keeps both facts in the same institution.
The naming is delivered as a line of dialogue with no institution behind it, so the name has no source and no cost.

entries.category: The Mask and the Two Lives
entries.name: The Life That Is the Disguise
entries.description: Which of the two lives is the performance — a structural decision that determines where the weight sits.

examples.text: Answers the question in the opposite direction to the reader's expectation and then builds twelve issues on the answer, which is why it is the definitive statement of the trope.
The transformation is a ritual performed in view, so the question of which self is real is asked visually every episode rather than argued.
Alternates between the two lives on a fixed schedule without ever deciding which one the character would keep, so the stakes migrate between them.

entries.name: The Archenemy
entries.description: The one antagonist who is about the protagonist rather than about a crime.

examples.text: Stages the archenemy relationship as a shared argument about whether one bad day is sufficient, which is the form at its most explicit.
Two positions on the same problem, held by people who like each other, which is why the relationship has outlasted every plot built on it.
Three antagonists, none of whom has any relationship to the protagonist's actual question, which is what a gallery looks like with the archenemy function removed.

entries.name: The Villain Who Was Right
entries.description: A sympathetic logic that compounds across a serial rather than resolving.

examples.text: The antagonist's diagnosis is endorsed by the film and only his method rejected, which is the strongest form of the trope and the hardest to sustain.
A whole line of heroes adopts the villain's position and the book follows the consequences to their end rather than reversing them.
States a sympathetic logic in one speech and never lets it constrain the plot, so the sympathy is asserted rather than felt.

entries.name: The Origin Shared With the Hero
entries.description: Same accident, opposite conclusion — the genre's neatest structural device and its most overused.

examples.text: Builds the entire film on the shared-origin structure and withholds the reveal until it reframes everything preceding it.
The shared origin is familial rather than accidental, which makes the opposite conclusion a betrayal instead of a coincidence.
The mentor-turned-antagonist in a copy of the protagonist's own suit is the laziest available version of the shared origin, and it arrives with no conclusion of its own to oppose the hero's.

entries.name: The Reformed Rogue
entries.description: The gallery member who joins, and the reversion that usually follows.

examples.text: A recruitment that held for decades because the book kept the history live rather than absolving it.
Established the pattern early enough that the genre treats the transition as ordinary rather than remarkable.
Coerced reform rather than chosen, which is a different and interesting structure that the concept's later uses flatten back into a team book.

entries.name: The Team-Up Against a Third Thing
entries.description: Temporary alliance, and what it reveals that a fight cannot.

examples.text: The alliance is forced by scale and the friction between allies supplies most of the characterisation the film has room for.

examples.work: Batman and the Joker in No Man's Land
examples.text: The alliance is bounded and the terms of the truce are the drama, which is the version that works.

examples.work: Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice
examples.text: Reaches the alliance by way of a misunderstanding fight, which supplies a reason for the team-up and undermines both participants on the way.

entries.name: The Villain Who Knows the Secret
entries.description: An antagonist holding the identity, and choosing not to use it.

examples.work: Norman Osborn in The Amazing Spider-Man
examples.text: The knowledge converts an antagonist into a permanent domestic threat and is the reason this rivalry reaches the protagonist's family at all.
The post-1986 version's decision to disbelieve what he has deduced is a characterisation through refusal, which is more interesting than the knowledge itself.
The antagonist learns the identity and the film does almost nothing with it before the climax removes the problem.

entries.name: The Successor Villain
entries.description: The gallery has legacies too, and they behave differently from the hero's.

examples.text: The recurring criminal office passed between holders makes the antagonist a position in the city rather than a person, which is what allows the gallery to outlive its members.
A successor villain who is also a failed legacy hero, which runs both succession structures through one character.
A successor built from the previous film's antagonist with no relationship to him, which is inheritance as branding.

entries.name: The Threat With No Face
entries.description: The impersonal antagonist, and why the genre keeps reaching for it despite knowing better.

examples.text: Makes the impersonal threat a principle with a face and a theology, which is the only reliable way to make one work.
A world-engine and a beam, with the antagonist's argument abandoned in the second act in favour of terrain destruction.
An antagonist reduced to an energy phenomenon in the final act, which removes the only thing the climax could have been about.

entries.name: The Roster That Cannot Agree
entries.description: The team book's engine is disagreement between people who are each individually right.

examples.text: The mid-film argument on the helicarrier is the film's actual subject and the invasion is its occasion, which is the correct ratio for a team book.
A team that agrees on method and disagrees on how far to take it, which produces friction that escalates rather than resets.
Assembles a roster with no articulated disagreement, so the friction has to be supplied by tone rather than by position.

entries.name: The Team-Up as Commercial Form
entries.description: Two properties in one book, and the structure that grew out of a sales device.

examples.text: An entire title built on the device, which forced the form to develop a reliable one-issue structure for two protagonists with incompatible tones.
The longest-running instance, and the one that demonstrates the format's real value: a guest supplies an outside perspective on a host the reader knows too well.
The team-up arrives only after a manufactured conflict, so the meeting the audience came for occupies the last twenty minutes.

entries.name: The Misunderstanding Fight
entries.description: Two heroes fight because neither will spend thirty seconds talking, and the genre keeps doing it.

examples.text: The device is used to introduce a new roster to an established one and to establish relative power in a single sequence, which is its honest function.
The Hulkbuster sequence is a misunderstanding fight with the misunderstanding removed, which leaves the spectacle and makes the cost purely municipal.

examples.work: Superman IV: The Quest for Peace
examples.text: A confrontation with no coherent disagreement at all, which shows what remains when the device is used without a position on either side.

entries.name: The Member Who Is Too Strong
entries.description: The roster problem that generates most of a team book's plotting difficulty.

examples.text: Solved the problem structurally rather than by coincidence, splitting an enormous roster into task-sized teams so that absence is a premise instead of an excuse — the most reusable answer the genre has produced.
Chose a roster whose powers are liabilities, which removes the problem at source and is the other durable solution.
Repeatedly separates its strongest member by circumstance, and the repetition teaches the reader that the roster rather than the plot is the difficulty.

entries.name: The Founding Charter
entries.description: The document, the vote, the membership rules — bureaucracy as characterisation.

examples.text: A team with a charter, a roster protocol and a reserve list, which supplies obstacles that no power set can solve.
The charter is a cover story and the book's central reveal is what the membership rules were actually for.
Institutional machinery presented as set dressing, so the school never generates a rule anyone has to obey.

entries.name: The Benched Member
entries.description: Removal from the roster as a disciplinary event, which most books stage as a sulk.

examples.text: Benching is used as a genuine consequence with a duration, so the return has to be earned rather than waited out.
Formal expulsion and reinstatement procedures, which make membership a status that can be lost and therefore worth something.
Departures and returns happen on emotional logic with no procedure behind them, so leaving the team costs nothing structural.

entries.name: The Traitor on the Team
entries.description: The betrayal that has to be survivable, because the roster is a standing asset.

examples.text: The betrayal is planned across years and its aftermath is played out over more, which is the only way the device pays for what it costs.
Betrayal inside a family, where expulsion is not available and the team therefore has to absorb it.
Betrayal applied at line scale, which diffuses it: when anyone might be a traitor, no particular betrayal lands.

entries.name: The Reserve Roster
entries.description: The bench, the alumni and the character who is technically still a member.

examples.text: The first team book, and the one that established a membership larger than any single story could use.
The reserve roster arriving at once is the payoff of a decade of accrual and works for exactly that reason and no other.
An assembled roster with no relationship to any existing team structure, which makes the assembly arbitrary.

entries.name: The Team as a Family That Cannot Leave
entries.description: Obligation rather than affinity, and the difference it makes.

examples.text: Membership follows from a shared condition rather than from a choice, which makes leaving a repudiation of the self rather than a resignation.
Adult siblings who cannot resign from a family assembled for a purpose none of them chose.

examples.work: Fantastic Four: Rise of the Silver Surfer
examples.text: Family framing asserted in dialogue with no obligation behind it, so the relationships are stated rather than binding.

entries.name: The Power-Up
entries.description: The permanent escalation, and the debt it creates for every subsequent writer.

examples.text: Escalation is licensed by an explicit training and inheritance structure, so each increase has a stated source and a cost.
The field's most-cited escalation ladder, and the standing demonstration that a depleting resource which refills between arcs is not a cost.
A power increase introduced to solve a story problem and quietly abandoned, which is the pattern that produces continuity debt.

entries.name: The Depowering
entries.description: Removing the capability, and the half-life of the change.

examples.text: The temporary loss used as a character test rather than as a plot obstacle, which is the version that survives being reversed.
Decline rather than removal, which cannot be reversed by the story's own logic and therefore actually costs something.
Depowering applied at population scale for line-wide effect, and substantially reversed within a decade, which is the reset teaching the reader not to invest.

entries.name: The Power Used Wrongly
entries.description: Competence turned to the wrong end, by the person the reader trusts.

examples.text: Builds the whole premise on capability without accountability and follows the consequences past the point of comfort.
The antagonist's power is coercion itself, which makes every scene a question about consent rather than about force.

examples.work: Man of Steel: the Smallville sequence
examples.text: Destruction staged as spectacle with the wrongness never registered by anyone in the film, so the misuse is the audience's observation rather than the story's.

entries.name: The Countermeasure Built for a Friend
entries.description: The contingency plan, and what its existence says about the person who made it.

examples.text: The contingency file as a betrayal that is also entirely in character, which is why it has never stopped being referenced.
Preparation shown as ordinary practice rather than as a reveal, which normalises it and makes the trust question quieter and harder.
Escalates the contingency to absurdity, at which point the trope stops being about trust and becomes a competence display.

entries.name: The First Full Demonstration
entries.description: The scene where the reader learns the ceiling, and it can only be played once.

examples.text: Spends the demonstration in the first chapter and builds the entire series on having no ceiling left to reveal, which converts the genre's most reliable escalation device into a subject.
The rescue sequence establishes capability, tone and public relationship in one scene, and every subsequent screen version is measured against it.
Delays the demonstration until the final act, so the audience reaches the climax without knowing what any of the four can do.

entries.name: The Power That Is a Disability
entries.description: Capability that costs the body carrying it — and the compensatory model the genre reaches for instead.

examples.text: Powers as conditions that are managed rather than deployed, which is the genre's most sustained treatment of the idea.
A power that makes contact impossible, so the cost is social and permanent rather than physical and temporary.
The compensatory sensorium so thoroughly offsets the condition that the condition stops being one, which is the model this pack's disability card names.

entries.name: The Restraint Broken
entries.description: The rule the character will not break, broken — and what the story owes afterwards.

examples.text: Inherits a broken restraint from its source and treats the consequence as the show's premise rather than as backstory.
Follows an unrestrained capability to its end and stays to describe the aftermath, which almost no work in the genre does.
Builds an entire premise on a broken restraint and then supplies the breaking as backstory, so the transgression is asserted rather than witnessed.

entries.name: The Fight the Reader Can Score
entries.description: The transitive ranking the genre pretends not to have, and which every reader keeps anyway.

examples.text: An interactive form has to state capability precisely, which makes the ranking explicit and playable rather than arguable.
Built entirely on a legible power hierarchy, which is why it works as spectacle and why it dates the moment the hierarchy is revised.
Relative capability shifts between scenes with no stated reason, so the reader cannot score the fight and stops trying.

entries.category: The City as the Hero's Jurisdiction
entries.name: The City That Is a Character
entries.description: A specific, fixed geography the reader learns — and can therefore lose.

examples.text: Renders the city from the police procedural's vantage, which establishes it as a functioning municipality with institutions rather than as a backdrop with gargoyles, and makes every costumed intervention an interruption of somebody's work.
The city is the protagonist and the heroes are its weather, which is the premise inverted and the most complete version of this trope.
A city with no geography, no institutions and no residents, present only to be threatened.

entries.category: The City as the Hero's Jurisdiction
entries.name: The Secret Headquarters
entries.description: The most reproduced image in the genre and among its least narratively necessary.

examples.text: The cave functions as a fixed geography the audience learns, so scenes located there carry information rather than atmosphere.
A headquarters that is also a school and a legal residence, which gives it obligations and therefore plots.
A satellite base whose only narrative function is to be somewhere the team can be assembled, and which is destroyed and rebuilt without consequence.

entries.category: The City as the Hero's Jurisdiction
entries.name: The Patrol
entries.description: The routine night, and what the genre does with the absence of a crisis.

examples.text: Opens on routine patrol rather than on a crisis, which establishes geography, exhaustion and the limits of one person covering a city before any plot arrives.
The procedural rhythm of ordinary shifts, which makes the exceptional case land because the ordinary one has been shown.
Patrol reduced to a montage between plot events, so the routine is asserted rather than experienced.

entries.category: The City as the Hero's Jurisdiction
entries.name: The Police Who Tolerate
entries.description: An institution that neither deputises nor arrests, and the arrangement nobody will put in writing.

examples.text: The signal on the roof read as an institutional embarrassment rather than as an alliance, which is the honest version of the arrangement.
Inverts the trope by making the police the powered characters, which exposes how much of the standard arrangement is about jurisdiction rather than capability.
The police alternately hunt and rely on the protagonist as each act requires, with no stated position holding between them.

entries.category: The City as the Hero's Jurisdiction
entries.name: The Neighbourhood That Pays
entries.description: Collateral with an address, and the residents who do not move away.

examples.text: Narrates the entire superhero era from street level, so the cost is always somebody's and never a skyline's.
Gentrification and reconstruction treated as the actual consequence of repeated destruction, which is the rare case of a story following the money.
Destruction at global scale with no named resident anywhere inside it, which removes the only thing that would have made the scale legible.

entries.category: The City as the Hero's Jurisdiction
entries.name: The Territory Dispute
entries.description: Two interveners, one city, and no authority to allocate between them.

examples.text: Jurisdictional friction between powered operators and the police handled as a standing procedural problem rather than as a one-off dispute, which is the version that treats it seriously.
Two unauthorised interveners with incompatible methods in one district, where the disagreement is about method rather than territory and is therefore unresolvable.
Jurisdiction handled entirely by a mentor telling the protagonist to stay small, which converts a structural question into a note from a supervisor.

entries.category: The City as the Hero's Jurisdiction
entries.name: The Villain's District
entries.description: Territory the antagonist holds, and the fact that holding it is administration.

examples.text: A city organised entirely by who controls which blocks, which makes territory the plot rather than the setting.
An antagonist whose power is property development, so his territory is acquired legally and cannot be punched.
A district seized by supernatural means in an afternoon, which removes the only interesting thing about controlling territory.

entries.category: The City as the Hero's Jurisdiction
entries.name: The City Rebuilt Between Issues
entries.description: The reconstruction nobody depicts, and the credibility it quietly spends.

examples.text: Spends a year on the reconstruction the genre normally elides, and demonstrates how much plot is available in it.
Keeps damage visible across episodes so that the accumulation is legible, which is the cheap version of the same discipline.
A power grid destroyed and a city restored between sequences with no acknowledgement, which teaches the audience that nothing depicted has weight.

entries.name: The Death That Sold Out
entries.description: The death as an event product, priced and scheduled before it is written.

examples.text: The genre's commercial high-water mark and the clearest case of a death designed as a sales event, with the reversal planned before publication.
Uses an event death to open a genuine succession argument, which is what the form can do when the reversal is not the point.
Builds a line-wide event out of the genre's accumulated deaths, and in doing so demonstrates how many there were to build from.

entries.name: The Funeral Issue
entries.description: The genre's one reliable format for grief, and its strange relationship to a reader who knows better.

examples.work: Batman: A Death in the Family
examples.text: The aftermath is played for years rather than for an issue, which is why this death did work that survived its eventual reversal.
Stages a funeral that also functions as a decade's reunion, so the grief and the accrual are spent in the same scene.
A funeral the audience already knew was provisional, which is the format running with its central tension removed.

entries.name: The Empty Costume
entries.description: The uniform in a case, and what an image can carry that a body cannot.

examples.text: A preserved costume is treated as an inheritance with legal and racial history attached, which is the trope used as evidence rather than as memorial.
The memorial case is the run's standing reproach and the reason its central return lands as an accusation.
Reproduces the memorial image with none of the history that gives it meaning, so it reads as set decoration.

entries.name: The Return Nobody Asked For
entries.description: The resurrection that costs the original death retrospectively.

examples.text: Kills at line scale to solve a continuity problem, and the subsequent restorations demonstrate how little a death holds when the reason for it was administrative.
Reverses a population-scale change and teaches a readership that line-wide events are provisional.
Returns a character to a status quo nobody had asked to have restored, which is the trope operating on a franchise rather than on a character.

entries.name: The Death That Held
entries.description: The rare permanent one, and what makes it stick.

examples.text: The death that held because it was a failure rather than a sacrifice — the protagonist's own intervention causes it — and the genre has spent fifty years unable to reverse it without destroying the character it made.
Placed outside continuity precisely so it could be permanent, which is the screen's version of the imaginary story.
A death staged as final at line scale and reversed within three years, which is the pattern the permanent ones are measured against.

entries.name: The Successor Takes the Name
entries.description: The mantle changing hands, and the reader who has to be won over twice.

examples.text: A succession held long enough to build its own readership, which is the only thing that makes a mantle transfer more than an interlude.
Makes the succession the film's subject and resolves it by refusing to treat the original as the standard.
Sets up a succession the franchise then defers for years, so the handover is announced rather than performed.

entries.name: The Original Comes Back
entries.description: The reversion, and the audience it disappoints.

examples.text: Stages the reversion as a contest rather than an inevitability, which at least makes the restoration a decision.
Runs the legacy structure on screen and hits the same reversion pressure the comics do, on a compressed schedule.
Four successors introduced and displaced inside a year, which teaches a reader that succession is a storyline rather than a structure.

entries.name: What a Death Can Still Cost
entries.description: In a form where death reverses, the decision is the only irreversible thing — and it belongs to the killer.

examples.text: Follows an unrestrained capability past the killing and stays to describe what it did to everyone left, which is the genre's most complete answer to the question this card asks.
Builds a whole continuity out of one irreversible decision, which is the structural point made at franchise scale.
A protagonist with a stated rule kills repeatedly without the film ever registering that he has, so the one irreversible act passes as staging.

entries.name: The Chest Symbol
entries.description: A single glyph that has to work at any size, in any medium, for ninety years.

examples.text: The symbol is treated as a heraldic device with a stated meaning, which is why the redesigns argue about the meaning rather than the shape.
A symbol chosen by the character as a deliberate act of homage, which makes the design a plot point rather than a given.
Puts a derived emblem on a new character's chest and never says what the borrowing is claiming, so the symbol arrives as a licence rather than as an argument.

entries.name: The Costume Redesign
entries.description: Every redesign is an argument about who the character is for.

examples.text: A redesign that states a standpoint and a period simultaneously, and which the art makes legible before any dialogue does.
Adapts a costume built from improvised materials and keeps the improvisation, which preserves the design's argument.
A redesign accompanying a reversal that remains disputed, where the costume change carried an argument the book did not make explicit.

entries.name: The Cape
entries.description: The genre's most recognisable object, and the one with the fewest practical defences.

examples.text: Gives the cape a stated engineering function and a supply chain, which is one honest way to keep the object once its impracticality has been admitted.
Paints the cape as vestment and treats the genre's iconography as explicitly religious, which is what the object is doing when it is doing anything.
A cape given elaborate physical rendering and no reason to be there beyond the design's inheritance.

entries.name: The Mask With No Eyes
entries.description: A convention that removes the actor's most expressive feature and survives anyway.

examples.text: Solves the blank-mask problem by animating the lenses, which is a lettering-and-design solution to an acting problem.
Faces the same constraint in a form where the player must read intent, and reaches the same solution independently.
Abandons the convention entirely for its costume design, which is a legitimate choice and one that removes a large part of the source's visual identity.

entries.name: The Colour Scheme as Allegiance
