entries.description: Palette as team membership, national claim or moral position, read before a word of dialogue.

examples.text: A costume that is a flag, worn by a character the film treats as a propaganda object before it treats him as a soldier.
Changes one palette and one origin and derives an entire alternate history from it, which is the trope stated as a premise.
Assigns the team its comics palette in a closing scene as a costume reveal, with no claim about what the colours align anyone to.

entries.name: The Costume Damaged
entries.description: The torn cowl and the exposed face — damage as the cheapest available signal of cost.

examples.text: Accumulated damage across the book functions as a wound ledger the reader can total up.
Damage that persists between scenes rather than resetting, which is the discipline the device requires to mean anything.
Runs its protagonist through structural collapse and a trench descent with the suit returning unmarked to every subsequent scene, which quietly tells the audience none of it weighed anything.

entries.name: The Merchandised Silhouette
entries.description: A design that has to work as a toy, which is a constraint before it is a compromise.

examples.text: A television form whose designs, vehicles and combinations are specified as a toy line first, which makes the constraint the production's stated starting point rather than a compromise arrived at later.
A silhouette so reduced it survives any reproduction, which is why it is the genre's most licensed image.
Costume decisions visibly driven by the toy line, with the design's own logic subordinated to it.

entries.name: The Costume Nobody Would Wear
entries.description: The design that cannot survive contact with a body, and what adaptation does about it.

examples.text: Builds the costume as period hardware with visible straps, buckles and a helmet that has to be put on, so the audience can see what wearing it would actually involve.
Comments on its own design inside the film, which is one way of paying for a costume the audience finds implausible.
Replaces a costume with a rendered energy field, which solves the plausibility problem by removing the object entirely.

entries.category: Love, Family and the Cost to Bystanders
entries.name: The Partner Who Waits
entries.description: The relationship structured around one person's absence, and who is asked to bear it.

examples.text: A relationship between two people who both do this work, which removes the waiting structure and shows how much of the trope was about asymmetry.
Takes the waiting partner's interiority as the entire subject, which the genre has almost never done.
The waiting is dramatised as patience rather than as cost, so it is characterisation of the hero rather than of the partner.

entries.category: Love, Family and the Cost to Bystanders
entries.name: The Family That Is a Target
entries.description: Concealment justified by danger, and the danger the concealment produces.

examples.text: Public identification is argued as a threat to families rather than as a matter of principle, which is the version with real stakes.
Runs the whole structure with the secret already shared inside the family, which relocates the tension from disclosure to consequence.
A family-in-danger structure resolved by a heist, so the danger and the resolution never touch.

entries.category: Love, Family and the Cost to Bystanders
entries.name: The Bystander With a Name
entries.description: One named person in the rubble, which does more than a skyline.

examples.text: Narrates the entire superhero era from a photographer's eye-level, so every act of heroism is also somebody's Tuesday — the definitive treatment, and the one that makes the standard climax unwatchable afterwards.
Builds a running series out of the people who clean up after the set pieces, which puts named civilians at the centre of the genre's own economy rather than in its rubble.
Attempts the eye-level shot in one sequence and then returns to the skyline, so the vantage is gestured at rather than held.

entries.category: Love, Family and the Cost to Bystanders
entries.name: The Civilian Who Chooses This
entries.description: Someone with no capability who decides to be here anyway.

examples.text: Gives half its pages to a police lieutenant with no capability who decides to work the same city anyway, and prices the decision in his marriage and his safety.
Civilians who take on the powered by means that cost them, which is the premise carried to its unpleasant conclusion.
Assembles civilians who have chosen this and then equips them well enough to win, which retires the question the premise opened.

entries.category: Love, Family and the Cost to Bystanders
entries.name: The Child of the Hero
entries.description: The next generation as an obligation nobody consulted them about.

examples.text: Makes the second generation's inheritance an obligation with a public standard attached, and lets the children fail it in ways nobody will permit them to refuse.
Makes the inheritance a parenting problem rather than a destiny, which is the rarer and more useful framing.

examples.work: Fantastic Four: Rise of the Silver Surfer
examples.text: Raises the question of children and the work and drops it inside one scene.

entries.category: Love, Family and the Cost to Bystanders
entries.name: The Relationship Continuity Will Not Allow
entries.description: The marriage or partnership an editorial line decides the character cannot have.

examples.text: The clearest case in the genre of an editorial position dissolving a relationship, and the clearest demonstration that readers experience it as an authorial act.
A marriage permitted, sustained for a decade and then removed by a continuity reset, which is the full arc of the problem.
Defers a relationship whose ending the audience already knows across ten seasons, which is the same pressure applied as delay rather than as dissolution.

entries.category: Love, Family and the Cost to Bystanders
entries.name: The Death That Motivates Someone Else
entries.description: A partner killed to give a protagonist a reason — a convention with a documented name and a compiler.

examples.text: The instance that gave the convention its name: Gail Simone's 1999 list, Women in Refrigerators, catalogued the pattern and took its title from this issue, and the list rather than any single story is what made the device visible.

examples.work: Batman: A Death in the Family
examples.text: The same structure applied to a sidekick rather than a partner, which is the version the genre treats as consequential and grieves properly.
A mother placed in jeopardy to resolve a conflict between two protagonists, which uses the device to end an argument rather than to start a story.

entries.name: The Hero Who Reads Comics
entries.description: Characters inside the genre who know the genre, and the frame it creates.

examples.text: Uses in-world comics scholarship as the mechanism by which a character understands what he is, which is also how the film claims membership of a genre it has none of the furniture for.
A protagonist whose entire model of heroism is drawn from comics, which is the premise and the critique at once.
A protagonist who knows the genre well enough to test his powers by its rules, and whose knowledge never costs him a decision.

entries.name: The In-Universe Fan
entries.description: The public that reads the heroes, which is where mode three lives inside the fiction.

examples.text: Heroism as broadcast entertainment with a ranked audience, so the in-universe fan is the economy the story runs on.
Fandom rendered as a managed marketing relationship, which is mode three depicted from inside the machine.
In-universe celebrity used for one joke about sponsorship without following the arrangement anywhere.

entries.name: The Retcon Acknowledged on the Page
entries.description: A story that admits its own history has been changed, and asks what that does to the people in it.

examples.text: A protagonist who discovers that his continuity is edited and confronts the editor, which is the device taken to its limit.

examples.work: Superman: Whatever Happened to the Man of Tomorrow?
examples.text: An explicit farewell to a continuity about to be replaced, written as a story rather than as an administrative act.
Acknowledges a change without permitting anyone to name what changed, which is the acknowledgement without the honesty.

entries.name: The Anniversary Issue
entries.description: A number on a cover as an occasion, and the accrual it is designed to spend.

examples.text: A final issue of a cancelled title that became the genre's most valuable single number, which is the anniversary logic operating in reverse.
Treats the genre's own history as its subject matter and reads as a commemorative issue for the whole form.
Renumbered back onto its original count so that milestone numbers could keep arriving, which is the occasion detached from the accrual it was supposed to spend.

entries.name: The Imaginary Story
entries.description: The genre's only reliable way to write an ending, and it works by stepping outside.

examples.work: Superman: For the Man Who Has Everything
examples.text: An out-of-continuity premise that turns out to be the most direct available statement about the character in continuity, which is the whole argument for the form in twenty-two pages.
An entire title built on the device, which institutionalised the escape hatch and demonstrated the appetite for endings the main line could not supply.
Changes one variable and follows it honestly, which is the imaginary story used as an argument rather than as a novelty.

entries.name: The Deconstruction Deconstructed
entries.description: The critique becoming a convention, and the reply to the reply.

examples.text: Answers the grim register by reconstructing the discarded material with full knowledge of why it was discarded.
Takes both the critique and the reconstruction as given and writes about the exhaustion of both.
Prosecutes the genre so completely that there is no position left from which to reply, which is where this line of argument ends.

entries.name: The Creator on the Page
entries.description: The writer or artist appearing inside the fiction, and what it costs the fiction.

examples.text: The author's appearance is the run's argument rather than its joke, and it is about authorship over a serial character specifically.
Renders the genre's own creators and their creations as archaeology, which is the device used as criticism.
Fourth-wall address used consistently and lightly, which works as a register and forecloses the story ever being about anything else.

entries.name: The Reader Addressed
entries.description: The narration that knows you are there, which this genre inherited from a house style rather than invented.

examples.text: Editorial address to the reader as an ordinary feature of the page, which is where the convention actually comes from.
Address used to strip the accumulated apparatus and demonstrate how much of the form is convention rather than necessity.
Narration that instructs the reader how to feel about events the pages have not established.

entries.name: The Serial That Cannot End
entries.description: A form whose commercial condition is that it never concludes, and what that does to every craft decision inside it.
entries.principle: A superhero serial is not a long story; it is a story that has been forbidden an ending, and almost every peculiarity of the genre follows from that one constraint. Endings are where meaning is assigned, so a form without them has to manufacture meaning some other way — through recurrence, through accrual, through the promise of an ending repeatedly offered and withdrawn. The writer's real position is not author but tenant: you inherit a property, you are expected to improve it, and you must leave it in a condition the next tenant can use. This is why the genre's most admired works are so often the ones that cheat the constraint — the out-of-continuity story, the alternate future, the licensed ending — and why the reader treats those as the real thing.
entries.example: *Superman: Whatever Happened to the Man of Tomorrow?* is explicitly framed as an imaginary story precisely so it can do the one thing the ongoing title cannot, which is stop.
entries.application: Before you plan an arc, write down what your successor inherits from it. If the answer is nothing, you have written a self-contained story inside a serial and the accrual will not compound. If the answer is a problem only you know how to solve, you have written a debt.

entries.name: Oneiric Time and Its Critics
entries.description: The oldest theoretical account of superhero time, and a live argument about whether it still holds.
entries.principle: Umberto Eco's 1962 essay on Superman describes a hero who consumes no time — each adventure begins from a start position that the previous one did not move, in what Eco calls a hazy oneiric climate the reader never quite notices. The claim has been the field's standing account for sixty years. It is now contested from two directions and the pack carries both. Angela Ndalianis and Henry Jenkins argue that contemporary superhero narrative has moved past Eco's iterative model into genuinely serial, multiple and intertextual construction. **Marc Singer's 2024 intervention argues that Eco has been misread and that the "Eco is obsolete" consensus is a populist reflex rather than a reading** — while conceding that Eco's observations were more historically contingent than Eco claimed. Note what Singer's position is and is not: it is an argument against Eco's critics, not a claim that nothing changed.
entries.example: *Action Comics #1* establishes a protagonist whose situation is restored at the end of every instalment, which is the pattern Eco described and the one the later scholarship argues the form has or has not left behind.
entries.application: Decide which model your book runs on and be consistent, because they demand opposite things. Iterative time wants a restored start position and rewards the single issue. Serial time wants accrual and punishes the reader who missed one. Most failed runs are a writer using serial techniques on a book the publisher is still selling as iterative.

entries.name: The Shared Universe as a Promise the Publisher Cannot Keep
entries.description: What the shared universe actually undertakes to the reader, and why it defaults.
entries.principle: The shared universe promises the reader that everything is happening in the same place at the same time and that this fact will be honoured. It cannot be. Honouring it requires every writer on every title to know and respect every other title's current state, at a scale no editorial apparatus has ever managed, and the failure is structural rather than a lapse of care. What actually happens is that the promise is honoured in the direction that sells — a crossover pulls titles into alignment for the duration of an event and releases them afterwards — and quietly broken the rest of the time. The reader knows this. The reader's tolerance is not for consistency but for **the appearance of good faith**, which is why an acknowledged contradiction costs almost nothing and an unacknowledged one costs a great deal.
entries.example: *Civil War* aligns a whole line around one argument, and the tie-ins that took the argument in incompatible directions demonstrate the default happening inside the very machine built to prevent it.
entries.application: When your book contradicts another, choose deliberately between three moves: acknowledge and explain, acknowledge and decline to explain, or stay silent. All three are legitimate. Only the fourth — contradicting without noticing — reads to the reader as contempt.

entries.name: Sliding Time
entries.description: The convention that keeps a character the same age across decades, and the bill it runs up.
entries.principle: Sliding time holds that a character's published history compresses into a fixed and short interior span — roughly a decade, perpetually — so that a figure who debuted in 1962 has still been active for about ten years. It is the genre's most successful piece of load-bearing dishonesty, and it works because readers want it to. The costs are specific and they accumulate at the edges rather than the centre. Anything anchored to real history — a war, a technology, a President, a fashion — has to be detached and re-floated, and every re-flotation weakens a character whose meaning depended on that anchor. Characters defined by a historical relationship are the ones sliding time slowly destroys.
entries.example: *The Amazing Spider-Man (Lee/Ditko run)* fixes its protagonist as a contemporary teenager in a specific New York, and every subsequent decade has had to decide which parts of that specificity to keep and which to let slide.
entries.application: List everything in your premise that is dated. For each, decide now whether it slides, is re-anchored, or is fixed — and if it is fixed, say so on the page, because a fixed anchor that nobody declares will be slid by the next writer without malice.

entries.name: The Reference That Ages
entries.description: Topicality as a loan against the future, taken out at a rate you cannot see when you sign.
entries.principle: A contemporary reference buys immediacy now and charges for it later, and the charge is not embarrassment but illegibility — the reader of twenty years hence does not find the reference dated, they find the scene incomprehensible and skip it. The rate varies enormously by what is referenced. A political event ages into history and can be footnoted. A technology ages into an obstacle the plot no longer needs solving. A slang register ages worst of all, because it makes the character rather than the world seem false. The genre's relevance moments are the clearest case study, because they are simultaneously the most admired and the least re-readable material in the form.
entries.example: *Green Lantern (O'Neil/Adams run)* is the genre's standing exhibit in both directions — the confrontation over who the hero has never helped still lands, and a good deal of the surrounding topicality now needs an apparatus.
entries.application: For each topical reference, ask what a reader who does not recognise it still gets. If the answer is "the scene still works, they just miss a layer," spend it. If the answer is "the scene stops," you have written a footnote and should convert it into an action.

entries.name: The Reader Who Arrives at Issue 400
entries.description: The genre's permanent accessibility problem, and the fact that it has no general solution.
entries.principle: Every long-running title has two readers with incompatible needs: the one who has been there and wants the accrual spent, and the one who arrived this month and needs the floor under their feet. Serving both perfectly is impossible, and the useful move is to stop trying and start choosing per scene. The craft insight is that new readers do not need history, they need **stakes and relationships**, and those can be conveyed entirely in the present tense. What actually loses the new reader is not the unexplained past but the unexplained **emotional weight** — a character reacting to something with an intensity the page has not earned. History can be omitted; the reaction cannot.
entries.example: *The Amazing Spider-Man (Lee/Ditko run)* solved this by restating the character's situation in nearly every issue, a discipline the industry abandoned and periodically rediscovers.
entries.application: Take any scene and ask what a first-time reader thinks is happening. Where the answer diverges from what a long-time reader thinks is happening, decide which one is the scene's audience. Do not attempt to write for both in the same panel.

entries.name: Continuity as Design, Not Lore
entries.description: The difference between a past that is stored and a past that is composed.
entries.principle: Most continuity is treated as inventory — a set of facts to be kept consistent — and the writers who do the most with it treat it instead as **material to be arranged**. The distinction is between remembering that something happened and placing it where it does work. Thierry Groensteen's account of comics describes **tressage**, or braiding: elements distributed across a work that speak to one another across the distance between them, so that meaning arises from the arrangement rather than from any one appearance. **Applying that to serial continuity is an extension, not Groensteen's own claim** — he theorises the page and the book, not the forty-year property — and the pack states this rather than borrowing his authority for a move he did not make.
entries.example: *Watchmen* is the demonstration case, where a recurring image is placed rather than merely repeated, and the reader assembles a meaning that no single panel states.
entries.application: Take three facts from your book's past. Instead of asking whether they are consistent, ask what they would mean if they were placed next to each other. If nothing, they are inventory. If something, that is your arc.

entries.name: Three Kinds of Continuity
entries.description: A typology that separates three things the word is doing at once.
entries.principle: Richard Reynolds distinguishes **serial** continuity — what happened in previous instalments of this title; **hierarchical** continuity — the fixed relationships and relative power levels that hold across the shared universe; and **structural** continuity — the accumulated body of meaning attached to a character, the thing a reader means when they say an act was out of character. They fail differently and they are repaired differently. A serial break is a factual error and can be fixed with a line of dialogue. A hierarchical break is a credibility problem and needs a scene. A structural break cannot be fixed at all, only lived down, which is why the reader response to it is anger rather than correction. **Research B could not retrieve Reynolds's enumeration verbatim and the flag stands unresolved through pass B2**; the three-way distinction is reported as the pack received it, and a writer relying on the exact wording should go to the source.
entries.example: *Fantastic Four #1* establishes all three at once — a first instalment, a set of relative capabilities, and a family whose behaviour toward one another becomes the thing later writers can violate.
entries.application: When a reader objects that something is wrong, sort the objection before answering it. Most editorial energy is spent fixing serial breaks, which are the cheapest kind, while structural breaks are argued with — which is the wrong response to the only one that does lasting damage.

entries.name: The Balance Sheet
entries.description: Continuity as an asset and a liability recorded in the same ledger.
entries.principle: Every element a story adds is simultaneously something a later story can spend and something a later story must service. A new character is an asset until they are an obligation; a revealed secret is capital until it is a constraint; a promise of consequence is a draw on credit that some successor has to honour or default on publicly. Writers routinely account for only one side. The generative habit is to ask both questions of every addition and to keep the ratio deliberate — a run that accrues without spending becomes unreadable, and a run that spends without accruing leaves the property poorer than it found it. **This is the same ledger `checklist-8` runs, stated as the principle the checklist operationalises.**
entries.example: *Planetary* is built on the asset side almost exclusively, mining a century of accumulated genre material as setting while obligating its successors to almost nothing.
entries.application: At the end of every arc, write two lists: what a later story can now use, and what a later story now has to explain. If the second list is longer, you have written a liability and should say so in the hand-over rather than letting it be discovered.

entries.name: The Reader Is the Storage Medium
entries.description: Where a serial's past is actually kept, and what follows from the fact that it is not kept by the publisher.
entries.principle: No publisher holds a complete, authoritative, accessible record of its own continuity, and the ones that have tried have produced documents that were obsolete on publication. The functional archive is distributed across readers, letter columns, handbooks, and now wikis — which means the past of a superhero property is **collectively remembered rather than institutionally recorded**, with all the properties of collective memory: it is selective, it is confidently wrong in places, and it is impossible to correct centrally. This has a craft consequence that is not obvious. What the audience "knows" about a character is not what was published; it is what has been retold. A writer working from the published record and a reader working from the retold one are working from different books.
entries.example: *Marvels* narrates the genre's own history from the vantage of someone assembling it from the outside, which is structurally what every reader is doing.
entries.application: Before contradicting a "well-known" fact, check whether it was ever actually published. A surprising amount of received continuity is retelling. Correcting it is legitimate; doing so without knowing it is received is how a writer gets a reputation for carelessness they did not earn.

entries.name: Where the Word Came From
entries.description: The retcon as a named practice, and what naming it changed.
entries.principle: Retroactive continuity is the alteration of a story's past by a later story, and it long predates its name — the practice is as old as the shared universe, because the moment two titles must agree about a third thing, somebody has to adjust what was already printed. What the name changed was the audience's relationship to it. An unnamed technique is invisible and reads as story; a named technique is visible and reads as an administrative act performed on a story. Once readers had the word, they could accuse, and a great deal of the genre's subsequent defensiveness about its own past is a response to being able to be accused. The craft point is not to avoid the technique but to recognise that it is now performed in public.
entries.example: The wartime generation carded at *All Star Comics #8* is the material the earliest large-scale retcons worked on, and *Crisis on Infinite Earths* is where the practice stopped being local repair and became a line-wide instrument.
entries.application: Ask whether your change is one the reader is meant to notice. Both answers are workable. What fails is a change large enough to be noticed and framed as though it were not.

entries.name: The Retcon That Adds and the Retcon That Deletes
entries.description: Two operations with the same name and opposite risk profiles.
entries.principle: An additive retcon inserts something into the past that was not there — a prior programme, an unrecorded relationship, an earlier holder of the office. A subtractive retcon removes something that was. They are not variants of one move. Addition is cheap and reversible: the reader who dislikes it can decline to weight it, and a later writer can quietly stop referencing it. Deletion is expensive and permanent: it invalidates stories the reader owns and remembers, and no later writer can restore the reader's original experience of them. The asymmetry is the whole practical lesson. **Frug's typology of retcon forms sorts these further, and its type 1a — the addition that reframes rather than contradicts — is the craft core**, because it is the only form that increases what the past can mean without spending any of it.
entries.example: *Truth: Red, White & Black* adds a prior programme and makes forty years of published stories mean something they did not previously mean; *The Man of Steel* deletes a boyhood career and a surviving population, and the stories that used them cannot be read the same way again.
entries.application: Sort your change before you write it. If it is deletion, name what the reader loses and decide whether the gain exceeds it. If you cannot name the loss, you have not understood the change.

entries.name: Repair, Land-Grab and Apology
entries.description: Three motives behind the same technique, and why the reader can always tell which one it was.
entries.principle: Retcons are performed for three reasons and the reason is legible in the result. **Repair** fixes something broken — a contradiction, an unusable premise, a dead end — and reads as maintenance. **Land-grab** clears ground so that the current writer can build, and reads as a writer preferring their own story to their predecessor's. **Apology** disowns something the property is now embarrassed by, and reads as an institution managing its reputation. Repair is uncontroversial. Land-grab is legitimate but should be paid for, by leaving the property better stocked than you found it. Apology is the difficult one, because it is often morally right and narratively costly at once, and because it invites the reader to ask what else is being quietly filed away.
entries.example: *Batman: Year One* is repair — it makes an origin usable by making it specific; *Truth: Red, White & Black* is the opposite of apology, since it refuses to disown the past and instead makes the past answer for itself; *Crisis on Infinite Earths* is land-grab at industrial scale, clearing a shared universe so it could be rebuilt.
entries.application: Name your motive privately and honestly before you write. Readers cannot see your motive but they can see its shape, and a land-grab presented as repair is the specific dishonesty this genre's audience is best at detecting.

entries.name: Hard, Soft and Partial
entries.description: Three depths of reboot, and the fact that the shallow ones are harder to write.
entries.principle: A **hard** reboot declares the past void and starts again from zero. A **soft** reboot leaves the past nominally intact but writes as though the reader need not know it, which is the most common form and almost never announced. A **partial** reboot resets some elements and preserves others, which sounds like a compromise and is in fact the most demanding of the three: it requires the writer to know exactly which load-bearing walls are being removed, and it leaves the reader without a general rule for what still counts. The hard reboot's advantage is clarity. Its cost is that it converts every reader's accumulated investment into nothing at a stroke, and a proportion of them do not come back.
entries.example: *Crisis on Infinite Earths* is the hard case and the one every later reset is measured against; *New X-Men* is a soft reboot conducted without announcement, keeping the numbering and simply behaving as though the premise were new; *Black Panther (Coates run)* is partial, preserving the character's history while resetting the political ground under him.
entries.application: State which of the three you are doing, in writing, to yourself and to your editor. Most reboot failures are a soft reboot that some participants believed was hard, or the reverse.

entries.name: The Reboot as a Sales Event
entries.description: The commercial function of the reset, which is not a cynical reading but the operating condition.
entries.principle: A reset is the direct market's most reliable instrument, because a first issue sells more than a fortieth and a reset manufactures first issues on demand. This is not a scandal to be exposed; it is the economic environment the writer works inside, and understanding it improves the work rather than souring it. The practical consequence is that the reset's **timing** is very often not yours, its **scale** is decided commercially, and its **reversal** may already be scheduled before you write the first page. The writers who do well under these conditions are the ones who ask what story is only tellable at this particular commercial moment, rather than the ones who write as though the moment were not happening.
entries.example: *The Death of Superman* is the clearest case in the genre of an event designed as a sales instrument with the reversal planned in advance; *X-Men #1 (1991 comic)* is the same logic applied to the object itself rather than to the story, sold on variant covers to a speculative market.
entries.application: Find out, before you plan, what is commercially fixed: the length, the relaunch, the reversal, the crossover you must service. Plan inside those. A plan that assumes they are negotiable is a plan for a book that will be rewritten by someone else.

entries.name: What Survives a Reboot
entries.description: The material that comes back regardless of intent, and what its returning tells you.
entries.principle: Every reboot declares certain things void, and a predictable subset of them returns within a few years — not because writers are sentimental but because the reboot removed something the property actually needed and the gap became visible in use. What survives is almost never what the publisher intended to preserve. It is, reliably, whatever was **doing structural work rather than occupying continuity space**: the relationship that generated conflict, the constraint that made the protagonist interesting, the supporting character who was the only person allowed to say the true thing. What does not come back is the accumulated incident. This is the most useful diagnostic the genre offers about its own characters, because it separates what a character **is** from what has merely happened to them.
entries.example: *The Man of Steel* removed a great deal and the elements that returned soonest were the ones that gave the protagonist someone to be measured against; *Batman: Year One* survived every subsequent reset because it is structure rather than incident.
entries.application: Ask what would have to come back if you deleted it. That list is your character. Everything else is history, and history is negotiable.

entries.name: The Reset as Consequence-Free Stakes
entries.description: The device's central hazard — a form that offers maximum apparent stakes and minimum real ones.
entries.principle: When any outcome can be reversed, stakes become a performance rather than a fact, and readers learn to price them accordingly. The genre's characteristic failure is not that it reverses things but that it keeps asking for a reaction it has trained the audience not to have. The escape is not to stop reversing. It is to locate the stakes in something the reset cannot reach: a decision, a reputation, a relationship altered by what a character was willing to do. **This is the superhero form of the problem `comedy:timing-34` describes in the sitcom reset — and the delta is that comedy's reset is a formal contract the audience accepts, whereas this genre's reset is denied even as it is performed.** Comedy resets and admits it; the superhero serial resets and insists this time is different.
entries.example: *The Death of Superman* promised finality and reversed it within a year; *Final Crisis* staged an ending at line scale and was superseded, which is the pattern that teaches readers what such promises are worth.
entries.application: For any threatened outcome, ask what remains true if it is reversed next year. If the answer is nothing, move the stakes into a choice — because a choice, unlike a death, cannot be undone by an editorial decision.

entries.name: What a Retcon Costs the Reader Who Was There
entries.description: The specific injury, stated precisely, because it is usually described wrongly.
entries.principle: The reader's objection to a retcon is routinely dismissed as nostalgia or entitlement, and it is neither. What a subtractive retcon takes is not a fact but **an experience the reader had and can no longer have had**: the stories they read are still on the shelf, but they no longer lead anywhere, and the anticipation with which they were read has been retrospectively falsified. That is a real loss and it is worth naming accurately, because a writer who understands it can mitigate it and a writer who thinks it is entitlement cannot. Mitigation is mostly acknowledgement — a story that says, inside itself, that something is being given up costs the reader far less than one that behaves as though nothing has happened.
entries.example: *The Man of Steel* falsified a great deal of prior reading in exactly this way, and the material carded at *All Star Comics #8* has been through the same operation more than once as successive continuities decided what the wartime generation had been.
entries.application: Write the sentence a long-time reader would say about your change, in their words, at their most reasonable. If you cannot write it without caricature, you do not yet understand the objection well enough to answer it.

entries.name: The Un-Reboot
entries.description: The reset that restores what a previous reset deleted, and what its existence proves.
entries.principle: The genre has produced a distinct and now-recurring event: the reboot whose content is the undoing of an earlier reboot. It is worth studying because it is an admission — the publisher is conceding, commercially and in public, that the previous reset removed something the property needed. Two things follow. First, no reset is final, which means the writer who plans as though theirs will be is planning badly. Second, and more useful, the un-reboot is the genre's only honest evaluation mechanism: it tells you, years later and with money behind it, which deletions were mistakes. Reading the pattern of what gets restored is a better guide to what a character requires than any amount of assertion about their essence.
entries.example: *Black Panther (Coates run)* was folded back into a restored legacy numbering mid-run, and *New X-Men* was substantially rolled back by successors who preferred the premise it had set aside.
entries.application: If you are restoring, say what the restoration is for, in story terms. An un-reboot justified only by the fact that readers missed something restores the element without restoring what made it work.

entries.name: The Numbering Tells the Truth
entries.description: The issue numbers as a public record of every editorial decision, readable by anyone who looks.
entries.principle: A title's numbering is the one part of a serial that cannot lie, because it is printed and archived and each change was a decision somebody made for a reason. Renumberings mark relaunches; restored numbering marks an un-reboot; a title change under continuous numbering marks a repositioning that the publisher wanted without the cost of a first issue; a run that begins mid-number marks a writer inheriting rather than launching. Reading the numbers before reading the run tells you what the commercial pressures were, which is context no amount of interviews will give you as reliably. **It is also where reference work goes wrong most often**: the span of a collected edition is not the span of a run, and a very large proportion of published claims about "runs" are actually claims about books.
entries.example: *Black Panther (Coates run)* runs #1–18 and then #166–172, which is two commercial decisions visible in the record; *New X-Men* has no first issue at all, being a retitling at #114; and *Luke Cage, Hero for Hire* changed title twice under continuous numbering as its market was repeatedly reassessed.
entries.application: Before writing about any run, get its first and last issue from the indicia rather than from the collection. If the boundary you have matches a trade paperback's contents, you have the book's boundary and not the run's, and you are about to publish somebody else's packaging as a fact.

entries.name: The Filing System for Contradiction
entries.description: What the multiverse was invented to do, before it was a marketing category.
entries.principle: The multiverse is not primarily a source of stories; it is an administrative solution to a bookkeeping problem. When a publisher owns two incompatible versions of the same character — an older one readers remember and a newer one currently selling — the parallel world lets both be true without either being wrong. Everything else the device does is downstream of that. Recognising this is useful because it tells you what the multiverse is **good** at: preserving something that would otherwise have to be deleted. It also tells you what it is bad at, which is generating stakes, since a device whose founding purpose is to make contradiction survivable is structurally poor at making anything feel irreversible.
entries.example: The wartime generation carded at *All Star Comics #8* was preserved rather than discarded by exactly this move, which is the origin case and still the clearest one.
entries.application: Before adding a parallel world, ask what would otherwise have to be deleted. If nothing would, you are not using the machinery, you are decorating with it.

entries.name: The Counterpart Self
entries.description: The same character under a changed premise, and why the comparison does the work.
entries.principle: The counterpart is the multiverse's one genuinely irreplaceable device: a version of a character altered in a single controlled respect, so that the difference between them isolates what the character actually is. It functions as an experiment, and like an experiment it is only informative if exactly one variable moves. The failure mode is the counterpart altered in every respect at once — evil, differently powered, from a different century — which teaches nothing because no comparison is possible. The discipline is severe and almost always skipped: change one thing, hold everything else, and let the reader do the arithmetic.
entries.example: *Squadron Supreme* runs the experiment at team scale, holding the analogue heroes' capabilities fixed and moving only the question of whether they govern.
entries.application: Write down the single altered variable before drafting. If you cannot state it in one clause, you are writing a different character wearing a familiar face, and the reader will feel the absence of the comparison without being able to name it.

entries.name: The Crisis as Compression Algorithm
entries.description: The line-wide event as a device for reducing accumulated state.
entries.principle: A crisis event is what a publisher reaches for when the accumulated continuity has become more expensive to service than it is worth. Its function is compression: many worlds become few, many versions become one, and a great deal of stored state is discarded in a single authorised act. The interesting craft fact is that compression is **lossy in a specific direction** — what survives is what is currently commercially legible, and what is discarded is disproportionately the odd, the regional and the aged, which are also the things that made the property distinctive. A crisis therefore reliably makes a shared universe simpler and slightly more generic at the same time, and the second effect is never in the pitch.
entries.example: *Final Crisis* attempts the operation at maximum scale and at maximum compression simultaneously, which is why it divides readers so sharply on legibility.
entries.application: List what your event discards, not what it keeps. If the list is all the strange material, you are not compressing a universe, you are normalising one — and the next writer will have to reinvent the strangeness at cost.

entries.name: Not an Escape Hatch
entries.description: The device's most common bad use, and the delta against how science fiction files it.
entries.principle: `scifi:trope-20` files the parallel world as an escape hatch — a way out of a corner the writer has written into — and for science fiction that is the honest description, because there the multiverse is usually a premise being explored. **In the superhero serial it is not a hatch, it is infrastructure**, permanently installed and always available, and that changes the failure mode completely. An occasional escape is a weak resolution; a permanently available escape is a solvent that dissolves every stake in the line, because the reader knows a bad outcome can always be relocated to a world that does not count. The delta is therefore not about the device but about its **standing availability**: science fiction's version is a door you open once, and this genre's is a door that is never shut.
entries.example: *Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse* is instructive precisely because it makes the availability itself the subject, so the counterparts cost the protagonist something rather than rescuing him.
entries.application: If a multiversal element resolves your plot, cut it and resolve the plot. Reserve the machinery for stories where the existence of counterparts is the problem rather than the solution.

entries.name: The Multiverse and the First-Time Viewer
entries.description: What the device costs an audience that has not been reading for thirty years.
entries.principle: On the page the multiverse is cheap, because a caption can establish a world in six words and the reader can reread. On screen it is expensive, because the audience cannot reread, cannot check, and has no prior investment in the versions being referenced. The specific cost is not confusion — audiences follow more than they are credited with — it is **unearned poignancy**: a scene built on the audience's affection for a version they have never seen plays as a scene about nothing. The workable screen approach is to establish the counterpart's difference in the present tense and let recognition be a bonus rather than a load-bearing beam.
entries.example: *Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse* builds each counterpart's difference into their first thirty seconds of screen time, so a viewer with no prior knowledge loses a layer and not the scene; *Logan* takes the opposite route and simply declines the machinery altogether.
entries.application: For every multiversal beat, write what a viewer with zero prior exposure understands. If the answer is "that these people know each other," you have written a reunion for an audience that was not at the party.

entries.name: The Fenced Universe
entries.description: The story deliberately walled off from continuity, and why the fence is what makes it good.
entries.principle: The out-of-continuity story — the elseworld, the what-if, the alternate future — is usually described as a freedom, and the more accurate description is a **constraint that supplies an ending**. Being unable to affect the ongoing line is precisely what allows the story to conclude, to kill permanently, to age its cast and to make an argument. The fence does not restrict the story; the fence is the story's only access to consequence. This is why the genre's most-cited standalone works are so often fenced, and why attempts to import their moves back into the ongoing line reliably fail: the move was never separable from the fence.
entries.example: *Kingdom Come* can stage an apocalypse and mean it because nothing in the ongoing line has to survive the ending; *Batman: The Dark Knight* ages its protagonist to the end of his usefulness, which no in-continuity book is permitted to do.
entries.application: If your story requires a permanent outcome, ask for the fence rather than fighting for the outcome. Writers routinely spend years arguing for a change the line will reverse, when the fenced version could have been published intact.

entries.name: The Counterpart Who Is the Villain
entries.description: The evil twin as the genre's laziest device and its sharpest one, depending on a single choice.
entries.principle: The dark counterpart is available in every superhero property and is nearly always wasted, because it is written as an opponent when its only real function is as an **argument**. A counterpart who merely fights the protagonist is a fight with extra costuming. A counterpart who reached a different conclusion from the same premises is an interrogation the protagonist cannot walk away from, because refuting them requires articulating a position rather than winning a contest. The test is simple: can the counterpart state a case the reader finds difficult to answer? If not, the doubling is decorative.
entries.example: *Invincible (comic)* places the argument in the protagonist's own inheritance and makes the case for the other side genuinely strong, which is why the confrontation reorganises the whole book rather than concluding an arc.
entries.application: Write the counterpart's argument as a speech you believe. If you cannot, either give the position to someone you can write sincerely or drop the doubling and write an antagonist with their own reasons.

entries.name: What a Reader Loses When Everything Is Possible
entries.description: The cost of unbounded possibility, which is not confusion but indifference.
entries.principle: A setting in which every configuration exists somewhere is a setting in which no configuration is significant, and readers arrive at this conclusion long before they can articulate it. The symptom is not complaint about complexity; it is a quiet drop in the intensity with which outcomes are received. `scifi:trope-38` treats infinite realities as a scale problem — how a narrative holds together across unlimited scope — and **the superhero delta is that the problem here is not scale but standing**: science fiction's infinite realities are usually the subject of the story, so their infinitude is what is being examined, whereas here they are the background against which ordinary stakes are supposed to register, and a background of unlimited possibility flattens whatever is placed on it.
entries.example: *Final Crisis* is the case where the machinery's full extent and the story's emotional demands are asked to operate at once, and readers divide precisely on whether the second survived the first.
entries.application: Bound the multiverse in your own book even if the line does not. A stated, small number of worlds that matter is worth more than an unbounded set, and the bound costs you nothing you were actually going to use.

entries.name: The Multiverse as a Trademark Container
entries.description: The commercial function that nobody puts in the pitch, and how it shapes what gets written.
entries.principle: Parallel worlds are useful to a rights holder in a way that has nothing to do with story: they allow a name to be kept in continuous use, allow two incompatible claims on a character to coexist, and allow a version acquired from elsewhere to be integrated without disturbing the one already selling. A working writer benefits from knowing this because it explains otherwise inexplicable editorial instructions — why a character must appear somewhere this year, why a version cannot be merged, why a world cannot be closed. These are rarely creative decisions and are almost never explained as what they are.
entries.example: *Marvelman / Miracleman* is the standing case in which a character's name, ownership and publishing continuity came apart from one another, and the fiction had to be arranged around the legal position rather than the other way round.
entries.application: When an editorial constraint makes no narrative sense, ask whether it is a rights constraint. If it is, stop trying to justify it in story and instead find the story that is best served by obeying it.

entries.name: The Merge and the Split
entries.description: The two operations the machinery actually performs, and their opposite consequences.
entries.principle: Everything the multiverse does reduces to combining worlds or dividing them, and the two have inverse effects on a line. A **merge** simplifies, resolves contradiction, and destroys the distinctness that made the merged elements worth keeping. A **split** preserves, permits contradiction, and multiplies what future writers must service. Publishers alternate between them on roughly generational cycles, and each cycle is presented as a permanent correction to the last. `trope-scifi-new-17` treats the reality-merge as a plot event; **the delta here is that it is a recurring administrative cycle rather than an event**, and a writer's real question is not what the merge means but where in the cycle they are standing.
entries.example: *Zenith* is the useful study because it treats the whole apparatus as a satire on the culture that produced it, which is only available to a writer who can see the cycle from outside.
entries.application: Find out which way the line is currently moving before you plan. A book that splits during a merge cycle, or accrues distinctness during a compression, will be corrected by editorial rather than by readers.

entries.category: The Legacy Character and the Sidekick
entries.name: Inheriting a Name
entries.description: The succession as this genre's most reliable engine, and the one thing it always needs.
entries.principle: A legacy character is not a replacement; it is a **relationship to an office**, and the story is always about the terms of that relationship rather than about the powers. What makes a succession work is the successor's stated reason for wanting the name, and what makes one fail is a successor who simply receives it. The genre's strongest legacy stories all give the successor a motive that is partly illegitimate — ambition, grief, a debt, a wish to be seen — because a purely worthy successor has no relationship to the office, only compliance with it. The office must cost something to hold, and the successor must want it anyway.
entries.example: *Ms. Marvel (2014 comic)* makes the taking of the name an explicit act of homage chosen by the character, which converts the succession from an assignment into a decision.
entries.application: Write the successor's reason for wanting the name in their own voice, at their least flattering. If the reason is "someone had to," you have a vacancy filled and not a succession.

entries.category: The Legacy Character and the Sidekick
entries.name: The Sidekick Is the Supply Line
entries.description: What the sidekick is structurally for, whatever the story says it is for.
entries.principle: A sidekick is a succession claim in advance, whether or not anyone intends one. The moment a younger figure is placed beside an established one and trained, the audience begins reading forward, and the property has acquired an heir it may not have meant to create. This has two consequences a writer should plan for rather than discover. First, the sidekick's danger reads differently from anyone else's, because harm to an heir is harm to the property's future. Second, a sidekick who never advances becomes an argument that the office is closed, which slowly makes the original look less like a mentor and more like an obstacle.
entries.example: *Young Avengers (2005 comic)* is the case that makes the mechanism its explicit subject, assembling successors whose claims nobody has agreed to and letting the awkwardness of that be the book.
entries.application: Decide at the outset whether this sidekick will inherit. If yes, plant the reason early. If no, give them a different destination, because a sidekick with nowhere to go decays into a reproach.

entries.category: The Legacy Character and the Sidekick
entries.name: The Mantle as Promotion and as Demotion
entries.description: The same event read two ways, and the fact that both readings are usually true.
entries.principle: Taking up an established name is presented as elevation and is simultaneously a reduction: the successor gains an audience and loses the ability to be read on their own terms, because every action is now measured against a predecessor the reader knows better. Writers tend to feel only the first half and readers tend to feel only the second, which is why successions so often land badly despite being well written. The move that resolves it is to give the successor a capability, a register or a problem the original never had — something the comparison cannot reach — so that the measurement stops being the only lens available.
entries.example: *Blue Beetle (Jaime Reyes)* gives the successor an intact family who know who he is, which is a structural condition none of the previous holders had and which the comparison therefore cannot touch.
entries.application: Name the thing your successor can do that the original could not. If the answer is only that they are newer, the demotion will outweigh the promotion and the reader will want the original back.

entries.category: The Legacy Character and the Sidekick
entries.name: The Route to a Readership
entries.description: The commercial reason legacy characters exist, stated without euphemism.
entries.principle: Succession is the genre's most reliable mechanism for changing who a property is addressed to, because it changes the protagonist without abandoning the trademark. This is a real and honourable function and it is also the source of the practice's worst failures, which occur when the demographic aim is the only aim. A successor introduced to reach an audience and given nothing else to do becomes a demonstration rather than a character, and the audience being courted is generally the first to notice. The successors that work are the ones where the change of address and the change of story are the same change: the new protagonist's situation generates plots the old one could not have had.
entries.example: *Ultimate Comics: Spider-Man* is the standing case, and it works because the successor's circumstances produce different stories rather than the same stories with a different lead.
entries.application: Ask what plots become available that were not available before. If the honest answer is none, the succession is a marketing decision wearing a story, and it will be reverted when the marketing decision changes.

entries.category: The Legacy Character and the Sidekick
entries.name: The Reversion That Was Always Scheduled
entries.description: The interregnum sold as a permanence, and the specific damage that does.
entries.principle: Most successions are planned as temporary before the first issue ships, and there is nothing wrong with an interregnum — the genre has produced excellent ones. The damage is done by the gap between how it is planned and how it is sold. A succession marketed as permanent and reverted on schedule teaches the audience that the property's announcements are not information, and that lesson generalises: the next genuine change is discounted in advance. Writers rarely control the marketing, but they do control whether the story itself makes a promise. A story that is honest about the shape of an interregnum can be moving; one that insists on permanence it has not been granted is simply setting up its own reader.
entries.example: *Ultimate Comics: Spider-Man* is again the useful case, because it is the succession that was **not** reverted on schedule, and the difference in how its successor is now regarded is the whole argument.
entries.application: Write the interregnum as an interregnum. A story about holding an office temporarily, well told, survives the reversion; a story that promised otherwise is retrospectively made false by it.

entries.category: The Legacy Character and the Sidekick
entries.name: The Successor Who Is Better
entries.description: The problem a genuinely superior successor creates, and why it is a good problem.
entries.principle: Occasionally a successor is simply the better character — better premise, better supporting cast, better fit to the present moment — and the property then faces a problem it has no mechanism for solving, because the trademark is attached to the original. What usually happens is that the successor is moved sideways into their own name, which preserves both and dilutes the office. What rarely happens, and works when it does, is that the original is allowed to become something else: a mentor, an antagonist, an absence. The genre's reluctance here is commercial rather than creative, and knowing that helps a writer argue for the better outcome in the right terms.
entries.example: *Static* is the case where the successor-shaped character carried a voice and a set of problems the line had no other access to, which is what made the property durable well beyond its publisher.
entries.application: If your successor is better, say so internally and propose a destination for the original. The proposal that gets accepted is the one that gives the trademark somewhere to live.

entries.category: The Legacy Character and the Sidekick
entries.name: The Vacancy Was Never Real
entries.description: The original's return as a structural certainty, and how to write toward it honestly.
entries.principle: In a form organised around a trademark, an office vacated by its principal holder is on loan rather than transferred, and every experienced reader knows it. `trope-56` describes the return as it plays on the page — the beat, the restoration, the successor's displacement. **The machinery-level fact is different and more useful: the vacancy is not a state the story entered but a period the property scheduled**, and the successor's tenure was bounded before it began. Writing toward that honestly does not mean undercutting the successor. It means giving the tenure a shape that completes — an argument made, a debt paid, a thing learned — so that the return ends a story rather than interrupting one.
entries.example: *Black Lightning* is instructive from the other direction, as a character whose own claim on his office was contested by the publisher's arrangements rather than by any successor.
entries.application: Give the interim tenure a completed arc, with its own last page, before the return is scheduled. A tenure that merely stops is what makes readers feel the successor was never real.

entries.category: The Legacy Character and the Sidekick
entries.name: The Legacy Character and the Trademark
entries.description: The legal fact underneath the narrative device, which determines more than any editor does.
entries.principle: A trademark must be used to be maintained, which means a name in continuous publication is a legal asset actively being preserved, and a name left dormant is one being risked. Succession is therefore among other things a **maintenance operation**: it keeps a mark in use when the original holder is commercially unviable. This explains patterns that look arbitrary from inside the fiction — why some names may never rest, why others reappear briefly and vanish, why a character can be renamed between territories. §0.20 records that the pack states this rather than leaving it as an unexplained editorial mood.
entries.example: *Whiz Comics #2* introduced a character whose name became the subject of one of the longest-running trademark disputes in the medium, and *Captain Marvel (Starlin run)* is the other side of it — a title kept in use, under a name whose ownership was the reason the title existed at all.
entries.application: Before proposing to retire a name, find out what depends on it being used. The answer is often the whole reason your proposal will be refused, and it is not a creative objection.

entries.category: The Legacy Character and the Sidekick
entries.name: The Office and the Person
entries.description: The distinction that resolves most legacy confusion, applied as a working test.
entries.principle: Almost every legacy muddle comes from failing to distinguish a claim about a person from a claim about an office. "He would never do that" may mean this individual would not, or it may mean nobody holding this office may — and those are different objections with different remedies. The distinction also determines what a succession can change: the office's obligations are inherited and the person's history is not, so a successor who is written as inheriting the predecessor's psychology has been given someone else's interiority and will read as a copy. The office travels; the person does not.
entries.example: *Black Panther (Priest run)* runs the distinction hardest, treating its protagonist as a head of state whose obligations exist independently of him, and filtering him through an outsider who keeps mistaking the office for the man.
entries.application: For every trait, mark whether it belongs to the office or the person. Successors inherit the first column only. Anything you find yourself moving from the second column is nostalgia with a plot attached.

entries.category: The Legacy Character and the Sidekick
entries.name: The Legacy Nobody Wanted
entries.description: Inheriting a name that carries a debt, and what the genre has learned to do with it.
entries.principle: Not every inheritance is a promotion. A successor can inherit a name that is compromised — by what a predecessor did, by what was done in the name's service, by a history the property spent decades not mentioning — and this is among the richest positions the device offers, because it converts the succession from an honour into a problem requiring a decision. The move that makes it work is refusing resolution: the successor neither disowns the name nor defends it, but carries it while knowing. What fails is the version where the inherited debt is discovered, acknowledged in one scene, and then stops operating.
entries.example: *Truth: Red, White & Black* makes the debt itself the inheritance, and the point of the book is that the knowledge cannot be discharged by anyone's good intentions afterwards.
entries.application: If your successor inherits a debt, decide what it costs them **in every subsequent story**, not in the story where they learn about it. A debt with no recurring cost was a revelation, not an inheritance.

entries.category: Death, Return and What a Death Can Still Cost
entries.name: Reversible Death as a Structural Condition
entries.description: The rule the whole section runs on, stated as a condition rather than a complaint.
entries.principle: In this genre death is a temporary state with an unpredictable duration, and this is a structural fact about the form rather than a failure of nerve by individual writers. Treating it as a scandal is a waste of the writer's attention; treating it as a condition to be designed around is the entire craft opportunity. The condition has one hard consequence: **the reader's belief is a finite resource that the form spends continuously**, and by the time any given writer arrives, most of it is already gone. `comedy:timing-34` describes the sitcom reset, and the delta is that comedy's reset is a **declared contract** the audience accepts in advance, whereas this genre's reset is performed while being denied — which is why the same device produces affection in one form and contempt in the other.
entries.example: *The Death of Superman* is the moment the condition became fully visible to a mass audience, because the scale of the event and the speed of the reversal were both unprecedented and both public.
entries.application: Assume your reader does not believe the death. Write the story that is still worth reading on that assumption, and you will have written something better than the story that depended on their belief.

entries.category: Death, Return and What a Death Can Still Cost
entries.name: The Death That Stuck
entries.description: The rare permanent case, and the conditions that actually produce permanence.
entries.principle: Deaths that hold are not the ones that were best written; they are the ones whose reversal would cost more than it earns. Three conditions produce that. The death **changed the protagonist structurally**, so undoing it would undo the character. It **was caused by the protagonist**, so reversal would remove a guilt the character is now built from. Or the character's absence **became load-bearing** for stories told since. Note what is absent from that list: solemnity, quality, and authorial intention. A beautifully written death with no structural consequence is reversed as easily as a careless one.
entries.example: *The Amazing Spider-Man #121–122* holds because all three conditions are present at once, and the genre has spent fifty years unable to undo it without dismantling the character it produced.
entries.application: Before writing a death, ask which of the three conditions you can supply. If none, the death is an event and will be reversed. If one, argue for it. If two, it will probably hold.

entries.category: Death, Return and What a Death Can Still Cost
entries.name: Death as an Event Product
entries.description: The commercial machinery around a death, and how it reaches the page.
entries.principle: A death at scale is a scheduled product with a print run, a media plan and, very often, a reversal date agreed before scripting. `trope-50` describes how that looks in the finished comic; **the machinery-level facts are the ones a working writer needs, and they are about sequencing**: the announcement usually precedes the script, the reversal is frequently commissioned from a different writer, and the tie-ins depicting the aftermath may ship before the death itself is drawn. A writer who understands the sequence writes a death that survives contact with it. One who does not writes a death that the surrounding apparatus contradicts before it is published.
entries.example: *The Death of Captain Marvel* is the counter-case worth studying, because it was published as a bounded volume with no line-wide apparatus around it — and it is the death from that era that held.
entries.application: Ask what is already scheduled around your death before you write it: the announcement, the tie-ins, the return. Write inside that timetable. A death whose meaning depends on facts the timetable will contradict is already lost.

entries.category: Death, Return and What a Death Can Still Cost
entries.name: Staging the Aftermath
entries.description: The mourning sequence as a structural instrument rather than an obligatory beat.
entries.principle: `trope-51` treats the funeral as a device on the page. At the machinery level the aftermath sequence does something more specific: it is the **only place in the form where the shared universe is required to agree about something**, because every character who appears has to have a position on the deceased. That makes it an unusually efficient instrument. It establishes relationships that decades of crossovers have left vague, it lets a writer state what a character meant without asserting it in narration, and it produces the one thing serial continuity is otherwise bad at — a consensus fact. Writers treat it as a duty; it is closer to a free structural resource.
entries.example: *The Death of Captain Marvel* devotes almost its whole length to the aftermath rather than the death, and the roll-call of who comes and what they say is the book's actual content.
entries.application: Use the aftermath to settle something. If your mourning sequence establishes no relationship and resolves no ambiguity, it is decoration, and the reader will experience it as a delay.

entries.category: Death, Return and What a Death Can Still Cost
entries.name: Designing a Death That Survives Its Reversal
entries.description: The section's reason for existing — what a death can still be made to do when it will not hold.
entries.principle: `trope-57` states the craft position: the decision belongs to the killer and is the only irreversible thing. **The machinery question is different — what can be built now that a later reversal cannot dismantle** — and it has three answers. A **decision** survives, because reviving the victim does not unmake the choice to kill. A **disclosure** survives, because what was said or learned in extremity stays said. And a **change in standing** survives, because a character who was arrested, deposed, divorced or believed capable of it remains so afterwards. Everything else is on loan. Building a death out of these three is the difference between a writer who is defeated by the form's condition and one who works inside it.
entries.example: *X-Men: Magneto Testament* is the extreme instance, withholding the entire superhero apparatus so that nothing in it is available to be reversed; *Marvelman / Miracleman* is the other extreme, following an unrestrained capability past the killing and describing what it did to the living, which no revival reaches.
entries.application: For your death, name the decision, the disclosure or the change in standing that it produces. If you cannot name one, you have written an absence, and absences are exactly what the form restores.

entries.category: Death, Return and What a Death Can Still Cost
entries.name: Dead in One Medium Only
entries.description: A character who is dead on screen and alive on the page, and what that does to both.
entries.principle: Once a property runs in several media at once, death becomes **medium-local**, and the audiences do not partition cleanly. A character killed in a film and continuing in the comics is simultaneously dead and alive for a large shared readership, which drains both versions: the screen death loses finality because the character is visibly still being published, and the ongoing comic acquires a faint air of denial. There is no fix at the level of an individual story. What there is, is a choice about which version's finality you are willing to spend, and that choice should be made deliberately rather than by whichever production schedule moves first.
entries.example: *Logan* buys its permanence by placing itself outside the ongoing continuity entirely — the same fence `continuity-26` describes, applied to a death; *Black Panther (2018 film)* is the case where an ending arrived in one medium for reasons wholly outside any fiction, and every other medium had to decide what to do about it.
entries.application: Ask which medium your death is final in, and write it as final there. A death hedged so it works in every medium at once is final in none.

entries.category: Death, Return and What a Death Can Still Cost
entries.name: The Death That Belongs to the Survivor
entries.description: The killing used as equipment for someone else, and the standing objection to it.
entries.principle: A death written to change a survivor is the most common form in the genre and the one with the worst record, because it makes a person into a mechanism. `horror:history-16` traces how horror's own reckoning with disposable victims proceeded; **the delta here is the serial's aggravating factor** — in a form where the dead return, a character killed to motivate someone else is often the one who does **not** come back, because their function was discharged on death and there is no story reason to restore them. The genre thus reserves its permanence for exactly the deaths that deserved it least. The remedy is not to ban the structure but to give the victim a position of their own that survives them: an unfinished argument, a decision they made, a claim the survivor cannot answer.
entries.example: *Batman: The Killing Joke* is the standing exhibit for the objection; *Suicide Squad #23 (Oracle)* is the standing exhibit for the answer, since the same event became the basis of a character who outgrew the story that produced her.
entries.application: Give the dead a position the living cannot resolve. If the survivor can honour the dead simply by acting well, the dead were equipment.

entries.category: Death, Return and What a Death Can Still Cost
entries.name: The Body That Comes Back Wrong
entries.description: The return as a horror event rather than a restoration, and why it repairs the form's biggest weakness.
entries.principle: If reversal is inevitable, the most productive response is to make the reversal itself carry the cost — to have the character return, but returned to a condition nobody would have chosen. This converts the form's central weakness into an engine: the reader who has stopped believing in deaths starts believing in returns, because a return that costs something is a new fact rather than a cancelled one. The mode is native to horror and imports cleanly, and it has a further advantage in a serial: a wrong return is an ongoing state rather than a single beat, so it keeps paying across issues in the way a death never does.
entries.example: *The Immortal Hulk* is the sustained demonstration, building fifty issues on the proposition that coming back is worse than dying and formalising the return as the book's recurring horror.
entries.application: If your character must return, decide what returns wrong. A restoration to the previous state is the reader being told the last year did not happen; a costly return is the last year being paid for.

entries.category: Death, Return and What a Death Can Still Cost
entries.name: The Death Nobody Was Allowed to Reverse
entries.description: The editorial fence around a permanent death, and the fact that it is a policy rather than a fictional law.
entries.principle: The genre's handful of durable deaths are held in place by **standing editorial policy**, not by anything inside the fiction, and the distinction matters because policies change and fictional laws do not. `trope-54` describes the deaths that held as a phenomenon on the page. At the machinery level the useful observation is that permanence is an institutional promise, maintained by people, renewed by each successive administration, and occasionally broken. A writer should therefore know which permanences are policy in their line, treat them as the most valuable material available — they are the only irreversible things in reach — and expect to be told no.
entries.example: *The Amazing Spider-Man #121–122* is protected by exactly such a policy, and the periodic attempts to work around rather than through it are instructive about what the policy is actually protecting.
entries.application: Find out which deaths are policy-protected before you plan around them. Building on one is the single strongest foundation the form offers; proposing to overturn one is the fastest way to have a pitch refused.

entries.category: Death, Return and What a Death Can Still Cost
entries.name: What the Reader Learns From the Fifth Return
entries.description: The cumulative effect of repetition on an audience, and the fact that it is not reversible either.
entries.principle: Each reversal in a property teaches its readers something about that property, and the lesson accumulates in one direction only. After the first return readers are surprised; after the third they are watching for the mechanism; after the fifth they are no longer reading the death as an event at all but as a scheduling announcement. **This is the one genuinely irreversible thing in a form built on reversal.** No later story can restore an audience's credulity, and the pattern is set by the property rather than by the individual writer, which means a writer inherits a credibility position they did not create and cannot repair. The workable response is to stop asking for a reaction the property has spent, and to ask for a different one.
entries.example: *Kingdom Come* is instructive because it addresses an audience already fully aware of the pattern and therefore never asks for surprise, spending its energy on consequence instead.
