entries.application: Count the property's previous returns before writing a death. That number tells you what emotional response is still available to you. Writing for a response the count has already spent is the most common single error in this material.

entries.category: The Mandate, the Format and the Trade
entries.name: The Event as an Economic Form
entries.description: The crossover as a financial instrument with a narrative attached, and what that means for the writer inside it.
entries.principle: A line-wide event is a mechanism for moving readers of successful titles onto unsuccessful ones, and its story exists to make that movement tolerable. This is not a cynical reading; it is the design brief, and events that ignore it fail commercially while events that serve it too nakedly fail with readers. The writer's actual craft problem is therefore **a distribution problem**: the story must be legible to someone reading only the core book, rewarding to someone reading everything, and non-fatal to someone reading only one tie-in. Very few events manage all three, and the ones that do are built that way from the outline rather than repaired in the scripting.
entries.example: *Civil War* is the standing case in both directions — a core book that carried its argument on its own, and a tie-in apparatus that took the argument in incompatible directions because nothing in the design required it not to.
entries.application: Write the three-sentence summary a reader of the core book only would give, and the one a tie-in-only reader would give. If they contradict each other, the event will be remembered as incoherent regardless of how good the core book is.

entries.category: The Mandate, the Format and the Trade
entries.name: The Tie-In You Did Not Choose
entries.description: Being conscripted into someone else's story, and the two honest ways through it.
entries.principle: A writer on an ongoing title will periodically be required to interrupt their own work to service an event they did not design, on a schedule they did not set, with an outcome they cannot alter. There are two workable responses and one common failure. The failure is to write the tie-in as an obligation discharged, which produces three issues the run's readers learn to skip and the event's readers learn nothing from. The responses that work are to **find the piece of the event that your character is uniquely positioned to see**, or to use the interruption as a pressure your ongoing story can absorb — the event becomes something that happens **to** your book rather than instead of it.
entries.example: *Captain America and the Falcon: Secret Empire* is the older and better model, where a line-level conspiracy is refracted entirely through what one book's protagonist can see and what it costs him to see it.
entries.application: Ask what your protagonist knows about the event that nobody else does. If the answer is nothing, invent it — an angle of view is the one thing the event's architects cannot take from you.

entries.category: The Mandate, the Format and the Trade
entries.name: The Editorial Mandate as a Formal Constraint
entries.description: The instruction from above treated as a formal problem rather than an indignity.
entries.principle: A mandate — a character must be alive by March, a status must be restored, a new figure must be introduced and made to matter — arrives as an external requirement and functions exactly like a formal constraint: a fixed element the work must accommodate. Writers who treat mandates as interference produce work that visibly resents itself. Writers who treat them as constraints produce solutions they would not otherwise have found, which is the standard argument for constraint in every other art form and holds here too. **Research B could not locate a scholarly treatment of the editorial mandate as a formal device**, which is a real gap: the most consistent shaping force on this genre's output has no critical literature, and this card is written on practitioner testimony rather than on scholarship. The pack states that rather than implying an authority it does not have.
entries.example: *Daredevil (Waid run)* was commissioned under an explicit brief to move the book out of a decade of grimness, and the brief is invisible in the result — which is what a mandate looks like when it has been used rather than endured.
entries.application: Write the mandate down as a formal specification — these elements fixed, these free. Then solve it. The resentment is not a craft position and it shows on the page.

entries.category: The Mandate, the Format and the Trade
entries.name: The Ending Belongs to the Publisher
entries.description: The condition underneath a craft problem Craft already covers.
entries.principle: `craft-31` treats the ending you are not allowed as a writing problem — how to give a run a shape when it cannot conclude. **The condition beneath it is contractual and worth stating separately: you are not withholding an ending, you do not own one.** The property's terminal state is an asset of the rights holder, and a run's last page is a hand-over rather than a conclusion. Two things follow. Your run's final issue may be decided by a sales report during your penultimate arc, so a shape that requires four more issues is a shape that may never exist. And anything you build that only **you** can resolve will be resolved by someone else, in a manner you would not have chosen, or abandoned — which is worse.
entries.example: *Planetary* is the useful exception that proves the rule, a creator-owned book that could hold its ending for three years and still deliver it, because the ending was not anybody else's asset.
entries.application: At every arc break, ask what happens if this is the last one. If the answer is that a promise is left unpaid, pay something now. Runs end without notice and the reader does not know you were not warned.

entries.category: The Mandate, the Format and the Trade
entries.name: The Direct Market and What Broke in 1996
entries.description: The distribution structure this genre is published into, and the collapse that produced it.
entries.principle: The superhero comic is sold into a non-returnable specialty market ordered two to three months in advance on solicitation copy — which means a book is bought by retailers on the strength of a description before a page is drawn, and cannot be reordered into success. That structure is not natural; it is the residue of a specific collapse. Marvel acquired the Heroes World distributor in December 1994 and went exclusive with it in July 1995; the competing distributors lost a large share of volume against fixed costs; DC, Image, Dark Horse and others signed exclusively with Diamond in response; Heroes World closed in 1997, leaving Diamond effectively alone. Marvel itself filed for Chapter 11 on 27 December 1996. **Every craft convention about first issues, relaunches and variant covers is downstream of that market shape.**
entries.example: *X-Men #1 (1991 comic)* is the peak of the speculative logic that market rewarded, sold on variant covers into a bubble; *Youngblood* is what the same conditions produced when the incentive was the creator's name rather than the story.
entries.application: Read your own solicitation copy before you write the issue. It is the only part of your book most retailers will ever see, and in this market their order is fixed before your pages exist.

entries.category: The Mandate, the Format and the Trade
entries.name: The Trade Is the Durable Object
entries.description: Which version of your work survives, and the condition that creates rather than the technique that follows.
entries.principle: `craft-35` treats decompression as a budget decision at the desk. **The condition underneath it is that the periodical is the promotional edition and the collection is the product** — the periodical is out of print within weeks, and the collected volume is what libraries, schools, translations and new readers receive for decades. This inverts several intuitions. The cliffhanger, which is the periodical's engine, is invisible in the collection. The recap, which the periodical needs, is redundant in it. And an arc's length is determined not by its story but by what makes a saleable book. A writer who does not know which edition they are being paid to serve will optimise for the one that disappears.
entries.example: *Marvels* was built as a bounded four-part work and has been continuously in print since, which is the collection behaving as the durable object rather than as a reprint.
entries.application: Ask which edition your book's success will be measured in. If it is the collection, the arc's length is a commercial specification and not a story judgement — and you should find that out before outlining, not after.

entries.category: The Mandate, the Format and the Trade
entries.name: Work-for-Hire as the Standing Condition
entries.description: The employment arrangement that determines what every other rule in this collection is for.
entries.principle: Nearly all superhero publishing is work-for-hire: the writer is paid for the work and the publisher owns it, including anything created inside it. This single fact explains most of the collection. Continuity must be maintained because the property is an asset. Deaths reverse because assets are not destroyed. Successions revert because the trademark is the thing being protected. Mandates exist because someone is responsible for the asset's condition and it is not you. Treating these as separate frustrations is the mistake; they are one condition seen from several angles. Knowing that does not change the terms, but it converts a series of arbitrary irritations into a coherent and predictable system, and predictable systems can be worked inside.
entries.example: *Marvelman / Miracleman* is the case in which every layer of this — authorship, ownership, the right to use a name — came apart in public and stayed apart for decades.
entries.application: For anything you create inside a work-for-hire book, assume it will be used by others, badly, without consulting you, and possibly with your name attached. If that is unacceptable for a given idea, that idea belongs in a different book.

entries.category: The Mandate, the Format and the Trade
entries.name: The Schedule Is a Collaborator
entries.description: Shipping dates as a formal force on the work, not an administrative fact around it.
entries.principle: A monthly book's schedule shapes its content more than most editorial notes do. A late issue acquires a fill-in artist, which means the arc's visual argument is interrupted at whichever point the calendar chose. A book shipping ahead of its crossover partner must avoid depicting a state that has not yet been established elsewhere. A delayed conclusion arrives after the tie-ins have already shown its outcome. None of this is visible to the reader as scheduling; it is visible as inconsistency, and the writer is who it is attributed to. The practical response is to design at the arc level for **interruptibility**: know which issues could survive a different artist and which could not.
entries.example: *The Ultimates* is the standing case, a thirteen-issue work whose actual shipping pattern bore no relation to the monthly cadence its structure assumed.
entries.application: Mark the issues in your arc that must be drawn by your artist. Tell your editor which they are. An interruption placed by the calendar lands wherever it lands; an interruption you have planned for lands where it costs least.

entries.category: The Mandate, the Format and the Trade
entries.name: The Page Rate Selects for Something
entries.description: How the work is paid for, and what that quietly rewards.
entries.principle: Payment by the page, on a fixed monthly count, with the writer and artist paid separately, produces predictable pressures. It rewards a consistent output rate over an uneven one, regardless of which serves the story. It makes an ambitious page expensive for the artist and free for the writer, which is why a script can casually specify what will cost someone else a week. And it makes the creator-owned book, paid on the back end, a different economic proposition demanding a different kind of risk. None of this determines quality — excellent work has been made under every arrangement — but it does determine what is **easy**, and what is easy accumulates.
entries.example: *Invincible (comic)* ran to a completed 144-issue ending under an arrangement where the creators held the property, which is a shape the standard rate structure makes very difficult to reach.
entries.application: When you specify a demanding page, know that you are spending someone else's time and say so in the script. The collaborators who do this get the ambitious pages they ask for; the ones who do not, stop being given them.

entries.category: The Mandate, the Format and the Trade
entries.name: The Property Has Other Owners Now
entries.description: The comic as one department among several, and what that does to the writer's latitude.
entries.principle: Once a property is generating substantially more revenue on screen than on the page, the comic's freedom narrows in a specific and non-obvious way. Direct instructions are rare. What happens instead is that the comic becomes **the version that must not diverge**: costumes converge on the screen designs, casts converge on the screen casts, and changes that would once have been routine now require a conversation with people who have no interest in comics. The writer experiences this as an inexplicable increase in caution. Understanding its source is worth a great deal, because it identifies which proposals are genuinely refusable and which are simply expensive to approve.
entries.example: *Ms. Marvel (2014 comic)* is the instructive sequence in reverse — a comic that established a character with enough force that the screen version followed it, which is the only reliable way a page-first property regains latitude.
entries.application: Find out where the property's revenue actually comes from. It tells you what your book is for this year, and a proposal framed against that is refused; framed with it, the same proposal is often approved.

entries.category: Canon, the Imaginary Story and Who Adjudicates
entries.name: Who Decides What Counts
entries.description: The question the whole section turns on, and the fact that it has no permanent answer.
entries.principle: Canon is not a property of stories; it is a **ruling made by somebody with standing to make it**, and the identity of that somebody has changed repeatedly. It has been the editor, the letter column, the handbook, the fan press, the wiki, and at present very often the screen. Nothing about a published story determines whether it counts — the same issue can be canonical, then not, then canonical again, without a word of it changing. For a writer this is more useful than it sounds, because it reframes "is this canon?" from a question about the text into a question about the current authority: who, right now, would have to agree, and what do they respond to?
entries.example: *The Brave and the Bold #28* ran the adjudication in public in its editorial pages as an ordinary feature of the form, which is the practice `trope-80` describes as a narrative device and which is here treated as what it also was — a court sitting.
entries.application: Before arguing that something counts, identify who currently rules on it. Arguing canon to a party without standing is the most common wasted argument in this field.

entries.category: Canon, the Imaginary Story and Who Adjudicates
entries.name: The Handbook and Its Authority
entries.description: The reference volume as an attempt to freeze a moving object, and what it actually achieves.
entries.principle: Every large property eventually publishes an official compendium, and every one is obsolete before it ships. Their real function is not accuracy but **arbitration**: by printing one version of a contested fact, the handbook settles arguments, and the settlement outlives the accuracy. This has a consequence writers underrate. A handbook entry, once printed, tends to become true through citation — later writers work from it, and the published stories it summarised become less influential than the summary. A great deal of what the audience believes about long-running characters originates in reference material rather than in fiction, which `continuity-10` describes from the reader's side and which this card describes from the institution's.
entries.example: *Detective Comics #27* has been re-narrated by handbooks and companion volumes far more often than it has been read, and the received account of it differs in details from the eleven pages themselves.
entries.application: When you cite a fact about a character's history, check whether your source is a story or a summary. If it is a summary, you are propagating an arbitration, which is legitimate — but know that you are doing it.

entries.category: Canon, the Imaginary Story and Who Adjudicates
entries.name: The Letter Column as a Court of Record
entries.description: The historical adjudication mechanism, and why its disappearance mattered more than it seemed to.
entries.principle: For roughly forty years the letter column was where continuity was argued, corrected and ruled on, in public, over the editor's signature, with the reader's name printed beside the objection. It did three things that nothing has fully replaced. It made the adjudicator **visible and accountable** — a named person had to answer. It made corrections **part of the archive**, printed in the same object as the error. And it gave readers standing, which is a different thing from giving them a voice. When letter columns were dropped for advertising space, the adjudication did not stop; it moved somewhere with no signature, no archive and no standing, and the tone of the genre's continuity arguments has never recovered.
entries.example: *The Brave and the Bold #28* is again the exhibit, where the editorial voice answering readers directly was an ordinary feature of the page rather than an occasional gesture.
entries.application: If your book has any channel to readers, use it to rule on things in your own name. The credibility gained by publicly conceding one error exceeds anything gained by never appearing to make one.

entries.category: Canon, the Imaginary Story and Who Adjudicates
entries.name: The Wiki as the Present Adjudicator
entries.description: Where the ruling is actually made now, and the specific ways it fails.
entries.principle: The functional canon of most superhero properties is now the fan-maintained wiki, because that is what everyone — readers, journalists, adaptation writers, and a good number of professionals — actually consults. It has genuine virtues: it is current, exhaustive and correctable. It also has three failure modes worth naming. It **flattens provenance**, presenting a 1963 story and a 2019 retcon in one voice. It **prefers the summarisable**, so a story whose meaning is in its execution is reduced to its plot. And it is **self-reinforcing**: an error, once entered, is cited by secondary sources which are then cited as corroboration. This build encountered all three while verifying its own Works roster.
entries.example: *Daredevil (Bendis/Maleev run)* is a concrete instance — this pack's own research found the run's issue span stated wrongly on the property's main reference page and correct on an adjacent one, caught only by cross-checking.
entries.application: Never take a run's boundaries, a first appearance or a creator credit from a single reference page. Two independent pages, or the indicia. This build made that a rule after finding the error, not before.

entries.category: Canon, the Imaginary Story and Who Adjudicates
entries.name: The Fan as Co-Author
entries.description: The audience's real authorial contribution, stated precisely enough to be useful.
entries.principle: The claim that fans co-author a serial is usually made too loosely to act on. Stated precisely, it comes to this: **the audience controls which published material remains in circulation**, and circulation determines what later writers build on. Fans do not write the stories, but by re-reading, recommending, collecting and arguing, they determine which stories stay available to be built on and which become inert. A run that nobody discusses is functionally decanonised regardless of its official status. This is why an unpopular story is rarely retconned away — it does not need to be. It is also why a writer's best protection against being overwritten is not editorial agreement but a story readers keep returning to.
entries.example: *Batman: Year One* has survived every subsequent continuity reset without protection, because it stayed in circulation and successive writers kept finding it easier to build on than to replace.
entries.application: Ask which of your stories a reader would hand to someone else. That is the one that will survive the next reset. The others are in circulation only while you are.

entries.category: Canon, the Imaginary Story and Who Adjudicates
entries.name: The Story Told Outside the Count
entries.description: The pre-adjudicated story, and what pre-adjudication is worth.
entries.principle: `trope-77` describes the imaginary story as a device on the page, and `continuity-26` describes the fence as what supplies an ending. **The adjudication angle is the third and least discussed: the out-of-continuity story is the only kind whose canonical status is settled before publication**, and settling it in advance is precisely what frees the work. Nobody will argue about whether it counts, so nobody has to be persuaded, and the story is released from the entire apparatus of standing and authority this section describes. That is a real and underused asset. The corollary is uncomfortable and true: several of the genre's most admired works owe part of their coherence to having been exempted from the process that governs everything else.
entries.example: *Kingdom Come* is the case where a work's whole argument depends on nobody needing to rule on it afterwards.
entries.application: If your story's value would survive nobody ever ruling it canonical, ask for the fence at the pitch. Writers routinely fight for in-continuity status that adds nothing to the story and subtracts a great deal of freedom.

entries.category: Canon, the Imaginary Story and Who Adjudicates
entries.name: The Annual and the Occasion
entries.description: The publishing occasion as an adjudication event, which is not how it is usually described.
entries.principle: `trope-76` treats the anniversary issue as a device — a number on a cover and the accrual it spends. At the adjudication level the occasion does something more specific: an annual, a milestone or a giant-sized issue is a **licensed opportunity to state what is currently true**. Because it stands slightly outside the monthly flow, it can summarise, formalise and settle in a way an ordinary issue cannot without looking like a recap. Historically this is where status quos are declared, rosters fixed, and disputed facts quietly resolved. Writers tend to treat these issues as obligations to fill with spectacle, which wastes the one slot in the schedule that carries standing.
entries.example: *Amazing Fantasy #15* is the extreme case of an occasion issue outliving its own occasion — a final issue of a cancelled title, and the accrual it started rather than spent.
entries.application: If you are handed a milestone issue, use it to settle something disputed. It is the only issue you will be given whose declarative tone the reader accepts without resistance.

entries.category: Canon, the Imaginary Story and Who Adjudicates
entries.name: When Adjudication Moves to Another Medium
entries.description: The screen version becoming the arbiter, and what that leaves the source line doing.
entries.principle: `craft-55` covers the craft problem of the adaptation becoming the canon — writing a source line whose readers know the screen version better. **The adjudication problem is separate and sharper: authority itself relocates.** When a screen version reaches an audience two orders of magnitude larger, the question "what is true about this character" is answered there, and the comics become a variant of their own property. The source line then has two viable positions and one unviable one. It can converge, becoming a supplement. It can diverge deliberately, becoming the place where the other version is available. What does not work is drifting — converging enough to lose distinctness without converging enough to be the reference.
entries.example: *Blade (1998 film)* is the early instance of a screen version establishing a property's public identity almost from nothing, and *Batman: The Animated Series* is the case where the adaptation originated material the source line then had to adopt.
entries.application: Ask whether your book is the reference or the alternative. Both are honourable. Decide, because the drift between them is where source lines lose the readers they still had.

entries.category: Canon, the Imaginary Story and Who Adjudicates
entries.name: The Two-Tier Canon
entries.description: The unofficial distinction every long-running property develops between what counts and what counts *more*.
entries.principle: In practice no large property has one canon; it has a small core of stories treated as load-bearing and a much larger body treated as technically true and practically ignorable. The tiers are never declared and are enforced by usage: the core is cited, adapted and reprinted, and the rest is what a writer may quietly contradict without consequence. Recognising the tiers is a practical skill. It tells you which contradictions will be noticed, which material is genuinely available to build on, and — most useful — which stories are in the lower tier and **should not be**, which is where the strongest unexploited material in any old property is found.
entries.example: *Jungle Action (McGregor run)* spent decades in the lower tier despite being one of the medium's first sustained long-form arcs, and its later promotion changed what the character could be used for.
entries.application: List the stories your property's core actually cites. Then read three good ones it does not. The gap between those lists is your least contested source of new material.

entries.category: Canon, the Imaginary Story and Who Adjudicates
entries.name: When the Adjudicator Changes
entries.description: What happens to established facts when the person with standing is replaced, and how to write across the transition.
entries.principle: Editors, editors-in-chief and rights holders change, and each change re-opens settled questions, because canon was never a property of the stories but a ruling by whoever held the office. A fact settled by a previous administration has exactly the durability of that administration's remaining tenure. The practical consequences are three. Anything you were told is permanent is permanent for a term. Anything refused may be available to the next holder. And the material most vulnerable at a transition is whatever the previous adjudicator personally championed. **Write so that your work does not depend on a ruling continuing to be made**, because the one thing no writer can secure is the continuity of the office.
entries.example: *Squadron Supreme* is the useful case, a self-contained argument whose meaning survives every subsequent administrative view of where it sits, because it never required a ruling to work.
entries.application: For each element you are building on, ask whether it is in the stories or in the ruling. Elements that live only in a ruling should not carry weight — not because the ruling is wrong, but because it is a term of office and your book is longer than one.

entries.name: A Power Is a Claim About a Person
entries.description: The foundational card for this section — what a capability is doing in a story before it does anything in a plot.
entries.principle: A power is a proposition about its holder: that this person's relation to the world is unlike yours in one specified way, and that the difference is worth a book. `fantasy:worldbuilding-4` gives the fuller treatment of magic systems as designed objects, and this collection's whole reason for existing is that its object is different — Fantasy designs a system a **world** runs on, and the superhero writer designs a system **one person** is, in a world otherwise exactly like the reader's. That difference is not cosmetic. A world-system is judged by consistency across a setting; a person-system is judged by whether it says something true about a character. The most common failure in this genre is a capability chosen for what it can do in a fight rather than for what it claims about the person doing it.
entries.example: *The Immortal Hulk* re-specifies a familiar capability as a claim about what its holder cannot stop being, and the whole book follows from the re-specification rather than from the power level.
entries.application: Write the sentence "this person is someone who —" and finish it with the power. If the sentence is only about capability, you have equipment rather than a character, and no amount of plot will convert one into the other.

entries.name: The Power That Is the Problem
entries.description: The capability designed as an affliction, and why it produces more story than an ability does.
entries.principle: A capability that solves problems yields a diminishing series of problems to solve. A capability that **is** the problem yields an inexhaustible one, because the protagonist cannot put it down. `fantasy:trope-19` covers the price-of-magic bargain, where cost is exacted in exchange for use; **the delta here is that there is no exchange and no bargain** — nothing was traded and nothing can be declined, so the structure is not a transaction but a condition. This also changes what the story can be about. A bargain story is about whether to pay. A condition story is about how to live, which is a subject rather than a decision, and subjects sustain serials.
entries.example: *Daredevil (Waid run)* is the instructive case because it takes a condition that had been written as affliction for decades and asks what it is like to refuse to be defined by it, which is a different story from the affliction itself.
entries.application: Ask whether your protagonist could stop. If they could and do not, you are writing a choice and will need to renew it every arc. If they could not, you have a condition, and conditions do not need renewing.

entries.name: Powers That Open Scenes and Powers That Close Them
entries.description: The scene-level economics of a capability, which determine how often it can appear.
entries.principle: Every capability is either generative or terminal. A generative power creates a situation that then has to be handled — it opens. A terminal power resolves the situation it is applied to — it closes. Both are necessary and the ratio is what matters: a roster of terminal powers produces short scenes and a plot that must keep the powers away from the problem, which readers experience as contrivance. `craft-21` **The Competence That Ends the Scene** treats this at the desk, as a scene-construction problem; `fantasy:craft-3` treats consequence as something a built world can simply let run; **the system-level question here is a design ratio**, fixed when the roster is specified rather than solved scene by scene, and a book whose ratio is wrong cannot be written out of it.
entries.example: *Fantastic Four #1* specifies four capabilities of which three are generative, which is why the configuration has sustained six decades of stories rather than six.
entries.application: Sort your roster into generative and terminal before writing. If more than a third are terminal, you will spend the series inventing reasons they are unavailable, and every one of those reasons costs you credibility.

entries.name: What Cannot Be Specified Cannot Be Bounded
entries.description: The link between a power with no clear image and a power with no clear limit.
entries.principle: `craft-13` **The Undrawable Power** treats the visual problem — what the reader sees when the capability has no natural image. `fantasy:worldbuilding-9` gives the fuller treatment of hard and soft systems, where an unspecified magic is a deliberate wonder-preserving choice; **the delta is that this genre cannot make that choice, because its unspecified powers sit beside specified ones in the same room.** The system-level consequence is the one that damages books: **a capability that cannot be depicted usually cannot be bounded either**, because both problems have the same source, which is that the power was never specified, only named. Telepathy, probability alteration, reality warping and magic-adjacent capability all share this. The reader cannot picture them, cannot predict them, and therefore cannot be surprised by them — and a power that cannot surprise cannot generate suspense, whatever it does to opponents.
entries.example: *New X-Men* is the useful case because it repeatedly specifies what a familiar unbounded capability actually does at the level of mechanism, which is what makes the scenes legible.
entries.application: Write the capability's specification as three sentences a reader could use to predict the next scene. If you cannot, the power is a name. Name-level powers are where every unearned resolution in this genre comes from.

entries.name: The Metaphor You Say Out Loud
entries.description: The capability that stands for something, and what happens when the story states what.
entries.principle: Superhero capabilities routinely carry a second meaning — adolescence, difference, trauma, inheritance — and the genre's standing question is whether to make the meaning explicit. `fantasy:worldbuilding-5` treats the allegorical system in a built world, where the meaning is a property of the setting. **The delta here is that the metaphor is attached to a person the reader is asked to identify with**, which changes the cost of stating it: naming the metaphor tells the reader what a character's life means, and a reader told what a life means stops examining it. The rule that emerges from the genre's practice is not "never state it" but **"state it once, from inside a character who has a reason to say it, and never from the narration."**
entries.example: *Uncanny X-Men #199* is the case where the metaphor and the actual history it borrows from are put in the same room and made to answer to each other, rather than one standing in for the other.
entries.application: Find every place the narration explains what the power means. Give the best line to a character who would say it and cut the rest. Narration that interprets its own metaphor is the genre's most common failure of nerve.

entries.category: Limits That Are Not the Plot's Convenience
entries.name: Stated Limit and Observed Limit
entries.description: The foundational card for this section — the two limits every powered character has, and the gap between them.
entries.principle: Every character has a limit the text asserts and a limit their published appearances actually demonstrate, and the two diverge immediately. `fantasy:worldbuilding-9` gives the fuller treatment of hard and soft magic systems and the rules-versus-wonder trade. **What this collection adds is the serial condition: neither limit is authored by one person.** The stated limit is a claim someone made once; the observed limit is the accumulated residue of forty writers, and where they conflict the observed one wins, because readers reason from what they have seen. That has a practical consequence Fantasy's account does not need: **a limit you state is a proposal, and a limit you demonstrate is a fact.**
entries.example: *Superman: Whatever Happened to the Man of Tomorrow?* works partly because it treats the observed limits of decades of stories as the real specification and the stated ones as decoration.
entries.application: List what your character has been shown doing, not what the handbook says. Where they disagree, write to the demonstration or spend a scene explicitly overturning it. Quietly writing to the stated limit reads as an error.

entries.category: Limits That Are Not the Plot's Convenience
entries.name: Specifying a Limit So It Survives Another Writer
entries.description: What makes a limit durable rather than merely present, in a form where you are not the last writer.
entries.principle: `craft-19` **A Limit the Reader Can Check** covers making a limit legible in a scene. `fantasy:worldbuilding-3` treats the internally consistent system, which one author maintains. **The delta is handover.** The system question here is durability: **a limit survives handover only if it is cheap to remember and expensive to break.** Cheap to remember means one clause, no conditions, no exceptions list — a limit requiring a paragraph will be misremembered within a year. Expensive to break means the limit is load-bearing for something a later writer wants, so that removing it costs them a story they would rather keep. Limits that are merely stated, however elegantly, are removed by the first writer who finds them inconvenient, and the removal will not read as vandalism to anyone but you.
entries.example: *All-Star Superman* specifies its limits as a small number of memorable clauses attached to things the story wants, which is why they hold across a work with no continuity to enforce them.
entries.application: State each limit in one clause. Then name what in your story would break if the limit were removed. A limit with nothing attached to it is a note to yourself, not a specification.

entries.category: Limits That Are Not the Plot's Convenience
entries.name: The Prohibition Is Part of the Specification
entries.description: The self-imposed rule as a system component, not a character trait.
entries.principle: `craft-18` **The Rule the Character Will Not Break** treats the prohibition as characterisation — what a refusal reveals. `fantasy:worldbuilding-4` treats costs and prohibitions as system components a designer sets. **The delta is that this one is chosen by the character and can be revoked by the next writer.** At the system level a prohibition functions **exactly as a capability limit does**, and should be specified with the same care: it determines what the character can do, it is checkable by the reader, it can be violated for effect, and it can be eroded by inattention. The difference from a physical limit is that a prohibition can be broken, which is its whole value — it is the only limit in the system that is also a decision. That makes it the most fragile part of any specification, because every writer who breaks it for one story permanently reduces what it means.
entries.example: *Kingdom Come* is built on the erosion of exactly such a prohibition across a generation, and treats the erosion as the setting's central historical fact rather than as a character beat.
entries.application: Write the prohibition into the specification beside the physical limits, and record every time it is broken. Three breaks and it is no longer a rule, it is a preference — and nobody will have decided that.

entries.category: Limits That Are Not the Plot's Convenience
entries.name: Who Else Is in the Room
entries.description: The limit that is other people — law, jurisdiction, and the rest of the roster.
entries.principle: The most underused limits in this genre are not physical. What a character may do is bounded by who can stop them, who can prosecute them, whose territory this is, and who else present would object — and these bounds have three advantages over physical limits. They **do not weaken the character**, so there is no power-creep pressure to remove them. They **generate scenes** rather than closing them, because each is a negotiation. And they **survive a reboot**, because they belong to the setting rather than the specification. `fantasy:worldbuilding-15` treats institutional constraint in built worlds; the delta is that this genre's institutions are the reader's own, so a jurisdictional limit needs no exposition at all.
entries.example: *Ex Machina* runs almost entirely on this class of limit, replacing the physical ceiling with a procedural one and finding a full book in it.
entries.application: For your next three plots, replace a physical limit with a person who would have to agree. The scenes get better and the character does not get weaker, which is the only trade in this section with no downside.

entries.category: Limits That Are Not the Plot's Convenience
entries.name: The Point-Buy Inheritance
entries.description: The tabletop tradition that formalised cost and limit decades before the comics did, and what it offers a prose writer.
entries.principle: Superhero tabletop games solved a problem the comics had left implicit: if capability is purchased from a fixed budget, then every power has a price, every limitation refunds part of it, and a character is a **balance sheet that must add up**. `fantasy:worldbuilding-19` covers the systematised magic economy in built worlds. The delta here is one of provenance and of use: this formalisation was developed for adjudication between players rather than for narrative, and it produces a specific discipline the comics rarely impose — **you cannot add a capability without removing something**, because the total is fixed. A writer who builds a roster this way arrives with limits already integral rather than bolted on.
entries.example: *Watchmen*'s cast reads as a balance sheet that adds up — one character with unbounded capability, priced against seven who have almost none. **The claim that it was designed that way is not made here.** What is documented is the reverse direction: the cast was **costed after the fact** in a point-buy system, in licensed supplements written concurrently with the comic using the author's own input, published 1987 and 1990. A closed system can be read off a finished work without having generated it, and the reading is the useful part. [gap: the design claim was searched 2026-08-24 and no statement by either creator was located]
entries.application: Give yourself a fixed budget and buy your roster from it. The characters you cannot afford are the ones you were going to have to write excuses for anyway.

entries.category: Cost in a Form That Cannot Accrue It
entries.name: Cost Must Land Inside the Arc
entries.description: The foundational card for the section that justifies this collection.
entries.principle: `fantasy:worldbuilding-5` and `fantasy:trope-19` both treat the price of power, and both assume something this genre cannot supply: **a story that ends, in which a debt incurred early is paid late.** A serial resets the ledger between arcs — the wound heals, the exhaustion passes, the sacrifice is undone by the next writer — so a cost deferred is a cost cancelled. This is the single largest divergence between the two genres' handling of the same idea, and it produces one hard rule. **Whatever a power costs must be paid inside the arc that incurs it**, in front of the reader, or it will not be paid at all. Everything else in this section follows from that.
entries.example: *Marvelman / Miracleman* pays inside the story it incurs in, describing the consequences of an unrestrained capability while the story is still running rather than promising them later.
entries.application: For every cost you introduce, name the issue in which it is paid. If the issue number is outside your arc, you have written a promise you cannot keep, and your successor will not keep it either.

entries.category: Cost in a Form That Cannot Accrue It
entries.name: Someone Else Pays
entries.description: Displacing the price onto a person the reset does not reach.
entries.principle: Costs paid by the powered protagonist are the ones the form restores fastest, because the protagonist is the asset. Costs paid by **someone else** are considerably more durable: a bystander's injury, a relationship's damage, a colleague's career, a city's rebuilt block. `horror:craft-17` covers the toll a supernatural capability takes on its holder; **the delta is direction** — horror's cost travels inward toward a protagonist whose destruction is available, and this genre's cost must travel outward, because the protagonist's destruction is not. The technique is not cruelty for its own sake. It is the recognition that in a form which protects its lead, the only people who can carry a permanent price are the ones the form does not protect.
entries.example: *Marvels* is the sustained demonstration, narrating the entire era from the position of someone who pays and has no capability to pay with.
entries.application: For each cost, ask who is holding it at the end of the arc. If it is the protagonist, expect it to be gone by the next one. If it is someone else, it may still be there in ten years.

entries.category: Cost in a Form That Cannot Accrue It
entries.name: Reputation and the Court Record
entries.description: The two kinds of cost the reset genuinely cannot reach.
entries.principle: A reset restores bodies, relationships and status quos. It does not restore **what people know** or **what is on record**, and those two categories are therefore the most valuable currency in this collection. A character who was seen doing something remains someone who was seen doing it; a charge filed, an injunction granted, a licence revoked, a public statement made — these persist because undoing them requires a story rather than an editorial decision. `fantasy:craft-3` treats consequence in built worlds where cause and effect can simply be allowed to run; the delta is that here consequence must be **stored somewhere the reset does not look**, and reputation and the record are the two available vaults.
entries.example: *Civil War* is the case where the durable residue was never the physical outcome but the positions characters took publicly and could not afterwards claim not to have taken.
entries.application: Convert one physical cost per arc into a reputational or legal one. It costs the same to write and it is still there when the bodies have healed.

entries.category: Cost in a Form That Cannot Accrue It
entries.name: When the Reversal Is the Price
entries.description: Making the restoration itself the thing that costs, rather than fighting it.
entries.principle: If the reset is inevitable, the most efficient move available is to charge for it — to design the restoration so that coming back is itself the expensive event. This converts the form's central weakness into its collection point, and it has an advantage no other cost structure has in a serial: **it is a recurring state rather than a single beat**, so it keeps paying across issues where a death or an injury pays once. `horror:craft-17` supplies the register — the body restored wrongly, the return that is worse than the loss — and the delta is structural rather than tonal: horror uses it for dread, and this genre needs it as **an accounting mechanism** in a form that otherwise cannot bank anything.
entries.example: *The Immortal Hulk* is the fifty-issue demonstration that the return, not the destruction, is where a serial can put a price.
entries.application: Ask what your character's restoration costs them. If the answer is nothing, you have written a delay rather than a loss, and the reader has already priced it.

entries.category: Cost in a Form That Cannot Accrue It
entries.name: The Debt You Cannot Discharge
entries.description: The cost written as a permanent condition rather than a payable amount.
entries.principle: The strongest costs in this genre are not paid at all; they are **carried**. A debt with a settlement price can be settled, and a serial will eventually settle it because settling is a story and carrying is not. A debt with no discharge mechanism — a thing done that cannot be undone, a knowledge that cannot be unlearned, an obligation with no defined end — becomes part of the character's specification rather than part of their plot, and specifications survive writers where plots do not. `fantasy:worldbuilding-4` builds costs into a system as prices; the delta is that here the durable form of cost is **not a price at all but a permanent term** in the character's definition.
entries.example: *Truth: Red, White & Black* installs exactly such a term, and its point is that no subsequent good conduct by anyone discharges it.
entries.application: Write one cost with no discharge condition. Then check that you have not, three issues later, invented one — which is what a writer does automatically unless they have decided not to.

entries.name: Different Systems, One Team
entries.description: The foundational card for this section — the superhero team as a collection of incompatible specifications.
entries.principle: `fantasy:worldbuilding-2` treats the internally consistent magic system, where one set of rules governs everyone and consistency is the design goal. **The superhero team is the opposite object: several unrelated systems, of different kinds and different scales, standing in one room and expected to cooperate.** One character's capability is technological, another's is physiological, another's is effectively divine — and no single rule set governs them. That is not a flaw to be tidied. It is the form's distinguishing feature and its main source of story, because every interaction between two incompatible systems is an unresolved question the writer gets to answer. The design problem is therefore not consistency but **adjudication**.
entries.example: *Fantastic Four #1* establishes four capabilities with four unrelated logics and no governing rule, and six decades of stories have come out of the gaps between them.
entries.application: Do not unify your team's systems. Instead write down, for each pair, what happens when they interact. The list of pairs is your plot generator; a unified system is a much shorter list.

entries.name: Who Wins, and Who Decides
entries.description: Inter-power adjudication as an explicit design responsibility rather than an argument to be avoided.
entries.principle: Readers will ask who wins, and the question is not childish — it is a request for the specification. In a form with no governing rule set, every match-up is adjudicated by whoever writes it, which means the answer changes by writer, and inconsistency here does more damage than almost anywhere else because it is the most easily checked thing in the book. `fantasy:worldbuilding-3` covers the internally consistent cost-and-limit system that makes such questions answerable in principle; **the delta is that this genre has no such system and must adjudicate case by case** — so the working requirement is not consistency but **a stated basis**: whatever decides the outcome must be visible in the scene, so the reader can see it was decided rather than assigned.
entries.example: *Watchmen* is unusually rigorous here, because the one character with unbounded capability is given an explicit reason to decline every confrontation, which removes the adjudication problem rather than fudging it.
entries.application: For every fight, name what decides it before you write it — reach, preparation, terrain, information, will. If the answer is "the plot", the reader will see that, and it is the one thing they will remember about the issue.

entries.name: The Member Who Solves the Plot
entries.description: The roster member whose capability short-circuits the story, and the four honest ways to handle it.
entries.principle: Every asymmetric roster acquires a member who can simply solve most problems, and the genre's standard response — inventing per-story reasons they are unavailable — is the most damaging option, because each excuse is a small withdrawal from the reader's credit. `craft-21` **The Competence That Ends the Scene** treats this as a scene-construction problem. `fantasy:worldbuilding-16` treats power tiers, where a designer can simply place a character below the problem. **The delta is that this roster's tiers were set by unrelated authors and cannot be rebalanced.** At the system level there are exactly four durable answers: **bound the capability** in the specification so it never had this reach; **give them a jurisdiction** so their absence is structural rather than convenient; **make the story about a problem their capability does not address**; or **remove them from the roster** and stop paying the tax. Anything else is an excuse renewed monthly.
entries.example: *Justice League Unlimited* handled this by rotating focus and letting the roster's size make absence structural, which is the second answer applied at production level.
entries.application: Name which of the four you are using, in writing. A team that has not chosen one is using the fifth option — excuses — and the reader is keeping count even if you are not.

entries.name: The Weakest Ceiling Is the Team's Ceiling
entries.description: How threat scale is actually set on an ensemble book, and the trap in setting it wrongly.
entries.principle: A threat must be survivable by the least capable member present or that member cannot be in the scene, which means **the roster's weakest specification governs the whole book's scale**, not the strongest. Writers reason from the top of the roster and then discover their least powerful characters have nothing to do, at which point those characters are either given a hasty upgrade — the beginning of creep — or quietly dropped. The alternative is to treat the weakest member's ceiling as the design constraint and to build threats that are dangerous **at that level**, letting the powerful members' contribution be scale rather than survival. `fantasy:worldbuilding-16` treats power tiers in built settings; the delta is that a comics roster's tiers are set by unrelated authors decades apart and cannot be rebalanced.
entries.example: *Gotham Central* takes the constraint to its conclusion and builds an entire book at the bottom of the roster's ceiling, where the powerful are weather rather than participants.
entries.application: Write your threat so it is lethal to your least powerful member. Then check every other member still has something to do. If they do not, the threat is scaled to the wrong end of the roster.

entries.name: Combination as a Scene-Form
entries.description: Powers that join — the mechanism a whole carded tradition is built on, and which the American form barely uses.
entries.principle: In the sentai and tokusatsu line, combination is not an occasional flourish but **a structural scene-form with a fixed position in the episode**: separate capabilities, separate machines, separate colours, joined into a single larger thing at the point where individual effort has been shown to be insufficient. The form's requirements are strict and instructive — every component must be individually established, the combination must be visibly effortful, and the whole must be able to fail. `fantasy:worldbuilding-17` treats collective and ritual magic; **the delta is that this is a production tradition with a fixed episodic slot and a merchandising logic attached**, not a worldbuilding option, and it encodes a lesson the American team book rarely learns: cooperation reads as an achievement only if the individual attempt visibly failed first.
entries.example: *Himitsu Sentai Gorenger* establishes the pattern the tradition still runs on, with combination as the episode's structural resolution rather than as a spectacle inserted anywhere.
entries.application: Before any combined effort, show the individual attempt failing. The combination's whole meaning is that it was necessary, and a combination that arrives before the failure is a set piece with no argument.

entries.category: Power Creep as a Production Artefact
entries.name: Creep Is a Production Process
entries.description: The foundational card for this section — why capabilities inflate, stated as a mechanism rather than a complaint.
entries.principle: Power creep is usually described as writers failing to restrain themselves. It is better understood as the predictable output of a production system: each writer must make their run feel consequential, escalation is the cheapest available way to do that, no single escalation is unreasonable, and nobody owns the aggregate. `horror:craft-11` treats escalation as a genre problem where the pressure is on the individual work; `comedy:timing-28` treats it where the pressure is on the joke. **The delta is ownership** — in both those cases escalation is authored, and here it is emergent, accumulated across decades by people who never met, each of whom made a locally defensible decision. That reframing matters because it identifies the only two effective interventions: **a specification somebody maintains, or a reset**, and the genre uses the second because the first requires an institution.
entries.example: *Dragon Ball* is the clearest case in any tradition of escalation as a sustained structural principle rather than a drift — Fantasy's own `fantasy:trope-19` cards it as its weak example, and the delta is that here it is examined as a production logic rather than dismissed as an excess. *(Shueisha, weekly serialisation, 1984–1995.)*
entries.application: You cannot fix creep in your run. You can decline to contribute, and you can leave a written specification for whoever follows. That is the whole of what an individual writer controls.

entries.category: Power Creep as a Production Artefact
entries.name: Retroactive Respecification
entries.description: Discovering that a character could always do this, and what the discovery costs.
entries.principle: `trope-34` **The Power-Up** covers the earned escalation as it plays on the page. `fantasy:worldbuilding-1` treats the magic system stated up front, where what a practitioner can do is fixed before the story runs. **The delta is that this genre's specification is amended after publication.** The system-level move is different and more damaging: the **retroactive** upgrade, in which a new capability is presented as having been latent all along. It costs more than a straightforward power-up for a specific reason — it does not only change the character going forward, it **re-reads every previous story**, in which the character now failed to use something they had. A power-up leaves the archive intact; a respecification invalidates it. The genre does this constantly, usually to explain a plot requirement, and almost always without noticing that it has spent something.
entries.example: *The Man of Steel* is the deliberate opposite case, a wholesale respecification done openly as a reboot, which is the honest form of the same operation — DC, 1986, six issues, and everything it changed was announced.
entries.application: If a capability must be new, make it new. Latency is a way of avoiding the scene where the character acquires something, and that scene is worth more than the tidiness you are buying.

entries.category: Power Creep as a Production Artefact
entries.name: The Depowering and Its Half-Life
entries.description: The correction that never holds, and the one form of it that does.
entries.principle: `trope-35` **The Depowering** covers the device as it appears in a story. `fantasy:worldbuilding-19` treats the systematised magic economy, where a reduction is a change to a ledger the author controls. **The delta is that this ledger has other users.** At the system level the observable fact is that depowerings have a **half-life measured in editorial regimes**: the reduction is dramatic, well received, and reversed within a few years by a writer who needs the capability back, because the property's other users — adaptations, merchandising, crossovers — continue to require the character as previously specified. The exception, and it is the only reliable one, is the depowering that is **built into the premise** rather than applied to a character: a book whose whole situation depends on the reduction cannot restore it without ending itself.
entries.example: *Logan* holds its reduction because the reduction is the film's premise and its ending, not an intervention in an ongoing specification.
entries.application: If you are reducing a character, ask what in your story becomes impossible if it is reversed. If nothing, you have written a temporary condition and should plan for its restoration rather than being surprised by it.

entries.category: Power Creep as a Production Artefact
entries.name: Escalation With an Owner
entries.description: The one condition under which escalation works, and how to tell whether you have it.
entries.principle: Escalation is not inherently a defect — it is the engine of an entire successful tradition — and the difference between escalation that works and creep that corrodes is whether **somebody owns the curve**. Owned escalation has a designed shape: a known ceiling, a planned rate, a purpose the increases serve, and an end. Unowned escalation has none of those and is simply the sum of local decisions. `horror:craft-11` and `comedy:timing-28` both describe escalation inside a work with a single author, where ownership is automatic. **The delta is that in serial superhero publishing ownership is the exception**, and a writer's first question on any long-running book should be whether anyone holds the curve — because if nobody does, restraint on your part is a donation rather than a policy.
entries.example: *Dragon Ball* is the owned case, escalating deliberately toward a designed conclusion; the American shared universe over the same period is the unowned one, escalating to no shape at all. *(Weekly Shonen Jump, 1984–1995, one author.)*
entries.application: Ask who owns the curve on your book. If the answer is nobody, escalate as little as you can and document the ceiling you assumed, because the document is the only thing that outlives you.

entries.category: Power Creep as a Production Artefact
entries.name: Naming the Period and the Publisher
entries.description: The discipline this whole section requires, stated as a card because the section is unusable without it.
entries.principle: Every claim about power levels is period-bound and publisher-bound, and a claim that omits both is false somewhere. A character's capability at one publisher in one decade under one editorial regime bears no reliable relation to the same character's capability elsewhere or later, and reference material routinely merges them into a single fictitious specification. `fantasy:worldbuilding-18` can speak of a magic system in general because a built world has one author and one edition. **The delta is that this genre has no such thing as a character's power level, only a character's power level in a run**, and C-09 requires every period-bound rule in this pack to name its period and publisher for exactly this reason.
entries.example: *Whiz Comics #2* introduced a character whose capability specification has been rewritten by three publishers under two names across eighty years, and no single statement about what he can do is true across that span.
entries.application: Attach a run, a publisher and a decade to every power claim you make, in your notes if not on the page. The habit costs nothing and it is the difference between a specification and a rumour.

entries.name: The Capability That Is Anatomical
entries.description: The foundational card for this section — the power that is a fact about a body rather than a skill or a possession.
entries.principle: A large proportion of this genre's capabilities are anatomical: not learned, not equipped, not granted, but simply what this body is. `fantasy:worldbuilding-20` treats inherent versus acquired magic as a design axis affecting who can be a practitioner. **The delta here is that the superhero's anatomical capability is attached to a body that is also the character's public identity, their vulnerability and their metaphor at once** — the same body wears the costume, is exposed by the unmasking, and carries whatever the power is supposed to mean. This is why the genre's power design and its body politics cannot be separated, and why the next four cards are about bodies rather than about capabilities.
entries.example: *Fantastic Four #1* specifies four permanent bodily alterations rather than four acquired skills, and the one character who cannot resume an ordinary appearance became the property's centre of gravity.
entries.application: Ask whether your character could put the power down. If not, every scene about their body is also a scene about their power, and you should be writing those deliberately rather than discovering them.

entries.name: Transformation and the Untransformed Body
entries.description: What the ordinary body is for, in a story about the extraordinary one.
entries.principle: Transformation is among the genre's oldest structures and its most frequently wasted, because writers treat the untransformed state as a waiting room. The form's whole tension lives there: the transformed body is capable and the untransformed one is where consequence, relationship and vulnerability are stored. The tokusatsu tradition understands this better than the American one and encodes it in structure — the henshin is withheld, the pre-transformation body does most of the episode's work, and the transformation is the moment the episode has been arguing toward. `fantasy:worldbuilding-20` covers inherent capability; **the delta is that transformation makes inherence intermittent**, and everything interesting is in the interval.
entries.example: *Kamen Rider (1971 tv)* fixes the pattern that the tradition still runs on, giving the untransformed body the episode's argument and reserving the transformed one for its conclusion. *(Toei, weekly, 1971.)*
entries.application: Count the pages your protagonist spends untransformed. If it is under half, you are writing the costume rather than the person, and the transformation has nothing to be a change from.

entries.name: Prosthesis and a Poor Record
entries.description: The genre's treatment of disabled bodies, stated as the record shows it rather than as the genre would prefer.
entries.principle: This genre has used disability as origin, as compensation and as spectacle far more often than as a fact about a person, and the pack states that rather than working around it. Three patterns recur and are worth naming: the **cure**, in which a body is restored and the character's situation with it; the **compensation**, in which a lost capability is repaid with a greater one, so that the disability is a trade rather than a condition; and the **prosthesis as upgrade**, in which assistive technology is written as enhancement and the actual experience of using it disappears. `trope-39` **The Power That Is a Disability** covers the device on the page. `fantasy:worldbuilding-20` treats inherent versus acquired capability as a neutral design axis. **The delta here is the record** — a pattern across the form's history, which is a claim about the genre rather than about any card.
entries.example: *Daredevil #9 (Echo)* is the counter-case worth studying, a deaf protagonist whose deafness is neither cured nor compensated and whose perception is rendered as a way of being in the world rather than as an ability.
entries.application: If your character is disabled, check which of the three patterns you are in. If you are in none of them, check again in the second draft, because the genre's defaults reassert themselves during revision more than during planning.

entries.name: The Costume as Second Skin
entries.description: The suit as part of the specification, and the question of where the body ends.
entries.principle: For a substantial number of characters the costume is not clothing but **equipment carrying part of the capability**, and this raises a specification question the genre usually leaves unanswered: how much of the power is the person? The answer determines what can be taken away, what an opponent can target, what a successor inherits, and whether the character exists without the suit. `fantasy:craft-13` treats the enchanted object and the question of where its power resides. **The delta is that the superhero's object is worn, public and identifying** — it is simultaneously the equipment, the trademark and the face, which means removing it is three different kinds of loss at once.
entries.example: *Blue Beetle (Jaime Reyes)* makes the boundary the actual subject, with a capability that is attached, not entirely under its holder's control, and not clearly separable from him.
entries.application: State how much of the capability is the suit. Then write the scene without it. If that scene is impossible, you have specified a device with a person attached and should know it.

entries.name: The Body That Cannot Be Hurt
entries.description: Invulnerability as a scene problem, and what a scene does when physical threat is unavailable.
entries.principle: Invulnerability removes the genre's default source of tension and is therefore treated as a design error, but the error is in the response rather than the specification. The usual response is to invent an exception — a substance, a magic, an opponent tiered above — which is creep by another name and works once. The alternative is to accept that threat must move to what the body does not cover: **the people around them, the record, the decision, the time it takes.** A character who cannot be hurt can still be too slow, too public, too late, or wrong. `fantasy:trope-1` treats the invulnerable figure in built settings, where an exception can be written into the world's rules; the delta is that here the exception is written into the character and every one of them is permanent.
entries.example: *Superman: Whatever Happened to the Man of Tomorrow?* threatens everyone except its protagonist and is the more frightening for it, which is the whole demonstration.
entries.application: Take a scene where your invulnerable character is threatened physically and rewrite it so the threat is to time, to reputation or to someone present. It is almost always the better scene, and it costs the specification nothing.

entries.category: Before 1938: the Pulp, the Strip and the Masked Man
entries.name: The Costumed Hero Existed Before the Superhero Did
entries.description: The furniture assembled decades early, in three separate media, by people who never met.
entries.principle: By the mid-1930s every visible component of the superhero was already in circulation and none of them were together. The concealed identity, the fixed method and the proprietary city came from the pulps; the costume and the recognisable silhouette came from the newspaper strip; the physical superlative came from prose science fiction and from the strongman traditions of stage and screen. What did not exist was the **combination**, and the combination is the invention. This matters for a writer because it dissolves the question of who invented the superhero into a more useful one: which component is your story actually built on, since each carries a different set of obligations.
entries.example: *The Scarlet Pimpernel* (1905) supplies the double identity and the deliberate public pose; *The Curse of Capistrano* (1919) adds the mark, the costume and the oppressed populace; *The Phantom* (1936) supplies the skin-tight costume and the mask before anyone flies.
entries.application: Name which prehistoric component your character is built from — the concealment, the method, the city, the costume, the physical superlative. The genre's conventions attach to the components separately, and a character built from two of five will feel thin in ways the missing three explain.

entries.category: Before 1938: the Pulp, the Strip and the Masked Man
entries.name: The Newspaper Strip Was the Senior Medium
entries.description: The form the comic book was a cheap reprint of, and what that inheritance fixed.
entries.principle: The comic book began as a **repackaging format for newspaper strips**, which is why its earliest conventions are strip conventions: the tier, the daily beat, the recurring cast, and the assumption that a reader arrives mid-story and must be re-oriented. The strip was the prestigious medium, with the larger audience and the better-paid creators; the comic book was the disposable derivative. Almost everything the form later treated as native to itself — the recap, the serialised arc, the fixed cast in a fixed city — arrived from a medium that had solved those problems for a daily audience decades earlier.
entries.example: *Flash Gordon* (1934) establishes the serialised adventure with a continuing cast and escalating scale in a medium of six panels a day, and the comic book inherits its pacing assumptions wholesale.
entries.application: When a comics convention seems arbitrary, check whether it is a strip convention that survived the change of container. Most of the ones that seem arbitrary are, and knowing that tells you which are load-bearing and which are habit.

entries.category: Before 1938: the Pulp, the Strip and the Masked Man
entries.name: The Prehistory Is a Lineage, Not an Origin
entries.description: What a claim about the prehistory can and cannot support.
entries.principle: It is accurate to say the superhero has ancestors and inaccurate to say it descends from them, and the distinction is not pedantry. A **lineage** claim identifies a documented transmission — this creator read that work, this convention was borrowed in this year. An **origin** claim asserts that the later thing is a continuation of the earlier one, which back-projects a category onto material that did not have it. The pack's standing position, carded at `subgenre-14`, is that the pulp relationship is a lineage; **this card's addition is historiographical rather than generic** — it is about what kind of evidence each claim needs, and the answer is that a lineage claim needs a document and an origin claim needs an argument nobody has successfully made.
entries.example: *Gladiator* (1930) is routinely named as a Superman antecedent, and what is actually documented is a resemblance plus a denial; the claim is repeated far more confidently than its evidence supports.
entries.application: Before writing that a genre came from somewhere, ask what would have to be true — a letter, an interview, a dated borrowing. If nothing would settle it, you are making an aesthetic claim in historical clothing, and you should say so.

entries.category: Before 1938: the Pulp, the Strip and the Masked Man
entries.name: What 1938 Actually Changed
entries.description: The single year that gets the credit, and what specifically happened in it.
entries.principle: The change *Action Comics* #1 made was not any of its components — a strong man, a costume, a secret identity and a city were all available — but the **assembly plus the commercial demonstration**. It proved a costumed figure with a concealed identity could carry a title, at a scale that reorganised an industry within two years, and the imitation was immediate and total. The useful framing for a writer is that 1938 is a **market event with a formal consequence**, not a creative singularity. What follows in the next four years is not a genre developing but a business copying a proven configuration as fast as it can print.
entries.example: *Action Comics #1* (1938) and *Detective Comics #27* (1939) are eleven months apart and the second is already an answer to the first — a figure defined by everything the first one is not.
entries.application: Study the second one rather than the first. Genres are defined by the answer to the founding work more than by the founding work, and the profitable positions are the ones the answer opened.

entries.name: The Boom and Its Arithmetic
entries.description: The scale of the first boom, and the production conditions it created.
entries.principle: Between 1938 and 1945 the superhero comic went from nonexistent to one of the highest-circulation periodical categories in the United States, and the arithmetic of that expansion determined the work. Demand outran the available talent by an enormous margin, which meant **anyone who could draw fast was hired**, most of them very young, most paid by the page, most working to a schedule no craft could survive intact. The formal consequences are visible on every page of the period and are usually misread as incompetence: the flat staging, the repeated poses, the resolved-in-eight-pages plot. They are the visible shape of a production rate.
entries.example: *Whiz Comics #2* (1940) and *Captain America Comics #1* (1941) are both products of a market absorbing every imitation it could get, eleven and eighteen months after the configuration was proven.
entries.application: When reading period work, separate the constraint from the choice. Almost everything a modern reader finds crude about 1940s superhero comics is a rate, and almost everything genuinely inventive in them happened despite it.

entries.name: The Studio That Was a Production Line
entries.description: The shop system, which is how most of this material was actually made.
entries.principle: A large share of the 1938–1945 output came from **packaging shops** — independent studios that produced complete comics to order for publishers who had a distribution slot and no editorial staff. The shop divided labour by task rather than by title: one hand pencilled, another inked, another lettered, another wrote, and the work was assigned by whoever was free. This is the origin of two things the genre still lives with. It is why authorship of the period is genuinely uncertain rather than merely undocumented, and it is why **the credit conventions of comics assume a division of labour** that most other narrative forms do not have.
entries.example: *The Spirit* (1940) is the counter-case that proves the rule — a strip produced under a named creator's control, in a period when almost nothing was, and remembered accordingly.
entries.application: When attributing period work, name the claim you are making — wrote, pencilled, inked, devised — and expect the record to answer at most one of them. `checklist-7` is the operational form of this.

entries.name: Publishing Into a War
entries.description: What the war did to the form, in three concrete ways rather than one thematic one.
entries.principle: The war is usually discussed as subject matter, and its three material effects mattered more. **Distribution**: comics went to servicemen in enormous volume, which expanded the audience beyond children and set circulation records the domestic market alone could not have produced. **Labour**: the men who drew them were conscripted, which opened the field to women and to older and younger workers for the duration, and closed it again afterwards. **Paper**: rationing constrained page counts and print runs, and publishers allocated scarce stock to proven sellers, which entrenched the leaders and suppressed new entrants.
entries.example: *Captain America Comics #1* is cover-dated March 1941 and was on sale **20 December 1940** — a costumed figure striking a head of state roughly a year before the United States entered the war, which is a fact about publishing lead times as much as about politics.
