entries.application: For any period claim, check the on-sale date rather than the cover date. In this era they differ by two to three months and the difference frequently changes what the work can have been responding to.

entries.name: Who Was Doing the Work
entries.description: The composition of the workforce, stated plainly, and the reason the record is thin.
entries.principle: The people who built this genre were disproportionately young, working-class, Jewish, and shut out of the better-paid commercial art and advertising markets that would have employed them otherwise; the wartime years also brought in a cohort of women who were largely gone from the field by 1950. The historical record of all of this is poor for structural reasons rather than accidental ones: **shop production obscured authorship, house names concealed individuals, and nobody was archiving a disposable product.** The consequence for anyone writing about the period is that absence of evidence here is genuinely not evidence of absence, and the honest form of a claim is bounded.
entries.example: *Police Comics #1* (1941) carries work whose attribution is still argued over, which is the ordinary condition of the period rather than an unusual case.
entries.application: State negatives as bounded searches — "no credit appears in the indicia and none is recorded in the standard indexes" — never as "she was not credited." `checklist-16` exists for this and this period is where it earns most.

entries.category: 1946-1956: the Collapse, Wertham and the Code
entries.name: The Genre Almost Ended
entries.description: The collapse that is skipped in most accounts, and what actually caused it.
entries.principle: The superhero did not survive the 1940s in any healthy form. By the early 1950s the category had shrunk to a handful of surviving titles at a single publisher while crime, horror, romance, western and funny-animal comics took the market. **The cause was readers leaving, not censorship** — the Code arrives in 1954, after the collapse was well advanced, and it killed the horror and crime lines that had replaced superheroes rather than the superheroes themselves. Getting this sequence right matters, because the popular account inverts cause and effect and produces the belief that the genre was suppressed when in fact it was abandoned and then rescued.
entries.example: The wartime generation carded at *All Star Comics #8* (1941) was substantially out of print within a decade, and *Showcase #4* (1956) is a revival of a discontinued form rather than a continuation of a living one.
entries.application: When a genre's decline is attributed to an external attack, check the dates of the decline against the dates of the attack. They are very often in the wrong order, and the real cause is usually the duller one.

entries.category: 1946-1956: the Collapse, Wertham and the Code
entries.name: Wertham Against the Received Version
entries.description: The most misreported figure in comics history, with both positions carried.
entries.principle: The received version — a crank psychiatrist claimed comics caused delinquency and had them banned — is wrong in nearly every part, and the accurate account is more interesting. *Seduction of the Innocent* (Rinehart, April 1954) argued that comics were a mass-culture pathogen harming ordinary children, on clinical case material rather than statistics. Its author had a substantial record: he founded the **Lafargue Clinic** in Harlem in 1946, and in October 1951 testified for the plaintiffs in the Delaware school-segregation cases, testimony that Chancellor Collins J. Seitz cited in ruling for the plaintiffs on 1 April 1952 — the only *Brown* companion case won at state level. He opposed censorship of adult reading and proposed restricting sales to under-15s. **And Carol Tilley's 2012 study in *Information & Culture* documents that he altered children's ages, condensed and rewrote quoted statements, and combined multiple subjects into composite testimony.** Both facts are true. **The pack carries both positions and adjudicates neither** (C-16): Tilley's finding is the settled account of his data handling, and Hall and Friedman's 2020 forensic-psychiatry treatment argues in turn that "Wertham as supervillain" is itself a constructed narrative that erases the civil-rights record.
entries.example: His objection to *Action Comics #1*'s protagonist was ideological rather than violent — that the figure taught children that strength is the desirable way to prevail — and his objection to the vigilante generally was that it made constituted authority look impotent, which is the objection that survived into the Code.
entries.application: If you repeat any claim about Wertham, name your source. This is the topic in comics history where the confident version is most reliably the wrong one, in both directions.

entries.category: 1946-1956: the Collapse, Wertham and the Code
entries.name: The Hearings That Recommended Nothing
entries.description: What the 1954 Senate subcommittee actually did, which was not what the genre believes.
entries.principle: The Senate Subcommittee to Investigate Juvenile Delinquency held comics hearings in New York on **21 and 22 April and 4 June 1954**, chaired by **Robert C. Hendrickson** — not Kefauver, who was a member and dominated the questioning, and whose name has attached itself to the proceedings ever since. Its 1955 interim report found crime and horror comics potentially harmful and then declined to act: *"The subcommittee flatly rejects all suggestions of governmental censorship as being totally out of keeping with our basic American concepts of a free press."* **It recommended no federal legislation and imposed none.** What it did instead was warn the industry to regulate itself and make the reputational consequences of failure obvious. The coercion was real; the mechanism was not law.
entries.example: The Code that followed was drafted and adopted by publishers, and the material that actually vanished — crime and horror — vanished because wholesalers would not carry unsealed books, which is a distribution decision rather than a legal one.
entries.application: Distinguish a legal prohibition from a distribution refusal. This genre's constraints have almost always been the second kind, and mistaking them for the first produces a false picture of who could have decided otherwise.

entries.category: 1946-1956: the Collapse, Wertham and the Code
entries.name: The Code the Industry Wrote for Itself
entries.description: The Comics Code as an industry instrument, its superhero-specific clauses, and how it ended.
entries.principle: The **Comics Magazine Association of America**, a trade body formed by publishers in September 1954, adopted the Code on **26 October 1954**, in force for comics cover-dated January 1955; the magistrate **Charles F. Murphy** was its first administrator and it ran to 41 provisions. It had no legal force and enormous practical force, because unsealed books did not reach the newsstand. Two clauses shaped superhero storytelling for a generation more than any editorial policy did: **"Policemen, judges, Government officials, and respected institutions shall never be presented in such a way as to create disrespect for established authority"** — a direct constraint on the genre's central premise — and **"In every instance good shall triumph over evil"**, which forecloses ambiguity and tragedy by rule. *(CMAA, United States, 1954–2011.)*
entries.example: The revision of January 1971 readmitted drug material and, separately, vampires and werewolves "in the classic tradition," which is why the supernatural re-enters shared universes in that year and not before; the Code ended not by repeal but by abandonment, DC dropping it on 20 January 2011 and Archie the following day, and the seal is now owned by the Comic Book Legal Defense Fund.
entries.application: When reading anything published between 1955 and 1971, treat the absent options as constraints rather than as choices. A period writer who never wrote a sympathetic criminal may have had opinions, or may have had a rulebook.

entries.name: The Reinvention Was a Method Before It Was a Style
entries.description: What actually changed in the revival, which was the production process.
entries.principle: The 1956–1970 revival is usually described stylistically — brighter, more scientific, more soap-operatic — and the durable change was **procedural**. Work moved from full-script toward a collaborative process in which the artist received a premise and constructed the story's pacing and staging on the page, with dialogue added afterwards. That single change put narrative authority in the artist's hands, produced the period's characteristic density of incident, and created the credit ambiguity that has generated litigation and argument ever since. A style can be imitated; a method changes what kinds of stories are producible.
entries.example: *Fantastic Four #1* (1961) and *Amazing Fantasy #15* (1962) are products of this process, and their pacing — several plots advancing at once, incident carried visually rather than narrated — is a property of the method rather than of a house taste. *(Marvel Comics, United States, 1961–1970.)*
entries.application: Ask who is deciding your story's beats. If it is the artist, write premises rather than panel descriptions and expect to dialogue what comes back. If it is you, expect the pages to be less dense and plan accordingly.

entries.name: The Method and Who It Credited
entries.description: The dispute that follows from the method, and why it cannot be settled.
entries.principle: A process in which one person supplies a premise, another constructs the narrative, and the first then writes the dialogue produces work whose authorship is **genuinely divided rather than merely disputed**, and no credit convention available at the time recorded that division. The resulting argument is not a case of one party lying. It is the predictable consequence of a production method that outran its paperwork, in an industry with no mechanism for recording joint authorship and every incentive not to. The pack states this rather than adjudicating it, and notes that the dispute's later phases are about ownership and money rather than about who did what.
entries.example: *The X-Men #1* (1963) and *My Greatest Adventure #80* (1963) are near-contemporaneous and carry credit information of quite different reliability, which is the ordinary condition of the period. *(Marvel and DC, United States, 1961–1970.)*
entries.application: For any work of this period, ask what the credit box was capable of recording. In most cases the answer is "one name and a job title," and everything else has to be reconstructed from testimony that is decades old and interested.

entries.name: Newsstand Decline and the Fan Who Stayed
entries.description: The audience change that made everything after it possible.
entries.principle: Through the 1960s the general newsstand audience contracted while a smaller, older, self-identifying readership consolidated — one that wrote letters, attended conventions, collected back issues and cared about continuity. This is the most consequential audience change in the genre's history, because it inverted the economics: circulation fell while the value of each remaining reader rose, and publishers began writing for people who would notice. **Continuity, the letter column, the in-joke, the cameo, and eventually the direct market are all downstream of this one shift.** It is also the origin of the genre's permanent tension between the readers it has and the readers it would need to grow.
entries.example: *Batman (1966 tv)* is the counter-case running in the same years — a mass general audience reached by treating the material as camp, producing an enormous short-term expansion and no durable readers at all. *(ABC, United States, 1966–1968.)*
entries.application: Know which audience your book is written for, because they want opposite things. The consolidating reader wants accrual and reward for attention; the general reader wants a self-contained thing that assumes nothing. Almost no work serves both.

entries.name: Against the Metal Ages
entries.description: Where the Golden/Silver/Bronze scheme came from, what it is for, and why this pack does not use it.
entries.principle: The metal ages are not a historiographical scheme. **"Golden Age" was coined by Richard A. Lupoff in the fanzine *Comic Art* #1 in 1960** — retrospective fan nostalgia naming a lost era. **"Silver Age" has no documented coiner**: it is widely traced to a 1966 letter column, and no issue, letter or name is verifiable. **"Bronze Age" has no documented first use at all.** All three hardened into back-issue grading categories through the price guides, which is what they are still doing. Benjamin Woo's "An Age-Old Problem" (*International Journal of Comic Art*, 2008) sets out the scholarly objection: no agreement on boundaries, dating by personal interpretation, no empirical grounding, a decline narrative smuggled in by the descending metals, and a scheme that periodises American superhero comics while presenting itself as a periodisation of comics. **This pack dates by year and condition instead** (§0.18), and Chris Gavaler's alternative — periodising by Comics Code revisions — is the one worth knowing, because Code eras correspond to what was permitted on the page.
entries.example: This collection's own six blocks are dated ranges with named conditions, and `history-12` is why: the Code's dates are documentary, and what a writer could put on a page changed on them.
entries.application: If you use an Age, say which years you mean. The term will otherwise be read as three different spans by three different readers, and none of them will be the one you meant.

entries.category: 1970-1986: Relevance, the Direct Market and the Creator-Rights Fight
entries.name: Relevance Arrives and Does Not Sell
entries.description: The period's best-remembered experiment and its commercial record.
entries.principle: The turn toward social subject matter around 1970 is the most-cited moment in the genre's middle period and it was, at the time, a commercial disappointment: the celebrated titles sold poorly and were cancelled or redirected within a few years. This is worth knowing for two reasons. It separates **critical memory from market performance**, which is a distinction the genre's own histories routinely collapse. And it explains the subsequent decade's caution: the relevance experiment's failure is the reason the mainstream returned to genre material until an entirely different economic structure made a second attempt viable.
entries.example: *Green Lantern (O'Neil/Adams run)* is the period's emblem and ran fourteen issues before the title ceased publication for four years, resuming only in 1976. *(DC Comics, United States, 1970–1972.)*
entries.application: When you cite a work as proof that an approach works, check whether it sold. Both facts are usable — "this was admired and did not sell" is a real finding — but conflating them will mislead whoever you are pitching.

entries.category: 1970-1986: Relevance, the Direct Market and the Creator-Rights Fight
entries.name: The Direct Market Had More Than One Inventor
entries.description: The change that made the modern industry, and a contested credit.
entries.principle: The direct market swapped **returnability for discount**: the retailer ordered firm and non-returnable, paid in advance, and received a much deeper discount, ordering from a catalogue months ahead so publishers could print to order rather than overprint speculatively. Under the newsstand system that preceded it, unsold copies were returned as stripped covers or, later, on unverified affidavit — an arrangement that invited fraud and made low-circulation titles impossible. **Phil Seuling**, through Sea Gate Distributors from 1972 and shipping under direct terms from autumn 1973, is the person usually credited. **The credit is contested by people who were there**: the underground "comix" had been distributed on these terms since 1968–69, the Donahue brothers ran direct arrangements earlier without scaling them, and the historian Bob Beerbohm argues that attributing it to one man does "disservice to the hundreds of others." What is not in dispute is that Seuling brought those terms to the mainstream publishers; whether that constitutes inventing the direct market, or scaling something several people were already doing, is exactly what the participants disagree about.
entries.example: Everything continuity-heavy, adult-oriented or niche in the subsequent forty years is downstream of guaranteed sell-through, which is the one thing this change supplied.
entries.application: When you hear that one person invented an industry practice, ask who else was doing it. In this case the other accounts are documented, and the shorthand version omits them.

entries.category: 1970-1986: Relevance, the Direct Market and the Creator-Rights Fight
entries.name: What Siegel and Shuster Actually Got
entries.description: The settlement everyone cites, with its actual terms.
entries.principle: In December 1975, with a large-budget Superman film in production and a public campaign led by Neal Adams and Jerry Robinson drawing national press, Warner Communications agreed terms with the character's creators. **They received an annual stipend of $20,000 each, medical benefits, and creator credit on future Superman material — and no ownership, no equity and no share of revenue**, in exchange for dropping their claims. The credit had been stripped in retaliation after their 1947–48 suit, disappearing from *Action Comics* #119 in February 1948, and was restored in 1976 after twenty-eight years. The settlement is routinely cited as the moment creators' rights were recognised. **It is more accurately the moment a company decided that public destitution was worse publicity than a pension.**
entries.example: The 1947–48 suit itself ended with the court holding that the publisher owned Superman, and a payment of $94,013.16 for both men — a figure worth stating, because the scale of it against the property's value is the whole argument. *(National/DC Comics, United States, 1938–1976.)*
entries.application: When citing this settlement as a precedent, state its terms. A pension and a byline is a real outcome and it is not a rights victory, and the difference is what every subsequent negotiation has turned on.

entries.category: 1970-1986: Relevance, the Direct Market and the Creator-Rights Fight
entries.name: Eighty-Eight Pages of Eight Thousand
entries.description: The original-art dispute, and the clause that made it a rights case.
entries.principle: In 1984 Marvel offered to return original artwork to the artist who had drawn well over eight thousand pages for it in the 1960s — and offered **eighty-eight pages**, roughly one percent, conditional on signing a four-page release, when other artists were being returned their art on a one-page form. The release barred him from displaying or reproducing his own art and reserved modification rights to the publisher, and included a clause **prohibiting him from assisting others in contesting the company's copyright ownership**. That clause is why the episode is a rights case rather than a property dispute: it attempted to buy silence with a man's own pages. *The Comics Journal* campaigned from summer 1985, a petition drew near-unanimous professional support through 1986, and in May 1987 Marvel dropped the four-page release and returned roughly 1,900 pages. *(Marvel Comics, United States, 1984–1987.)*
entries.example: Thousands of pages were never accounted for, and the later copyright-termination litigation brought by the estate is a separate matter of a different decade, settled in 2014 — the two are routinely conflated.
entries.application: Read what a rights document asks you to give up, not what it offers to give back. The offer in this case was one percent and the ask was the right to help anyone else.

entries.category: 1986-2000: the Turn, the Boom and the Crash
entries.name: The Turn Was Not One Year
entries.description: The period label this pack uses, and the honest span behind it.
entries.principle: The deconstructive turn is conventionally dated to 1986 and the dates do not support a single year. Moore's *Marvelman / Miracleman* had been running in a British anthology since March 1982; *Crisis on Infinite Earths* began in April 1985 and *Squadron Supreme* in September 1985, the latter putting analogue heroes in government a full year before the year that gets the credit; *Batman: Year One* is February 1987 and *Batman: The Killing Joke* is 1988. **1986 is the year the market noticed, not the year the work began.** The block is dated 1986–2000 because that is when the commercial and formal consequences run, and the card states the span so the label does not do work it cannot bear.
entries.example: *Watchmen* itself is a 1986–87 serial; only its first issue is 1986, and the collected edition that most readers know is later still.
entries.application: When you date a movement, date the earliest work rather than the most famous one. The gap between them is usually four or five years and it usually contains the thing that actually explains the movement.

entries.category: 1986-2000: the Turn, the Boom and the Crash
entries.name: The Speculative Boom
entries.description: The early-1990s expansion, and the fact that it was not a readership.
entries.principle: Between roughly 1991 and 1993 the direct market expanded enormously on the strength of buyers who were purchasing comics as appreciating assets rather than as reading matter — multiple copies, variant covers, sealed and unread. The critical fact, and the one that makes the subsequent collapse legible, is that **the peak was substantially fictitious**: Comichron's own caveat on the record month of April 1993, when 48 million comics moved into the direct market, is that many were for the speculator market, many were never sold to consumers, and many were never paid for. A boom measured in orders rather than in readers is a boom in inventory.
entries.example: *X-Men #1 (1991 comic)* sold over eight million copies on five covers, a record that still stands and that measures collectors completing sets rather than people reading a comic. *(Marvel Comics, United States, 1991–1993.)*
entries.application: Distinguish orders from readers whenever you meet a sales figure in this industry. The two diverge most exactly when the numbers are most impressive, and every reference work quotes the impressive one.

entries.category: 1986-2000: the Turn, the Boom and the Crash
entries.name: The Crash and Who Paid For It
entries.description: The collapse's mechanism, and the people it actually fell on.
entries.principle: The correction had two engines running at once. The speculative demand evaporated, leaving retailers holding non-returnable inventory bought at the peak — the direct market's founding trade, firm orders for a deeper discount, working exactly as designed and in the worst possible direction. And the distribution structure was destroyed from inside: Marvel bought the Heroes World distributor on 28 December 1994 and went exclusive with it for books shipping in July 1995; DC, Image and Dark Horse signed exclusively with Diamond in response; the remaining distributors lost 35–40% of volume against fixed costs and collapsed. Marvel filed for Chapter 11 on **27 December 1996**, and announced in April 1997 that it was closing Heroes World and returning to Diamond, leaving one distributor. **The retailers absorbed the inventory and a great many of them did not survive it.**
entries.example: Documented totals show the top 300 comics selling roughly $244 million at retail in 1997 and falling again in 1998, with 100.3 million copies in 1997 against 84.5 million in 1998. *(United States direct market, 1994–1998.)*
entries.application: When a market's terms transfer risk to one party, find out who that party is before predicting what a downturn does. Here it was the shops, and the industry's shape since is a consequence of how many of them closed.

entries.category: 1986-2000: the Turn, the Boom and the Crash
entries.name: The Statistic That Cannot Be Counted
entries.description: The industry's most-repeated number, and the fact that it has no source.
entries.principle: The claim that comic shops fell from around nine thousand to around four thousand is the single most-cited statistic about this period, and **neither endpoint is verifiable**. The best available archive puts the 1993 peak at somewhat over **six thousand storefronts** against roughly **eleven thousand ordering accounts** — and the two are different units, because accounts included flea-market vendors, mail-order sellers and buying clubs that were never shops. Trade reporting that quotes the larger figures describes them as unsourced. **No census of comic shops has ever been conducted.** The useful card is not a corrected number but the condition: an industry with no membership body and no registration requirement cannot produce the statistic everyone quotes about it, and every figure in circulation is an estimate of an estimate.
entries.example: Distributor reporting itself begins late — indexed sales from September 1996 and actual copies shipped only from February 2003 — so the commonly quoted collapse from a billion dollars cannot be reconstructed from documented data at either end.
entries.application: Before repeating a number about this industry, ask who counted and when they started. For most of the period the answer is nobody, and a bounded "not documented" is worth more than a confident figure.

entries.category: Identity, Adolescence and the Two Lives
entries.name: Erikson Is Scaffolding, Not Evidence
entries.description: The developmental framework the genre borrows, and what it can actually bear.
entries.principle: The reading of the secret identity as adolescent identity work borrows Erik Erikson's stage model, and the borrowing is usually presented as though it imported empirical authority. It does not. Erikson's model is psychosocial theory developed from clinical observation, and its empirical standing is weak in a specific and documented way: Dunkel and Harbke's 2017 review pooled 62 correlation matrices from 50 samples, N = 20,326, and found the stage measures load on **a single general factor rather than eight separable stages**. James Marcia's operationalisation — crossing exploration against commitment to give four identity statuses — is the empirically usable part, and the useful thing for a writer is the second dimension. **Foreclosure**, high commitment with no exploration, is a distinct and dramatically rich state that writers routinely collapse into either confusion or resolution: the character who became the hero without ever having questioned it is not the same as one who explored and chose. (robustness: contested)
entries.example: The genre's most common identity arc runs from diffusion straight to achievement and skips foreclosure entirely, which is why so many origin stories feel as though a step is missing — it is.
entries.application: Place your character on both axes, not one. If they are highly committed and have explored nothing, write that as a state rather than as a stage on the way somewhere, because it is one.

entries.category: Identity, Adolescence and the Two Lives
entries.name: The Mutant Body as a Reading
entries.description: The best-known critical account of the superhero body, labelled as what it is.
entries.principle: Scott Bukatman's *Matters of Gravity: Special Effects and Supermen in the 20th Century* (Duke University Press, 2003) collects, as its third chapter, the essay "X-Bodies: The Torment of the Mutant Superhero," originally published in 1994. It reads the mutant body as a figure for adolescent bodily anxiety and social stigma — a body that changes without permission, marks its owner, and is both the source of power and the reason for concealment. **This card carries no robustness tier because there is nothing to replicate.** Bukatman's method is cultural criticism and phenomenological analysis; the essay offers no data, no sample and no measurement, and does not purport to. The pack states this explicitly because a reader who mistakes it for evidence about actual adolescent readers has misread the genre of the source rather than the source.
entries.example: The reading applies to any body that alters involuntarily and must then be hidden, which is why it has been extended well past the X-Men and why the extensions are also readings rather than findings.
entries.application: Use the argument, and cite it as an argument. If you need to claim something about real adolescents, you need a different kind of source and this pack's `psychology-1` and `psychology-6` are where to start.

entries.category: Identity, Adolescence and the Two Lives
entries.name: The Costume Does Not Do It to You
entries.description: The single most-cited piece of psychology in writing about costumes, and its actual status.
entries.principle: "Enclothed cognition" is the claim that wearing a garment affects cognition when its symbolic meaning is held in mind — in the original, a coat described as a doctor's coat improved attention while the identical coat described as a painter's coat did not (Adam & Galinsky, *JESP* 48(4), 2012). **A preregistered direct replication with a larger sample failed to find the effect** (Burns et al., *JESP* 83, 2019), and an earlier attempt failed on working memory. A 2025 meta-analysis argues post-2015 work retains evidential value while conceding replicability concerns about the early studies — **and it is authored by Adam and Galinsky**, which is a defence rather than an adjudication and must not be cited as independent. Note also what the original claim was: not that the garment acts on the wearer, but that **believing what it means does**, which is a claim about a character's beliefs rather than about textiles. (robustness: unreplicated)
entries.example: The genre's own best treatments have always written it as belief rather than as fabric — the mask as a licence the wearer grants themselves — which is on firmer ground than the citation was.
entries.application: Write the costume's effect as something your character believes, and you need no psychology at all. Cite the study as an empirical warrant and you are resting weight on an effect that did not survive a direct replication.

entries.name: Wish-Fulfilment Is an Argument
entries.description: The genre's oldest psychological reading, and the literature that does not exist behind it.
entries.principle: The claim that superhero fiction serves wish-fulfilment — that readers borrow an agency they lack — is the oldest psychological account of the genre and it is a humanities and psychoanalytic argument, not a finding. **This card carries no robustness tier because there is nothing to tier.** A search of the empirical literature for any work connecting superhero fiction to locus of control, self-efficacy as a trait, or compensatory control returns **nothing**; this is a bounded negative from a search conducted for this pack in August 2026, not an assumption. The nearest adjacent evidence is not about superheroes at all and is carded separately at `psychology-5`. The argument remains worth using — it is generative and it describes something readers report — but it should be offered as a reading, and a writer who cites it as psychology is citing a vacancy.
entries.example: The reading long predates any of the measurement traditions it is usually dressed in, and the genre's own critical literature has always treated it as interpretation rather than as result.
entries.application: If you want the wish-fulfilment frame, take it from the criticism and say so. If you want an empirical claim about what your reader gains, you will have to make do with `psychology-5`, which is smaller and about something else.

entries.name: Transportation, Not Superpowers
entries.description: The closest thing to evidence for the empowerment claim, stated at its real size.
entries.principle: The nearest empirical support for the idea that heroic fiction changes a reader's sense of agency is Isberner and colleagues (*Discourse Processes* 56(8), 2018): narratives featuring protagonists who display high self-efficacy shifted readers' own control beliefs — **but only when transportation into the story was strong, and the effect was temporary.** A second experiment showed it was mediated by transportation and identification. Three limits are load-bearing and are usually dropped in the retelling. It is about **strong protagonists generally**, not superheroes. It is a **temporary** shift, not a trait change. And it is a **single lab with no replication located**. The genuinely useful implication is not about power at all: whatever effect exists runs through **absorption**, which is a property of craft rather than of capability. (robustness: unreplicated)
entries.example: On this evidence a well-written competent protagonist in any genre would do the same work, and a badly written flying one would not do it at all.
entries.application: If you want a reader to leave feeling more capable, spend your effort on transportation — on whether they are absorbed — rather than on how much your protagonist can lift.

entries.name: What the Longitudinal Studies Actually Found
entries.description: The research on superhero media and children, and the effect it looked for and did not find.
entries.principle: Coyne and colleagues (*Journal of Abnormal Child Psychology* 45(8), 2017) followed 240 preschoolers across a year, explicitly to test whether superhero media teaches **defending** — sticking up for victimised peers, the behaviour adults hope is being modelled. Engagement predicted **increased physical and relational aggression** a year later, and was **unrelated to prosocial behaviour and unrelated to defending**. A five-wave study following 430 children from around 29 months (*Frontiers in Psychology* 16, 2025) reproduces the direction and disaggregates engagement: early identification, toy play and media each predicted higher aggression, while **dressing up was related to very few outcomes**. Both are longitudinal and correlational, both use parent report for predictor and outcome, neither randomises exposure, and no meta-analysis of superhero media specifically exists. (robustness: contested)
entries.example: The distinction between identification and dress-up is the finding a writer can use: wearing the costume carried almost nothing, and believing you are him carried the signal.
entries.application: If you write a character who claims superhero stories taught them to protect people, you are writing the belief rather than the finding — which is legitimate, and worth knowing you are doing.

entries.category: Attachment, Parasocial Relationship and the Fan
entries.name: The Parasocial Bond Is Real
entries.description: The best-evidenced construct in this collection, and the distinction inside it.
entries.principle: Horton and Wohl named "para-social interaction" in *Psychiatry* 19(3), 1956 — an essay, not a study, reporting no data. The construct that grew from it is now well evidenced and splits in two, and the split matters. **Parasocial interaction** is the in-the-moment sense of mutual awareness during exposure; **the parasocial relationship** is the enduring bond that persists between exposures. A meta-analysis of 120 studies across four decades (Tukachinsky, Walter & Saucier, *Journal of Communication* 70(6), 2020) establishes that parasocial relationships are measurable and predict involvement and persuasion, and that the two constructs are only **moderately correlated** and should not be treated as one thing. The evidence thins considerably when narrowed to **fictional** characters specifically, where the studies are few, mostly correlational and largely built on non-standardised measures. (robustness: robust)
entries.example: A reader's relationship with a character across a decade of issues is the second construct, not the first, and it is the one that survives a bad issue.
entries.application: Decide which one your story is about. A single overwhelming encounter is interaction; a bond that governs how a fan reads the next twenty years is a relationship, and they respond to different things.

entries.category: Attachment, Parasocial Relationship and the Fan
entries.name: The Lonely Fan Is the Disconfirmed Version
entries.description: The most common fictional treatment of the fan, and the fact that the evidence fails to support it.
entries.principle: The standard portrayal — the isolated person whose attachment to a character substitutes for relationships they cannot form — is a specific empirical hypothesis, and the 120-study meta-analysis **fails to find it**. Parasocial relationships were **not** significantly predicted by loneliness, social deficiency or poor social skills. They correlate instead with homophily and identification, which is to say they run through the same machinery as ordinary liking, and they are found in socially well-connected people. This is a rare case where a genre's stock character is not merely unkind but **empirically the wrong way round**, and knowing it opens better material: the interesting fan is not compensating for an absence but extending a capacity they already use well. (robustness: contested)
entries.example: Written as disconfirmed, the fan becomes someone whose attachment to a character is continuous with their attachments to people, which is both truer to the evidence and harder to condescend to.
entries.application: If your fan character's devotion is explained by their isolation, you have written the hypothesis the meta-analysis failed to support. Try writing it as the same faculty that makes them good at friendship.

entries.category: Attachment, Parasocial Relationship and the Fan
entries.name: The Impossible Body and the Bond That Buffers It
entries.description: Three claims about muscularity and media that are routinely merged into one, at three different strengths.
entries.principle: Pope and colleagues (*International Journal of Eating Disorders* 26(1), 1999) measured the most popular American action figures across three decades and found them growing markedly more muscular, with many exceeding the largest human bodybuilders when scaled to adult height. **That study measures plastic; it studied no children and claims only that cultural expectations "may contribute."** Cited as evidence that superhero toys harm boys, it is being asked to say something it does not say. Separately, the media-to-male-body-dissatisfaction link does have meta-analytic support (Barlett, Vowels & Saucier, 2008), at small-to-moderate effect sizes and mostly short-term exposure. And separately again, the one superhero-specific experiment found the opposite of the intuitive result: men with **no** parasocial bond to a muscular hero showed lower body satisfaction, while men **with** a bond showed no harm (Young, Gabriel & Hollar, *JESP* 49(2), 2013) — a single lab, 98 undergraduates, no replication located. (robustness: unreplicated)
entries.example: The depicted ideal became physically impossible over thirty years, which is a documented fact about manufacturing and a claim about the culture rather than about any child.
entries.application: Cite the action-figure study for what it measured. If you want a claim about readers, use the media-effects literature and halve your confidence; if you want the buffering effect, treat it as a suggestive lead and say so.

entries.category: Moral Licensing and the Appeal of Unaccountable Force
entries.name: Licensing Needs an Audience
entries.description: The mechanism the genre most relies on, and the version of it that survives scrutiny.
entries.principle: Moral licensing — a prior good act making a subsequent bad one easier — is the implicit engine of the hero who is permitted his cruelty because of his record. The evidence is weaker and stranger than the genre assumes. Blanken, van de Ven and Zeelenberg (*PSPB* 41(4), 2015) pooled 91 studies, N = 7,397, and found **d = 0.31 with publication bias present by their own assessment** and no supported moderator. A registered-report replication of the founding credentials study with N = 932 found **no consistent effect and a reversal in one domain**, supporting moral *consistency* instead. A 2025 meta-analysis of 115 experiments, N = 21,770, finds the effect substantial when participants are **observed** and near zero when they are not. **What survives is interpersonal, not intrapsychic**: people relax when credit has been banked in public. (robustness: contested)
entries.example: The private moral ledger — the hero who feels entitled because of what he has done — is the version the evidence least supports; the hero trading on a public record is the version that does.
entries.application: Put witnesses in the room. A licensing beat played in front of people who know what the character has done is both the better scene and the defensible one.

entries.category: Moral Licensing and the Appeal of Unaccountable Force
entries.name: Why the Unaccountable Hero Appeals
entries.description: The structural account of who is permitted to use force, and the limit of what it claims.
entries.principle: Menaka Philips (*American Political Science Review* 116(2), 2022) argues that the genre distributes what she calls **the privilege of violence** — the force individuals may deploy according to normative expectations of gender and race — in three modes: the **unrestricted** rage of the white male vigilante, the **vulnerability** of the feminist heroine whose violence is licensed only alongside displayed woundedness, and the **sacrificial control** of the Black male hero whose disciplined force performs respectability. The occasion of the argument is the adoption of a specific vigilante's insignia by law enforcement. **This card carries no robustness tier: it is political theory, a claim about what texts license their characters to do, and it says nothing about what audiences then do.** `craft-4` states the same argument as a craft instrument; this card states its scope, because the commonest misuse is to read it as an audience-effects finding.
entries.example: The three modes are visible as a distribution across a single ensemble, which is why the argument is most legible on a team book and least legible on a solo one.
entries.application: Use it to ask who your story permits to be unrestrained and on what basis. Do not use it to claim anything about your reader — for that, the honest answer in this collection is that the work has not been done.

entries.category: Moral Licensing and the Appeal of Unaccountable Force
entries.name: The Costumed Stranger on the Metro
entries.description: The priming literature, its poor record, and one field study that declines to use it.
entries.principle: A small literature reports that exposure to superhero imagery increases helping — images raising helping intentions, a poster raising actual helping against a control (Van Tongeren et al., *Frontiers in Psychology* 9, 2018). This is **social priming**, the paradigm class with the worst replication record in the field, and the pack states that rather than quoting the result bare. The more interesting item is a 2025 field study on the Milan metro (Pagnini et al., *npj Mental Health Research* 4, 57): seat-offering to a visibly pregnant woman rose from 37.7% to 67.2% when a person in a Batman costume boarded, across 138 observation sessions. **The authors themselves decline the priming interpretation**, citing the replication record, and propose a disruption-of-automaticity mechanism instead — and note that 44% of those who gave up a seat reported not having seen the costume at all. (robustness: unreplicated)
entries.example: A costumed stranger changing a carriage's behaviour without being consciously registered is a better scene than a costumed stranger inspiring anyone, and it is what the data actually shows.
entries.application: If you write the costume changing a crowd, write it as interruption rather than as inspiration. That is both the more defensible reading and the one that does not require anybody to be looking.

entries.category: Latino, Indigenous and Asian American Creators
entries.name: George Pérez
entries.description: The genre's definitive ensemble draughtsman, self-taught, and one of very few to hold four of the five authorship claims.
entries.meta: American, of Puerto Rican parentage, 1954–2022. **This card is for the penciller and inker claims, and for co-plotting; he also wrote.** Holding four of the five — writer, penciller, inker, plotter — is rare enough in this industry to be the fact a writer should notice first. Self-taught; the clarity is constructed rather than inherited.
entries.knownFor: *Wonder Woman* vol. 2, drawn throughout from 1987 and scripted through issue 62; *Crisis on Infinite Earths* with Marv Wolfman, 1985–86.
entries.signature: Twenty figures in a panel with the eye directed to one of them — density that stays legible because the composition, not the caption, decides where you look.

works.title: Crisis on Infinite Earths
works.note: with Marv Wolfman; the compression event carded at `history-21`'s span

entries.category: Latino, Indigenous and Asian American Creators
entries.name: Gabby Rivera
entries.description: The clearest documented case in the pack of what changes when the writer shares the protagonist's position — and of what does not.
entries.meta: American; queer Puerto Rican writer from the Bronx; living. **This card is for the writer claim only.** She did **not** create America Chavez: the character pre-existed as Marvel's first queer Latina hero and Rivera was brought in to write the solo book. That distinction — creator *of* a background versus creator brought *to* a character — is one this pack keeps rather than collapses, and it is why the card states it in the first sentence.
entries.knownFor: *America*, 2017. Came to comics from YA prose.
entries.signature: A protagonist whose ethnicity and queerness shape texture, family and pressure without ever becoming the plot's subject.

entries.category: Latino, Indigenous and Asian American Creators
entries.name: Jeffrey Veregge
entries.description: A formline design system with fixed rules, applied to superheroes — and the demonstration of how much of a superhero is silhouette.
entries.meta: American; enrolled member of the Port Gamble S'Klallam Tribe, with Suquamish and Duwamish heritage; 1974–2024. **This card is for the artist claim; the credits do not decompose into penciller, inker and colourist** and pass C could not establish that they do. He described his own style as "Salish Geek" — a style label rather than a byline.
entries.knownFor: *Marvel's Indigenous Voices* #1, 2020, on which he led development; Marvel variant covers, 2020; the *Red Wolf* relaunch, 2015.
entries.signature: A traditional Coast Salish design grammar with its own rules, made to hold a figure the reader already knows — so the recognition happens on silhouette alone.

entries.category: Latino, Indigenous and Asian American Creators
entries.name: Arigon Starr
entries.description: Superhero comedy built from an in-group premise, and creator-owned rather than work-for-hire.
entries.meta: American; enrolled member of the Kickapoo Tribe of Oklahoma, of Muscogee ancestry; living. **This card is for the writer, artist and colourist claims** — she colours her own work, self-taught. No letterer credit is recorded. Birth year is not documented in any source pass C reached and is deliberately absent here.
entries.knownFor: *Super Indian* — a radio series from 2006, printed as *Super Indian Volume One* in 2012. **The dates are genuinely split across three formats** (radio 2006, webcomic 2011 per one source, print 2012 per her own site) and the card gives the print volume.
entries.signature: Powers derived from tainted commodity cheese — parody carrying political specificity that a straight-faced origin could not.

works.title: Super Indian
works.note: print volume one; radio series from 2006

entries.category: Latino, Indigenous and Asian American Creators
entries.name: Larry Hama
entries.description: The widest claim-spread in this batch, and the most practical anti-drift discipline in serial writing.
entries.meta: American; Sansei Japanese American, born in New York in 1949; living. **This card is for the writer claim, but he also holds penciller, inker and editor** — four roles across a career. His family were sent to relocation camps during the war; **he was born after it, and the card says so** because the compressed version of this biography routinely gets it wrong.
entries.knownFor: *Wolverine* #31–118; *G.I. Joe: A Real American Hero*, 1982–94. Inducted into the Harvey Awards Hall of Fame in 2024 — **the body's own name for that category in that year, not an earlier one**.
entries.signature: Every character modelled on a specific real person, so that traits stay consistent across a hundred and fifty issues written by one hand.

works.title: Wolverine
works.note: #31–118; the issue range is documented, the year span is inferred from it

works.title: G.I. Joe: A Real American Hero
works.note: the licensed line treated as a continuity

entries.category: Latino, Indigenous and Asian American Creators
entries.name: Gene Luen Yang
entries.description: A borrowed icon used as a critical instrument rather than as a tribute.
entries.meta: American; Chinese American, father from Taiwan and mother from Hong Kong; living. **This card is for the writer claim on the carded work** — art by Viktor Bogdanovic and later Billy Tan — though he is a cartoonist on his own graphic novels. Raised Catholic, which is relevant to the pack's religion block and is not what this card is for.
entries.knownFor: *New Super-Man*, 2016–18; *Shang-Chi*, 2020, where he inherits a character built from 1970s Orientalist pulp and retrofits a family, a language and a diaspora onto him.
entries.signature: The critique carried by the premise rather than argued in dialogue — a Chinese Superman interrogates nationalism simply by existing.

works.title: New Super-Man
works.note: DC; his own site dates the first collected volume 2017

works.title: Shang-Chi
works.note: Marvel; repairing an inherited stereotype rather than retiring it

entries.category: Women Writing and Drawing the Superhero
entries.name: Tarpé Mills
entries.description: A costumed heroine authored end to end by one hand, in 1941, under a name chosen to hide that the hand was a woman's.
entries.meta: American, 1918–1988; born June Tarpé Mills. **This card is for the writer, penciller and inker claims — she held all three.** The byline is a **personal pen name adopted to conceal gender**: she told a newspaper it "would have been a major let-down to the kids if they found out that the author of such virile and awesome characters was a gal." Her legal first name appears in biography only; **every strip carries Tarpé Mills, and the pack does not "restore" June to the credit line.**
entries.knownFor: *Miss Fury*, a newspaper strip from 6 April 1941, reprinted in comic-book form.
entries.signature: Wardrobe as characterisation — a fashion-drawn action idiom that committee-made superhero comics have never reproduced, because no committee has one hand.

works.title: Miss Fury
works.note: newspaper strip, 6 April; comic-book reprints followed

entries.category: Women Writing and Drawing the Superhero
entries.name: Joye Murchison Kelly
entries.description: Seventy-plus stories published under someone else's name, and the pack's clearest case of voice surviving anonymity.
entries.meta: American, 1924–2021; born Joye Evelyn Hummel, later Joye Murchison. **This card is for the writer claim.** The stories were published under **"Charles Moulton", a publisher-owned house byline** — she received no on-page credit at the time. **The credit is retroactive**: her authorship was not publicly established until she was interviewed for a 2014 history, and the Bill Finger Award followed in 2018. That gap between writing and credit is the card.
entries.knownFor: More than seventy *Wonder Woman* stories, 1944–47, beginning with a story published in spring 1945.
entries.signature: A second hand inside an established character's moral logic, undetectable at the time — which is what a house byline is designed to produce.

entries.category: Women Writing and Drawing the Superhero
entries.name: Ramona Fradon
entries.description: A working theory of how much rendering a superhero page can carry before the storytelling drowns.
entries.meta: American, 1926–2024; née Ramona Dom, professional name from her 1948 marriage. **This card is for the penciller and inker claims; she did not write her superhero work.** Her *Metamorpho* co-creator credit with Bob Haney **was not consistently given at the time and is now routinely acknowledged** — a standing case study in how comics credit is retroactively redistributed (C-14).
entries.knownFor: *Aquaman*, 1951–61; *Metamorpho*, co-created 1965; *Super Friends*, 1977–81.
entries.signature: Her own stated preference — "less shadow", "bigger open patterns" — which is a legibility argument disguised as a taste.

works.title: Metamorpho
works.note: co-creation with Bob Haney; credit now generally acknowledged

entries.category: Women Writing and Drawing the Superhero
entries.name: Marie Severin
entries.description: The pack's best argument that colour is authorship, from a creator who also held three other claims.
entries.meta: American, 1929–2018. **This card is for the colourist claim — her primary one — and she also held penciller, inker and letterer: four of the five.** Her method, in her own words from the EC years: "I would mix colors — golds, greens, blues — and you would intensify them." Reported co-creator and costume designer of the original Spider-Woman, 1976; **creator credit for that character is not uniform across sources and the card says reported, not settled.**
entries.knownFor: Marvel's head colourist to 1972; *Doctor Strange* in *Strange Tales* #153–160, 1967; *Not Brand Echh* from 1967.
entries.signature: Colour as a deliberate emotional grammar rather than as local hue — intensified, not described.

works.title: Not Brand Echh
works.note: parody used as a diagnostic on her own genre

entries.category: Women Writing and Drawing the Superhero
entries.name: Louise Simonson
entries.description: Child protagonists inside a superhero cosmology, written without condescension.
entries.meta: American; born Mary Louise Alexander; living. **This card is for the writer claim; she was also an editor, which is an authorship role outside the five.** **Credited as Louise Jones on 1970s and early-1980s editorial work** and as Louise Simonson from 1980. A search under one name misses half the career, and the pack carries both.
entries.knownFor: *Power Pack*, 1984–88; *X-Factor*, 1986–91; *Superman: The Man of Steel*, 1991–99.
entries.signature: Children given real stakes and no reduction in their intelligence, which is the harder half of writing them.

works.title: X-Factor
works.note: a team book metabolising a retcon it did not ask for

entries.category: Women Writing and Drawing the Superhero
entries.name: Janice Chiang
entries.description: The reader's pacing instrument, controlled by someone who did not write the script.
entries.meta: American, born 1955; living. **This card is for the letterer claim — the only one of the five she holds, and the point of the card.** Guest of Honor and Inkpot Award recipient at San Diego Comic-Con in 2023.
entries.knownFor: *Alpha Flight*, 1987–94; *Conan the Barbarian*, 1982–90; *Iron Man*, 1987–90; *Impulse*, 1999–2002.
entries.signature: Balloon placement and sound design deciding a page's rhythm — the script proposes a pace and the letterer sets it.

works.title: Impulse
works.note: a book whose premise is speed, lettered accordingly

entries.category: Women Writing and Drawing the Superhero
entries.name: Jordie Bellaire
entries.description: Colour as lighting design and structural device rather than decoration.
entries.meta: American; living. **This card is for the colourist claim — her primary one; she also writes.** Birth year is not documented in the sources pass C reached and is deliberately absent. Five Eisner Awards for Best Coloring — **a category string that exists in the years awarded and must not be back-dated onto earlier work** (V-22).
entries.knownFor: *Absolute Wonder Woman*, from 2024.
entries.signature: A deliberately narrow palette doing the work a caption box would otherwise have to do.

entries.category: Women Writing and Drawing the Superhero
entries.name: Gail Simone
entries.description: Ensemble voice as a learnable craft, and the compiler of a piece of critical vocabulary the genre now uses about itself.
entries.meta: American, born 1974; living. **This card is for the writer claim.** She compiled the 1999 list that gave the genre its standing term for the convention of killing a partner to motivate a protagonist — **the pack names the list and its compiler rather than treating the coinage as anonymous folklore**, which is the same discipline `trope-72` applies.
entries.knownFor: *Birds of Prey*, 2003–07 and 2010–11; *Secret Six*, 2005–11; *Wonder Woman*, 2007–10.
entries.signature: Every character audibly distinct in dialogue alone, with no attribution needed — demonstrated across an ensemble, repeatedly, which is what makes it teachable.

works.title: Secret Six
works.note: the ensemble-voice demonstration at its clearest

entries.category: Japanese Creators: Tokusatsu, Shonen and Mahou Shoujo
entries.name: Eiji Tsuburaya
entries.description: The man who built the grammar of the suited hero, working in a role the five-claim model has no name for.
entries.meta: Japanese, 1901–1970; born Tsumuraya Eiichi, the surname characters and reading both altered professionally. **None of the five comics claims applies.** He was a *tokusatsu kantoku* — special-effects director — a film craft of miniature, optical and suit-based effects. **Pass C's finding is that tokusatsu splits "creator" across four credited people**: the credited originator, the head writer, the effects director and the suit actor. This card is the third of those. This creator is carded in a superhero pack because the Manga pack is planned and not yet built; when it is, the tokusatsu line is its material as much as this one's.
entries.knownFor: *Ultraman*, 1966; *Ultra Q*, 1966; *Godzilla*, 1954.
entries.signature: Scale established by what the miniature does to the camera, and a costume that must read as a body under strain rather than as a costume.

entries.category: Japanese Creators: Tokusatsu, Shonen and Mahou Shoujo
entries.name: Shozo Uehara
entries.description: The head writer, which in this tradition is the role the credited creator often did not fill.
entries.meta: Japanese, 1937–2020. **None of the five comics claims applies: he was a screenwriter and head writer (脚本家).** In tokusatsu the head writer sets series arc and tone while the credited "creator" may have written nothing — pass C's most transferable finding about how this tradition assigns authorship. **His death date is contested**: an obituary published 9 January 2020 states he died on 2 January **2019**, which is internally inconsistent with its own publication date; the Japanese record gives 2 January 2020, and the card follows that with the conflict stated. Carded here because the Manga pack is planned and not yet built, and the head-writer role this card names belongs to that pack's taxonomy as much as to this one's.
entries.knownFor: *Himitsu Sentai Gorenger*, 1975; *Ultraseven*, 1967; *Kaettekita Ultraman*, 1971.
entries.signature: Five archetypes, rotating focus episodes, and a monster-of-the-week that still carries the season's theme — the structure the team-hero format runs on worldwide.

entries.category: Japanese Creators: Tokusatsu, Shonen and Mahou Shoujo
entries.name: Bin Furuya
entries.description: A character built entirely from silhouette and posture, with no face and no voice.
entries.meta: Japanese, born 1943; living. **None of the five comics claims applies: he is a suit actor** — the physical performer inside the costume, distinct from both the on-screen face actor and the voice actor. **His professional given-name reading (Bin) differs from the ordinary reading of the same characters (Satoshi)**, and databases split him between the two. Carded here because the Manga pack is planned and not yet built; the suit actor has no slot in an American comics taxonomy and will need one there.
entries.knownFor: The suit performance in *Ultraman*, 1966; also on screen as Amagi in *Ultraseven*, 1967.
entries.signature: Physical characterisation with every ordinary instrument removed — the purest available lesson in what posture alone can carry.

entries.category: Japanese Creators: Tokusatsu, Shonen and Mahou Shoujo
entries.name: Mitsuteru Yokoyama
entries.description: One hand that drew both poles the Japanese power fantasy swings between.
entries.meta: Japanese, 1934–2004. **Sole author — story and art undivided, which is the manga norm and not a division of the five claims.** Manga is serialised in monochrome, so **there is no colourist role at all**, a structural fact rather than a gap in the record. Carded here because the Manga pack is planned and not yet built, and both of this creator's poles belong at least as much to that pack.
entries.knownFor: *Mahōtsukai Sally* (*Sally the Witch*), serialised from July 1966; *Tetsujin 28-gō*, 1956. **The "first magical girl" claim is qualified in the sources** — a rival predates it in print while its anime came later — and the card does not print an unqualified first.
entries.signature: The remote-controlled giant and the secretly-magical schoolgirl, invented by the same person a decade apart, which is the clearest evidence that the two forms are one tradition.

works.title: Mahōtsukai Sally
works.note: manga, from July; anime the same year

entries.category: Japanese Creators: Tokusatsu, Shonen and Mahou Shoujo
entries.name: Gō Nagai
entries.description: Escalation with no floor — what happens when a hero's power is genuinely monstrous and the story refuses to reassure you.
entries.meta: Japanese, born 1945 as Nagai Kiyoshi; living; **Gō Nagai is a personal pen name.** Sole author working through a **studio system** — Dynamic Productions, founded with his brothers in 1969, supplies assistants who are employees rather than co-credited creators. That arrangement is the manga answer to the American bullpen and it produces a single credited name. Carded here because the Manga pack is planned and not yet built; the studio-system authorship this card describes is that pack's problem to formalise.
entries.knownFor: *Devilman*, 1972–73; *Mazinger Z*, 1972–73; *Cutie Honey*, 1973–74.
entries.signature: A protagonist whose power is indistinguishable from the thing he is fighting, sustained rather than resolved.

works.title: Cutie Honey
works.note: manga; the transforming heroine as an engine rather than a premise

entries.category: Japanese Creators: Tokusatsu, Shonen and Mahou Shoujo
entries.name: Akira Toriyama
entries.description: Improvised serial plotting done well — writing without a plan and staying legible.
entries.meta: Japanese, 1955–2024. **Sole author: wrote, drew and inked, with assistants "mostly for backgrounds."** His editor functioned as a de-facto story editor, **a role with no American comics equivalent and holding none of the five claims** while exercising authority a US writer would hold — pass C's sharpest structural finding about manga authorship. Carded here because the Manga pack is planned and not yet built, and the de-facto story editor named above is a role that pack will have to name properly.
entries.knownFor: *Dragon Ball*, 1984–95; *Dr. Slump*, 1980–84.
entries.signature: Escalation that keeps its stakes readable because each new ceiling is established before it is exceeded — the owned curve `powers-24` describes.

entries.category: Japanese Creators: Tokusatsu, Shonen and Mahou Shoujo
entries.name: Masami Kurumada
entries.description: Armour as a power system, and the shonen team assembled from a fixed roster of designs.
entries.meta: Japanese, born 1953; living. **Sole author, story and art.** Carded here after pass C's assembly moved Shōtarō Ishinomori to the Screen Creators block, where his credited claim — the origination of *Kamen Rider* and *Super Sentai* as television — actually sits. Carded here because the Manga pack is planned and not yet built; the armour-inventory power system belongs to its taxonomy.
entries.knownFor: *Saint Seiya*, 1986–89; *Ring ni Kakero*, 1977–82.
entries.signature: A capability located in a wearable object with a fixed inventory, so that escalation is a matter of which armour rather than how much power — the design constraint `powers-29` treats as the costume question.

entries.category: Japanese Creators: Tokusatsu, Shonen and Mahou Shoujo
entries.name: Kōhei Horikoshi
entries.description: The deliberate graft of American superhero furniture onto shonen structure.
entries.meta: Japanese, born 1986; living. **Sole author, story and art**; formerly an assistant to another mangaka — the apprentice pipeline rather than a bullpen. Series concluded August 2024. Carded here because the Manga pack is planned and not yet built, and this is the title where the two traditions are most directly in contact.
entries.knownFor: *My Hero Academia*, 2014–2024.
entries.signature: Licensing, hero schools and public rankings — the conferred-mandate mode built into the premise rather than argued as a plot, which is why the American registration story reads as a rupture and this one as a world.

entries.category: Japanese Creators: Tokusatsu, Shonen and Mahou Shoujo
entries.name: Naoko Takeuchi
entries.description: The fusion that produced the modern magical-girl form — mahou shoujo crossed with sentai.
entries.meta: Japanese, born 1967; living. **Sole author, story and art.** Carded here because the Manga pack is planned and not yet built; the mahou shoujo lineage is that pack's spine, not this one's.
entries.knownFor: *Sailor Moon*, 1991–97; *Codename: Sailor V*, 1991–97.
entries.signature: A *team* of transforming girls with colour-coded roles and a combined attack — sentai structure imported wholesale into a form that had been solitary.

entries.category: Japanese Creators: Tokusatsu, Shonen and Mahou Shoujo
entries.name: Ageha Ohkawa
entries.description: Four women publishing under one name, and the closest thing manga has to a divided authorship.
entries.meta: Japanese; living; leads **CLAMP**. Credited Nanase Ohkawa until 2004, when **all four members renamed themselves** — a collective adoption of new personal pen names, and the card carries both forms. **This card is for the writer, storyboarder and producer-director roles.** CLAMP divides labour — writer/storyboarder, chief character designer, background artists — **but not along American lines: there is no inker and no letterer, and the last three roles rotate.** The members' legal names are not disclosed in any source pass C reached and **the pack does not assert them.** Carded here because the Manga pack is planned and not yet built, and collective authorship of this kind has no American equivalent for that pack to inherit.
entries.knownFor: *Cardcaptor Sakura*, 1996; *Magic Knight Rayearth*, 1993; *X*, 1992.
entries.signature: A single authorial voice surviving genuinely collective production — the counter-example to every assumption that one voice needs one hand.

entries.name: Marcel Gotlib
entries.description: A superhero built entirely out of a country's self-image, which is what the American form does without admitting it.
entries.meta: French, 1934–2016; born Marcel Gottlieb, **a personal pen name simplifying his own surname.** **The five-claim model does not divide here: he is a BD *auteur*, script and art undivided**, which is the tradition's norm. Also a publisher.
entries.knownFor: *Superdupont*, co-created with Jacques Lob in *Pilote*, 21 September 1972; moved to *Fluide Glacial* in 1975. **Sources disagree, one giving 1977; the card follows the specific 1972 citation and states the conflict.**
entries.signature: National caricature as a power set — the beret and the baguette treated with exactly the seriousness the cape usually receives.

entries.name: Jacques Lob
entries.description: The same machinery worked as parody for twenty years and then turned to straight dystopia.
entries.meta: French, 1932–1990. **This card is for the writer claim — he is one of the few BD figures the American writer/artist split actually fits**, a pure scenarist who needed a different artist each time.
entries.knownFor: *Superdupont*, 1972; *Submerman*, a superhero parody with Georges Pichard; *Le Transperceneige*, 1982.
entries.signature: One skeleton, two tones — the superhero structure played for absurdity and then, unchanged, for horror.

works.title: Le Transperceneige
works.note: the same machinery, no longer funny

entries.name: Jean Giraud
entries.description: A BD sensibility applied directly to an American superhero, producing a story with no fights and no plot engine.
entries.meta: French, 1938–2012. **Personal pen names split by genre**: **Mœbius** for science fiction and fantasy, **Gir** for westerns — a function-split byline rather than a concealment. **This card is for the artist and writer claims.**
entries.knownFor: *Silver Surfer: Parable* with Stan Lee, 1988–89 — **an Eisner for best limited series in 1989, the body's own category string for that year**; *Arzach*, 1974–75; *The Airtight Garage*, 1976.
entries.signature: A superhero rendered as a phenomenon moving through a world that does not organise itself around him — the American form's own furniture with its narrative engine removed.

works.title: Arzach
works.note: the wordless sequence that made the reputation

entries.name: Aabid Surti
entries.description: A hero built from a specific Indian social wound rather than from an imported costume.
entries.meta: Indian, born 1935; living. Also credited **Abid Surti** — the romanisation is unstable across sources and the pack carries both. **This card is for the writer claim on the carded work**; the art was by other hands, and he holds penciller claims elsewhere. **Authorship of the run is scoped, not asserted**: he conceived and wrote it from December 1976, and after he left the publisher the writing passed to another hand and the art from father to son.
entries.knownFor: *Bahadur*, Indrajal Comics, December 1976.
entries.signature: The antagonist's sociology — the dacoit belt of Chambal — generating the series engine, so the hero's power is never the reason the stories exist.

entries.name: Pratap Mullick
entries.description: A penciller carrying a franchise — design language as the thing that survives every later hand.
entries.meta: Indian, 1936–2007. **This card is for the penciller claim.** Inking and lettering are **not separately documented**, which pass C establishes is the ordinary condition outside the American industrial system rather than a gap in this particular record. **His name in Devanagari could not be verified and is deliberately omitted here** rather than reconstructed.
entries.knownFor: *Nagraj*, Raj Comics, 1 April 1986 — he drew roughly the first fifty issues to 1995. **The character has no single creator**: it was conceived by the publisher's team, the debut issue was written by a third party, and Mullick drew it. **A card saying "created by" any one of them would be wrong**, and this one does not.
entries.signature: A figure silhouette strong enough to function as the brand, which is why the design outlived his run on it.

works.title: Nagraj
works.note: Raj Comics, 1 April; c. 50 issues to 1995

entries.name: Anupam Sinha
entries.description: A superhero with no superpowers, in a market defined by powers.
entries.meta: Indian, born 1962; living. **This card is for the writer and penciller claims — an undivided authorship rare in this pack**, and rarer still in a work-for-hire line. Inker, colourist and letterer are not separately documented.
entries.knownFor: *Super Commando Dhruva*, first appearance in Raj Comics, April 1987.
entries.signature: Deduction, equipment and a stated prohibition against killing, substituted for the power fantasy — the constraint generating the plots that the power would have foreclosed, which is `powers-9`'s argument demonstrated at book length.

entries.name: Matt Baker
entries.description: The era's finest figure stylist, working in a period that did not print artists' names.
entries.meta: American, 1921–1959; born Clarence Matthew Baker, the byline a shortened form of his own middle name rather than a pseudonym. **This card is for the penciller claim, with occasional inking.** **Attribution for this period is provisional by construction**: much of his labour was pencilled figures and backgrounds inside other artists' pages with the inker credited, and the standard reference describes 1940s attribution as difficult if not impossible to establish. Every Baker credit in this pack is worded as attributed, not certain. **Do not resolve his name against the encyclopedia article titled simply "Matt Baker" — that is a British television presenter born in 1977**, a collision an agent hit directly while verifying this card.
entries.knownFor: *Phantom Lady* #13–23, 1947–49; *It Rhymes with Lust*, 1950; *Voodah*, 1945.
entries.signature: A page blocked around one body in motion, with posture rather than caption carrying the emotional beat.

entries.name: Orrin C. Evans
entries.description: The editorial frame as an authorial act — who gets to be the hero of which strip, decided before any script.
entries.meta: American, 1902–1971; born Orrin Cromwell Evans, a journalist by trade. **He holds none of the five claims**: he was publisher and president of the company and co-creator of the features. **The book could not obtain newsprint for a second issue**, an account attributing this to hostile distributors and competing publishers. One contributing artist is credited only as "Cravat" — **a pseudonym of unknown type, and the pack records the uncertainty rather than guessing.**
entries.knownFor: *All-Negro Comics* #1, June 1947 — the first comic book created entirely by Black creators, carrying the Lion Man feature.
entries.signature: An anthology's contents page as the argument: the decision about which strips exist is prior to, and larger than, any of them.

works.title: All-Negro Comics
works.note: #1, June; no second issue was published

entries.name: Billy Graham
entries.description: Sustained-arc visual pacing on the genre's first long-form serialised novel, and a contested writing credit.
entries.meta: American, 1935–1997; born William Henderson Graham. **This card is for the inker and penciller claims across the run, and it names a contested writer claim**: he is formally credited co-writer on two issues of *Luke Cage*, and a co-writer on the same book has stated he received only pencilled pages to script, questioning what Graham contributed. **The pack states both positions and adjudicates neither** (C-16). **A secondary aggregator gives his death year as 1999; two independent sources give 4 April 1997**, and the card follows those. **Not the evangelist of the same name (1918–2018).** He was largely forgotten until a 2018 film revived interest, his granddaughter having posted his art after his death.
entries.knownFor: *Jungle Action* #6–24, the Black Panther run, 1973–76; *Luke Cage, Hero for Hire*, 1972–74.
entries.signature: Escalation made legible across thirteen issues — the staging that lets a single arc read as a novel rather than as a serial.

works.title: Jungle Action
works.note: #6–24 with Don McGregor; the arc is #6–18 and #6–24 is what the collections hold

works.title: Luke Cage, Hero for Hire
works.note: inks and pencils; co-writer credit on #14–15 is contested

entries.name: Dwayne McDuffie
entries.description: The series bible as a method — build the city's economics and class structure, and motive falls out of the setting.
entries.meta: American, 1962–2011; died the day after his forty-ninth birthday. **This card is for the writer claim; he was also an editor and the author of the line's bible.** **Litigation must be disclosed**: in 2017 his widow sued the revival entity alleging his share of the original company was excluded from the relaunch; reported settled, terms unread. **The pack discloses the existence of the suit and does not characterise fault.**
entries.knownFor: *Hardware* #1, February 1993 — the line's first published title; *Icon*; *Justice League Unlimited* as producer and writer, where his contribution is routinely omitted from short credits.
entries.signature: Continuity written as infrastructure before it is written as story, so that a character's choices are constrained by a world rather than by an author.

works.title: Hardware
works.note: #1, on sale 25 February; the line's first release

entries.name: Denys Cowan
entries.description: Deliberately imperfect line and heavy blacks, making a costumed figure read as physically vulnerable.
entries.meta: American, born 1961; living, documented active into the 2020s. **This card is for the penciller claim; he is not a writer on the carded work**, and has also held editor-in-chief and creative-director roles. **Milestone's own account names four founders; a widely used reference names five**, adding a figure who left before any title was published. **The pack gives the four and footnotes the fifth** rather than picking.
entries.knownFor: *Hardware*, 1993; *The Question*, 1987–90.
entries.signature: A scratchy, unresolved line on a genre built from clean ones — the drawing arguing with the costume.

entries.name: Christopher Priest
entries.description: The unreliable, non-linear superhero narrator — and the most structurally ambitious modern run in the genre.
entries.meta: American, born 1961 as James Christopher Owsley; living. **The name change is legal, not a pen name** — he has said so explicitly, and **credits before roughly 1993 read Jim Owsley** while everything after, including the carded run, reads Christopher Priest. **This card is for the writer claim; he was also the first African American editor in mainstream comics**, at Marvel from 1979 — a claim that itself carries a counter-note, since a 1947 Black-owned publisher had both Black writers and a Black editor. **Three-way disambiguation is required**: not the English novelist Christopher Priest (1943–2024, deceased), and not the film director Christopher Guest. **A pack that confuses the first two reports a living creator as dead.**
entries.knownFor: *Black Panther* vol. 3, 1998–2003 — and **he did not write #57–58**, so "Priest #1–62" overstates it by two.
entries.signature: A hostile, comic outsider narrator through whom the reader must earn access to the protagonist — point of view as a political argument.

works.title: The Falcon
works.note: credited as Jim Owsley, the byline he used before the 1993 legal change

entries.name: Ta-Nehisi Coates
entries.description: A working essayist rebuilding a superhero book as a political-legitimacy novel.
