entries.meta: American, born 1975; living. **This card is for the writer claim only; he holds no art claims and came to the form from journalism and memoir.** **Also carded at `historical:author-111` for his first novel — that card is for the prose and this one is for the comics**, which is the delta this pack owes (verification line 17). **Public controversy over his political writing is not a conduct allegation and the pack does not conflate the two.**
entries.knownFor: *Black Panther* vol. 6, from 2016, art by Brian Stelfreeze. **The numbering is two commercial decisions in the public record**: #1–18, then #166–172 under a legacy renumbering. **Never write "#1–25."**
entries.signature: A king facing an insurgency he cannot punch — and the visible friction of essay-weight interiority meeting a medium that shows.

entries.name: Afua Richardson
entries.description: Worldbuilding done in ornament rather than in dialogue.
entries.meta: American; living, profiled as actively working in 2025. **Birth year is not documented in any source pass C reached and is deliberately absent.** **This card is for the artist claim; the credits do not decompose into penciller, inker and colourist** — she delivers finished full-colour art, and pass C could not establish a separate inker or colourist. Also uses the personal alias "Docta Foo" alongside her legal byline.
entries.knownFor: *Black Panther: World of Wakanda*, 2016–17 — covers for five issues and interior art on the first issue's backup.
entries.signature: Ghanaian Adinkra symbols introduced into a fictional nation's visual language, so the setting argues through decoration.

entries.name: Pat Mills
entries.description: The editor-author — an anthology designed as an engine for tone.
entries.meta: British, born 1949; living. **This card is for the writer claim; he was also an editor**, and the two are inseparable in his case because the design decision preceded the scripts.
entries.knownFor: *2000 AD*, co-created 1977; *Nemesis the Warlock*; *Marshal Law*, from 1987.
entries.signature: A weekly anthology built so that its house tone survives any individual writer — the format doing the work an editorial policy would otherwise have to.

works.title: 2000 AD
works.note: co-created; Judge Dredd appears in Prog 2, not Prog 1

works.title: Marshal Law
works.note: #1–6 to 1989; "Fear and Loathing" is the collection's title, not the run's

entries.name: Alan Moore
entries.description: A kitsch children's character placed in the real world of 1982 — the move that made deconstruction a genre.
entries.meta: British, born 1953; living. **This card is for the writer claim.** **Carded twice already in this library** — `fantasy:author-101` for formal architecture and `horror:author-123` for his horror body and his criticism of the industry — **and neither is about the superhero**, which is this card's delta. **He uses "The Original Writer" on reprints of work he does not own: a byline whose function is to deny authorship**, and the same protest move another creator made under a different invented name. He has his name removed from adaptations of work he does not own and refuses payment for them.
entries.knownFor: *Marvelman* in *Warrior* #1, March 1982 — **not 1985, which is the recoloured US reprint and the single most common error on this work**; *Watchmen*, 1986–87.
entries.signature: The genre's own furniture taken literally and followed to its consequences, without parody and without rescue.

works.title: Marvelman
works.note: Warrior #1, March; the US Miracleman #1–5 of 1985 are recoloured reprints

entries.name: Grant Morrison
entries.description: The opposite bet to deconstruction — the superhero's absurdity treated as a strength to be argued for.
entries.meta: British, born 1960; living. **They are non-binary and use they/them**, and older reference material uses he/him; **the pack carries the current pronouns and says why the older sources differ.** **This card is for the writer claim.**
entries.knownFor: *Zenith*, from *2000 AD* Prog 535, 15 August 1987 — **a date on which sources disagree by a week, and the pack follows the prog record**; *All-Star Superman*, 2005–08; *New X-Men*, #114–154, 2001–04. **There is no "New X-Men #1"**: the title is a retitling under continuous numbering.
entries.signature: Reconstruction as an argument rather than a retreat — the case that the form's excesses are its subject.

works.title: All-Star Superman
works.note: on sale November 2005, cover-dated January 2006 — both years circulate

entries.name: Neil Gaiman
entries.description: Inheriting another writer's superhero and extending it without imitating the voice.
entries.meta: British, born 1960; living. **This card is for the writer claim.** **From 2024, multiple women publicly alleged sexual assault and abuse. He denies non-consensual conduct. Civil suits were filed in February 2025; one was dismissed on jurisdiction without any ruling on the facts. No criminal charges have been filed.** Every element of that is an allegation, attributed and dated, and the pack states the allegations, the denial and the absence of charges together — **the same treatment `horror:author-124` and `fantasy:author-30` already give it**, so the library is consistent. **Also carded in those two packs for prose and for *The Sandman*; this card is for the superhero inheritance**, which neither covers.
entries.knownFor: *Miracleman* #17–24, from June 1990, left unfinished at the publisher's collapse.
entries.signature: A successor voice that declines to imitate its predecessor and changes the question the book is asking instead.

entries.name: Garry Leach
entries.description: The art that made a deconstruction land, by refusing to be cartoon.
entries.meta: British, 1954–2022. **This card is for the penciller, inker, letterer and colourist claims — four of the five, and the fullest art claim in this block.** Also an editor and publisher.
entries.knownFor: *Marvelman* in *Warrior* #1–3, #5–7, 1982.
entries.signature: Photographic gravity applied to a children's character, so that the premise's cruelty has nowhere to hide.

entries.name: Brian Bolland
entries.description: Line as total control — stillness carrying the menace.
entries.meta: British, born 1951; living, with documented digital practice from 1997. **This card is for the penciller claim; he inks and colours his own work**, which is unusual and is the reason the next fact matters. **He was dissatisfied with another hand's colouring of his best-known book and recoloured it himself for a 2008 edition** — two published colourists for one work, and any citation must name the edition.
entries.knownFor: *Judge Dredd*, 1977–80; *Camelot 3000*, 1982–85; *Batman: The Killing Joke*, 1988.
entries.signature: A precision so complete that motion is unnecessary — the threat is in what is held still.

works.title: Judge Dredd
works.note: art from 1977; created by John Wagner and Carlos Ezquerra. 2000 AD

entries.name: Dave Gibbons
entries.description: Layout as authorship — the nine-panel grid as an argument rather than a container.
entries.meta: British, born 1949; living. **This card is for the penciller, inker and letterer claims, and he later wrote: four of the five.**
entries.knownFor: *Watchmen*, 1986–87; *2000 AD* from February 1977.
entries.signature: A fixed grid used until its exceptions become the loudest events on the page.

works.title: Watchmen
works.note: with Alan Moore and John Higgins

entries.name: Kim San-ho
entries.description: A hero grammar improvised at nineteen, in a market that had no precedent to copy.
entries.meta: Korean, born 1939 — **a state encyclopedia gives 1939 and another source 1940, and the card follows the encyclopedia**; living, with documented work to 2016. Credited **Sanho Kim** in the United States. **산호 is a personal pen name adopted over the legal name 김철수.** **This card is for the writer and penciller claims; in his US work he was also credited as inker, cover artist and art director.** **His later career is devoted to nationalist historical work that Korean sources themselves flag as controversial: this card is for the 1959 comic and does not imply endorsement of that work.** **Romanisation is badly unstable** — the creator appears in three clusters and the work in five title variants, and a naive deduplication produces two or three phantom people.
entries.knownFor: 정의의 사자 라이파이 (*Rai Pai, Lion of Justice*), 1959, serialised to 1962. **Relationship to the American form runs the unusual direction**: the work predates his 1966 emigration, after which he drew for American publishers — a documented exchange running Korea to America.
entries.signature: A masked orphan-avenger whose insignia is a letter of the Korean alphabet — an imported form localised at the level of the emblem.

entries.name: Mars Ravelo
entries.description: The transformation as a ritual — an object and a word rather than an origin accident.
entries.meta: Filipino, 1916–1988. **This card is for the writer claim on the carded work**, which was illustrated by another hand; he wrote **and drew** the 1947 predecessor. **The debut date is contested**: a standard reference gives *Pilipino Komiks* #77, 13 May 1950, and another source gives 1949 as a remodelling of the earlier character. The card follows the specific citation and states the conflict.
entries.knownFor: *Darna*, 1950, from the 1947 predecessor *Varga*.
entries.signature: Power obtained by swallowing a stone and speaking a name — a transformation that is repeatable, performable, and therefore adaptable across seventy years of film.

entries.name: Gedeone Malagola
entries.description: The only creator in this pack working from a documented editorial brief to copy a specific American hero.
entries.meta: Brazilian, 1924–2008. **This card is for the writer and penciller claims** — the sources describe the work as drawn and scripted by him, except one issue. **The copy brief is on the record**: an academic paper documents the publisher asking him to create a hero based on a specific American character, and identifies the deliberate subtractions — no lantern symbol, no colour weakness, a black uniform and a full-face mask. **This is the pack's study case for the gap between derivation and invention.** **Three sources give three years — 1964, 1965 and 1966**; the card follows the academic paper's 1965 and states the range.
entries.knownFor: *Raio Negro*, 1965, 24 issues to 1966.
entries.signature: A borrowed origin structure rebuilt around a national air force and a real rocket programme — the copy localised at the level of institutions.

entries.name: Kunt Tulgar
entries.description: Resource-constrained genre translation — which elements of a genre are load-bearing when the budget forbids the rest.
entries.meta: Turkish, died 16 March 2022 aged 76; **birth year is not printed in the obituaries pass C reached and is deliberately absent.** **He holds none of the five comics claims: a film director, screenwriter, producer, actor and dubbing artist**, with the screenplay credit shared. **Turkey is carded with a film director for a reason**: a peer-reviewed history of Turkish comics identifies **no** Turkish-created costumed superhero, and the country's canonical comics heroes are historical adventure. **Turkey's superhero tradition is cinematic, not comics-based** — a bounded negative, not an assumption.
entries.knownFor: *Süpermen Dönüyor*, 1979, an unauthorised Turkish adaptation. **An obituary dates it 1976; two film-specific sources give 1979** and the card follows those.
entries.signature: Flight achieved with rear projection and a doll — the genre reduced to the two or three things an audience will not forgive being absent.

entries.name: Roye Okupe
entries.description: A shared universe with its continuity architected before the first volume shipped.
entries.meta: Nigerian-American; living, documented developing new work in 2026. **Birth year is not documented in any source pass C reached, including his own publisher's site, and is deliberately absent.** **This card is for the writer claim; he does not draw.** **Relationship to the American form is documented exchange running both directions** — the universe was conceived in the American idiom, later distributed by an American publisher, and adapted to animation. **No pre-2000 Nigerian superhero creator was verified, and pass C notes it did not search for one**, so the pack must not imply the tradition begins in 2015.
entries.knownFor: *E.X.O.: The Legend of Wale Williams*, 31 August 2015.
entries.signature: Universe architecture treated as a first-draft problem rather than as something a line accretes.

works.title: E.X.O.: The Legend of Wale Williams

entries.name: Sunkanmi Akinboye
entries.description: Action choreography as a trained-body problem rather than a drawing problem.
entries.meta: Nigerian, working from Lagos; living. **Birth year is not documented and is deliberately absent.** Also formally rendered **Akinboye Olasunkanmi** in Yoruba naming order, and **the order is unstable across sources** — confirm before merging or splitting records. **This card is for the penciller claim**; inking, colour and lettering on the carded volumes are credited to others.
entries.knownFor: Lead artist on the YouNeek line including *E.X.O.*, 2015; professional since 2002 with Nigerian publishers.
entries.signature: Martial-arts training and animation vocabulary driving the staging, so the fight is choreographed before it is drawn.

works.title: E.X.O.: The Legend of Wale Williams

entries.name: Wong Yuk-long
entries.description: The founding text of Hong Kong action manhua, and the model for the Asian comics studio.
entries.meta: Hong Kong Chinese, born 1950 as 黃振隆; 黃玉郎 is a **personal pen name**, and he also uses an adopted English byline. **This card is for the penciller and writer claims, and for a publisher role that holds none of the five.** **A conviction must be disclosed: he was convicted of a financial offence in Hong Kong, sentenced to two and a half years and served eighteen months.** **This rests on English-language sources only** — the Chinese-language references were unreachable — **so the precise charge and year require confirmation before ship**, and the card says so. **Relationship to the American form is parallel invention**: every source frames the work as founding a new fighting genre from Hong Kong street life and martial arts, and **no source draws a superhero comparison**, so the pack does not.
entries.knownFor: 小流氓 (*Little Rascals*), 1970, retitled 龍虎門 (*Oriental Heroes*) after a 1975 indecent-publications law — **censorship visibly rewriting an in-progress hero comic**.
entries.signature: Studio production at newspaper speed, with pencils, backgrounds, effects and colour split across many hands under one brand — serial output as a craft constraint.

entries.category: Queer Creators and the Queer Superhero
entries.name: Rachel Pollack
entries.description: Succeeding a signature voice by changing the question the book is asking.
entries.meta: American, 1945–2023. **This card is for the writer claim.** A trans woman; **all comics work is credited Rachel Pollack**, and her only pre-transition byline is on a 1971 prose story. **The pack does not surface it: a craft pack has no use for it**, and the rule generalises to every creator whose name has changed. Jewish, from Brooklyn — relevant to the pack's religion block and not what this card is for.
entries.knownFor: *Doom Patrol* #64–87, 1993–95, introducing Coagula, a trans superhero in a mainstream title; *New Gods* vol. 4, 1995–96.
entries.signature: A character whose powers are her body politics — the least allegorical fusion of identity and superpower in mainstream comics.

entries.category: Queer Creators and the Queer Superhero
entries.name: Phil Jimenez
entries.description: Maximum density — background detail loaded with plot rather than decoration.
entries.meta: American, born 1970; living, with work released in 2025. **This card is for the penciller, inker and writer claims — three of the five.** **A "first" claim attaches to him and the pack marks it as reported rather than settled**: one source states his coming out in a letters page is believed to be the first time a creator came out in the pages of a comic book, and **two sources disagree on the year**, giving 1996 and 1997 for the issue.
entries.knownFor: *Wonder Woman* vol. 2 #164–188 as writer and artist, 2000–03; *Wonder Woman Historia: The Amazons* #1, 2021.
entries.signature: A page that rewards a second reading because the first one could not have held it all.

entries.category: Queer Creators and the Queer Superhero
entries.name: Ivan Velez Jr.
entries.description: A superteam built out of an actual neighbourhood — powers distributed by geography and grievance rather than by archetype.
entries.meta: American, born 1961; living, though **the most recent documented activity pass C could reach is 2017 — the largest currency gap among this batch's living creators, and the card states it rather than implying he is currently working.** **This card is for the writer claim**; he is also a cartoonist and editor. **The "Jr." is load-bearing and is dropped in some credits.**
entries.knownFor: *Blood Syndicate*, 1994–97; *Tales of the Closet*, 1987–93; *Ghost Rider* vol. 3 #70–93.
entries.signature: A roster whose composition is a map of a place, so that the team's frictions are the neighbourhood's.

works.title: Tales of the Closet
works.note: not a superhero work, and the reason he was publishing openly before 1989

entries.category: Queer Creators and the Queer Superhero
entries.name: Magdalene Visaggio
entries.description: Genre immortality used as a formal device rather than as a premise.
entries.meta: American, born 1984; living, publishing through 2025. **This card is for the writer claim.** **Pre-transition credits stand under her earlier name; everything from 2016 forward, including the carded work, is credited Magdalene Visaggio.** **The pack does not retro-credit earlier work to the current name and does not use the earlier name for later work** — and any automatically generated bibliography will do one or the other, so hers must be assembled by hand.
entries.knownFor: *Eternity Girl* #1–6, 2018.
entries.signature: A superhero book about the impossibility of ending, in a form that structurally cannot end — the genre's condition made the subject.

entries.category: Queer Creators and the Queer Superhero
entries.name: Andy Mangels
entries.description: A primary source for how the genre's queer readership organised itself before the industry acknowledged it.
entries.meta: American, born 1966; living. **This card is for the writer claim**; he is also a historian and journalist of the field, and the carded work is criticism rather than comics. **A publicly reported housing crisis in 2019 is public and is not craft; it is noted here and does not appear on the card.**
entries.knownFor: "Out of the Closet and Into the Comics," *Amazing Heroes*, summer 1988 — **a contemporaneous document, not a retrospective**; and the founding of a long-running convention panel, **whose year is given as 1987 by one source and 1988 by another and is carried as disputed**.
entries.signature: The essay written from inside the moment rather than about it, which is why it functions as evidence.

works.title: Out of the Closet and Into the Comics

entries.name: Peter David
entries.description: A power-set written as a psychological structure rather than as a plot engine.
entries.meta: American, 1956–2025. **This card is for the writer claim.** **He had an ischaemic stroke in December 2012 affecting his right side and vision, and discussed it publicly along with his rehabilitation** — the basis for this block's inclusion is his own disclosure, not inference. **Also carded at `scifi:author-127` for tie-in fiction; that card is for the novels and this one is for the comics.** **A defect found while writing this card: SF's `meta` reads "b. 1956" with no death, and he died on 24 May 2025. Owed to the changelog and to SF's maintainers.**
entries.knownFor: A twelve-year run on *The Incredible Hulk* from the mid-1980s; *X-Factor*; *Young Justice*, 1998–2003.
entries.signature: The transformation treated as characterisation — what the change is *of*, rather than what it enables.

entries.name: Bill Mantlo
entries.description: A merchandising mandate given an interior life the merchandise did not have.
entries.meta: American, born 1951; living. **He sustained a severe brain injury in a hit-and-run collision on 17 July 1992 and has required full-time care since; the driver was never identified.** **He cannot consent to or comment on his inclusion, and the pack states the injury factually and briefly, does not dramatise it, and does not write a living man as a closed book.** **This card is for the writer claim.** **A 1983 adaptation shipped without initially crediting its source author; the publisher acknowledged the error and the author requested only standard payment, proper credit and a subscription** — disclosed because this card treats him as a model of adaptation craft.
entries.knownFor: *Rom* #1–75, 1979–86; *Micronauts*, 1979–84; *Cloak and Dagger*, co-created 1982.
entries.signature: A licensed toy written as a tragedy — the mandate accepted completely and then made to carry something it was not built for.

entries.name: Marieke Nijkamp
entries.description: The working answer to the genre's cure reflex.
entries.meta: Dutch; living, with work published in October 2025 and solicited into 2026. **Birth year is not documented and is deliberately absent.** **Publicly self-identified as disabled and autistic**; uses she/her and they/them. **This card is for the writer claim.** **This block's shape is itself a finding**: two of its three acquired their disabilities mid-career, which is what the industry's record captures more readily than it captures disabled people entering the field. **She is the counterweight, and the pack says so rather than smoothing it.**
entries.knownFor: *The Oracle Code*, March 2020, art by Manuel Preitano; *Hawkeye: Kate Bishop* #1–5, 2021–22.
entries.signature: A disabled protagonist written as a life rather than as a problem awaiting a plot solution — the direct refusal of the pattern `powers-28` names.

entries.category: Latin American Creators and the Luchador Film
entries.name: José G. Cruz
entries.description: The photographed body composited into fictional space — a superhero whose art style is the documentary photograph.
entries.meta: Mexican, 1917–1989; born José Guadalupe Cruz Díaz. **This card is for the writer claim and for a photomontage practice that sits outside the five-claim model entirely** — he is neither penciller nor colourist but an assembler of photographed bodies against painted backgrounds. He was also the publisher. **A disclosure the pack states with its status intact: in 1961 he was accused of the homicide of Laura Esperanza Córdova Navarro, and on 18 October 1961 a judge decreed *formal prisión* — an indictment-stage detention order under Mexican procedure, not a conviction. The outcome could not be verified. It must not be reported as a conviction.**
entries.knownFor: *Santo, el Enmascarado de Plata*, from 3 September 1952 — weekly, at its peak three thirty-two-page issues a week, running into the early 1980s.
entries.signature: A real masked body, photographed and cut out, placed into drawn space — so the reader's belief attaches to a person rather than to a drawing.

entries.category: Latin American Creators and the Luchador Film
entries.name: Rodolfo Guzmán Huerta
entries.description: A fictional identity maintained in public for forty-two years, with no separation permitted between performer and character.
entries.meta: Mexican, 1917–1984. **He holds none of the five comics claims: a wrestler and film actor, and the subject and licensed persona of the comic rather than an author of it.** **The persona is the pack's clearest character-persona byline, and it is structurally unlike a pen name** — a role occupied by a body, governed by a rule of non-disclosure of the face. **One documented public unmasking, on television in late January 1984; he died days later and was buried in the mask.** The persona then passed as heritable property to his son.
entries.knownFor: The persona adopted in 1942; the comic from 1952; fifty-three or more films, 1958–1982.
entries.signature: An identity with legal and commercial weight, transferable by inheritance, defended by trademark, and terminable only by unmasking or death.

works.title: El Santo
works.note: persona adopted; first Arena México bout 26 July

works.title: Santo contra el cerebro del mal
works.note: shot in Havana; released 1961, and he is not the star

entries.category: Latin American Creators and the Luchador Film
entries.name: Alejandro Muñoz Moreno
entries.description: Antagonist-shaped stardom — an icon who exists in narrative terms because another one does.
entries.meta: Mexican, 1922–2000. **He holds none of the five claims: a wrestler and film actor.** Never publicly unmasked; buried in the mask. **The clearest case of a persona separating from the legal person: his successor is not his biological son, and the trademark position followed the split — Muñoz's actual son holds the "Blue Demon" mark, while the successor holds the mark to "Blue Demon Jr."** **Any card implying an unbroken father-to-son lineage is inaccurate**, and this one does not.
entries.knownFor: The persona from September 1948; roughly twenty-five films, 1964–1979.
entries.signature: The rival as necessary complement — a genre sustaining two icons who each require the other to mean anything.

works.title: Blue Demon
works.note: persona first appears, Mexico City, September

entries.category: Latin American Creators and the Luchador Film
entries.name: Héctor Germán Oesterheld
entries.description: The strongest structural counter-argument to the single-protagonist superhero, written from inside the genre.
entries.meta: Argentine, born 1919. **Forcibly disappeared in 1977 under the Argentine dictatorship; his four daughters were also disappeared. No death date exists — that is the nature of the crime, and the pack states 1977 as the date of disappearance rather than of death.** **This card is for the writer claim**; the art is by another hand. Relationship to the American form is parallel invention written against it: no source documents derivation.
entries.knownFor: *El Eternauta*, from *Hora Cero Semanal*, 4 September 1957.
entries.signature: An ordinary middle-aged man in an improvised suit, and the doctrine that the only valid hero is the collective hero — the genre's premise refused at its root.

entries.category: The Founders and the Work-for-Hire Generation
entries.name: Jerry Siegel
entries.description: Power inseparable from a secret social humiliation — the disguise as the story engine.
entries.meta: American, 1914–1996. **This card is for the writer claim.** Used the personal pen names Joe Carter, Jerry Ess and Herbert S. Fine. **Creator-rights status, both directions (line 22)**: rights sold in March 1938 for $130; a 1947–48 suit held the publisher owned the character and settled for just over $94,000; **the byline was then stripped in retaliation, disappearing from *Action Comics* #119 in February 1948**. A 1975 public campaign produced a $20,000 annual stipend, medical benefits and restored credit — **a pension and a byline, not a rights victory**, and the distinction is what every subsequent negotiation has turned on. **A credit restored later is a different claim from one held from the start (C-14).**
entries.knownFor: *Action Comics* #1, 1938.
entries.signature: The hero's strength and the man's embarrassment written as the same fact, so that neither can be removed without the other.

entries.category: The Founders and the Work-for-Hire Generation
entries.name: Joe Shuster
entries.description: The low-angle heroic figure and the impossible-feat splash — the original grammar.
entries.meta: American, 1914–1992. **This card is for the penciller and inker claims.** **A disclosure the pack states plainly because a reader researching him will meet it**: he produced unsigned art for a 1950s fetish publication. By the 1975 campaign he was nearly blind and living in poverty, which is what made the publicity unanswerable.
entries.knownFor: *Action Comics* #1, 1938.
entries.signature: How little rendering is needed when the pose is doing the work.

entries.category: The Founders and the Work-for-Hire Generation
entries.name: Bill Finger
entries.description: The superhero as detective — mood, city, and the villain as thematic mirror.
entries.meta: American, 1914 – c. January 1974; **the death date is approximate and the card prints the "c."** Born Milton Finger. **This card is for the writer claim.** **He had no credit at all until 2015**, and the co-creator recognition then given applied going forward. **The other party privately conceded on 1980s audio that Finger was responsible for "50–75% of all the creativity" while publicly denying it for decades** — the pack states both the concession and the denial.
entries.knownFor: *Detective Comics* #27, 1939; the Joker, the Riddler, the Penguin and the Scarecrow.
entries.signature: A city written as a moral climate, so the detective's method and the villain's pathology are the same material.

entries.category: The Founders and the Work-for-Hire Generation
entries.name: Bob Kane
entries.description: Authorship contracted rather than performed — the case study for any fiction touching credit or ghosting.
entries.meta: American, 1915–1998; born Robert Kahn. **This card is for a byline rather than for a craft claim**: he held penciller and writer credits that are both contested, and functioned as a **byline-as-brand** over a rotating stable of ghosts. **The disclosable fact is the concealment itself** — the arrangement was hidden from his own publisher for fourteen years. **Not to be confused with Gil Kane**, unrelated, also working under an adopted name, in superhero comics at the same time.
entries.knownFor: *Detective Comics* #27, 1939.
entries.signature: A signature functioning as a trademark over work by other hands — authorship as a contractual position rather than an activity.

entries.category: The Founders and the Work-for-Hire Generation
entries.name: Jerry Robinson
entries.description: Visual design as characterisation, by a man who entered the industry as a letterer.
entries.meta: American, 1922–2011; born Sherrill David Robinson. **This card is for the letterer, inker and penciller claims — three of the five, climbed in that order**, which is why he is carded here rather than in the crafts block. Early work appeared under another man's byline. **The Joker's creation is contested three ways and the pack adjudicates none of it**: one account limits his role to a playing-card design, he maintained he created the character, and a third party recalled the silent-film visual source. He later co-led the campaign that won the 1975 settlement.
entries.knownFor: The Joker, *Batman* #1, 1940.
entries.signature: A villain designed before he is written — the face deciding what the character can be made to mean.

entries.category: The Founders and the Work-for-Hire Generation
entries.name: Sheldon Moldoff
entries.description: Fourteen years of invisible authorship, and what a house style costs an individual voice.
entries.meta: American, 1920–2012. **This card is for the penciller and inker claims.** **He ghosted the Batman line from 1953 to 1967 under another man's byline with the publisher unaware of the arrangement** — his own account of the terms was that he did the work, said nothing, and had steady employment. Mr. Freeze, the second Clayface, Bat-Mite, Batwoman and the original Bat-Girl all trace to that period and were credited elsewhere.
entries.knownFor: The Batman line, including *Batman* #81–199, 1954–68.
entries.signature: A style so successfully impersonal that its author left no trace in it — which is what the arrangement was purchasing.

entries.category: The Founders and the Work-for-Hire Generation
entries.name: Otto Binder
entries.description: Premise-generation at industrial scale, under deadline.
entries.meta: American, 1911–1974. **This card is for the writer claim.** **"Eando Binder" is a shared family pen name** — from "E and O", begun with his brother Earl and retained solo from January 1936, which makes it a category of its own: neither a publisher's name nor a solo invention. He wrote 986 of 1,743 stories in one character family, and originated Supergirl, Brainiac, Bizarro and the Phantom Zone. **He mortgaged his home and could not afford to retire** — a work-for-hire outcome the pack states rather than implies.
entries.knownFor: *Captain Marvel Adventures* and the Marvel Family, 1941–53.
entries.signature: Concept density as a working method — a new premise per issue, sustained past the point where invention should have failed.

entries.category: The Founders and the Work-for-Hire Generation
entries.name: C. C. Beck
entries.description: Cartoony clarity, and the proof that a simplified line can carry sincerity that rendering kills.
entries.meta: American, 1910–1989; born Charles Clarence Beck. **This card is for the penciller and inker claims; he was also art director.**
entries.knownFor: *Whiz Comics*, 1939 — a character whose name became the subject of one of the medium's longest trademark disputes, which is why `powers-25` cards him from the other direction.
entries.signature: A line reduced until nothing is left but the intention — the opposite bet from photographic anatomy, and equally deliberate.

entries.category: The Founders and the Work-for-Hire Generation
entries.name: Will Eisner
entries.description: The page as a unit of rhetoric — and the employer's side of the work-for-hire arrangement.
entries.meta: American, 1917–2005; born William Erwin Eisner. **This card is for the writer, penciller, inker and letterer claims — four of the five.** Used the reversal pen names **Willis Rensie** and **Erwin**, self-chosen to inflate the apparent size of his shop — **not publisher-owned house names, which is precisely the distinction he is quoted about.** **He is the pack's source for how house names worked** — *"We just handed them out with the salary"* — **and three things qualify that**: he attributes the system to publishers rather than to his own shop; it is a 1999 recollection of 1930s practice, so the pack cards it as **testimony, not documentation**; and **court transcripts surfaced in 2010 indicate he testified in a 1939–40 suit in support of a publisher he spent decades saying he testified against.** **He is a documented unreliable narrator of his own era, and the pack discloses that on the card it quotes him from.** He was also the **employer** here, not a casualty. A separate disclosure: *The Spirit*'s Black sidekick is a minstrel-derived caricature that a reader meets on the first page of any reprint.
entries.knownFor: *The Spirit*, from 2 June 1940 — and he retained ownership of it while running a shop that handed publisher-owned names to its staff.
entries.signature: A city block rather than a protagonist as the organising subject, with the title folded into the architecture of the scene.

entries.name: Todd Klein
entries.description: Lettering as characterisation — a distinct hand per speaker, so the page carries voice without attribution.
entries.meta: American, born 1951; living, documented working through 2022 and describing himself as semi-retired rather than retired. **This card is for the letterer claim, which is his primary one**; he is also a logo designer and an occasional writer.
entries.knownFor: *The Sandman*, 1989–96.
entries.signature: A speaker identifiable from the shape of the balloon alone, which lets a writer drop attributions entirely.

entries.name: Gaspar Saladino
entries.description: Per-character display lettering — a monster's voice solved as a design problem before it is a diction problem.
entries.meta: American, 1927–2016. **This card is for the letterer claim, primary**; also a logo designer, with cover lettering from 1949.
entries.knownFor: Character-designated lettering on *Swamp Thing*, early 1970s.
entries.signature: A typeface invented for one speaker, so that the reader hears a register the script never has to describe.

entries.name: Tom Orzechowski
entries.description: The engineering that makes a famously dense script readable.
entries.meta: American, born 1953; living, **with the most recent documented activity in 2017 — a nine-year gap the card states rather than papering over.** **This card is for the letterer claim, primary**; also a logo designer.
entries.knownFor: *Uncanny X-Men*, 1979–93, roughly six thousand pages.
entries.signature: How much prose a page can actually hold, and exactly where it must break — a limit discovered by someone other than the writer.

entries.name: Tatjana Wood
entries.description: Palette establishing genre, threat level and tone before a word is read.
entries.meta: German-born American, 1926–2026, dying three days before her hundredth birthday; born Tatjana Amalie Weintraub. **This card is for the colourist claim, primary.** **Her 1950s–60s work is recorded as uncredited**, done alongside her then-husband's projects — **the concrete instance of the under-recording this block exists to name, and it is gendered.**
entries.knownFor: DC cover colouring through the 1970s and into the mid-1980s, plus interiors including *Swamp Thing* and *Animal Man*.
entries.signature: The cover as the industry's shop window, coloured for a decade by one hand — world-building done in the one image most readers ever see.

entries.name: Adrienne Roy
entries.description: A consistent palette doing world-building work that dialogue never has to.
entries.meta: American, 1953–2010. **This card is for the colourist claim, primary.** **No awards are recorded against roughly seventeen unbroken years on a flagship line** — pass C reads this as a record gap rather than an absence of merit, and the card says so. Her birth is recorded only as a year.
entries.knownFor: The Batman line, including *Detective Comics* and *Batman*, 1978–95.
entries.signature: One city's colour held steady across two decades, so that a change in it becomes an event.

entries.name: Laura Martin
entries.description: Digital colour as lighting design — each era given its own film stock.
entries.meta: American; living, documented as an awards ambassador appointed 2014. **Born Laura DePuy; credited Martin since her 2001 marriage — a married-name credit change, not a pseudonym, and a search under one name misses the other half of her career.** **Birth year is contradicted between sources, one giving 1975 and one 1971, and the card prints neither.** **This card is for the colourist claim, primary**; she also writes.
entries.knownFor: *Planetary*, from 1999; *Astonishing X-Men*, from 2004.
entries.signature: A palette that dates a scene without a caption, which is a structural device a writer can script for.

works.title: Planetary
works.note: colours, to 2009; by Warren Ellis and John Cassaday

works.title: Astonishing X-Men
works.note: with Joss Whedon and John Cassaday

entries.name: Joe Sinnott
entries.description: The last hand on a page defining a publisher's identity.
entries.meta: American, 1926–2020; born Joseph Leonard Sinnott. **This card is for the inker claim, primary.**
entries.knownFor: *Fantastic Four*, 1965–81, finishing another artist's pencils.
entries.signature: A finish so consistent that a house look survives every change of penciller under it.

entries.name: Vince Colletta
entries.description: The negative case — inking as an editorial act, and what a finisher removes.
entries.meta: American, 1923–1991; born Vincenzo Colletta. **This card is for the inker claim, primary**; later an art director. **The dispute is not whether he inked the pages but what he did to them**: named professionals accused him of eliminating figures and reducing crowds to silhouettes to save time. **His own defence is on the record — deadline and rate pressure — and the pack carries it and adjudicates nothing.** No conviction or criminal matter is on record.
entries.knownFor: *The Mighty Thor*, 1964–70.
entries.signature: Scale silently rewritten at the inking stage, so that what a writer specified and what a reader receives are different scenes.

entries.name: Mort Weisinger
entries.description: A mythos built as a rule system, so that a tightly specified world generates plots automatically.
entries.meta: American, 1915–1978. **He holds none of the five claims: an editor**, sole editor of one line for twelve years. **This block's damaging-mandate case, and the pack states it**: documented mistreatment of colleagues, including an artist reportedly suffering migraines from the confrontations, corroborated by his own son as extending beyond work.
entries.knownFor: The Superman line, 1958–70 — Kandor, the Phantom Zone, the kryptonite varieties, and the imaginary story as a licensed form.
entries.signature: Specification as a generator: name the rules tightly enough and the stories fall out of them.

entries.name: Jim Shooter
entries.description: The company-wide crossover event invented — the commercial machinery every shared-universe writer now plots inside.
entries.meta: American, 1951–2025. **He holds none of the five claims here: carded as editor-in-chief**, though he also wrote. **Two disclosures.** He enforced a policy **prohibiting the portrayal of gay characters**, a documented editorial policy with a discriminatory effect rather than a criminal matter. And his tenure is directly contested — the standard formulation among his critics is that he arrived when the company needed him and stayed too long — with several major creators leaving over conflicts with him. **The pack presents the legacy as contested, not settled.**
entries.knownFor: Editor-in-chief, 1 January 1978 – 15 April 1987; *Secret Wars*.
entries.signature: An event architecture that moves readers between titles — the structure `continuity-51` describes as an economic form.

entries.name: Archie Goodwin
entries.description: Editing that raises a writer's own voice instead of overwriting it.
entries.meta: American, 1937–1998. **He holds none of the five claims here: carded as editor**, though he was a substantial writer. Widely described as the best-liked editor in the field, which is a fact about a working method rather than a temperament.
entries.knownFor: The Epic imprint in the 1980s; DC editing, 1989–98.
entries.signature: The counter-model to the mandate — an editorial hand whose effect is invisible because it is additive.

entries.name: Karen Berger
entries.description: The imprint logic behind every mature take on a legacy character.
entries.meta: American, born 1958; living, with an imprint founded in 2017. **She holds none of the five claims: carded as editor.** **A scoping note the pack makes rather than glossing**: her imprint was horror- and fantasy-led, and **her superhero claim rests on one title and on recruiting the British writers who then reshaped a superhero line** — defensible, and stated as such rather than described as a superhero editorship.
entries.knownFor: Vertigo, founded 1993, led to 2013; the *Swamp Thing* recruitment that preceded it.
entries.signature: An imprint as a permission structure — the institutional move that makes a certain kind of book pitchable at all.

entries.name: Jenette Kahn
entries.description: The structural reformer — changing who could get published, which is upstream of every craft question.
entries.meta: American, born 1947; living, with a production company founded 2002. **She holds none of the five claims: carded as publisher, president and editor-in-chief**, and the block framing is accurate because she held the last of those titles from 1989 to 2002.
entries.knownFor: DC, 1976–2002; the royalties plan introduced in 1981; Vertigo and Milestone as mandates.
entries.signature: A royalty structure as a craft intervention — the change that determines what a writer can afford to attempt.

entries.category: Creators Working from Religion and Ethnicity
entries.name: Jack Kirby
entries.description: Force rather than accuracy — anatomy broken on purpose so the panel communicates impact.
entries.meta: American, 1917–1994; born Jacob Kurtzberg, the surname anglicised. **This card is for the penciller, inker and writer claims**, plus conceptual design; not a letterer. Early work also appeared under the personal pen names Curt Davis, Jack Curtiss and Fred Sande. Born to poor Jewish immigrants on the Lower East Side; the historical record documents his mother's Yiddish folktales and his youth-gang experience feeding directly into the work. **Creator-rights status, both directions**: his heirs' termination notices were settled in 2014 **without adjudication**, and he is in one Hall of Fame and has never been inducted into another that shares his name — **two facts that each circulate as the whole truth, and each names a different body** (V-01).
entries.knownFor: *Captain America Comics* #1, 1941; the Fourth World, 1970.
entries.signature: A figure powerful because the panel cannot contain it — a drawing decision doing work no script can.

works.title: The Fourth World
works.note: begun at DC; the anchor issue's date is itself disputed between August and October

entries.category: Creators Working from Religion and Ethnicity
entries.name: G. Willow Wilson
entries.description: Religious observance rendered as plot mechanics rather than as flavour.
entries.meta: American, born 1982; born Gwendolyn Willow Wilson — **the initialised byline is her own choice, not a concealment.** **This card is for the writer claim.** She studied several religions at university and **converted to Islam in 2003**, initially practising privately.
entries.knownFor: *Ms. Marvel* vol. 3, February 2014, co-created with her editor.
entries.signature: Prayer, dietary rules and a family curfew functioning as the structural obstacles a double life runs into — belief as an engine rather than a theme.

entries.category: Creators Working from Religion and Ethnicity
entries.name: Sana Amanat
entries.description: The editorial half of authorship — specificity protected through development rather than written in one pass.
entries.meta: American, born in New Jersey to Pakistani immigrant parents; living, with documented production work to 2022. Birth year is not documented and is deliberately absent. **She holds none of the five authorship claims, and this card states that on its face**: she is credited as co-creator in an editorial capacity, and the writing and art are other people's. **Credit is shared five ways and "creator of Ms. Marvel" is imprecise.** **The childhood-anecdote origin is documented as her own dated first-person statement — but the anecdote itself is never specified in the reporting, so the accurate form is that the character grew out of an anecdote she told her editor, per her own account.**
entries.knownFor: *Ms. Marvel* vol. 3 #1, February 2014.
entries.signature: A legacy identity inherited by a new protagonist who was a fan of the previous one — a reusable structural solution to writing inside an existing continuity.

entries.category: Creators Working from Religion and Ethnicity
entries.name: Naif Al-Mutawa
entries.description: One-to-one allegorical design — instant clarity, and a hard ceiling on character change.
entries.meta: Kuwaiti; living, with the last hard documentation in 2015 — **the weakest currency in this block and the card says so.** Birth year not documented. **He holds none of the five claims on the published comics**: a clinical psychologist by profession, he is the creator, founder and chief executive, and the issues were written and drawn by hired industry veterans. **Disclosures, all of them things done to him rather than by him**: a Saudi grand mufti condemned the work; he faced a 2014 blasphemy suit in Kuwait **which he won**, and won the 2015 appeal; ISIL members issued death threats in 2014.
entries.knownFor: *The 99*, launched 2006 in Kuwait; a crossover with an American publisher, October 2010.
entries.signature: Ninety-nine heroes each fixed to one divine attribute — a design that buys immediate legibility and forecloses the character arc, which is a live trade-off for any themed team.

entries.name: Steve Ditko
entries.description: The most under-credited writer of the revival — he plotted the run everyone quotes.
entries.meta: American, 1927 – c. 29 June 2018; **the death date is approximate and the card prints the "c."** — he was found deceased and the date is estimated. **This card is for the penciller, inker and writer claims: he self-inked, and held a plot credit from *The Amazing Spider-Man* #25 in 1965.** **Co-creation proportions are disputed and the pack adjudicates nothing**: his own itemisation of his contribution is on the record, and the other party assigned a character's first name. Held no letterer claim.
entries.knownFor: *Amazing Fantasy* #15, 1962; *The Amazing Spider-Man* #1–38, 1963–66.
entries.signature: Page design making anxiety a spatial property — the panel arrangement doing what a caption would otherwise have to say.

works.title: Amazing Fantasy
works.note: #15; the on-sale date is disputed between June and August

entries.name: Carmine Infantino
entries.description: He solved how to draw speed, and the answer launched a period.
entries.meta: American, 1925–2013. **This card is for the penciller and inker claims**; later art director and publisher. **Creator-rights status, both directions (line 22)**: he sued his former publisher in 2004 claiming ownership of four characters, and **the suit was dismissed the same year** — the pack states the outcome, not only the filing.
entries.knownFor: *Showcase* #4, October 1956 — the issue the revival is dated from.
entries.signature: The motion line as a vocabulary, and the costume designed as a graphic logo rather than as clothing.

entries.name: Gil Kane
entries.description: He taught superhero art to use the camera.
entries.meta: American, 1926–2000; born Eli Katz, Latvian Elija Kacs. **This card is for the penciller claim**, plus cover art. **Pseudonym type is contract-evasion**: he worked at one publisher as *Scott Edward* while under contract to another, and used two earlier names, one of them jointly. **Not to be confused with Bob Kane** — unrelated, both under adopted names, both in superhero comics simultaneously, and routinely conflated.
entries.knownFor: The Green Lantern redesign, 1959; the Atom, 1961; *His Name Is… Savage*, 1968, an early attempt at the long form.
entries.signature: The foreshortened up-shot — a figure lunging at the reader rather than posed across the panel.

entries.name: Gardner Fox
entries.description: He invented the shared multiverse and the team book — the two most load-bearing structural ideas in the genre.
entries.meta: American, 1911–1986; born Gardner Francis Cooper Fox. **This card is for the writer claim.** **Nine personal pen names** across genres, which is the largest count in the pack. **A work-for-hire outcome the pack states as what it was**: he stopped receiving work in 1968 after the publisher refused health insurance and other benefits to its older creators — **a benefits dispute, not a retirement.** *(A widely repeated version of this account was not verified in pass C and the card claims only what was.)*
entries.knownFor: "Flash of Two Worlds!", *The Flash* #123, 1961; the Justice League, from *The Brave and the Bold* #28, 1960.
entries.signature: A contradiction turned into a setting — two incompatible versions made compatible by making the incompatibility the premise.

entries.name: Stan Goldberg
entries.description: He chose the colour identities of a publisher's entire line, and got no credit box.
entries.meta: American, 1932–2014. **This card is for the colourist claim, primary**; also penciller and inker. **He worked uncredited through the period in question**, and his claim to have set those colour schemes **rests on his own testimony — which is what being uncredited means: there is, by construction, no credit-box evidence.** The pack presents it as a claim and says why it can be no more than that.
entries.knownFor: The colour schemes of a publisher's superhero line, late 1950s to mid 1960s.
entries.signature: A character recognised by palette before silhouette — the fifth authorship claim doing work the record never recorded.

entries.name: Robert Kanigher
entries.description: The man who scripted the issue the revival is dated from, and who is almost never named when that date is cited.
entries.meta: American, 1915–2002. **This card is for the writer claim**; also an editor. Used at least five byline pseudonyms. **Precision the pack insists on: he wrote the lead origin story of *Showcase* #4, "Mystery of the Human Thunderbolt!" — not the whole issue.** The second story is John Broome's, and *"Kanigher wrote Showcase #4"* is an overstatement that will be caught. **Creation credits for several of his characters are shared with artists in the ordinary manner of the period and he is not carded as sole creator of any of them.** **A disclosure: a documented reputation for volatility as a collaborator, from first-hand accounts by two artists who worked with him.**
entries.knownFor: *Showcase* #4's lead story, 1956; simultaneous output across war, romance, western and superhero.
entries.signature: Compressed reinvention — a discarded property re-premised, re-costumed and given a working origin inside a handful of pages.

entries.name: Denny O'Neil
entries.description: The template for the issue-driven superhero story, and the counter-lesson in how fast topicality dates.
entries.meta: American, 1939–2020; born Dennis Joseph O'Neil. **This card is for the writer claim**; also an editor. **Pseudonym type is a literary-allusion personal pen name**, taken from the protagonist of a 1955 novel and used at a different publisher.
entries.knownFor: *Green Lantern* #76–89, 1970–72 — **the title was never called *Green Lantern/Green Arrow* at the time; that is the 1983 reprint series and the trades.**
entries.signature: A cosmic officer confronted by a question he has no procedure for — the genre's furniture turned to face the reader's own street.

works.title: Green Lantern
works.note: vol. 2 #76–89; the title resumed only in 1976

entries.name: Neal Adams
entries.description: Photographic anatomy imported into superheroes — then the industry's most effective activist.
entries.meta: American, 1941–2022. **This card is for the penciller and inker claims**; also writer, editor and publisher. **He co-led the 1975 campaign that won the founding creators their settlement**, which is the more consequential half of his record. **A disclosure for any card quoting him as an authority beyond craft**: he promoted an expanding-Earth theory contradicting plate tectonics and built it into a superhero book.
entries.signature: Panel borders broken deliberately, so the figure's motion is an argument with the page's own geometry.

entries.name: Steve Englehart
entries.description: Long-form continuity as thematic argument rather than bookkeeping.
entries.meta: American, born 1943; living, with documented activity to 2021. **This card is for the writer claim.** **Pseudonym type is a protest pen name** — adopted during editorial disputes to withdraw his name from his own work, which is the same move Alan Moore makes under a different invented name and which `author-40` cards from the other side. **Pass C found two spellings of a second, house pseudonym and could not resolve which is correct; the card does not print either.**
entries.knownFor: *Captain America and the Falcon* #169–176, 1974 — **"Secret Empire" is the trade's title, not the run's**; *Avengers*, 1972–76.
entries.signature: A conspiracy that runs to the top and is never named — allegory that refuses to close, so the reader must.

entries.name: Don McGregor
entries.description: The first fully self-contained superhero novel told in issues.
entries.meta: American, born 1942; living, with documented work to 2018. **This card is for the writer claim.** Also a creator-ownership pioneer.
entries.knownFor: "Panther's Rage", *Jungle Action* #6–18, 1973–75. **The arc is #6–18; #6–24 is what the collections hold**, and the trailing issues are a separate, unfinished story. **#5 is a reprint and #23 is a reprint**, so the run's own page count is smaller than its issue span implies.
entries.signature: A closed cast, a mapped geography and a thesis, sustained across thirteen issues — arc planning treated as architecture.

works.title: Jungle Action
works.note: #6–18, the arc; the series ran to #24

entries.name: Frank Miller
entries.description: Caption and image as two deliberately mismatched narrators.
entries.meta: American, born 1957; living, with documented activity to 2024. **This card is for the writer, penciller and inker claims.** **His deconstructive turn begins in 1979–83, not 1986** — see `author-102`. **A disclosure, and the pack does not conflate categories**: political and content controversies from 2011, including public criticism from a peer, and his own later statement that he had not been thinking clearly during a difficult period. **No conduct allegation.**
entries.knownFor: *Daredevil*, 1979–83; *Ronin*, 1983–84; *Batman: The Dark Knight*, 1986 — **the indicia series title, not "The Dark Knight Returns", which is issue #1's chapter title applied to the whole by the collection.**
entries.signature: Compression — a caption that contradicts the picture it sits on, so the reader must decide which is lying.

entries.name: Howard Chaykin
entries.description: The formal vocabulary credited to 1986, arriving in 1983.
entries.meta: American, born 1950; living, with documented activity to 2023. **This card is for the writer and penciller claims.** **A disclosure: content controversies on two works, in 1988 and 2017 — content, not conduct.** **This card carries the block's own correction.** Sorted by first appearance, the block runs **1982 · 1983 · 1983–84 · 1984 · 1986 · 1986–91**: four of its six people are not 1986, and one of them is not deconstructive at all but the reconstructive counter-current running alongside. **"The 1986 Generation" is the year the market noticed, not the year the work began.** Two independent verification passes reached that conclusion from different evidence. **The category string is kept because it is declared in config and in a locked blueprint; the failure is stated here instead, and the rename is a §17 row for the full-pack review.**
entries.knownFor: *American Flagg!*, 1983.
entries.signature: Signage, media chatter and diegetic text layered into the panel until the page reads as an environment rather than a frame.

works.title: American Flagg!
works.note: three years before the year the block is named for

entries.name: Walt Simonson
entries.description: The reconstructive counter-case — proof that the block's label is a periodisation rather than a description.
entries.meta: American, born 1946; living, with documented activity to 2022. **This card is for the writer, penciller, inker and letterer claims — four of the five**, and **he hand-lettered his own sound effects**, which is why the letterer claim is not incidental. **He is not deconstructive**, and he runs 1983–87 — the two facts that together make him this block's most useful card.
entries.knownFor: *The Mighty Thor* #337–382, 1983–87.
entries.signature: The sound effect as a design element rather than an annotation — lettering promoted into the composition.

entries.name: Bill Sienkiewicz
entries.description: Paint, collage and mixed media inside a work-for-hire superhero book.
entries.meta: American, born 1958; born Boleslav William Felix Robert Sienkiewicz — **shortened, not anglicised: the surname is retained in full.** Living, with documented activity to 2024. **This card is for the penciller and inker claims**; he later wrote. **His break lands in 1984**, two years before the block's year.
entries.knownFor: *New Mutants*, 1984–85; *Elektra: Assassin*, 1986–87.
entries.signature: A superhero page that abandons the line entirely — the most radical formal break of the period, executed inside a monthly.

entries.name: Lynn Varley
entries.description: Colour carrying decay, era and irony rather than local hue.
entries.meta: American. **Living status is unconfirmed: no death is reported in any source pass C reached, and the most recent documented activity is 2007** — the weakest currency in the Authors collection, and the card states it rather than implying either answer. **Birth year is not documented and is deliberately absent.** **This card is for the colourist claim, primary.**
entries.knownFor: *Ronin*, 1983–84; *Batman: The Dark Knight*, 1986. Awards for colouring in 1999.
entries.signature: A palette that dates and degrades a world, so that the reader knows how late it is without being told.

entries.name: Ann Nocenti
entries.description: Superhero comics used for ecological, media and gender argument, with a genuinely destabilised antagonist.
entries.meta: American; living, with an award in 2018 and continuing work in comics and film. **This card is for the writer claim**; she was also an editor from 1984 to 1988. **Her defining work is 1988–90 — after the year the block is named for**, which is the fourth of the block's six datings to fall outside it.
entries.knownFor: *Daredevil*, 1986–91.
entries.signature: An antagonist whose instability is structural rather than decorative — she cannot be resolved because the argument she embodies has not been.

entries.name: Brian Michael Bendis
entries.description: Decompression as a deliberate technique, and what it costs as well as what it buys.
entries.meta: American, born 1967; living, with documented activity to 2025. **This card is for the writer claim**; he was **artist as well as writer on his early crime work**, which is where the dialogue method comes from. **Run-boundary warning: a widely used reference page states his *Daredevil* run as #26–50. It is #26–81**, with the artist off the book for five issues and a later reunion issue — **the pack's own research found the error on one page and the correction on an adjacent one**, and `continuity-64` cards the lesson.
entries.knownFor: *Ultimate Spider-Man*, from 2000; *Daredevil* #26–81, 2001–06; *Alias*, 2001.
entries.signature: An eleven-page origin expanded to seven issues — pace as a claim about what deserves the reader's time.

entries.name: Kelly Sue DeConnick
entries.description: A character's status treated as a writing problem rather than a marketing one.
entries.meta: American, born 1970; living, with work solicited into 2026. **This card is for the writer claim**; she is also an editor and a manga translator. **She uses her full name deliberately so that readers register a woman author** — a byline decision, not a pseudonym. **Run-boundary warning, and it is the trap this pack keeps meeting: the run is routinely cited as 2012–2015, a span that silently fuses two volumes.** This card is **vol. 7 #1–17, on sale 18 July 2012 to 6 November 2013**; the relaunched vol. 8 is a separate run, and the omnibus is a collected-edition span belonging to neither. **A disclosure: an organised fan backlash accusing the run of an agenda began before the first issue shipped — harassment directed at her, not an allegation against her.**
entries.knownFor: *Captain Marvel* vol. 7 #1–17, 2012–13.
entries.signature: A promotion earned inside the prose — voice, professional idiom and peer relationships doing the work a power upgrade would otherwise be asked to do.

entries.name: Ed Brubaker
entries.description: Crime-genre discipline applied to a legacy superhero — consequence, memory and succession as plot mechanics.
entries.meta: American, born 1966; living, with documented activity to 2024. **This card is for the writer claim**; also a cartoonist.
entries.knownFor: *Captain America*, November 2004 – October 2012.
entries.signature: A returning figure written as an intelligence problem rather than a resurrection — the reveal earned by procedure.

entries.name: Richard Donner
entries.description: Verisimilitude — the fantastic made to feel true within the story's own terms.
entries.meta: American, 1930–2021; born Richard Donald Schwartzberg. **He holds none of the five comics claims: a film director.** **Authorship of the sequel is genuinely divided and must never be attributed to one director**: he was removed after a dispute with a producer, replaced, and declined screen credit for material he had shot; a restored cut appeared in 2006. **Line 28 applies — director, writer, producer and "based on" are four separate claims** and this card makes only the first.
entries.knownFor: *Superman*, 1978.
entries.signature: The stated principle that the audience will accept anything once, provided the film never winks — sincerity as a technical requirement.

entries.name: Bruce Timm
entries.description: A self-contained tragedy in twenty-two minutes — how much backstory a writer can simply refuse to explain.
entries.meta: American, born 1961; living, announced as an executive producer in 2021. **He holds none of the five comics claims here: an animation producer, designer, director and writer.** **Line 28's four television claims are distinct** and this card names producer and designer first. **The series originated material the source line then adopted**, which `continuity-68` cards as authority relocating between media.
entries.knownFor: *Batman: The Animated Series*, 1992–95.
entries.signature: Design as compression — a city and a mood established by shape and palette so the script never has to describe either.

entries.name: Shōtarō Ishinomori
entries.description: The transformation sequence and the colour-coded team — the two structures most of the world's non-American superhero television runs on.
entries.meta: Japanese, 1938–1998; born 小野寺章太郎 Onodera Shōtarō. **石ノ森 is a personal pen name, respelled in 1986 — pre-1986 credits read 石森 Ishimori, and they are the same man, not two people.** **He holds the manga claims of a sole author, and his television "creator" credit is a licensing credit rather than an authorship claim**: the 1971 scripts are by other named writers and the direction by others again. **This is line 28 and line 21 colliding, and the card states both** — one character, several credited bodies, and a creator credit that describes ownership rather than work. **He receives co-creator credit on the later American adaptation and must not be described as its creator outright.**
entries.knownFor: *Kamen Rider*, 1971; *Himitsu Sentai Gorenger*, 1975; *Cyborg 009*, 1964.
entries.signature: A ritual of transformation with a fixed position in the episode — identity, cost and recurrence bound into one repeatable sequence.

entries.name: Sam Raimi
entries.description: The tonal contract most superhero fiction still signs — sincere melodrama under escalating spectacle.
entries.meta: American, born 1959; living, with a film released January 2026. **He holds none of the five comics claims: a film director.**
entries.knownFor: The *Spider-Man* trilogy, 2002–07.
entries.signature: The secret-identity misery played entirely straight while the set pieces grow — the refusal to let scale make the private life ironic.

entries.name: Ryan Coogler
entries.description: An antagonist whose political case is stronger than the hero's, and is never refuted — only defeated.
entries.meta: American, born 1986; living, with a 2025 feature and a confirmed next project. **He holds none of the five comics claims: a film director and co-writer — two of line 28's four claims, and the card names both.**
entries.knownFor: *Black Panther*, 2018.
entries.signature: The villain given the better argument and beaten anyway, so the victory is a cost rather than a resolution.

entries.name: Umberto Eco
entries.description: The structural trap behind every status-quo reset a writer will be asked to write.
entries.meta: Italian, 1932–2016; semiotician, Professor Emeritus at Bologna. **He holds none of the five claims and this is not an empirical source: humanities, a semiotic reading with no data.** **Also carded at `mystery-crime-thriller:author-126` for his novel — that card is for the novelist and this one for the semiotician**, and the two have nothing in common but the man. **The English translation is fully verified — *Diacritics* 2:1, Spring 1972, 14–22, trans. Natalie Chilton. That the essay first appeared in a 1964 Italian volume was NOT verified, and the pack cites the translation only.**
entries.knownFor: "The Myth of Superman", 1972.
entries.signature: A hero who consumes no time, in a haze the reader never quite notices — the observation the whole field has argued with for sixty years.

entries.name: Richard Reynolds
entries.description: The first serious attempt to state the genre's rules as rules.
entries.meta: **The person cannot be documented.** Pass C found no birth year, no institutional affiliation and no living status, despite the book appearing on two publishers' lists — **so this card is for the book and leaves the person blank, which is the honest form.** **A same-surname author on a related recent title surfaced in the same searches and must not be merged with him.** **Humanities: close reading and genre taxonomy, not empirical.** **His three-way continuity typology is carried elsewhere in this pack with research B's verbatim-UNCONFIRMED flag, which pass B2 did not clear** — see `continuity-8`.
entries.knownFor: *Super Heroes: A Modern Mythology*, Batsford 1992; University Press of Mississippi 1994.
entries.signature: Seven laws extracted from three books — the move that makes a genre arguable rather than merely describable.

entries.name: Peter Coogan
entries.description: The most usable working definition in print — a test a writer can run against their own protagonist.
entries.meta: American; living, with documented employment to 2024. Birth year not documented and deliberately absent. **He holds none of the five claims. Humanities: genre definition, not empirical.** **This pack's own organising claim is argued partly against his**, and §1 concedes what it takes from him — which is why the card is here rather than in a bibliography.
entries.knownFor: *Superhero: The Secret Origin of a Genre*, MonkeyBrain Books, 2006.
entries.signature: Mission, powers, identity — three tests stated tightly enough that the edge cases become visible instead of invisible.

works.title: Superhero: The Secret Origin of a Genre

entries.name: Ramzi Fawaz
entries.description: The sharpest account of why superhero bodies carry meaning beyond plot.
entries.meta: American; living, publishing to 2022; Associate Professor of English. **He holds none of the five claims. Humanities: queer and feminist theory, not empirical.**
entries.knownFor: *The New Mutants: Superheroes and the Radical Imagination of American Comics*, NYU Press, 2016.
entries.signature: The mutant body read as a form that makes political difference visible — the metaphor treated as a mechanism rather than a message.

entries.name: Carolyn Cocca
entries.description: The broken gender pattern quantified rather than asserted.
entries.meta: American; living, publishing to 2020; Professor of Politics, Economics and Law. **She holds none of the five claims.** **Her work is mixed and the pack says so on the card**: systematic counting of character appearances and creator demographics is **empirical**, and the political-theory argument built on it is **interpretive**. **Cite the counts as evidence and the conclusions as argument** — the distinction §5e exists to enforce.
entries.knownFor: *Superwomen: Gender, Power, and Representation*, Bloomsbury, 2016.
entries.signature: A count instead of an impression, so a writer can see exactly which conventions they are inheriting.

entries.name: Carol Tilley
entries.description: The pack's methodological conscience — she went to the primary records.
entries.meta: American; living, with a keynote in 2023; Associate Professor at Illinois. **She holds none of the five claims. Empirical: archival research on a critic's own case files** — the one card in this block whose method is evidence rather than reading. **`history-10` carries her finding, and carries the counter-argument beside it** (C-16): a 2020 forensic-psychiatry treatment accepts her methodological criticisms while arguing that the villain narrative built on them erases a documented civil-rights record.
entries.knownFor: "Seducing the Innocent: Fredric Wertham and the Falsifications That Helped Condemn Comics", *Information & Culture* 47:4, 2012, 383–413.
entries.signature: Going to the case files — the demonstration that a field's founding villain and its founding orthodoxy can both be wrong.

entries.category: The Prehistory: Pulp, Strip and Masked Man
entries.name: The Scarlet Pimpernel
entries.author: Baroness Emmuska Orczy
entries.awards: No award located; no award body covering genre or adventure prose existed in the period. [gap: thehugoawards.org consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: The double identity arrives fully formed and a third of a century early: a public persona built deliberately to be dismissed, concealing an…
entries.text: The double identity arrives fully formed and a third of a century early: a public persona built deliberately to be dismissed, concealing an operative whose whole method depends on being underestimated. What the superhero later adds is capability; what it inherits here is the **structure of concealment as active misdirection** rather than as mere secrecy. The pack cards it as a lineage claim and not an origin claim — the distinction `history-3` exists to hold.

entries.category: The Prehistory: Pulp, Strip and Masked Man
entries.name: The Curse of Capistrano (Zorro)
entries.author: Johnston McCulley
entries.awards: No award located; no award body covering genre or adventure prose existed in the period. [gap: thehugoawards.org consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Adds to the concealment the three things the pulp hero hands forward intact: a costume, a mark left deliberately at the scene, and an oppressed…
entries.text: Adds to the concealment the three things the pulp hero hands forward intact: a costume, a mark left deliberately at the scene, and an oppressed populace whose condition supplies the mandate nobody conferred. It is the clearest single ancestor of the American masked avenger, and the clearest case of the pack's boundary rule at work — the furniture is present, the capability is not, and the work sits in the prehistory rather than in the genre.

entries.category: The Prehistory: Pulp, Strip and Masked Man
entries.name: Detective Story Hour (The Shadow as narrator)
entries.author: Street & Smith, narrator credited to the house name Maxwell Grant
entries.awards: No award located; the Peabody Awards were not established until 1939. [gap: Peabody Awards database consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Radio serial. A narrator invented to advertise a magazine became more popular than the magazine, and the character was retro-fitted into prose to…
entries.text: Radio serial. A narrator invented to advertise a magazine became more popular than the magazine, and the character was retro-fitted into prose to meet the demand — the genre's first documented case of a persona escaping its medium. **The byline is a publisher-owned rotating house name used by at least five different writers**, which makes this the pack's earliest working example of authorship as a company asset, carded from the other side at `author-73`.

entries.category: The Prehistory: Pulp, Strip and Masked Man
entries.name: Gladiator (Philip Wylie)
entries.author: Philip Wylie
entries.awards: No award located; no award body covering genre prose existed in the period. [gap: thehugoawards.org consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: The physical superlative without the mandate: a man of extraordinary capability who never settles on what to do with it, and whose story is a series…
entries.text: The physical superlative without the mandate: a man of extraordinary capability who never settles on what to do with it, and whose story is a series of failed vocations rather than a career. It is routinely named as an antecedent of the American superhero and **what is actually documented is a resemblance plus a denial** — which is why the pack cards it as a lineage claim requiring evidence rather than as a source.

entries.category: The Prehistory: Pulp, Strip and Masked Man
entries.name: The Living Shadow
entries.author: Credited to the house name Maxwell Grant; written by Walter B. Gibson
entries.awards: No award located; no award body covering genre or pulp prose existed in the period. [gap: thehugoawards.org consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: The proprietary city, the network of agents, the fixed method and the identity that is itself a disguise — the operational apparatus the costumed…
entries.text: The proprietary city, the network of agents, the fixed method and the identity that is itself a disguise — the operational apparatus the costumed hero inherits whole. **The authorship is the finding as much as the book is**: the byline is a house name, the actual writer produced the great majority of the run, and at least four other people wrote under it, so a single-name attribution here is a claim about a trademark rather than about a person.

entries.category: The Prehistory: Pulp, Strip and Masked Man
entries.name: Doc Savage Magazine: The Man of Bronze
entries.author: Credited to the house name Kenneth Robeson; written by Lester Dent
entries.awards: No award located; no award body covering genre or pulp prose existed in the period. [gap: thehugoawards.org consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: The team as a set of specialisms around a central superlative, the headquarters, the recurring supporting cast, and a protagonist perfected by…
entries.text: The team as a set of specialisms around a central superlative, the headquarters, the recurring supporting cast, and a protagonist perfected by training rather than by accident — a self-made superman whose origin is a regimen. **A second publisher-owned house name**, used by at least ten writers across the line, and a reminder that the pulps had solved serial production a decade before the comic book had to.

entries.category: The Prehistory: Pulp, Strip and Masked Man
entries.name: The Phantom
entries.author: Lee Falk
entries.awards: No award located; no comic-strip or comic-book award body covering this material existed in 1936. The National Cartoonists Society was founded in 1946. [gap: National Cartoonists Society awards record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Comic strip. The skin-tight costume and the full mask arrive here, two years before the capability does — which is the single most useful fact in…
entries.text: Comic strip. The skin-tight costume and the full mask arrive here, two years before the capability does — which is the single most useful fact in the prehistory, because it separates the genre's iconography from its premise and shows they were invented by different people for different reasons. Also the first hero to operate as an inherited office rather than as an individual, a structure the genre spends the next ninety years rediscovering.

entries.name: Action Comics #1
entries.author: Jerry Siegel and Joe Shuster
