entries.awards: No award located; no comic-book award body existed. The earliest, the Alley Award, first honoured calendar year 1961. [gap: Alley Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Single issue. Not the invention of any component but the **assembly plus the commercial demonstration** — proof that a costumed figure with a…
entries.text: Single issue. Not the invention of any component but the **assembly plus the commercial demonstration** — proof that a costumed figure with a concealed identity could carry a title, at a scale that reorganised an industry inside two years. The mandate is assumed rather than conferred and never questioned, which makes it the purest available specimen of the pack's first mode. Its rights history is carded at `author-65` and is not incidental to it.

entries.name: Detective Comics #27
entries.author: Bill Finger and Bob Kane
entries.awards: No award located; no comic-book award body existed in 1939. [gap: Alley Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Single issue. Eleven months after the founding work and already an answer to it: no powers, no daylight, a city rather than a world, and a mandate…
entries.text: Single issue. Eleven months after the founding work and already an answer to it: no powers, no daylight, a city rather than a world, and a mandate warranted by grief rather than by capability. **Study the answer rather than the founding work** — genres are defined by the reply more than by the opening, and every position the reply opened is still occupied. The credit was single-named for seventy-six years and `author-67` carries what that cost.

entries.name: Whiz Comics #2
entries.author: Bill Parker and C. C. Beck
entries.awards: No award located; no comic-book award body existed in 1940. [gap: Alley Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Single issue. The wish-fulfilment line at its most literal — a child speaks a word and becomes the adult hero — and for a period the best-selling…
entries.text: Single issue. The wish-fulfilment line at its most literal — a child speaks a word and becomes the adult hero — and for a period the best-selling superhero in the United States. It is also the origin of the medium's longest trademark dispute, which is why `powers-25` cards it from the specification side: a character whose capability description was rewritten by three publishers under two names across eighty years.

entries.name: The Adventures of Superman (radio series)
entries.author: Robert Maxwell and Allen Ducovny for the radio serial
entries.awards: No award located. The Peabody Awards were established in 1939 with an Entertainment category from 1942 and a Programs for Children & Youth category from 1944; the official winners database returns no entry for this programme. [gap: Peabody Awards database consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Radio serial. The medium that supplied the character's most durable furniture — kryptonite, the cub reporter, the flying — invented for broadcast…
entries.text: Radio serial. The medium that supplied the character's most durable furniture — kryptonite, the cub reporter, the flying — invented for broadcast and imported back into the comics, which is `continuity-68`'s adjudication problem arriving in the genre's second year. **A 1946 on-air commendation from a veterans' organisation is a civic endorsement rather than a prize and this card does not present it as an award**, which is the distinction the pack's award rule exists for.

entries.name: The Spirit
entries.author: Will Eisner
entries.awards: No award located; no comic-book award body existed in 1940. [gap: Alley Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Comic strip. A newspaper insert whose author retained ownership in a period when almost nobody did, and which treats a city block rather than a…
entries.text: Comic strip. A newspaper insert whose author retained ownership in a period when almost nobody did, and which treats a city block rather than a protagonist as the organising subject. The splash page here is architecture rather than a title card. **Its Black sidekick is a minstrel-derived caricature a reader meets on the first page of any reprint**, and the pack states that rather than letting it be discovered.

entries.name: Captain America Comics #1
entries.author: Joe Simon and Jack Kirby
entries.awards: No award located; no comic-book award body existed in 1941. [gap: Alley Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Single issue. Cover-dated March 1941 and **on sale 20 December 1940** — a costumed figure striking a foreign head of state roughly a year before the…
entries.text: Single issue. Cover-dated March 1941 and **on sale 20 December 1940** — a costumed figure striking a foreign head of state roughly a year before the United States entered the war, which is a fact about publishing lead times as much as about politics. The pack's standing instruction to check on-sale against cover date comes from cases like this, where the two dates support different claims.

entries.name: Police Comics #1
entries.author: Jack Cole and others
entries.awards: No award located; no comic-book award body existed in 1941. [gap: Alley Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Single issue. The anthology as the era's actual unit of publication, and the home of the period's most formally inventive strip — a body that can…
entries.text: Single issue. The anthology as the era's actual unit of publication, and the home of the period's most formally inventive strip — a body that can become any shape, drawn by a cartoonist who used the premise to break the panel rather than to win fights. **Attribution across this issue is provisional**: shop production, house names and unprinted credits make the 1940s the period where `checklist-7` earns most.

entries.name: Superman (Fleischer/Famous shorts)
entries.author: Fleischer Studios; later Famous Studios
entries.awards: Academy Award nomination, Best Short Subject (Cartoons), 1942, for the first entry. It did not win. A nomination is not an award and this card does not present it as one.
entries.description: Feature film. Seventeen theatrical shorts that fixed the character's flight, palette and physical scale for every subsequent adaptation — the first…
entries.text: Feature film. Seventeen theatrical shorts that fixed the character's flight, palette and physical scale for every subsequent adaptation — the first time the genre's iconography was authored outside comics and imported back. **The award line is the pack's clearest small instance of V-03's third case**: a nomination is neither a win nor a documentation gap, and it is stated as what it is.

entries.name: All Star Comics #8
entries.author: William Moulton Marston and Harry G. Peter
entries.awards: No award located; no comic-book award body existed in 1941. [gap: Alley Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Single issue. Cover-dated December 1941 and **on sale 21 October 1941**. The genre's first major woman lead arrives inside a team anthology rather…
entries.text: Single issue. Cover-dated December 1941 and **on sale 21 October 1941**. The genre's first major woman lead arrives inside a team anthology rather than in her own title, which is a fact about how the form distributed attention. The character's later authorship — a second writer produced seventy-plus stories under a publisher-owned byline and went uncredited for seven decades — is carded at `author-2`.

entries.name: Showcase #4
entries.author: Robert Kanigher, Carmine Infantino and Joe Kubert
entries.awards: No award located; the Alley Award, the first American comic-book award, first honoured calendar year 1961. [gap: Alley Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Single issue. The revival's starting gun, and a masterclass in compressed reinvention — a discarded property re-premised, re-costumed and given a…
entries.text: Single issue. The revival's starting gun, and a masterclass in compressed reinvention — a discarded property re-premised, re-costumed and given a working origin in a handful of pages. **The lead story is Kanigher's; the second story in the same issue is another writer's**, and "he wrote Showcase #4" is the overstatement this pack's own verification caught before it was carded.

entries.name: The Brave and the Bold #28
entries.author: Gardner Fox and Mike Sekowsky
entries.awards: No award located; the first American comic-book award honoured calendar year 1961. [gap: Alley Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Single issue. Cover-dated February–March 1960 and **on sale 29 December 1959**. The team book as a commercial instrument — assembling proven…
entries.text: Single issue. Cover-dated February–March 1960 and **on sale 29 December 1959**. The team book as a commercial instrument — assembling proven characters so that each title's readers are exposed to the others — which is the mechanism `continuity-51` describes as an economic form, operating twenty-five years before it acquired a name.

entries.name: Fantastic Four #1
entries.author: Stan Lee and Jack Kirby
entries.awards: No award located; the Alley Awards for calendar year 1961 record no entry for this issue. [gap: Alley Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Single issue. Four capabilities with four unrelated logics and no governing rule, which is the asymmetric roster `powers-16` cards as this genre's…
entries.text: Single issue. Four capabilities with four unrelated logics and no governing rule, which is the asymmetric roster `powers-16` cards as this genre's distinguishing design object. It also establishes all three of Reynolds's continuity types at once — a first instalment, a set of relative power levels, and a family whose behaviour toward each other becomes the thing later writers can violate.

entries.name: Amazing Fantasy #15
entries.author: Stan Lee and Steve Ditko
entries.awards: No award located; no Alley Award entry located for this issue. [gap: Alley Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Single issue. The final issue of a cancelled title, which is the anniversary logic running in reverse — an occasion that started an accrual rather…
entries.text: Single issue. The final issue of a cancelled title, which is the anniversary logic running in reverse — an occasion that started an accrual rather than spending one, and the case `trope-67` cards. **The on-sale date is disputed between June and August 1962 and the pack states the dispute rather than choosing.** The origin's engine is a failure to act rather than an act, which is why the death it causes has never been reversible.

entries.name: The Amazing Spider-Man (Lee/Ditko run)
entries.author: Stan Lee and Steve Ditko
entries.awards: Alley Award, 1963 and subsequent years, in categories whose exact strings this pack does not reproduce. [gap: year-by-year Alley ballots consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. The run in which the method becomes visible: several plots advancing at once, incident carried by the page rather than by narration, and a…
entries.text: Run. The run in which the method becomes visible: several plots advancing at once, incident carried by the page rather than by narration, and a protagonist whose problems are rent and homework. **The award line is deliberately unspecific about categories.** The Alley category strings changed year to year and the year-by-year ballots could not be reached, so the pack names the body and declines to invent a category — the named-prize trap avoided by omission rather than by guess.

entries.name: The X-Men #1
entries.author: Stan Lee and Jack Kirby
entries.awards: No award located; no Alley Award entry located for this issue. [gap: Alley Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Single issue. A premise that makes the capability hereditary and therefore a social category rather than an accident — the move that lets the book…
entries.text: Single issue. A premise that makes the capability hereditary and therefore a social category rather than an accident — the move that lets the book be read as being about something, and the reading `psychology-2` labels as criticism rather than as evidence. It sold poorly for a decade before the premise found its audience, which is the commercial fact most accounts of it omit.

entries.name: Batman (1966 tv)
entries.author: William Dozier, executive producer
entries.awards: Emmy nominations, 1966; no win located. Nominations are not awards and this card does not present them as such. [gap: Television Academy record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Television series. The counter-case running inside the revival: a mass general audience reached by treating the material as camp, producing an…
entries.text: Television series. The counter-case running inside the revival: a mass general audience reached by treating the material as camp, producing an enormous short-term expansion and almost no durable readers. **It is also mode three's most consequential specimen** — the furniture complete, the mandate never at issue anywhere, and the whole thing legible as a superhero work on iconography alone.

entries.name: The Fourth World
entries.author: Jack Kirby
entries.awards: No award located for the original run; the Shazam Awards began with the ceremony of 1971. [gap: Academy of Comic Book Arts record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. A closed pantheon-scale myth built inside a work-for-hire line and cancelled mid-sentence — simultaneously the best model for…
entries.text: Run. A closed pantheon-scale myth built inside a work-for-hire line and cancelled mid-sentence — simultaneously the best model for cosmology-as-serial and the best cautionary tale about it. **The anchor issue's date is itself disputed between August and October 1970 and the pack states the dispute**, because it is the date the entire sequence is reckoned from.

entries.category: Bande Dessinee and the French Prosecution
entries.name: Fantax
entries.author: Pierre Mouchot, as Chott
entries.awards: No award located; the Angoulême festival was not founded until 1974 and awarded no album prize before 1976. [gap: Angoulême prize lineage consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. France's costumed vigilante before the law, and the clearest single case in any tradition of a superhero line legally extinguished. **Its…
entries.text: Run. France's costumed vigilante before the law, and the clearest single case in any tradition of a superhero line legally extinguished. **Its creator shut it down pre-emptively in 1949 to avoid prosecution under the new statute, was pursued from 1954 regardless, and was convicted in 1961** — seven years of proceedings over a comic that had already ceased. The pen name is personal, not a house name.

entries.category: Bande Dessinee and the French Prosecution
entries.name: Superdupont
entries.author: Marcel Gotlib and Jacques Lob
entries.awards: No award located for the original serialisation; the festival's first album prize was awarded in 1976. [gap: Angoulême prize lineage consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. What the form's French fate produced once the law had done its work: the superhero survives as parody, with national identity itself as the…
entries.text: Run. What the form's French fate produced once the law had done its work: the superhero survives as parody, with national identity itself as the superpower and the satire aimed at French chauvinism as much as at American comics. **Authorship moved across at least six artists after 1977 and a single-creator attribution would be false**, which is why this card names two and says so.

entries.category: Bande Dessinee and the French Prosecution
entries.name: La Brigade chimérique
entries.author: Serge Lehman, Fabrice Colin and Gess
entries.awards: Grand Prix de l'Imaginaire, 2011, in the bande dessinée category. This is not an Angoulême prize and the two are routinely confused.
entries.description: Bande dessinée. An archaeology of the European superhero that never was — it makes the **absence** the story, tracing a vanished 1920s and 1930s…
entries.text: Bande dessinée. An archaeology of the European superhero that never was — it makes the **absence** the story, tracing a vanished 1920s and 1930s continental tradition of *surhommes* and the appropriation that ended it. The model for writing a genre's suppressed history as plot rather than as preface, and the counterpart to `history-16`'s argument that a period label can conceal what it claims to describe.

entries.category: Shonen Battle Manga and Mahou Shoujo
entries.name: サイボーグ009 / Cyborg 009
entries.author: 石ノ森章太郎 Shōtarō Ishinomori
entries.awards: No award located for the original serialisation; the Shogakukan Manga Award existed from 1955 but no entry for this work was located. [gap: Shogakukan Manga Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Manga. Nine people rebuilt as weapons by the organisation that abducted them, whose mandate is taken rather than conferred — the team assembled from…
entries.text: Manga. Nine people rebuilt as weapons by the organisation that abducted them, whose mandate is taken rather than conferred — the team assembled from the wreckage of somebody else's programme. It is the earliest of this pack's Japanese entries to satisfy all three clauses of the organising claim without qualification, and the mandate question is the story rather than its premise. Carded here because **the Manga pack is planned and not yet built**.

entries.category: Shonen Battle Manga and Mahou Shoujo
entries.name: 魔法使いサリー / Sally the Witch
entries.author: 横山光輝 Mitsuteru Yokoyama
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Shogakukan Manga Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Manga. The transformation heroine before the team, the costume or the ritual — a girl with power concealing it inside an ordinary life, which is the…
entries.text: Manga. The transformation heroine before the team, the costume or the ritual — a girl with power concealing it inside an ordinary life, which is the secret-identity structure arriving in a form the American tradition had not thought to apply to a child. **Sources describe it as "one of the first" rather than the first, and a rival title preceded it in print while its own animated version preceded that rival's**; the pack states the contest rather than printing an unqualified priority. Carded here because **the Manga pack is planned and not yet built**.

entries.category: Shonen Battle Manga and Mahou Shoujo
entries.name: キューティーハニー / Cutie Honey (1973 manga)
entries.author: 永井豪 Gō Nagai
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Kodansha Manga Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Manga. The transformation sequence made explicit as spectacle, and an android protagonist whose capability is literally the assumption of other…
entries.text: Manga. The transformation sequence made explicit as spectacle, and an android protagonist whose capability is literally the assumption of other identities — the mask taken to its logical end, where there is no face underneath to unmask. It moves the magical-girl form into a shonen register, which is why it sits in this block rather than beside the earlier title. Carded here because **the Manga pack is planned and not yet built**.

entries.category: Shonen Battle Manga and Mahou Shoujo
entries.name: ドラゴンボール / Dragon Ball
entries.author: 鳥山明 Akira Toriyama
entries.awards: No award located for the original serialisation. [gap: Shogakukan Manga Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Manga. **This work enters the pack in mode three and the card says so.** It fails the mandate clause — nobody confers the protagonist's licence to…
entries.text: Manga. **This work enters the pack in mode three and the card says so.** It fails the mandate clause — nobody confers the protagonist's licence to act and nobody could revoke it, and the question is never at issue anywhere in the work — so it is admitted on iconographic legibility alone, exactly as §2's cost 3 rules. **The exclusion from modes one and two is argued from the primary text rather than inherited**, which matters because a neighbouring pack cards this work as its weak example and this pack declines to inherit that judgement. What it is unmatched at is **owned escalation**: a power curve with a designed shape, a known ceiling and an author holding it, which `powers-24` cards as the condition creep requires. Carded here because **the Manga pack is planned and not yet built**.

entries.category: Shonen Battle Manga and Mahou Shoujo
entries.name: 美少女戦士セーラームーン / Sailor Moon (1991 manga)
entries.author: 武内直子 Naoko Takeuchi
entries.awards: Kodansha Manga Award, shōjo category, 1993. The category existed in that year; the award's earlier lineage is discontinuous and this pack does not back-date it.
entries.description: Manga. **Mode one, per §2** — the mandate is assumed, never conferred, and never revocable. Its structural move is the fusion of the magical-girl…
entries.text: Manga. **Mode one, per §2** — the mandate is assumed, never conferred, and never revocable. Its structural move is the fusion of the magical-girl transformation with the sentai team: a *group* of transforming girls with assigned colours and a combination finish, which is where the modern form actually begins and which no single-heroine predecessor supplies. The transformation is a ritual the audience learns to anticipate, in `powers-27`'s sense. Carded here because **the Manga pack is planned and not yet built**.

entries.category: Shonen Battle Manga and Mahou Shoujo
entries.name: カードキャプターさくら / Cardcaptor Sakura
entries.author: CLAMP
entries.awards: Seiun Award, Best Comic, 2001. [gap: Kodansha and Shogakukan records consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Manga. **Authorship here does not fit the five-claim model and the card states it**: a four-woman studio publishing under one name, with a…
entries.text: Manga. **Authorship here does not fit the five-claim model and the card states it**: a four-woman studio publishing under one name, with a writer-storyboarder, a chief character designer and two background artists who rotate roles — no inker, no letterer, no colourist, and no individual to card. The work itself makes collection rather than combat the engine, so escalation is replaced by accumulation. Carded here because **the Manga pack is planned and not yet built**.

entries.category: Shonen Battle Manga and Mahou Shoujo
entries.name: 魔法少女まどか☆マギカ / Puella Magi Madoka Magica
entries.author: Gen Urobuchi and Studio Shaft
entries.awards: Seiun Award, Best Media, 2012; Television Academy of Japan animation award, 2011. [gap: Japan Media Arts Festival record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Animated series. **Anime-original rather than adapted**, which is why it is `tv` and not `manga` — the manga followed it. It is the magical-girl…

It is the magical-girl form's deconstruction from inside, and its mechanism is precisely the mandate clause: the licence to act is **conferred by a party whose terms are concealed**, and the story is the discovery of what was signed. That makes it the block's clearest mode-two work and the counterpart to this pack's registration cards. Carded here because **the Manga pack is planned and not yet built**.

Carded here because **the Manga pack is planned and not yet built**.

entries.text: Graphic novel. The working answer to the genre's cure reflex: a disabled protagonist written as a life rather than as a problem awaiting a plot solution, by an openly disabled author. **It is the counter-case `powers-28` names**, and the only card in this block whose creator's disability is self-disclosed rather than acquired mid-career — which is itself the block's shape, and the pack states that rather than smoothing it.

entries.text: Single issue. The first Black superhero in mainstream American comics arrives as **a head of state who out-thinks the visiting protagonists on his own ground** — the debut is structured as an ambush and a test rather than as a rescue, which is why it still reads as un-condescending sixty years on. **A causal claim runs the wrong way in most accounts and the pack corrects it: the political party of the same name was founded three months after this issue.**

The stakes are not academic: one of the three died destitute and his funeral costs were raised by an industry charity.

The most technically radical superhero run of its era: **non-linear narration filtered through a hostile, comic outsider** who keeps mistaking the office for the man, so the reader has to earn access to the protagonist. **Priest did not write #57–58**, so the commonly cited span of sixty-two overstates it by two. Point of view deployed as a political argument rather than as a device.

entries.text: Feature film. The film that proved a Black-led superhero text could carry a **genuinely contested political antagonist** — the challenger's diasporic claim is never refuted, only defeated, which is the harder and rarer construction. **It is the first superhero film nominated for Best Picture, under the expanded field introduced in 2009**; the pack notes that the expansion's rationale named a different superhero film as an example, and that a named example is not the same as a demonstrated cause.

The form has no American equivalent and the direction of export runs outward, to Colombia and Venezuela. **The persona is a character-persona byline of a kind no pen name matches** — a role occupied by a body, heritable, trademarked, and ended only by unmasking or death, which `author-62` cards from the person's side.

entries.text: Feature film. **The three-way trap this card exists to resolve.** A 1952 film with a silver-masked title is *not* a Santo film — he declined it and another wrestler took the lead. This is his **first film appearance**, shot in Havana in late 1958 and released in Mexico City in July 1961, **in which he is not the star**. His first starring role is a different film again. The carded year is the year the work was made in the form it was made as, and the release gap is stated rather than smoothed.

entries.text: Feature film. **His first starring role**, and the film that fixes the template: the wrestler as an investigator with police sanction, moving between the ring and the crime plot without changing costume, because the costume is not a disguise but an identity he never sets down. The mandate here is **conferred and explicit** — he works with the authorities — which makes the luchador film a mode-two tradition rather than the vigilante one an American reader expects.

The Latin American tradition's entry point and its widest-reaching work — a serial that ran for decades and generated a comic rather than the reverse, which inverts the usual order and is why it is carded in its original medium. The protagonist's capabilities are mental and disciplinary rather than physical, and the mandate is a moral code stated aloud, which places the work closer to the pulp lineage than to the costumed one.

The issue in which a character disabled by a notorious earlier work is rebuilt as an intelligence operative rather than restored — **the genre's single most consequential refusal of the cure reflex**, and the origin of a role that outgrew the story that produced it. **Her first appearance in that role is here; the identity is not named until a later issue**, and the pack states which is which rather than collapsing them.

entries.text: Single issue. A deaf Cheyenne protagonist whose perception is rendered as a way of being in the world rather than as a compensating ability — **neither cured nor traded, which is the counter-case to all three patterns `powers-28` names**. **Her tribal affiliation was changed for a screen adaptation**, which is the pack's clearest instance of an adaptation altering a character's specificity for production convenience.

entries.author: Mark Waid and Paolo Rivera

entries.description: Run. Commissioned under an explicit brief to move the book out of a decade of grimness, and the brief is invisible in the result — **what a mandate…
entries.text: Run. Commissioned under an explicit brief to move the book out of a decade of grimness, and the brief is invisible in the result — **what a mandate looks like when it has been used rather than endured**, which `continuity-53` cards as the formal-constraint reading. Its treatment of the protagonist's disability is neither affliction nor superpower but a **method**, and the run's refusal to be defined by the affliction is the argument.

entries.description: Criticism. The scholarly treatment this block is answerable to, and the reason the block exists in the shape it does. **It is humanities rather than…
entries.text: Criticism. The scholarly treatment this block is answerable to, and the reason the block exists in the shape it does. **It is humanities rather than empirical** — close reading of a genre's record, not a study of readers — and the pack labels it as such, because a card that cited it as evidence about disabled readers would be misreading the genre of the source. Its account of the cure reflex is what `powers-28` states as a pattern and what `work-51` and `work-52` are carded against.

entries.description: Tokusatsu series. The Japanese live-action costumed hero arrives here, on television rather than in print, with a masked figure whose warrant to act…
entries.text: Tokusatsu series. The Japanese live-action costumed hero arrives here, on television rather than in print, with a masked figure whose warrant to act is announced rather than granted. **The lineage clause of this pack's organising claim does not apply to it**: the tradition is a parallel invention and not a borrowing, and this work is admitted on iconographic legibility alone. It is frequently called **"Japan's first superhero"** and this pack declines the phrase, which is on its forbidden list: at least three works are advanced for the priority under three different definitions, and the contest is worth stating where the winner is not. What it does establish beyond argument is the **serialised television hero as the tradition's native form**, which is why the block that follows is mostly television and the American block is mostly print. Carded here because **the Manga pack is planned and not yet built**.

entries.text: Tokusatsu series. **The lineage clause does not apply**: this is the parallel tradition, admitted on iconography, and the card states it rather than letting the shared silhouette imply descent. Its mandate is **mode two and unusually explicit** — the hero is fused to a member of an official science patrol, so the licensing question sits in the premise rather than arriving as a complication, and the organisation that briefs and equips him can also stand him down. **The Author field carries three names because one would be false**: pass C's finding is that tokusatsu divides among creator, head writer, effects director and suit actor what a comic collapses into a single credit, and the giant-scale effects work is the contribution the genre exported. Carded here because **the Manga pack is planned and not yet built**.

entries.name: 仮面ライダー / Kamen Rider (1971 tv)
entries.author: 石ノ森章太郎 Shōtarō Ishinomori, credited creator; Toei, production
entries.awards: No award located; the Japan Media Arts Festival was not founded until 1997 and cannot reach this year. [gap: Japan Media Arts Festival record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Tokusatsu series. **The lineage clause does not apply**; the work enters on iconographic legibility, as every card in this block does. The…
entries.text: Tokusatsu series. **The lineage clause does not apply**; the work enters on iconographic legibility, as every card in this block does. The transformation is fixed, repeated and announced, which converts the costume from a disguise into a **ritual the audience learns to anticipate** — and it is what `powers-27` puts to every transformation hero, which is the question of what the untransformed body is for. The repeated change is the structural signature the block is named for. Its mandate is taken rather than conferred: the hero is a defector from the organisation that built him, so the licence is seized from the party that would have granted it. **Two honesties about the credit.** Pass C establishes that the television "creator" credit here is a **licensing credit** and the 1971 scripts are by other hands; and **the name is spelled Ishinomori throughout this pack, including on work published before he respelled it in 1986** — Ishimori and Ishinomori are one man, and this pack's house style is the creator's own final spelling throughout. Carded here because **the Manga pack is planned and not yet built**.

entries.description: Tokusatsu series. **The lineage clause does not apply.** This is the founding of the colour-coded team with a combination finish — the single most…
entries.text: Tokusatsu series. **The lineage clause does not apply.** This is the founding of the colour-coded team with a combination finish — the single most exported structure in the tradition, and the one an American audience met decades later in adaptation without meeting its origin. Its mandate is **mode two throughout**: an organisation recruits, assigns, colour-codes and directs, and the individual hero has no standing outside it, which is the opposite of the American default and is why this pack's mandate test is worth running on non-Western material rather than assuming the answer. The colour-coding is `trope-62` built into a format rather than left to a costume designer, and the combination finish is the scene-form `powers-20` cards as the mechanism the American tradition largely declined to use. Carded here because **the Manga pack is planned and not yet built**.

entries.description: Tokusatsu series. **The lineage clause does not apply**, and this card states it for a work made twenty-nine years into the tradition, where the…
entries.text: Tokusatsu series. **The lineage clause does not apply**, and this card states it for a work made twenty-nine years into the tradition, where the reflex would be to treat the statement as settled and drop it. The series reopens the mandate question the block had let harden: the police are a **procedural counterweight** who investigate, doubt and eventually cooperate with the hero, so the licence is negotiated across a season rather than assumed in an opening narration. That is `trope-45`'s arrangement — the institution that neither deputises nor arrests — given a whole season to resolve rather than left as standing furniture: the transformation is unchanged, the paperwork around it is entirely new. **Its award negative is bounded rather than structural**: unlike the block's four earlier entries, a qualifying body existed in this year, so the negative names a search rather than a founding date. Carded here because **the Manga pack is planned and not yet built**.

entries.description: Tokusatsu series. **The lineage clause does not apply.** Late-night, adult-audience tokusatsu with a hereditary armoured knighthood, and it is…
entries.text: Tokusatsu series. **The lineage clause does not apply.** Late-night, adult-audience tokusatsu with a hereditary armoured knighthood, and it is carded because it demonstrates that the henshin form is **not intrinsically a children's television format** — the assumption the American reception of the tradition has mostly made. Its mandate is **conferred and revocable in the strictest sense in this pack**: the title is inherited, held under a governing order, subject to a time limit on the armour and forfeitable for failure, so the licence has both a grantor and a clock. That makes it the block's best answer to what `checklist-1` audits: not whether the protagonist has a warrant, but what holding on to it costs. Carded here because **the Manga pack is planned and not yet built**.

entries.description: Manga. **The category is a compromise and the card says so.** This is a manga in a block named for a live-action television form, placed here…
entries.text: Manga. **The category is a compromise and the card says so.** This is a manga in a block named for a live-action television form, placed here because the pack's twenty-five Works categories have no slot for the founding Japanese hero manga outside the shonen block, which is full at ten. The genuine connection is that its **1959 live-action adaptation is among the earliest Japanese costumed-hero television series**, which is this block's actual subject. **The lineage clause does not apply** here either, and for the same reason as the rest of the block. The carded year is the 1952 serialisation rather than the 1951 strip the character first appeared in, per S-10 — the year the work first appeared in the form it was written as — and the earlier appearance is a precursor with a different premise, not the same work under another name. Carded here because **the Manga pack is planned and not yet built**.

entries.name: 仮面ライダー / Kamen Rider (1971 manga)
entries.author: 石ノ森章太郎 Shōtarō Ishinomori
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Shogakukan and Kodansha Manga Award records consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Manga. **The manga and the television series are the same year and are not the same work**, which is why the pack disambiguates both and cards them…
entries.text: Manga. **The manga and the television series are the same year and are not the same work**, which is why the pack disambiguates both and cards them separately. Here the credit is not a licensing credit: Ishinomori drew this himself, concurrently with the broadcast, and the divergence is the point — **the manga is markedly bleaker, and its ending is not the television ending.** **The lineage clause does not apply.** The pair is the cleanest case in the pack of a single property whose two simultaneous versions answer the mandate question differently, and a writer looking for what adaptation actually costs should read them side by side rather than treating either as the source. Carded here because **the Manga pack is planned and not yet built**.

entries.author: John Wagner and Carlos Ezquerra
entries.awards: No award located, and no category string is cited. [gap: Eagle Award ballot record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. **The mandate is the whole subject and it is monstrous.** A judge who is police, court and executioner in one body holds the most explicitly…
entries.text: Run. **The mandate is the whole subject and it is monstrous.** A judge who is police, court and executioner in one body holds the most explicitly conferred licence in this pack, granted by a state whose legitimacy the strip never endorses — so the reader is asked to enjoy a competence they are not permitted to approve of. That is satire that survives forty years of serialisation because the joke is structural rather than topical, and it is the British line's founding move: **take the American mandate seriously enough to ask who signed it.** Its real-time ageing, in which the character ages a year for every publication year, is the **road not taken** by the convention `continuity-4` cards — sliding time, and the bill it runs up.

entries.name: Marvelman / Miracleman
entries.author: Alan Moore, with Garry Leach and Alan Davis

entries.description: Run. **The carded year is 1982 and the character is from 1954**, which S-10 resolves rather than obscures: the object carded is Moore's revival,…
entries.text: Run. **The carded year is 1982 and the character is from 1954**, which S-10 resolves rather than obscures: the object carded is Moore's revival, which is a different work from the Mick Anglo original it continues, and the pack dates it by the form it was written as. The revival's method is the one the whole decade then borrows — **take an existing children's hero literally and follow the consequences** — and it arrives at deposed governments and levelled cities four years before the American books that get the credit for it. **The dual title is not a variant spelling**: the name changed for trademark reasons on export, and the ownership dispute that followed kept the work out of print for decades, which `continuity-38` cards as the clearest case of a rights position determining what a canon contains.

entries.category: The British Line: 2000 AD and Marvelman
entries.name: Captain Britain (Moore/Davis run)
entries.author: Alan Moore and Alan Davis
entries.awards: No award located, and no category string is cited. [gap: Eagle Award ballot record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. **The name in the card is the run, not the character**, per §8's convention for a work whose carded object is a creative tenure rather than a…
entries.text: Run. **The name in the card is the run, not the character**, per §8's convention for a work whose carded object is a creative tenure rather than a title — the character dates from 1976 and the run carded here begins in 1982. Its structural contribution is the **multiverse used as a moral instrument rather than a filing system**: parallel Britains are visited and destroyed, and the destruction is neither reversed nor absorbed — which is `continuity-28`'s cost of unbounded possibility answered by refusing to make the possibilities free. It is also the point at which the British writers entering the American industry acquire the habit the next decade is built on: **treating a licensed corporate character as material rather than as a job**.

entries.category: The British Line: 2000 AD and Marvelman
entries.name: Bananaman
entries.author: Steve Bright, Dave Donaldson and John Geering
entries.awards: No award located, and no category string is cited. [gap: Eagle Award ballot record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Comic strip. **A children's humour strip is carded in this pack deliberately**, because the British tradition's relationship to the American genre…
entries.text: Comic strip. **A children's humour strip is carded in this pack deliberately**, because the British tradition's relationship to the American genre is substantially parodic and a block that carded only its serious end would misrepresent it. The transformation is triggered by eating a banana, the hero is a schoolboy, and every element of the American template is present and deflated — which is a genuine mandate case rather than a joke about one: **the licence is self-assumed, comically unearned, and never once questioned by anyone in the strip**, which is the assumption mode taken to its limit. That is `trope-14` taken to its comic limit — the costume as permission, granted by nobody and questioned by no one. Its animated adaptation reached an audience the serious British line never did.

entries.category: The British Line: 2000 AD and Marvelman
entries.name: Zenith
entries.author: Grant Morrison and Steve Yeowell
entries.awards: No award located, and no category string is cited. [gap: Eagle Award ballot record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. A superhero who is a pop star and declines the job, which makes **refusal of the mandate the premise** rather than a third-act crisis — the…
entries.text: Run. A superhero who is a pop star and declines the job, which makes **refusal of the mandate the premise** rather than a third-act crisis — the licence is available, legible and offered, and the protagonist would rather not. It is the British line's answer to the American deconstruction of the same years, and it differs in method: where those books take the mandate seriously and find it appalling, this one finds it **boring**, which is a harder position to sustain and a rarer one in the genre. Its own rights history mirrors *Marvelman*'s: **the ownership dispute kept it uncollected for decades**, and the two together are why this block's cards state rights positions where American cards state print runs.

entries.category: The British Line: 2000 AD and Marvelman
entries.name: Marshal Law
entries.author: Pat Mills and Kevin O'Neill
entries.awards: No award located. The Eisner Awards were first presented in 1988, for 1987 work; no entry for this series was located. [gap: Eisner Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Limited series. **A period-bound publishing fact the card names rather than assumes**, which is `powers-25`'s discipline applied to a work rather…
entries.text: Limited series. **A period-bound publishing fact the card names rather than assumes**, which is `powers-25`'s discipline applied to a work rather than to a capability: this is British-created work published by an American house — Marvel's creator-owned imprint — in 1987, and that arrangement is the reason the British line's influence arrives inside the American industry rather than beside it. The premise is a state-licensed hero-hunter, so the mandate is conferred **in order to be turned against other holders of it**, and the satire is aimed at the genre's militarism rather than at its earnestness. It is the most hostile book in this pack toward its own subject, and it is carded because a genre reference that omits its own strongest internal critic is doing advocacy.

entries.category: The British Line: 2000 AD and Marvelman
entries.name: Jack Staff
entries.author: Paul Grist
entries.awards: No award located, and no category string is cited. [gap: Eisner and Eagle Award records consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. **Self-published, single-authored, and carded partly for that** — the block's other six entries are all company or imprint work, and the…
entries.text: Run. **Self-published, single-authored, and carded partly for that** — the block's other six entries are all company or imprint work, and the British line's later history is substantially a small-press one that a roster built from famous names would erase. Its formal move is a **fractured chronology used as a continuity method**: the book jumps decades between pages and asks the reader to assemble the history, which is the opposite of the recap-and-restate discipline the American mainstream uses and is `continuity-10`'s claim adopted deliberately — the reader is the storage medium, and this book knows it. The mandate here is a British wartime hero's, assumed under an emergency that ended fifty years earlier and never formally revoked — which is a joke and also a real answer to what happens to a licence nobody withdraws.

entries.name: नागराज / Nagraj

entries.description: Run. India's flagship costumed hero, and the point at which the Indian industry stops adapting mythological material and builds a serial superhero…
entries.text: Run. India's flagship costumed hero, and the point at which the Indian industry stops adapting mythological material and builds a serial superhero line of its own. **The mandate is assumed and its origin is criminal**: the character begins as a weapon built by others and turns, which is the same shape as *Kamen Rider* arrived at independently fifteen years earlier and is worth noting as convergence rather than influence. The powers are drawn from **Indian serpent mythology rather than from science or accident**, which is the tradition's actual difference from the American template and a more useful one than the surface differences of costume and setting. **Who inked, coloured or lettered this work could not be established**: pass C found the same for thirteen of fourteen people in this pack's Indian, other-national and Latin American blocks, and that is a finding about what was recorded, not an indication that the roles did not exist.

entries.name: Mr. India (1987 film)
entries.author: Shekhar Kapur, director; Salim–Javed, writers
entries.awards: No award verified in this pass; Filmfare Award nominations for this film are in circulation and none was confirmed against the awarding body's own record. [gap: Filmfare Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Feature film. **The disambiguating suffix is doing real work**: a 1961 film shares the title and is unrelated, and §8's convention resolves it. The…
entries.text: Feature film. **The disambiguating suffix is doing real work**: a 1961 film shares the title and is unrelated, and §8's convention resolves it. The hero's capability is invisibility from a device his father built, so the power is **inherited technology rather than a body**, and the mandate is assumed under a specific and dated pressure — the film is explicit that its villain is a hoarder and its hero's constituency is hungry children. That makes it the pack's clearest case of the genre's social contract being written **locally rather than imported**, and it is carded ahead of better-known Indian titles for exactly that reason. It is also a musical, which the pack notes without treating as an anomaly: the genre's forms are national, and a reference that carded only the American shape of a superhero film would be describing one industry and calling it the genre.

entries.description: Feature film. The Indian superhero franchise as a commercial structure — sequels, merchandising and a costumed silhouette designed to be legible on…
entries.text: Feature film. The Indian superhero franchise as a commercial structure — sequels, merchandising and a costumed silhouette designed to be legible on a poster — which is the industrial half of this genre and is usually carded only in its American form. **Its mandate is inherited across two films**: the powers come from the previous film's protagonist, the father, so the licence is a family matter rather than an institutional one, and the story is a son deciding whether to take up something he did not ask for. **This entry replaced Super Commando Dhruva in the roster at pass D**, which moved the block from three comics and one film to two and two — a change the card records because the block's medium balance is an argument about where the Indian tradition actually lives.

entries.name: മിന്നൽ മുരളി / Minnal Murali
entries.author: Basil Joseph, director
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Kerala State Film Award and Filmfare South records consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Feature film. A Malayalam-language origin story in which lightning strikes **two** people, and the pack cards it for that structural decision: the…
entries.text: Feature film. A Malayalam-language origin story in which lightning strikes **two** people, and the pack cards it for that structural decision: the antagonist is made by the same accident in the same instant, so the film's question is not what power does to a man but **why the same event produces a hero and a villain**, which the American origin story almost never asks directly. The mandate is assumed and immediately contested by a village that has known the protagonist all his life — a small-scale legitimacy problem the metropolitan version of this genre cannot stage. It is the most recent work in this pack's international blocks and evidence that the tradition is **still originating rather than only adapting**, which the block's other three entries, all at least fifteen years older, would otherwise leave open.

entries.description: Run. The Philippines' foundational costumed hero, a village girl who swallows a stone and transforms — so the tradition's central heroine is **a…
entries.text: Run. The Philippines' foundational costumed hero, a village girl who swallows a stone and transforms — so the tradition's central heroine is **a transformation hero rather than a disguised one**, arriving at the henshin structure independently of Japan and eight years before it. **The carded year is the 1950 serialisation and an earlier version of the character ran in 1947 under a different name**, which the card states rather than smoothing: the pack's rule is that a precursor with a different premise is a precursor, not the same work. The mandate is conferred by a dying guardian and is conditional on the stone, which makes it revocable in a way the American assumed mandate is not. **Who inked, coloured or lettered could not be established** — pass C's finding about the record outside the American system, stated rather than left to inference.

entries.description: Run. Korea's first serial costumed hero, in a decade when the country had a comics industry and almost no surviving archive of it — which is why…
entries.text: Run. Korea's first serial costumed hero, in a decade when the country had a comics industry and almost no surviving archive of it — which is why this card is short on production detail and says so instead of padding. **The name is a research hazard the pack records**: pass C found this creator in three romanisation clusters and this work in five title variants, and a naive dedupe produces two or three phantom people from one man. The hero flies, wears a costume legible at a glance, and operates against an external threat in a country five years out of a war, so the **mandate is national and assumed** in the most literal sense this pack cards. **Who inked, coloured or lettered could not be established.**

entries.name: Raio Negro
entries.author: Gedeone Malagola
entries.awards: No award located; no Brazilian comics award body covering this period was identified in this pass. [gap: Brazilian comics award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. A Brazilian masked hero from the domestic publishing boom of the 1960s, carded alongside this pack's 1954 Brazilian television entry so that…
entries.text: Run. A Brazilian masked hero from the domestic publishing boom of the 1960s, carded alongside this pack's 1954 Brazilian television entry so that the block holds **both halves of one national tradition rather than a single convenient example**. Its interest is the mandate: the hero operates with police knowledge and without police authority, which is the **tolerated-vigilante position** that the American books of the same decade were forbidden by their own code to depict honestly. Brazil's superhero line is usually summarised as derivative and pass D found the summary is doing work the record does not support — the borrowing is of costume and format, not of the licence question, which is answered locally. **Who inked, coloured or lettered could not be established.**

entries.name: 小流氓 → 龍虎門 / Oriental Heroes
entries.author: 黃玉郎 Wong Yuk-long
entries.awards: No award located; no Hong Kong comics award body covering this period was identified in this pass. [gap: Hong Kong comics award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. **The arrow in the name is not a typographic flourish**: the title changed mid-run, from *Little Rascals* to *Oriental Heroes*, and the pack…
entries.text: Run. **The arrow in the name is not a typographic flourish**: the title changed mid-run, from *Little Rascals* to *Oriental Heroes*, and the pack cards both because the change tracks the work's own move from street-gang realism to costumed martial-arts spectacle. That trajectory is the block's most useful case, because it shows a superhero form **assembling out of a non-superhero genre in real time** rather than being imported whole. The mandate is fraternal and assumed — a licence held from a brotherhood rather than a state — and the powers are trained rather than granted, which is the martial-arts tradition supplying what radiation supplies elsewhere. It is also the commercial anchor of an entire industry: this run is what made Hong Kong comics an export business. **Who inked, coloured or lettered could not be established.**

entries.name: 3 Dev Adam
entries.author: T. Fikret Uçak, director
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Turkish film award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Feature film. **An unlicensed film in which Captain America and a Mexican luchador pursue a murderous Spider-Man**, and it is carded straight rather…
entries.text: Feature film. **An unlicensed film in which Captain America and a Mexican luchador pursue a murderous Spider-Man**, and it is carded straight rather than as a curiosity. It is the clearest evidence in the pack for **mode three of the organising claim**: the iconography travels without the rights, the mandate, the continuity or the publisher, and it remains legible to an audience with no access to any of them. That is what "iconography in circulation" means as a mode of entry, and this film is the case that makes the mode necessary rather than merely available. The villain casting is the finding: the costume signifies **hero** so reliably that inverting it is the film's whole engine, which is `trope-62`'s point — palette read as moral position before a word of dialogue — demonstrated by an unauthorised production three continents from the source.

entries.description: Television series. **Brazil's costumed hero arrives on television in 1954 and in comics only in 1959**, which pass B2 established and the pack cards…
entries.text: Television series. **Brazil's costumed hero arrives on television in 1954 and in comics only in 1959**, which pass B2 established and the pack cards accordingly: the television original is the historically primary object and the comics line is the adaptation, not the other way round. **This entry exists because a check refused an earlier answer.** The pass-D addendum proposed removing a different work to pay for a new category; the citation check found that work cited by a merged card and rejected the removal, and this substitution was made instead — **the roster is better for having been overruled by its own tooling.** The mandate is sponsor-shaped in a way no other card in this pack can show: the series was built around an advertiser and the hero's mission and the product were not separable, which is the commercial licence in its most literal form. **The individual creator could not be established**, and the pack states the gap rather than assigning the credit to the broadcaster by default.

entries.name: Süpermen Dönüyor
entries.author: Kunt Tulgar, director
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Turkish film award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Feature film. **Turkey's superhero tradition is cinematic and not comics-based, and this card carries the finding** rather than leaving the medium…
entries.text: Feature film. **Turkey's superhero tradition is cinematic and not comics-based, and this card carries the finding** rather than leaving the medium to look like an accident of what was available: pass C searched for an indigenous Turkish superhero *comics* creator, found a peer-reviewed generic history of Turkish comics that identifies none, and established that Turkey's canonical heroes are historical adventure. Both Turkish entries in this block are therefore films. The work itself is an unlicensed Superman made on a budget that cannot stage the iconography it needs and stages it anyway, which is **mode three again and from the other direction** — where the 1973 entry inverts the costume's meaning, this one reproduces it exactly and lets the gap between ambition and resource become the film's texture. A pack that cards only well-resourced examples of a genre describes a market rather than a form.

entries.name: E.X.O.: The Legend of Wale Williams
entries.author: Roye Okupe, writer; Sunkanmi Akinboye, artist
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Eisner and Glyph Comics Award records consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Graphic novel. **This entry replaced Powerman in the roster, and the reason is an authorship distinction the pack takes seriously**: the earlier…
entries.text: Graphic novel. **This entry replaced Powerman in the roster, and the reason is an authorship distinction the pack takes seriously**: the earlier candidate was British-written for a Nigerian market, which makes it a work about Nigeria rather than a work of the Nigerian tradition, and pass D flagged the difference rather than letting the flag of convenience stand. This work is Nigerian-written, Nigerian-drawn and published by a Nigerian studio into a global market. Its hero returns to a **near-future Lagos rendered as a functioning city rather than as a problem**, which is a genre decision before it is a political one — the superhero form requires a city worth defending, and the card notes how rarely African settings have been granted one. The mandate is inherited technology and a father's unfinished work, the same shape as this pack's Indian film entry and arrived at independently.

entries.name: The Brave and the Bold #57 (Metamorpho)
entries.author: Bob Haney and Ramona Fradon
entries.awards: No award located, and no category string is cited. The Alley Awards existed in this year but their year-by-year ballots were not located and their categories demonstrably changed. [gap: Alley Award ballot record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Single issue. **A woman co-created a headline character for a major publisher in 1965 and the credit was carried**, which is why this issue is the…
entries.text: Single issue. **A woman co-created a headline character for a major publisher in 1965 and the credit was carried**, which is why this issue is the block's earliest entry rather than a better-remembered one. `history-8` states the general case — the composition of the workforce and the reason the record is thin — and this is the specific instance where the record is not thin: Fradon's co-creation is documented, and the character's design language is hers. The work itself is a body-horror premise played as adventure, a hero whose transformation is permanent and disfiguring and whose story is about being unable to change back, which the genre would not return to at this register for two decades. `author-9` cards the creator.

entries.name: Power Pack
entries.author: Louise Simonson and June Brigman
entries.awards: No award located. The Eisner Awards were not first presented until 1988 and the Kirby Awards not until 1985, so no comic-book award body applicable to this year's work had yet issued. [gap: Eagle Award ballot record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. Four children with powers and **no adult supervising the mandate**, which makes it the cleanest test in the pack of what the licence question…
entries.text: Run. Four children with powers and **no adult supervising the mandate**, which makes it the cleanest test in the pack of what the licence question looks like when nobody involved could plausibly hold a licence. It sits in `subgenre-16`'s line — the all-ages book — and is carded to prevent that line reading as a lesser one: the constraint of a young readership produced a book that had to answer where the parents are, a question the adult titles of the same years were free to ignore. **Woman-written and woman-drawn at a major publisher in 1984**, which the block cards as a fact about the industry as much as about the book. `author-11` cards the writer.

entries.author: Gail Simone
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Eisner Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. **The carded object is the run rather than the title**, per §8, because the title predates this tenure and the tenure is what the pack is…
entries.text: Run. **The carded object is the run rather than the title**, per §8, because the title predates this tenure and the tenure is what the pack is pointing at. Its engine is `trope-25`'s — a roster whose members disagree and are each individually right — built from an all-women team in which the field operative and the intelligence operative have incompatible methods and neither is written as the sensible one. The run is also the pack's clearest case of a disabled lead whose capability is **information rather than a body**, and it is carded here rather than in the disability block because the block it displaces would then lose a work the citation check has locked. `author-14` cards the writer.

entries.author: Kelly Sue DeConnick
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Eisner and Harvey Award records consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. **The costume redesign is the story rather than a marketing note**, which is `subgenre-28`'s subject stated as a specific case: a character…
entries.text: Run. **The costume redesign is the story rather than a marketing note**, which is `subgenre-28`'s subject stated as a specific case: a character carried for decades in a swimsuit is put in a flight suit, and the run treats the change as a claim about what the character is for rather than as a concession. The name is taken from a predecessor, so the mandate is inherited and the run's arc is the decision to accept an inheritance nobody offered. **The disambiguating suffix is load-bearing**: several unrelated works share this title across four decades and two publishers, and §8's convention resolves the collision rather than trusting context. `author-108` cards the writer.

entries.name: The Secret History of Wonder Woman (Jill Lepore)
entries.author: Jill Lepore
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Eisner and National Book Critics Circle records consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Narrative history. **Humanities rather than empirical** — archival history built from family papers and legal records, not a study of readers — and…
entries.text: Narrative history. **Humanities rather than empirical** — archival history built from family papers and legal records, not a study of readers — and the pack labels it as such, because a card citing it as evidence about audiences would be misreading the genre of the source. It is the block's methodological anchor: the origin of the genre's most-cited woman character turns out to rest on a private history that the character's own publisher did not know, which is `checklist-16`'s case for running the inherited-claim pass on the sentences you did not think you were asserting. **Its value to this pack is negative as much as positive** — several claims the genre repeats about this character's creation do not survive it.

entries.name: Jessica Jones (2015 tv)
entries.author: Melissa Rosenberg, showrunner
entries.awards: No award located. Both the Emmy Awards and the Peabody Awards had applicable categories in this year and no entry for this series was confirmed against either body's own record. [gap: Emmy and Peabody records consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Television series. `subgenre-11`'s street-level book moved to screen, and the pack cards it because the move exposes what that subgenre actually is:…
entries.text: Television series. `subgenre-11`'s street-level book moved to screen, and the pack cards it because the move exposes what that subgenre actually is: **the powers are real, rarely used, and structurally irrelevant to the antagonist**, whose capability is coercion. The mandate is refused rather than assumed — the protagonist is a private investigator who declines the licence and is dragged into using it — which makes it the pack's best screen example of `craft-8`'s territory approached from the far side. Its treatment of assault is the genre's most sustained, and the card notes that the work's reputation for it rests on the adaptation rather than on the source run.

entries.name: Wonder Woman (2017 film)
entries.author: Patty Jenkins, director
entries.awards: No Academy Award nomination located in any category. **No superhero film has won the Academy Award for Best Picture**, and this pack states that rule wherever it states a Best Picture fact. [gap: Academy Awards database consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Feature film. The first theatrical feature in this genre's modern era directed by a woman, and carded for a craft reason as well as a historical…
entries.text: Feature film. The first theatrical feature in this genre's modern era directed by a woman, and carded for a craft reason as well as a historical one: the costume problem `craft-54` describes is solved here by **designing for movement rather than for fidelity**, and the film's most-reproduced sequence works because the armour was built to be run in. Its mandate is mode one in the purest form the pack cards on screen — assumed absolutely, from a source no human institution could revoke, and never once questioned by the protagonist. **The award line is a documented absence rather than an omission**: a commercially dominant film in this genre receiving no nomination in any category is itself the fact, and claims about the genre's critical standing should be checked against it rather than against its box office.

entries.name: Ms. Marvel (2022 tv)
entries.author: Bisha K. Ali, head writer
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Emmy Awards database consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Television series. **The adaptation changed the capability and the comics followed**, which is `craft-55` demonstrated rather than argued: the…
entries.text: Television series. **The adaptation changed the capability and the comics followed**, which is `craft-55` demonstrated rather than argued: the source character's power is a malleable body and the screen version's is hard light with an inherited origin, and the later comics adopt the screen version. That is the direction of travel a reference pack has to be able to describe, because the assumption runs the other way. It is carded in the women's block rather than the religion block, where its source run sits, **because the two entries answer different questions and the pack states which** — the source run is about a Muslim American teenager's religious life, the adaptation is about a woman-led screen production and an inheritance rewritten in transit. `work-93` is the source and the two cards cross-refer.

entries.author: Gerard Jones and Mike Parobeck
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Eisner and Harvey Award records consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. A Latino city councilman in a Texas border town who puts on a costume, and the book's whole interest is `craft-5`'s question — what the…
entries.text: Run. A Latino city councilman in a Texas border town who puts on a costume, and the book's whole interest is `craft-5`'s question — what the intervention buys and for whom — because the protagonist already holds an office with actual power and the costume gets him less done than the council seat does. **That is a rare and genuinely useful inversion**: the mandate is available to him legitimately, and he takes an illegitimate one anyway, so the story has to explain why. Commercially it failed and was cancelled inside two years, which the card states rather than implying a lost classic. **The disambiguating suffix separates it from an unrelated later character of the same name.**

entries.category: Latino, Indigenous and Asian American Superheroes
entries.name: Blue Beetle (Jaime Reyes)
entries.author: Keith Giffen, John Rogers and Cully Hamner
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Eisner Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. The third holder of the name, so it is `trope-55`'s situation — the successor who has to win the reader over twice — and it solves the problem…
entries.text: Run. The third holder of the name, so it is `trope-55`'s situation — the successor who has to win the reader over twice — and it solves the problem by making the inheritance **involuntary and unexplained**: the artefact chooses him and the previous holder is dead before the first issue. Its structural contribution is `craft-24`'s: **the family finds out early and stays in the book**, which removes the concealment engine the genre defaults to and replaces it with a household that has opinions about the mandate. The card notes what the run does not do — it does not make the protagonist's ethnicity the plot — and that this is a choice with costs on both sides rather than a neutral default.

entries.author: Brian Michael Bendis and Sara Pichelli
