entries.description: Run. A new Spider-Man in a parallel line, and `continuity-34` is the card that explains why he exists there and not in the main line: **the…
entries.text: Run. A new Spider-Man in a parallel line, and `continuity-34` is the card that explains why he exists there and not in the main line: **the commercial reason legacy characters are created, stated without euphemism.** The separate-continuity berth is what made the character possible and is also what made him provisional, and the run is written knowing both. Its craft interest is the inheritance handled as `checklist-10` requires — the predecessor's death is the premise, the successor's competence is not assumed, and the book spends a year on whether he is entitled to the name. **The character was later merged into the main line, which is a continuity event the card names rather than treating this run as self-contained.** `author-107` cards the writer.

entries.category: Latino, Indigenous and Asian American Superheroes
entries.name: Ms. Marvel (2014 comic)
entries.author: G. Willow Wilson and Adrian Alphona; edited by Sana Amanat
entries.awards: Hugo Award, Best Graphic Story, 2015. The category was created in 2009 as Best Graphic Story; "or Comic" was ratified 2019 and took effect in 2020, so the suffix is not used for a 2015 award.
entries.description: Run. A Pakistani American Muslim teenager takes a name her predecessor has vacated, so the inheritance is doubled — a legacy mantle **and** a claim…
entries.text: Run. A Pakistani American Muslim teenager takes a name her predecessor has vacated, so the inheritance is doubled — a legacy mantle **and** a claim on an American genre by someone the genre had carded as a subject rather than a hero. Its mandate is assumed and immediately domestic: the constraint on the protagonist is not the police or a licensing body but a family and a religious community with standing to object, which is a genuinely different limit from the ones `powers-9` enumerates. **The editor is carded in the Author field deliberately**: pass C's five-claim model treats editorial origination as a claim the record usually loses, and this book's premise is documented as originating with its editor. `author-88` and `author-89` card both. Its screen adaptation is `work-89` and the two differ in the capability itself.

entries.category: Latino, Indigenous and Asian American Superheroes
entries.name: Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings
entries.author: Destin Daniel Cretton, director
entries.awards: No Academy Award nomination located in any category. [gap: Academy Awards database consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Feature film. `craft-52`'s claim — adaptation selects for iconography — with an unusually clear result: **the source character's most portable…
entries.text: Feature film. `craft-52`'s claim — adaptation selects for iconography — with an unusually clear result: **the source character's most portable element was a martial-arts discipline rather than a costume**, and the film keeps the discipline and discards nearly everything else, including the source's original antagonist, whose rights and racial construction made him unusable. That substitution is the card's real content, because it is a case where **the adaptation's departure from the source is the ethical improvement rather than the compromise**, which is the opposite of the direction `craft-55` usually describes. This entry replaced a 2020 comic run in the roster at pass D, moving the block from five comics to four and one film — a change the card records because the block's medium balance is a claim about where the tradition is currently being made.

entries.name: Alpha Flight #106
entries.author: Scott Lobdell and Mark Pacella
entries.awards: No award located. The GLAAD Media Awards existed from 1990; no ballot for this year was located and no category string is cited. [gap: GLAAD Media Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Single issue. The first explicit coming-out of an established costumed hero at a major American publisher, and it arrives **fourteen years after the…
entries.text: Single issue. The first explicit coming-out of an established costumed hero at a major American publisher, and it arrives **fourteen years after the character was created and roughly a decade after the reading was an open secret** — the delay is the card's subject. `continuity-53` is the frame: the silence was a formal constraint imposed from above, not an authorial choice, and the issue exists because the constraint was lifted rather than because a writer won an argument. **The issue was not written by a queer creator**, and the pack states this rather than letting a landmark of representation imply an authorship it did not have: pass C found no openly queer creator documentable on a mainstream superhero title before 1989, and the five queer creators in this pack's Authors block all have later superhero credits. **The gap is between the community and the mainstream page, not in the record of queer creators.**

entries.name: The Authority (Ellis run)
entries.author: Warren Ellis and Bryan Hitch
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Eisner and Eagle Award records consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. **A precise credit the card will not blur**: this run establishes the two male leads as a couple and treats the fact as unremarkable; the…
entries.text: Run. **A precise credit the card will not blur**: this run establishes the two male leads as a couple and treats the fact as unremarkable; the marriage and the domestic material that the book is chiefly remembered for belong to the **following** run, and the pack cards the tenure it names rather than absorbing a successor's work into it. Its wider argument is `subgenre-13`'s — superhumans who decide the state is the problem and act on it — which makes the queer content structurally inseparable from the political content: the couple are the book's only stable institution, in a book whose subject is institutions failing. The card notes the run's widely copied visual grammar, and notes that the copying reached the page faster than the politics did.

entries.name: Young Avengers (2005 comic)
entries.author: Allan Heinberg and Jim Cheung
entries.awards: No award located, and no year is cited. A GLAAD Media Award for Outstanding Comic Book is widely reported for this run and appears as both 2005 and 2006 depending on the source, which is the ceremony-year-for-work-year confusion this pack refuses to resolve by choosing. [gap: GLAAD Media Award ballot record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. `subgenre-8`'s legacy title with the inheritance made literal — a team assembled entirely from successors and relatives — and the queer…
entries.text: Run. `subgenre-8`'s legacy title with the inheritance made literal — a team assembled entirely from successors and relatives — and the queer relationship at its centre is **introduced without a coming-out issue**, which is the structural difference from `work-95` thirteen years earlier and the reason both are carded. The run's method is `craft-30`'s: write the arc, inherit the character, and leave the two leads in a position a later writer could not easily undo. **The award line is the card's second lesson**: a named prize with a guessed year looks more verified than a bounded negative and is worth less, so the body is named, the convention problem is named, and nothing is cited.

entries.name: Detective Comics #854–860 (Batwoman)
entries.author: Greg Rucka and J. H. Williams III
entries.awards: No award located, and no category string is cited. The Eisner Awards label by ceremony year and this run's work year is 2009; no ballot entry was confirmed against the administering body's own record. [gap: Eisner Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. **The mandate is revoked by a named body and the card can point at it**, which `craft-1` asks of every costumed figure and which almost no…
entries.text: Run. **The mandate is revoked by a named body and the card can point at it**, which `craft-1` asks of every costumed figure and which almost no American superhero work can actually supply: the protagonist is discharged from military service under a specific policy on a specific ground, and the costume is what she does instead. That makes it the pack's strongest case that a real institution is a better limit than an invented one. Its formal achievement is `craft-43`'s at an extreme — panel architecture that changes shape between the two identities, so the page layout itself carries which life the reader is in — and it is one of the few runs in the genre where the art's structure is the argument. **Neither creator on this run holds an Author card**, which the pack notes rather than hides: the Authors roster is closed at 120 and this run's writer and artist both lost their slots to creators whose claims the presence blocks needed more.

entries.name: Uncanny X-Men #199
entries.author: Chris Claremont and John Romita Jr.
entries.awards: No award located. The Kirby Awards were instituted in 1984 and first presented in 1985; no entry for this issue was located. [gap: Kirby Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Single issue. A Holocaust memorial ceremony, a survivor in attendance, and a costumed arrest — the issue in which the genre's most-used ethnic…
entries.text: Single issue. A Holocaust memorial ceremony, a survivor in attendance, and a costumed arrest — the issue in which the genre's most-used ethnic backstory is made explicit on the page rather than implied. `subgenre-30` is the frame, and this card is its clearest instance: **the character's ethnicity is not decoration on a power set but the origin of a political position the book takes seriously enough to argue against.** The card notes what the issue does not settle — the survivor's identification of the character is not a legal finding and the story does not treat it as one — because the received version of this scene is more conclusive than the scene. It is also the point from which the character's decades-long oscillation between antagonist and colleague becomes readable as a consistent position rather than as editorial drift.

entries.name: Disguised as Clark Kent (Danny Fingeroth)
entries.author: Danny Fingeroth
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Eisner Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Criticism. **Humanities rather than empirical** — close reading and interview material, not a study of readers — and the pack labels it as such,…
entries.text: Criticism. **Humanities rather than empirical** — close reading and interview material, not a study of readers — and the pack labels it as such, following the same rule `work-86` and `work-54` follow. It is the standard treatment of the genre's Jewish authorship and the assimilation reading of the secret identity, and this pack cards it **because the reading is repeated everywhere and sourced almost nowhere**: `checklist-16`'s inherited-claim pass has no target if the claim has no attributable statement behind it. The card states the sourcing rather than the conclusion — the author is himself a former editor at one of the two publishers, which is access and interest at once, and the pack names both rather than treating insider status as neutral.

entries.name: X-Men: Magneto Testament
entries.author: Greg Pak and Carmine Di Giandomenico
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Eisner and Harvey Award records consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Limited series. **A superhero-line comic about the Holocaust in which no power is depicted at any point**, which is the formal decision the card is…
entries.text: Limited series. **A superhero-line comic about the Holocaust in which no power is depicted at any point**, which is the formal decision the card is here for: the series removes the genre's own apparatus from a story its continuity had always claimed, and what remains is a historical comic with a licensed character's name on it. **The pack states the sourcing** — the series was researched against Holocaust-museum material and shipped with a teachers' guide — and **does not rule on whether the result is adequate to its subject**, because that is a judgement a reference pack is not the place to issue and a card that issued it would be doing criticism under cover of description. It sits in `subgenre-37`'s territory rather than this genre's, and the tension between the two is the reason it is carded at all.

entries.name: The Amazing Adventures of Kavalier & Clay
entries.author: Michael Chabon
entries.awards: Pulitzer Prize for Fiction, 2001. The prize is labelled by award year, one year after the book's publication year, and the card prints both rather than collapsing them.
entries.description: A literary novel about two Jewish cousins inventing a costumed hero in 1939, and the pack cards it as a **work about the genre that is also evidence…
entries.text: A literary novel about two Jewish cousins inventing a costumed hero in 1939, and the pack cards it as a **work about the genre that is also evidence about it** — the escape-artist framing of the secret identity and the golem lineage are advanced here as fiction and have since been cited as though they were history, which is `checklist-16`'s exact failure mode running in the opposite direction. `history-8` covers the workforce this novel dramatises and should be read against it rather than through it. **This entry replaced a 2004 comic run in the roster at pass D**, which is what closes the `novel` medium at six, and the substitution is recorded because a fictional source doing historical work is a specific hazard this block otherwise had no card for.

entries.name: Green Lantern (O'Neil/Adams run)
entries.author: Denny O'Neil and Neal Adams
entries.awards: No award located, and no category string is cited. The Shazam Awards were administered in this period but two year conventions are in circulation for them and the specialist index flags its own entries as uncertain. [gap: Shazam Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. **The most-cited run in the genre's history and the one whose commercial record is most consistently misreported**, which is why `history-17`…
entries.text: Run. **The most-cited run in the genre's history and the one whose commercial record is most consistently misreported**, which is why `history-17` exists and why this card points at it: relevance arrived, was praised, and did not sell. The run's structural move is to give the mandate a **critic inside the book** — one hero holds a licence from a cosmic authority and the other refuses to recognise it — so the argument the period is remembered for is staged between two protagonists rather than delivered by a narrator. What it actually changed was editorial permission rather than sales, and the card states the distinction because the received version collapses them.

entries.name: The Amazing Spider-Man #96–98
entries.author: Stan Lee and Gil Kane
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Shazam Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. **Three issues published without the Code seal**, which is the fact the card is here for: the publisher printed an anti-drug story the Code…
entries.text: Run. **Three issues published without the Code seal**, which is the fact the card is here for: the publisher printed an anti-drug story the Code forbade, shipped it unsealed, and the Code was revised afterwards. `history-12` covers the Code as an industry instrument the industry wrote for itself, and this is the clearest instance of a member using that authorship against the instrument. **The received version has the Federal government requesting the story**, and the card states that this is the version in circulation rather than asserting it, because the request's documentation is not something this pack has seen. The story itself is weaker than its reputation and the card says so — it is carded for what it did to the Code, not for what it does on the page.

entries.name: The Amazing Spider-Man #121–122
entries.author: Gerry Conway, Gil Kane and John Romita Sr.
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Shazam Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. The death that the genre did not reverse for decades, and `craft-22`'s claim — killing is a one-way door — established as a fact about this…
entries.text: Run. The death that the genre did not reverse for decades, and `craft-22`'s claim — killing is a one-way door — established as a fact about this form rather than as advice. Its mechanism is the card's real content: **the hero's own intervention is what kills her**, so the death is not a failure to arrive in time but a consequence of arriving, which is the hardest version of the beat and the one almost nobody copies. The panel's sound effect and its ambiguity have generated fifty years of argument about whether the story means what it appears to mean, and the pack notes that **the ambiguity is on the page rather than in the reception** — a rare case where the received controversy is accurate.

entries.name: Master of Kung Fu
entries.author: Steve Englehart, Doug Moench and Paul Gulacy
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Shazam Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. A licensed book built on a rented antagonist, and **both halves of that arrangement are problems the card names**: the licence made long…
entries.text: Run. A licensed book built on a rented antagonist, and **both halves of that arrangement are problems the card names**: the licence made long stretches of the run unreprintable for decades, and the rented character is one of the genre's most durable racial constructions. `work-94` cards the 2021 film that solved the second problem by **deleting the character entirely and substituting another**, and the two cards cross-refer deliberately — a reader meeting only one of them would take this genre's handling of the material to be either worse or better than the record supports. What the run itself is good at is unrelated to either: a protagonist whose mandate is **refused rather than assumed or conferred**, acting against the person who conferred it, in a book whose fight staging was among the most legible of its decade.

entries.name: Howard the Duck
entries.author: Steve Gerber and Frank Brunner
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Shazam and Eagle Award records consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. `subgenre-36`'s parody written from **inside** the line it parodies and published by the company being parodied, which is the arrangement that…
entries.text: Run. `subgenre-36`'s parody written from **inside** the line it parodies and published by the company being parodied, which is the arrangement that makes it interesting and the one that eventually broke it. Its target is not the costume but the seriousness: an existential comedy in a shared universe, running the genre's furniture past a protagonist who finds all of it absurd and is nonetheless subject to it. **The creator's later dispute with the publisher over the character is part of the work's meaning rather than a postscript to it**, and the card states it as such — the book is about an outsider with no standing in a system that owns him, written by one.

entries.name: Seal of Approval (Amy Kiste Nyberg)
entries.author: Amy Kiste Nyberg
entries.awards: No award located; the Eisner Awards' comics-related book category existed in this period and no entry for this title was located. [gap: Eisner Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Narrative history. **Humanities rather than empirical** — archival and institutional history, not a study of readers — and labelled as such,…
entries.text: Narrative history. **Humanities rather than empirical** — archival and institutional history, not a study of readers — and labelled as such, following `work-54`, `work-86` and `work-100`. **This pack cards it because three of its own history cards rest on it.** `history-10` on Wertham against the received version, `history-11` on the hearings that recommended nothing, and `history-12` on the Code as an industry instrument all draw substantially from this book, and carding the source makes the dependency visible rather than leaving three cards to look independently derived. **Where three cards share one source, card the source** — C-14's requirement to state the sourcing, applied to the pack's own structure rather than to a sentence.

entries.name: The Eternals
entries.author: Jack Kirby
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Shazam Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. Written and drawn by one man on a premise that **did not want to be part of the shared universe it was published into**, and absorbed into it…
entries.text: Run. Written and drawn by one man on a premise that **did not want to be part of the shared universe it was published into**, and absorbed into it anyway — which is `craft-37`'s subject stated at its most concrete: the book outlives you, and what it becomes is not yours to decide. The work's argument is that the genre's gods are ancient astronauts and its heroes are their unfinished experiments, a cosmology the line then had to reconcile with the pantheon it already published. **It is carded in this block rather than the cosmic one because its subject is the period's appetite for a bigger frame, not the theological line proper**, and the pack states the placement because the alternative reading is available. `author-87` cards the creator.

entries.name: Captain Marvel (Starlin run)
entries.author: Jim Starlin
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Shazam Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. `subgenre-18`'s line arrives here in the form the genre still uses: **cosmic scale as a moral register rather than a power register**, in which…
entries.text: Run. `subgenre-18`'s line arrives here in the form the genre still uses: **cosmic scale as a moral register rather than a power register**, in which the threat is a nihilist with a theology and the fight is about what the universe is for. The run establishes the antagonist the genre's largest commercial property would be built on four decades later, which the card notes without letting the later use determine the earlier work's value. **The disambiguating suffix is doing heavy work here**: three unrelated carded entries in this pack share a form of this title across four decades, and §8's convention is the only thing keeping them apart.

entries.name: Warlock (Starlin run)
entries.author: Jim Starlin
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Shazam Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. **The protagonist's archenemy is his own future self**, which makes it `trope-17`'s structure taken to the only place it cannot be taken twice:…
entries.text: Run. **The protagonist's archenemy is his own future self**, which makes it `trope-17`'s structure taken to the only place it cannot be taken twice: the antagonist is about the protagonist not thematically but literally, and the resolution requires the hero to kill the person he is going to become. It is the pack's clearest case of a messianic frame used **structurally rather than decoratively** — the sacrifice is load-bearing, the resurrection is refused for years, and the theology is the plot rather than the paint. The run is also where this line's characteristic failure mode is visible: a cosmology so complete that later writers can only add to it, which `powers-24` names as escalation without an owner.

entries.name: The Silver Surfer: The Ultimate Cosmic Experience
entries.author: Stan Lee and Jack Kirby
entries.awards: No award located; no comic-book award body with an applicable long-form category existed in this year. The Eisner Awards were not first presented until 1988 and the Kirby Awards not until 1985. [gap: Eagle Award ballot record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Graphic novel. **Frequently described as the first American graphic novel and this pack does not print the claim.** At least two other 1978 books…
entries.text: Graphic novel. **Frequently described as the first American graphic novel and this pack does not print the claim.** At least two other 1978 books hold the same position under different definitions — of format, of distribution, of intent — and the priority turns entirely on which definition is used, which is the same shape as the tokusatsu priority contest this pack declines at `work-55`. **What is not contested is the format decision**: an original long-form superhero work sold as a book, by the genre's two most-cited creators, a decade before the industry had an award category that could recognise one. The work reunites its creators on a character whose ownership and origin they publicly disagreed about, and the card names the disagreement rather than presenting the reunion as a resolution.

entries.name: The Death of Captain Marvel
entries.author: Jim Starlin
entries.awards: No award located; the Kirby Awards were not instituted until 1984. [gap: Eagle Award ballot record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Graphic novel. **A costumed hero dies of cancer, in bed, and is not brought back for decades** — the genre's most-used character death is here made…
entries.text: Graphic novel. **A costumed hero dies of cancer, in bed, and is not brought back for decades** — the genre's most-used character death is here made unavailable to every device the genre has for undoing one. `powers-15`'s debt you cannot discharge, written as an entire book: the protagonist's capability is irrelevant to what kills him, and the work's subject is the gap between what he can do and what is happening to him. It is the counter-case to `continuity-43`'s death-as-event-product, published a decade before that machinery existed, and the pack cards both so the contrast is available rather than implied. The cosmic frame is used here for **scale of witness rather than scale of threat**: the antagonists attend the deathbed.

entries.name: Kingdom Come
entries.author: Mark Waid and Alex Ross
entries.awards: No award located, and no category string is cited. The Eisner Awards' limited-series categories existed in this period and no ballot entry was confirmed against the administering body's own record. [gap: Eisner Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Limited series. `subgenre-4`'s reconstruction with a theological armature: the narrator is a clergyman, the frame is an apocalypse, and the argument…
entries.text: Limited series. `subgenre-4`'s reconstruction with a theological armature: the narrator is a clergyman, the frame is an apocalypse, and the argument is that the genre's older generation was **right about restraint and wrong about withdrawal**. It is the most direct published answer to the deconstruction decade, and its method is the reason it works — it does not refute the darker books, it **grants their premises and disputes their conclusion**, which is a harder rhetorical position and a rarer one. The painted art is doing argumentative work rather than decorative work: the figures are aged, heavy and photographic, so the case for the older heroes is made by the drawing before the script makes it.

entries.name: Final Crisis
entries.author: Grant Morrison and J. G. Jones
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Eisner Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Event crossover. The theological line and `subgenre-10`'s commercial form in one object, which is why it is carded here rather than with the events:…
entries.text: Event crossover. The theological line and `subgenre-10`'s commercial form in one object, which is why it is carded here rather than with the events: the premise is that **evil wins and the story is told from inside the defeat**, and the narrative technique — elliptical, non-consecutive, assuming the reader will assemble it — is a claim about what a shared universe can hold. `continuity-51` describes the event as a financial instrument with a narrative attached; this is the case where the narrative attempted to be worth more than the instrument and the tension between the two is legible on the page. **It is the pack's most divisive carded work and the card states that rather than adjudicating**, because a reference that reports contested reception as settled is doing advocacy.

entries.category: The Patriotic, Military and State Line
entries.name: Captain America and the Falcon: Secret Empire
entries.author: Steve Englehart and Sal Buscema
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Shazam Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. **The patriotic hero renounces the identity after uncovering a conspiracy reaching the highest office**, published while the equivalent real…
entries.text: Run. **The patriotic hero renounces the identity after uncovering a conspiracy reaching the highest office**, published while the equivalent real events were still unfolding — which is `craft-8`'s mandate withdrawal performed by the holder rather than the grantor, and the genre's most consequential example of it. The card notes the work's own care: **the office is never named on the page**, and the pack does not name it either, because the identification is a reading the story invites and does not make. What follows the renunciation is the part that matters structurally — the character operates under a different name for a year, which tests whether the mandate was in the costume or in the person, and the book's answer is neither.

entries.category: The Patriotic, Military and State Line
entries.name: The Ultimates
entries.author: Mark Millar and Bryan Hitch
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Eisner and Harvey Award records consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Limited series. `subgenre-13`'s state superhuman built as a **defence programme with a budget, a chain of command and a public-relations problem** —…
entries.text: Limited series. `subgenre-13`'s state superhuman built as a **defence programme with a budget, a chain of command and a public-relations problem** — the mandate is not merely conferred but administered, and the book's recurring scene is a briefing. Its influence on the genre's screen era is large enough that the card has to state the direction of travel carefully: this book's visual and structural choices reached the films, and the films then reached back into the comics, so a reader tracing the resemblance in the wrong direction will misdate the invention. **The work's politics are contested and the pack carries both positions** (C-16) rather than presenting the book's satire as either endorsed or evidently critical, because published readings run both ways.

entries.category: The Patriotic, Military and State Line
entries.name: Truth: Red, White & Black
entries.author: Robert Morales and Kyle Baker
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Eisner and Glyph Comics Award records consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Limited series. **The super-soldier programme retold as a medical experiment on Black soldiers**, which retroactively places the genre's founding…
entries.text: Limited series. **The super-soldier programme retold as a medical experiment on Black soldiers**, which retroactively places the genre's founding patriotic origin inside a documented history of American state medicine. `subgenre-40` is the frame; this card is where that frame stops being formal. Its structural achievement is that it **does not correct the earlier story so much as make it expensive**: the original origin still stands and now has a cost attached that no later writer can remove without removing this book. The card notes that its reception was strongly divided at publication and that the division was substantially about whether a licensed corporate character should carry the material — **both positions are on the record and the pack carries both.**

entries.category: The Patriotic, Military and State Line
entries.name: Ex Machina
entries.author: Brian K. Vaughan and Tony Harris
entries.awards: No award located, and no category string is cited. [gap: Eisner Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. A costumed hero is elected mayor, so `craft-3`'s intervener without a constituency **acquires one**, and the entire book is the consequence:…
entries.text: Run. A costumed hero is elected mayor, so `craft-3`'s intervener without a constituency **acquires one**, and the entire book is the consequence: every action now has a jurisdiction, a budget line and voters who can remove him. It is the pack's strongest case that the genre's licence problem is not solved by legitimising it — the mayor is less able to act than the vigilante was, and the book is honest that this is what legitimacy means. **Its handling of a specific real catastrophe is the card's caveat**: the work opens on it, uses it as premise, and the pack notes that readings of whether the use is earned differ sharply and that both are published.

entries.category: The Patriotic, Military and State Line
entries.name: Civil War
entries.author: Mark Millar and Steve McNiven
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Eisner and Harvey Award records consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Event crossover. The registration question staged as a line-wide argument, and `checklist-6`'s jurisdiction pass is the card to read against it,…
entries.text: Event crossover. The registration question staged as a line-wide argument, and `checklist-6`'s jurisdiction pass is the card to read against it, because the event's most-discussed weakness is jurisdictional: **the two sides are written to be arguable and the tie-in books disagree about which one the reader is meant to hold.** That inconsistency is a fact about how an event is produced rather than a failure of a script, and the pack cards it as such — a crossover is written by many hands under a schedule, and coherence is the first thing the schedule takes. Its premise remains the genre's clearest articulation of the mandate question at scale, which is why it is carded despite the execution being contested. **Both readings of the ending are published and the pack carries both.**

entries.category: The Patriotic, Military and State Line
entries.name: The Boys (2006 comic)
entries.author: Garth Ennis and Darick Robertson
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Eisner Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. `subgenre-5`'s satire aimed at the **institution rather than the costume**: superheroes as a corporate product line with a defence contract,…
entries.text: Run. `subgenre-5`'s satire aimed at the **institution rather than the costume**: superheroes as a corporate product line with a defence contract, and the protagonists as the state's deniable answer to them. The mandate question is inverted — the licensed party is the villain and the unlicensed party is the state's own — which makes it a genuine structural contribution rather than only a tonal one. **The disambiguating suffix separates it from its screen adaptation, which this pack cards separately in Batch 25 and which differs from it substantially**; the two are not interchangeable and a card citing "The Boys" without a suffix would be citing neither. Its excess is deliberate and is also the reason its argument is easy to dismiss, which the card states rather than defends.

entries.category: The Direct Market and the Nineties
entries.name: X-Men #1 (1991 comic)
entries.author: Chris Claremont and Jim Lee
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Eisner and Harvey Award records consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Single issue. **The best-selling single comic book on record, and the card's subject is the mechanism rather than the number.** `history-22` covers…
entries.text: Single issue. **The best-selling single comic book on record, and the card's subject is the mechanism rather than the number.** `history-22` covers the speculative boom and the fact that it was not a readership; this issue is where the two became indistinguishable, sold in five variant covers to an audience buying multiples of one comic. **The suffix is load-bearing and this is the batch's real collision risk**: a different first issue of this franchise, carded in this pack thirty years earlier, has almost the same name. Its creative content is not the reason it is carded, and the card says so — what it demonstrates is that a format decision made in the sales department can be the most consequential authorial act of a year.

entries.category: The Direct Market and the Nineties
entries.name: Youngblood
entries.author: Rob Liefeld
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Eisner and Harvey Award records consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. The founding title of a creator-owned publisher formed by artists leaving the two majors, and the card is here for **what the departure was…
entries.text: Run. The founding title of a creator-owned publisher formed by artists leaving the two majors, and the card is here for **what the departure was about rather than what the book contains**: ownership, and the precedent `history-20` cards — the original-art dispute and the clause that turned it into a rights case. That precedent is what the founders had watched happen to the previous generation. **The book itself is widely held to be poor and the pack neither endorses nor disputes that**, because its carded significance is structural: a top-selling launch from a company that had not existed the previous year proved the direct market could be entered without a distributor's permission. What followed is `history-23`'s crash, and the two cards should be read together.

entries.category: The Direct Market and the Nineties
entries.name: The Death of Superman
entries.author: Dan Jurgens, Jerry Ordway, Louise Simonson and Roger Stern
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Eisner and Harvey Award records consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Event crossover. `continuity-43`'s death as an event product, and the instance from which that card's machinery is drawn: a polybagged issue, a…
entries.text: Event crossover. `continuity-43`'s death as an event product, and the instance from which that card's machinery is drawn: a polybagged issue, a black armband, national news coverage and a scheduled return. **The card states the scheduling** — the reversal was planned before the death was published — because the received version has a publisher surprised by demand, and the difference between those two stories is the whole of `continuity-35`'s reversion that was always scheduled. It is carded in the Direct Market block rather than the Modern Run block because **its significance is as a selling mechanism**, and the pack would rather be honest about that than card it as a story. `author-11` is among the credited writers.

entries.category: The Direct Market and the Nineties
entries.name: Marvels
entries.author: Kurt Busiek and Alex Ross
entries.awards: No award located, and no category string is cited. The Eisner Awards label by ceremony year and this work's year is 1994; no ballot entry was confirmed against the administering body's own record. [gap: Eisner Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Limited series. **The entire thirty-year history of a shared universe retold from street level by a news photographer who never once meets a hero on…
entries.text: Limited series. **The entire thirty-year history of a shared universe retold from street level by a news photographer who never once meets a hero on equal terms**, which is `craft-6`'s claim — the bystander is a character or the story is lying — executed as a whole book rather than as a panel. Published in the middle of the speculative boom and arguing the opposite case: that the genre's accumulated continuity is an asset if you stand somewhere it can be seen from. Its painted art serves the same argument as its viewpoint, since photorealism from below is what makes the scale legible. The card notes that its nostalgia is **selective and self-aware**, and that the book's final movement is about the cost of that selectivity rather than a celebration of it.

entries.category: The Superhero at Play: Tabletop and Video Game
entries.name: Batman: Arkham Asylum
entries.author: Rocksteady Studios; Paul Dini, writer
entries.awards: BAFTA Video Games Awards, 2010: Best Game, and Gameplay. Also Game Developers Choice Awards, 2010, Best Game Design. Its Guinness World Record for "most critically acclaimed superhero game" is a record derived from an average review-aggregator score and is not a jury award; it is described in the text and is deliberately not listed here.
entries.description: Video game. **The award line is this card's methodological content as much as its factual content**: two jury awards are printed and a widely cited…
entries.text: Video game. **The award line is this card's methodological content as much as its factual content**: two jury awards are printed and a widely cited third honour is withheld from the field, because a Guinness World Record awarded on an average Metacritic score of 91.67 is a **measurement wearing an award's vocabulary**, and a reader scanning an awards field would take it for a judgement. Its contribution to the genre is `craft-46`'s: **the rogues gallery as a portfolio, converted into a level structure** — each antagonist is a different set of rules, so the gallery's variety becomes the game's design rather than its flavour. The confined single-location setting is the other half, and it is what lets a licensed property with ninety years of continuity be entered without any of it.

entries.category: The Superhero at Play: Tabletop and Video Game
entries.name: Marvel's Spider-Man (2018 game)
entries.author: Insomniac Games; Bryan Intihar, creative director; Jon Paquette, lead writer
entries.awards: D.I.C.E. Awards, 22nd Annual, 2019: Outstanding Achievement in Animation. No BAFTA win and no Game Awards win were confirmed against the administering bodies' own records. [gap: BAFTA and Game Awards records consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Video game. **The delta against every other medium in this pack is motion**, and the card states it as a delta rather than as praise: `craft-15` is…
entries.text: Video game. **The delta against every other medium in this pack is motion**, and the card states it as a delta rather than as praise: `craft-15` is about producing speed on a static page, and this work's central achievement is that it does not have that problem and builds its entire appeal on not having it. Traversal is the game's argument — the pleasure is locomotion rather than combat, which is a claim about what the character is that comics had made in single panels and never sustained. The mandate here is assumed and domestic in the same shape as `work-93`'s, and the work's other decision worth carding is **that the civilian life is playable**: the identity the genre usually treats as an interruption is given mechanics of its own.

entries.category: The Superhero at Play: Tabletop and Video Game
entries.name: City of Heroes
entries.author: Cryptic Studios; Rick Dakan, writer and lead design
entries.awards: No award located. Four D.I.C.E. nominations in 2005, including Computer Game of the Year, produced no win; the 2006 D.I.C.E. Massively Multiplayer Game of the Year went to a different title in the same franchise and must not be attributed here. A ninth-place magazine list position for 2004 is not an award. [gap: D.I.C.E. Awards record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Video game. **The mandate question asked of the audience rather than of a character** — who is licensed to make a superhero — and it is the one case…
entries.text: Video game. **The mandate question asked of the audience rather than of a character** — who is licensed to make a superhero — and it is the one case in this pack where that question reached a court. The publisher of one of the two majors sued in November 2004, alleging the game promoted infringing character creation; **the plaintiff subsequently admitted that some of the allegedly infringing characters cited in its own complaint had been created by its own investigators**, and the case settled on 12 December 2005. The operators asserted the settlement required no change to the character creation engine. **The pack states both attributions and neither as a holding**: a settlement is not a merits finding, and the second fact is the operators' claim rather than a court's. The engine itself is `trope-14` given to the player — the costume as permission, self-issued, ten thousand times over. Servers closed 30 November 2012.

entries.category: The Superhero at Play: Tabletop and Video Game
entries.name: Champions
entries.author: George MacDonald, Steve Peterson, Rob Bell, Bruce Harlick and Ray Greer; Hero Games
entries.awards: No award located. The Origins Awards existed in this period and no ballot entry was confirmed against the administering body's own record. [gap: Origins Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Tabletop game. **This is not the first superhero role-playing game and the card corrects the claim rather than repeating it.** *Superhero: 2044*…
entries.text: Tabletop game. **This is not the first superhero role-playing game and the card corrects the claim rather than repeating it.** *Superhero: 2044* (1977) is the earliest professionally produced example and *Villains and Vigilantes* (1979) also precedes this work, which is inspired by the first of them and says so in its own reference record. **Neither of those two titles is carded here** — the category holds four, and naming is not carding. What this work has priority in is the mechanism: it is **one of the first published role-playing games to build characters from a points budget rather than from dice**, and the pack takes that weaker phrasing deliberately, because its source offers a stronger one in the same article and a claim available at two strengths is usually a summary sitting beside a record. `powers-10` is the card this work sits under: capability purchased from a fixed total, limitations refunding part of the price, and a character who is a balance sheet that has to add up.

entries.name: Crisis on Infinite Earths
entries.author: Marv Wolfman and George Pérez
entries.awards: No award located; the Kirby Awards were instituted in 1984 and first presented in 1985, and no entry for this series was located. [gap: Kirby Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Event crossover. **The carded year is 1985 and the category string says 1986, and the pack states the discrepancy rather than hiding it**: this…
entries.text: Event crossover. **The carded year is 1985 and the category string says 1986, and the pack states the discrepancy rather than hiding it**: this block spans 1985 to 1988 and `history-21` argues the turn was not one year. The category was called *The 1986 Turn* through Batches 20–25 and **was renamed to *The 1986 Generation* at the patch batch** — a cohort rather than an event, which is what these eight works are. The rename also removed a second fault nobody had booked: **the Authors block for the same material was already called The 1986 Generation**, so the pack had been carrying one block under two names. The work itself is `continuity-13`'s three motives in one object — repair, land-grab and apology — executed as a **deliberate destruction of a company's accumulated continuity** in order to sell a simplified one. Its lasting effect is not the simplification, which failed within a decade, but the establishment of the line-wide reset as a **repeatable commercial instrument**, which is what `continuity-51` cards and what every subsequent event inherits. `author-1` cards the artist.

entries.name: Squadron Supreme
entries.author: Mark Gruenwald and Bob Hall
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Kirby Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Limited series. **It precedes the two books this period is named for and almost no account of the period mentions it**, which is the card's reason…
entries.text: Limited series. **It precedes the two books this period is named for and almost no account of the period mentions it**, which is the card's reason for existing: `subgenre-3`'s deconstruction is here already, complete, and executed on a cast openly modelled on another publisher's heroes. Its premise is the mandate taken to its conclusion — superhumans decide to run the world properly, and the book follows the programme through utopian legislation to behaviour modification to the deaths of most of the cast. **The priority claim is a bounded one and the card makes it carefully**: this work is earlier, and being earlier is not being more influential. What it demonstrates is that the argument was available before the books that made it famous, which complicates the received story of a single year in which the genre grew up.

entries.name: Batman: The Dark Knight
entries.author: Frank Miller, Klaus Janson and Lynn Varley
entries.awards: No award located, and no category string is cited. The Kirby Awards were being presented in this period and no ballot entry was confirmed against the administering body's own record. [gap: Kirby Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Limited series. `subgenre-2`'s turn arrives with this book and the label most often hung on what followed — the **"Dark Age"** — is on this pack's…
entries.text: Limited series. `subgenre-2`'s turn arrives with this book and the label most often hung on what followed — the **"Dark Age"** — is on this pack's forbidden list and is quoted here only in order to refuse it: it is a periodisation, it does the same work the metal scheme does, and `history-16` is the card that argues against both. The work's own achievement is the **aged hero as an argument about the genre's refusal to age**, staged in a nine-panel-derived grid and a television-feed chorus that treats the costumed act as a public-order controversy. **What it is blamed for is mostly what its imitators took from it** — the violence without the formal argument — and the card distinguishes the two rather than defending or condemning the book wholesale. **The colourist is carded and her living status is unconfirmed** — pass C found no documentation after 2007 and no birth year, and her Author card leaves both blank rather than estimating.

entries.name: Watchmen
entries.author: Alan Moore and Dave Gibbons
entries.awards: Hugo Award, 1988, in the one-off Other Forms category. It did not win Best Graphic Story, which was not created until 2009.
entries.description: Limited series. The mandate is the subject rather than the premise: **every costumed figure in it is asked by what warrant they act, and the book's…
entries.text: Limited series. The mandate is the subject rather than the premise: **every costumed figure in it is asked by what warrant they act, and the book's answer differs for each of them.** Its formal achievement is the nine-panel grid used as an argument about determinism rather than as a layout preference, and its reputation for ending the genre's innocence is the received wisdom this pack's history blocks exist to complicate — `work-131`, published the previous year, had already made the argument. **One flag this card raises against the pack itself.** `powers-10` cites this work as *"famously developed with this kind of costed, closed-system thinking"*; research pass E flagged **"famously"** as an attribution to nobody and routed it to the full-pack review. The claim is plausible and unsourced, this card does not repeat it, and **a Works card quietly declining to repeat its own Powers card's claim would be an invisible disagreement**, so the flag is stated here instead.

entries.name: Superman: Whatever Happened to the Man of Tomorrow?
entries.author: Alan Moore and Curt Swan
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Kirby Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. **`craft-31`'s ending you are not allowed, delivered by a publisher that had decided to allow it exactly once.** The story was commissioned as…
entries.text: Run. **`craft-31`'s ending you are not allowed, delivered by a publisher that had decided to allow it exactly once.** The story was commissioned as a farewell to a continuity being replaced by `work-135`, which is what made a terminal ending commercially possible: the character continues, so this ending costs nothing. That arrangement is the card's real content — **the genre can produce a genuine ending only when a reboot has already made it non-binding**, which is a structural fact about corporate serial fiction rather than a failure of nerve by any writer. Its epilogue does the thing the form almost never does and the pack notes it: the survivors are ordinary afterwards, and the story treats that as the good outcome.

entries.name: The Man of Steel
entries.author: John Byrne
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Kirby Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Limited series. `continuity-12`'s two operations with the same name, and this is the **deleting** one performed at maximum scale on a single…
entries.text: Limited series. `continuity-12`'s two operations with the same name, and this is the **deleting** one performed at maximum scale on a single character: the previous fifty years are declared not to have happened, the supporting cast is rebuilt, and the powers are reduced to a level a story can be written against. **The reduction is the part worth carding.** A character whose stated limit and observed limit had drifted for decades — `powers-6`'s pair — is given a ceiling low enough to be checkable, which is `craft-19`'s requirement and the single most useful thing a reboot can do. The card notes that the deletion's costs arrived later and fell on other books, which is `checklist-8`'s continuity debt incurred by one title and paid by a line.

entries.name: Batman: Year One
entries.author: Frank Miller and David Mazzucchelli
entries.awards: No award located, and no category string is cited. [gap: Kirby and Eisner Award records consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. `subgenre-9`'s origin story as a form, and the version that fixed the form for thirty years: **the origin retold as a procedural**, with a…
entries.text: Run. `subgenre-9`'s origin story as a form, and the version that fixed the form for thirty years: **the origin retold as a procedural**, with a competent police detective as co-protagonist and the costume arriving late and badly. Its structural argument is that the hero's first year is interesting **because he is bad at it**, which the genre's origin retellings had systematically avoided. It is also the pack's clearest case of `craft-30` — write the arc, inherit the character — since the run changes nothing that a subsequent writer must honour and is nonetheless the version every subsequent writer honours. The card notes that its police procedural half has aged into a different reading than it had at publication, and that both readings are published.

entries.name: Batman: The Killing Joke
entries.author: Alan Moore and Brian Bolland
entries.awards: No award located, and no category string is cited. The Eisner Awards were first presented in 1988; no ballot entry was confirmed against the administering body's own record. [gap: Eisner Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Graphic novel. **The 1988 end of a block whose label named a single year, and the card states the failure as `work-130` states it at the 1985 end**…
entries.text: Graphic novel. **The 1988 end of a block whose label named a single year, and the card states the failure as `work-130` states it at the 1985 end** — the two entries bracket a three-year span, which is why the category is now *The 1986 Generation* and was *The 1986 Turn* until the patch batch. The work's carded significance is `continuity-18`'s: **what a retcon costs the reader who was there.** A supporting character is shot, paralysed and photographed in an act of violence staged as a message to a man, and the injury was neither planned as permanent nor authorised as such at the time. What followed is the genre's most-cited case of a maiming becoming a character: `work-84` cards the run built from it, and the two entries are the pack's best paired argument that **the industry's worst decisions and its most durable characters are sometimes the same event.** Its own writer's later public repudiation of the book is on the record and the card notes it.

entries.name: Planetary
entries.author: Warren Ellis and John Cassaday
entries.awards: No award located, and no category string is cited. [gap: Eisner Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. A team who investigate the twentieth century's secret history and find **the genre's own furniture buried in it** — each issue excavating a…
entries.text: Run. A team who investigate the twentieth century's secret history and find **the genre's own furniture buried in it** — each issue excavating a pulp, a kaiju film, a Hong Kong ghost story or a founding superhero premise as an archaeological site. That structure makes it the pack's most self-aware carded work and its most useful one for a writer learning what the form is assembled from. `craft-42`'s claim — the cover as a separately authored object — is executed here more systematically than anywhere else in the genre: each cover is a pastiche of a different publishing tradition, so the object announces its subject before the story does. Its glacial publication schedule is part of its record and the card states it rather than presenting the run as it reads collected.

entries.name: Daredevil (Bendis/Maleev run)
entries.author: Brian Michael Bendis and Alex Maleev
entries.awards: No award located, and no category string is cited. The Eisner Awards label by ceremony year and no ballot entry for this run was confirmed against the administering body's own record. [gap: Eisner Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. **The identity is published by a tabloid in the second year and never satisfactorily put back**, which makes it `craft-25`'s disclosure as a…
entries.text: Run. **The identity is published by a tabloid in the second year and never satisfactorily put back**, which makes it `craft-25`'s disclosure as a jurisdictional event sustained over dozens of issues rather than resolved in one. Every consequence the genre normally waives arrives: the licence to practise law, the admissibility of the hero's own testimony, the federal interest, the impossibility of a private life. It is the strongest argument in the pack that **the secret identity is a legal structure before it is an emotional one**, which `trope-12` states and this run proves by removing it. The card notes the run's method — decompressed, crime-fiction paced, drawn from photo reference — and that this became a house style widely copied and rarely understood. `author-107` cards the writer.

entries.name: New X-Men
entries.author: Grant Morrison and Frank Quitely
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Eisner Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. `powers-22`'s retroactive respecification applied to an entire population: a **secondary mutation** is introduced as a mechanism, which…
entries.text: Run. `powers-22`'s retroactive respecification applied to an entire population: a **secondary mutation** is introduced as a mechanism, which licenses any existing character to acquire a new capability without a new origin, and the run is honest that this is a licence rather than a discovery. Its wider argument is that the franchise's central metaphor had been mishandled by treating a persecuted minority as a paramilitary team — so the school becomes a school, the costumes become uniforms, and the threat becomes demographic rather than criminal. **Nearly all of it was undone within two years of the run ending**, which the card states because a run's influence and a run's continuity survival are different measurements and this one scores oppositely on them.

entries.name: Runaways
entries.author: Brian K. Vaughan and Adrian Alphona
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Eisner Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. `trope-33`'s team as a family that cannot leave, made literal in the only way the genre had not tried: **the parents are the villains, and the…
entries.text: Run. `trope-33`'s team as a family that cannot leave, made literal in the only way the genre had not tried: **the parents are the villains, and the team is what the children become by fleeing them.** That premise solves the mandate question by refusing it — nobody licenses these protagonists and nobody could, they are minors acting against the adults who would hold the authority — and it produces the rarest structure in the form, a superhero team with **no headquarters, no funding and no adult supervision** that the book does not quietly restore. Its capabilities are inherited from the parents, so every power in the cast is a piece of evidence about what was done to them.

entries.name: Invincible (comic)
entries.author: Robert Kirkman and Cory Walker
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Eisner Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. `trope-3`'s inherited mission set up conventionally for a year and then inverted: **the father who conferred the mission is an advance agent…
entries.text: Run. `trope-3`'s inherited mission set up conventionally for a year and then inverted: **the father who conferred the mission is an advance agent for an invasion**, and the inheritance the protagonist accepted is the thing he has to fight. The card notes what makes the reversal work structurally rather than as a shock — the first year is written straight, at full sincerity, so the reversal costs the reader something they had actually invested in. Its other contribution is **consequence carried at panel level**: injuries persist, the supporting cast is depleted permanently, and the book runs to a planned ending rather than an indefinite one, which is the discipline creator ownership makes available and corporate serialisation does not. **The disambiguating suffix separates it from its animated adaptation**, which this pack does not card.

entries.name: All-Star Superman
entries.author: Grant Morrison and Frank Quitely
entries.awards: No award located, and no category string is cited. [gap: Eisner Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Limited series. `powers-30`'s problem — a body that cannot be hurt, and what a scene does when physical threat is unavailable — answered by **making…
entries.text: Limited series. `powers-30`'s problem — a body that cannot be hurt, and what a scene does when physical threat is unavailable — answered by **making the character dying the premise** and then declining to make the dying dramatic. The book's solution to invulnerability is that the stakes are time and obligation rather than damage, which is the most-copied answer in the modern genre and the one most often copied without the discipline that makes it work. It is also the pack's clearest instance of a reconstruction that **does not argue with the deconstruction at all** — it simply proceeds as though the argument had been settled, which is a rhetorical position `work-114` could not take nine years earlier.

entries.name: The Vision (2015 comic)
entries.author: Tom King and Gabriel Hernández Walta
entries.awards: No award located, and no category string is cited. [gap: Eisner Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Limited series. `trope-16`'s question — which of the two lives is the performance — asked of a family that **built the ordinary life on purpose, as…
entries.text: Limited series. `trope-16`'s question — which of the two lives is the performance — asked of a family that **built the ordinary life on purpose, as an experiment, and cannot tell whether it is working.** A synthezoid constructs a wife and two children and moves to the suburbs, and the horror is procedural: each small concealment is reasonable, each is recorded, and the narration tells the reader the ending from the first page. That foreknowledge is the formal decision worth carding, because it converts suspense into dread and makes the reader complicit in watching a family that cannot be warned. **The disambiguating suffix is required**: the character has been the subject of several unrelated titles under the same name.

entries.name: The Immortal Hulk
entries.author: Al Ewing and Joe Bennett
entries.awards: No award located, and no category string is cited. [gap: Eisner Award record consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Run. `powers-2`'s capability designed as an affliction, restored to a character whose affliction had been steadily rewritten as an asset over fifty…
entries.text: Run. `powers-2`'s capability designed as an affliction, restored to a character whose affliction had been steadily rewritten as an asset over fifty years — and the restoration is done by **reclassifying the genre of the book** rather than by changing the character. It is a horror comic with a superhero in it, which `subgenre-35` covers and which this run demonstrates is a re-registration available to almost any long-running property. The theological frame it builds is the other half: a resurrection that is involuntary, a hell that is administrative, and a body that will not stay dead because something requires it. **The run's artist was removed after antisemitic imagery was identified in published pages**, which is part of this work's record and is stated here rather than omitted; the card names the fact and does not narrate beyond it.

entries.name: The Dark Knight
entries.author: Christopher Nolan
entries.awards: Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor, 2009 (Heath Ledger, posthumous). Best Picture nominations were expanded from five to ten for the following ceremony; the Academy president's own announcement supports the connection, and the expanded field was not stable in later years and must not be described as fixed. **No superhero film has won the Academy Award for Best Picture.**
entries.description: Feature film. **The award line is this card's substance and §0.22 is discharged on it.** The version of this story in general circulation has an…
entries.text: Feature film. **The award line is this card's substance and §0.22 is discharged on it.** The version of this story in general circulation has an institution silently conceding an error; **the record has an announcement, which is a weaker and better-documented claim**, and the card states what was announced rather than what was concluded. The film's own contribution is `craft-47`'s enemy who cannot be beaten: an antagonist with no origin, no demand and no capability, whose entire power is that he will not stop — which removes every lever the genre's plots run on and forces the film to be about the protagonist's rules instead. Its escalation logic, in which each intervention produces the next threat, is the most-imitated structure in the genre's screen era.

entries.name: Superman (1978 film)
entries.author: Richard Donner
entries.awards: Special Achievement Academy Award for Visual Effects, 1979. No competitive Academy Award was won. [gap: Academy Awards database consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Feature film. `craft-52`'s selection for iconography, performed before anyone knew it was a selection: the film keeps the costume, the flight, the…
entries.text: Feature film. `craft-52`'s selection for iconography, performed before anyone knew it was a selection: the film keeps the costume, the flight, the origin and the mythic register and discards the four decades of continuity around them, and **that discard is the template every subsequent adaptation follows.** Its structural achievement is tonal rather than technical — it plays the material entirely straight for two hours after a decade in which the only screen version anyone remembered had played it as comedy, and the straightness is what made the genre filmable. **The award line carries a distinction that matters**: a Special Achievement award is conferred outside the competitive categories and is not a win in one, and this pack does not print it as though it were.

entries.name: Batman (1989 film)
entries.author: Tim Burton
entries.awards: Academy Award for Best Art Direction, 1990. [gap: Academy Awards database consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Feature film. Carded for `trope-64`'s subject rather than for the film: **the merchandised silhouette**, and the marketing campaign that proved a…
entries.text: Feature film. Carded for `trope-64`'s subject rather than for the film: **the merchandised silhouette**, and the marketing campaign that proved a superhero property's logo could sell more than its story. The design language — a city built as expressionist set rather than as a place, a costume moulded rather than sewn — became the genre's default screen look for a decade and is the reason the art-direction award is the appropriate one. The film's treatment of its source is the card's caveat: it rewrites the protagonist's origin to connect it to the antagonist's, a change the comics did not adopt and that later adaptations mostly abandoned, which makes it a useful counter-case to `craft-55`'s usual direction of travel.

entries.name: Blade (1998 film)
entries.author: Stephen Norrington
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Academy Awards and Saturn Awards records consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Feature film. `subgenre-35`'s monster hero, and **the commercially successful superhero film that immediately precedes the genre's screen era and is…
entries.text: Feature film. `subgenre-35`'s monster hero, and **the commercially successful superhero film that immediately precedes the genre's screen era and is left out of nearly every account of how that era began.** It is adapted from a minor supporting character in a horror line, made for an adult audience, and its success is what made the studio's subsequent franchise strategy arguable internally — a sequence the received history begins two years later with a different film. The card states the omission as a fact about the received history rather than as a grievance. Its hero's mandate is self-conferred and hereditary at once, and the film is unusual in the genre for **treating the protagonist's own biology as the antagonist's strongest recruiting argument.**

entries.name: X-Men (2000 film)
entries.author: Bryan Singer
entries.awards: No award located. [gap: Academy Awards database consulted 2026-08-24]
entries.description: Feature film. `craft-54`'s hardest problem answered by **abandoning it**: the costumes are black leather, the source designs are referred to once as…
entries.text: Feature film. `craft-54`'s hardest problem answered by **abandoning it**: the costumes are black leather, the source designs are referred to once as a joke, and the film's own line about yellow spandex became the genre's shorthand for the position. The card cards the decision rather than endorsing it, because the position was reversed within a decade by films that solved the problem instead of avoiding it, and **the reversal is more instructive than the original choice.** What the film establishes durably is the ensemble structure — a large cast introduced through one newcomer's arrival — and the treatment of the source metaphor as a civil-rights allegory delivered straight, which the comics had done for decades and no screen version had attempted.

entries.text: Feature film. `craft-27`'s question — which life is the real one — made the plot rather than the theme: the protagonist's powers fail as his civilian life collapses, so the film's mechanism is that **the two lives are one resource and spending it on either depletes the other.** That is the single best dramatisation in this pack of what a secret identity costs, and it works because the film is willing to let him quit for a whole act and be happier. Its train sequence is the genre's most-copied set piece and the card notes why it works structurally rather than technically: the capability is used to its stated limit, the limit is one the audience already knows, and the bystanders are `craft-6`'s characters rather than scenery.

entries.text: Feature film. An original property rather than an adaptation, which is why it is carded: **the genre's assumptions are visible in a film that inherited none of them.** Its premise is the mandate withdrawn by litigation — heroes banned because rescue produces liability — which is `craft-8`'s withdrawal enacted by a mechanism the comics had never used and which reads as more plausible than any of theirs. The family is `powers-16`'s incompatible-systems team with the incompatibility written as domestic rather than tactical. The card notes the film's contested politics: readings of its position on exceptional ability run sharply both ways, **both are published, and the pack carries both** rather than settling it.

entries.text: Feature film. `craft-53`'s problem — ninety years will not fit in a film — solved by **not fitting any of it**: the film is a coda that assumes a history it never depicts, and the absence is what gives the character weight the depicted history never managed. Its mandate is entirely spent; the protagonist has no licence, no institution and no constituency, and the plot is a delivery job. **The award line is the card's second content**: a nomination is not a win and V-03 requires the shapes to stay distinct, and this pack found no earlier screenplay nomination in the genre, which is a claim about what was searched rather than about what exists. The film's violence is the first in this franchise permitted by its rating and the card notes that the permission is a commercial fact before it is an artistic one.

entries.text: Feature film. **`craft-57` says the screen cannot do a splash page and this film is the counter-case the card needs**, which is why it is carded rather than the several live-action films with better-known box office: it builds a rendering style out of comics grammar — halftone, registration offset, panel inserts, lettered sound — and proves the limitation was a convention rather than a property of the medium. Its structural content is the legacy question `trope-55` describes, resolved by putting six holders of one name on screen at once so that succession is argued rather than asserted. The card notes that the film's animation technique required an unusual production model, and that the model's labour conditions are part of its record.

entries.description: Television series. The genre's first sustained television presence, and the card is here for `craft-56`'s claim: **casting is a continuity…
entries.text: Television series. The genre's first sustained television presence, and the card is here for `craft-56`'s claim: **casting is a continuity decision.** For a generation this actor was the character, in a way no comics artist's version had been, and the identification survived his death and shaped the property's handling for decades. The series itself establishes the economics screen superheroes ran on until the 1990s — a small standing cast, a fixed set, capability shown as rarely as the budget required — and `craft-13`'s undrawable power becomes the unaffordable one, which is a different constraint producing similar prose. **The disambiguating suffix separates it from the 1980s series of nearly the same name**, which this pack does not card.

entries.text: Animated series. **`craft-55`'s adaptation becoming the canon, in the clearest instance the genre has**: a character created for this series entered the comics, became a permanent fixture of the line, and is now among the property's most valuable assets — the direction of travel that a reference pack has to be able to describe because the assumption runs the other way. Its design language, painted on black card and scored orchestrally, is the version most subsequent adaptations answer to rather than the comics of its own decade. The card notes what the series did to the antagonist roster: it rebuilt several rogues with motives sufficient to carry a half-hour, which `craft-46`'s portfolio requires and which the source line had not consistently done.

entries.description: Animated series. `trope-32`'s reserve roster as a **production method rather than a plot device**: the series carries dozens of members, uses three…
entries.text: Animated series. `trope-32`'s reserve roster as a **production method rather than a plot device**: the series carries dozens of members, uses three or four per episode, and treats the bench as a casting pool — which solves the ensemble problem that defeats most team adaptations and which no live-action production has been able to afford. Its serialised spine runs underneath episodic instalments, so a viewer can enter anywhere and a viewer who stays is rewarded, which is `continuity-6`'s accessibility problem answered structurally. **The spine's subject is the mandate**: an unaccountable superhuman organisation acquires a weapon, a government responds, and the series argues both sides for a season. `author-34` cards the writer.

entries.text: Television series. `trope-42`'s city that is a character, carded on screen because **the neighbourhood is the series' organising unit** — the antagonist is a developer, the crime is property, and the hero's jurisdiction is a handful of blocks he can reach on foot. That scale is the pack's clearest demonstration that the genre's street-level register is a **geographic** decision before it is a tonal one. The series is also where the screen adaptation of `work-139`'s run is most visible, and the card notes the relationship rather than treating either as free-standing. Its fight staging, built on long takes and visible exhaustion, is the counter-argument to the genre's default of impact without cost.

entries.text: Television series. **The adaptation differs from `work-121` substantially enough that `checklist-14`'s fidelity pass is the card to run against the pair**, and the pack cards both rather than letting one stand for the other: the source is a satire of the genre's readers as much as its heroes, and the adaptation redirects the satire onto media consolidation, celebrity and nationalist branding. That redirection is the card's content — **an adaptation can be less faithful and more current at once**, and the pack states this without ranking them. The series' recurring structural move is corporate: every atrocity is followed by a communications meeting, which is `subgenre-13`'s state superhuman relocated to a shareholder-owned one.

entries.description: Television series. **The final card in this pack's Works collection, and it is a grief structure**: `continuity-44`'s mourning sequence as a…
entries.text: Television series. **The final card in this pack's Works collection, and it is a grief structure**: `continuity-44`'s mourning sequence as a structural instrument rather than an obligatory beat, extended to a whole series in which the genre's most-used device — a reality altered to undo a loss — is shown from inside as an act of harm the mourner is committing against a town. The formal method is pastiche: each episode adopts a different decade's situation-comedy grammar, so the **audience's own nostalgia becomes the mechanism of the concealment**. Its final act reverts to the genre's default mode and the card states that the reversion is widely held against it, that both readings are published, and that the pack carries both. It is a fitting last entry for a collection whose organising question is by what warrant a person acts: here the answer is grief, and the series is clear that grief is not a warrant.
